Unit 1 · Foundations of Nursing Care for Adult Clients · Chapter 1

Health, Wellness, and Illness

Health and wellness are individualized and dynamic. In this chapter, the nurse connects a client's usual functioning, modifiable risks, environment, health beliefs, and support systems to practical health-promotion planning.

TL;DR - Wellness Is Individualized

Do not judge wellness by diagnosis alone. Compare the client with the client's usual baseline, identify modifiable risks, assess barriers to adherence, and build health education around the client's beliefs, resources, and support system.

Priority Lens

  • Health and wellness include physical function plus emotional and social contentment.
  • Illness is the client's altered functioning; disease is the physiologic alteration.
  • The illness-wellness continuum centers on the client's normal state of health.

Common Test Move

  • Choose interventions that strengthen coping, activate support, improve education, and reduce barriers.
  • Classify risks as modifiable or nonmodifiable before planning education.
  • Look for denial, mistrust, cultural mismatch, finances, or weak support as adherence barriers.

High-Yield Framework

Core Concepts

Foundations

Health/wellness

Optimal functioning and adaptation within the client's own life situation.

Ask what "normal" and "well" mean for this client.

Illness

Altered functioning in response to a health problem.

Assess how the client perceives the change and how daily roles are affected.

Disease

Physiologic alteration in body structure or function.

Do not assume the disease label predicts the client's wellness level.

Continuum

A way to compare severe illness, usual baseline, and optimal wellness.

Set goals that move the client toward the best achievable wellness state.

Variables That Shape Wellness

Assess first

Tobacco and health-risk behaviors

Tobacco or other health-risk behaviors.

Modifiable

Nutrition and activity patterns

Nutrition, weight, activity, and exercise patterns.

Modifiable

Education and preventive care

Access to health education and preventive care.

Modifiable

Behavior-linked risks

Sexual practices and other behavior-linked risks.

Modifiable

Developmental and genetic traits

Age, sex, developmental level, and genetic traits.

Nonmodifiable

Inherited or lifelong conditions

Some inherited or lifelong conditions.

Nonmodifiable

Past experiences

Past life experiences that influence current beliefs.

Nonmodifiable

Stable chronic baseline

Current baseline when a chronic condition is stable.

Nonmodifiable

Education target

Education works best when it targets what the client can actually change.

Do not spend the priority intervention on a fixed trait when a modifiable risk is present.

Health/Wellness Assessment

Adherence

ATI frames health promotion around assessment plus barrier reduction. Before teaching, determine what the client believes, what resources exist, and what is blocking follow-through.

Focused physical assessment

Complete a focused physical assessment and compare findings with the client's usual state.

Illness perception

Ask how the client perceives the illness, its severity, and the prescribed plan.

Access barriers

Identify access barriers: cost, transportation, health care availability, and education needs.

Trust, beliefs, roles, and support

Assess trust in the provider, belief in the therapy, cultural or religious fit, family roles, and support systems.

Financial restrictions

Look for financial restrictions that can force the client to prioritize one health need over another.

Nursing Actions That Promote Wellness

Intervene

Coping resources

Provide resources that strengthen coping, such as dietitian referral, support groups, or practical home tools.

Support system

With permission, involve the client's support system during illness and stress.

Obstacle reduction

Identify obstacles to health and create realistic strategies to reduce them.

Education methods

Use education methods that increase awareness and reduce risk.

Concrete adherence supports

Improve adherence with concrete supports: written materials, medication organizers, and follow-up planning.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Smoking With Cardiovascular Family History

Active Learning Scenario

A clinic client continues to smoke after several quit attempts and has a family history of cardiovascular disease. Build the Basic Concept template around reducing obstacles and strengthening health-promotion behaviors.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
Related contentIdentify barriers to adherence and health promotion, including stress, coping, support, beliefs, access, and prior experiences.
Underlying principleHealth promotion and disease prevention improve when nursing care addresses the client's real barriers, not just the risk label.
Nursing interventionsOffer coping resources, encourage support systems, identify obstacles, build risk-reduction education, and create practical adherence strategies.

Application Exercises

1

A client with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes says meal planning is difficult and prescribed medications are easy to forget. Which actions support adherence? Select all that apply.

  • A. Ask a dietitian to assist with meal planning.
  • B. With consent, involve the client's support system.
  • C. Focus only on age-related cognitive changes.
  • D. Encourage use of a daily medication dispenser.
  • E. Provide written home education materials.
A, B, D, E These actions reduce barriers, strengthen coping/support, and make the plan easier to follow.
C Cognitive assessment can matter, but it is not the best adherence intervention in this scenario.
2

Which client best represents the center of the illness-wellness continuum?

  • A. A student with influenza.
  • B. An older adult with a new diabetes diagnosis.
  • C. A postpartum client with a urinary tract infection.
  • D. A client with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis that is well controlled.
D The center reflects the client's usual state. A stable chronic condition can be the client's normal baseline.
3

At a health fair, which variables should the nurse treat as modifiable? Select all that apply.

  • A. Social smoking.
  • B. BMI of 28.
  • C. Genetic alopecia.
  • D. Trisomy 21.
  • E. Reflux symptoms that can improve with treatment and lifestyle changes.
A, B, E These are realistic targets for education and behavior or treatment planning.
C, D Genetic or chromosomal traits are nonmodifiable.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

Basic Concept: health promotion, wellness variables, adherence barriers, and smoking risk reduction. Worked AMS Templates will be linked after the Templates page receives source-supported examples.

Unit 1 · Foundations of Nursing Care for Adult Clients · Chapter 2

Emergency Nursing Principles and Management

Emergency nursing starts with rapid recognition, triage, and a systematic primary survey. The nurse prioritizes life-threatening problems first, communicates deterioration early, and follows emergency protocols for toxic, thermal, and cardiac events.

TL;DR - ABCDE Before Everything Else

Use triage to sort urgency, then use the ABCDE primary survey to find threats to life: airway/cervical spine, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure/environment. Call rapid response for signs of sudden decline and follow BLS/ACLS-based protocols for arrest rhythms.

Immediate Priorities

  • Airway is first; without oxygenation, the rest of the survey cannot help.
  • Use jaw-thrust when trauma or cervical spine injury is suspected.
  • Control visible bleeding, obtain large-bore IV access, and replace volume as ordered.

Exam Traps

  • Do not induce vomiting or use ipecac for ingested toxins.
  • Asystole is not a shockable rhythm; prioritize CPR, IV access, epinephrine per protocol, and reversible causes.
  • Use SBAR when activating or documenting a rapid response event.

Emergency Framework

Five-Level ED Triage

Sort first

Triage sorts urgency by how quickly the client needs treatment to prevent death, limb threat, or deterioration.

1 - Resuscitation

Immediate treatment is needed to prevent death. Examples include cardiac arrest, stroke, pulmonary embolus, and overdose.

2 - Emergent

Time-sensitive problem could become life- or limb-threatening. Examples include traumatic amputation, head/neck injury, and venomous bite.

3 - Urgent

Treatment is needed, but the problem is not immediately life-threatening. Examples include kidney stone, gallbladder colic, and fracture.

4 - Less Urgent

The client can wait for a period of time without immediate treatment. Examples include bladder infection, laceration, and infected toe.

5 - Nonurgent

Simple evaluation and minor care management are expected. Examples include rash, minor cut, and backache.

Primary Survey: ABCDE

Life threats

The primary survey moves from oxygenation to circulation, neurologic status, and full exposure while correcting life threats as they appear.

A - Airway/Cervical Spine

Assess responsiveness, obstruction, blood, vomitus, broken teeth, secretions, and trauma risk. Open airway. Use head-tilt/chin-lift only when trauma is not suspected; use modified jaw-thrust with suspected cervical spine injury.

B - Breathing

Assess breath sounds, chest expansion, respiratory effort, rate, depth, and oxygenation. Support ventilation with oxygen, bag-valve mask, or advanced airway support as indicated.

C - Circulation

Assess heart rate, blood pressure, pulses, capillary refill, bleeding, and shock risk. Start CPR if needed, control hemorrhage, establish large-bore IV access, give isotonic fluids or blood products as ordered.

D - Disability

Assess rapid neurologic status using AVPU or Glasgow Coma Scale. Repeat neuro checks often so deterioration is not missed.

E - Exposure/Environment

Assess the full body, hidden injuries, chemical/thermal exposure, and hypothermia risk. Remove clothing as needed, preserve evidence, and prevent heat loss.

Thermal and Toxic Emergencies

Rapid support

Thermal and toxic emergencies still begin with support of ABCDE, then removal of exposure, toxin control, and prescribed antidotes.

Frostbite

Frostbite can require rewarming in warm water and tetanus protection.

Hypothermia

Prevent or treat hypothermia by removing wet clothing, warming the room, using warm blankets, and infusing warmed fluids as prescribed.

Heat Stroke

Heat stroke is an emergency: prioritize ABCDE, oxygen as needed, large-gauge IV access, cooling measures, and urine output monitoring.

Poisoning Priorities

Identify the agent, provide supportive care, stop absorption, remove the toxin when appropriate, and administer antidotes when ordered.

Ingestion Care

For ingestion, ATI supports activated charcoal, gastric lavage with aspiration when appropriate, and aspiration procedures; ipecac is not recommended.

Antidote and Seizure Support

Use naloxone for opioid toxicity and benzodiazepine therapy for seizures when prescribed.

Rapid Response and Cardiac Emergency

Escalate

Escalation prevents deterioration from becoming arrest, and rhythm response depends on whether the rhythm is shockable.

Rapid Response Activation

Activate the rapid response team for early signs of sudden decline before arrest or stroke occurs.

Critical-Care Support

Expect critical-care support such as an ICU nurse, respiratory therapist, provider, or hospitalist based on facility policy.

SBAR

Use SBAR to communicate and document the event.

Shockable Rhythms

For ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, begin BLS components and defibrillate according to protocol.

PEA or Asystole

For PEA or asystole, begin BLS components, establish IV access, administer epinephrine per protocol, and consider reversible causes.

PEA Reversible Causes

Think Hs and Ts - hypovolemia, hypoxia, acidosis, potassium imbalance, hypothermia, toxins, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, coronary thrombosis, and pulmonary thrombosis.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Five-Level ED Triage

Active Learning Scenario

A nurse in the ED is implementing triage. Complete the Basic Concept template by naming the levels, defining each one, and matching example clients.

LevelDefinitionExample Client
ResuscitationNeeds immediate treatment to prevent death.Cardiac arrest, stroke, pulmonary embolus, overdose.
EmergentTime-sensitive, with risk of life- or limb-threatening progression.Traumatic amputation, head/neck injury, venomous bite.
UrgentNeeds treatment, but not immediately life-threatening.Kidney stone, gallbladder colic, fracture.
Less urgentCan safely wait for a period of time.Bladder infection, laceration, infected toe.
NonurgentRequires simple evaluation or minor care.Rash, minor cut, backache.

Application Exercises

1

On a medical-surgical unit, which client should trigger rapid response team activation?

  • A. Pressure injury with blood glucose of 300 mg/dL.
  • B. New right calf pain with shortness of breath.
  • C. Blood visible on a femoral pressure dressing after cardiac catheterization.
  • D. Dark red toes with absent pedal pulse.
B Calf pain plus shortness of breath can signal pulmonary embolism and rapid respiratory decline.
A, C, D These require assessment and provider notification, but they do not match the same immediate deterioration pattern in this ATI item.
2

A client ingested a toxic agent. Which actions are expected? Select all that apply.

  • A. Induce vomiting.
  • B. Instill activated charcoal as prescribed.
  • C. Prepare for gastric lavage with aspiration when appropriate.
  • D. Administer syrup of ipecac.
  • E. Infuse IV fluids as prescribed.
B, C, E These support toxin binding/removal and circulation.
A, D Vomiting and ipecac increase aspiration risk and are not recommended in this ATI-supported item.
3

An unresponsive client collapsed while pulling weeds. There is no indication of trauma. Which airway technique should the nurse use?

  • A. Head-tilt/chin-lift.
  • B. Modified jaw-thrust.
  • C. Hyperextension of the head.
  • D. Flexion of the head.
A Use head-tilt/chin-lift for an unresponsive client when cervical spine trauma is not suspected.
B Reserve modified jaw-thrust for suspected trauma or cervical spine injury.
4

Which action belongs in the emergency plan for asystole?

  • A. Defibrillate immediately.
  • B. Prepare transcutaneous pacing as the priority.
  • C. Administer IV epinephrine per protocol.
  • D. Elevate the lower extremities as the main intervention.
C ATI supports epinephrine with BLS components, IV access, and evaluation for reversible causes during asystole management.
A Asystole is not a shockable rhythm.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 3

Neurologic Diagnostic Procedures

Neurologic diagnostic care is about matching the test to the risk: contrast, bleeding, sedation, metal, infection, intracranial pressure, or postprocedure CSF leak. The nurse protects the client before, during, and after the scan or procedure.

TL;DR - Know the Test Risk

For neuro diagnostics, ask: Is contrast used? Is the client pregnant or allergic? Is kidney function adequate? Is bleeding risk present? Is metal or claustrophobia a concern? Does the procedure enter the CNS or dura? Those answers drive the nursing priorities.

High-Yield Safety Checks

  • Contrast procedures: check allergy history and kidney function.
  • Angiography: assess bleeding risk and distal circulation after catheter removal.
  • MRI: remove metal, screen implants, and address claustrophobia.

Priority Follow-Up

  • After lumbar puncture, keep the client flat as prescribed and monitor for headache.
  • For ICP monitoring, preserve system integrity and sterile technique.
  • Use GCS trends to communicate neurologic change quickly.

Diagnostic Procedure Map

Contrast and Imaging Procedures

Pre/Post

Imaging safety depends on contrast, sedation, metal, pregnancy risk, bleeding risk, renal function, and postprocedure circulation checks.

Cerebral Angiography

Visualizes cerebral blood vessels; can identify aneurysm, obstruction, narrowing, tumor vascularity, or guide therapy. NPO as prescribed, assess allergies/bleeding risk/renal function, remove jewelry, monitor puncture site and distal circulation after the procedure.

CT Scan

Cross-sectional cranial images; can identify tumors, infarctions, abnormalities, and guide biopsy needles. If contrast or sedation is used, check NPO status, allergy history, BUN/creatinine, and monitor for reaction or renal changes.

MRI

Magnet-based cross-sectional images; useful for soft tissue, tumor size, and blood vessel location without radiation exposure. Remove metal and foil-backed patches, screen for implants, assess claustrophobia, use MRI-approved equipment, and monitor for contrast reaction.

PET/SPECT

Nuclear medicine images of brain activity or metabolism. Discuss pregnancy risk, assess diabetes management needs, keep the head still during imaging, and monitor for radioisotope reaction when used.

X-Ray

Images skull/spine structures to identify fractures, curvature, erosion, dislocation, or calcification. Determine pregnancy status, remove jewelry/clothing over the area, and explain that the procedure is quick and requires stillness.

Function, Consciousness, and Pressure

Trend changes

Function tests and pressure monitoring help trend neurologic changes, guide escalation, and protect invasive monitoring systems.

EEG Purpose

EEG assesses brain electrical activity and is commonly used for seizure activity, sleep disorders, and behavioral changes.

EEG Teaching

Teach the client to wash hair, avoid oils/gels/sprays, stay awake as instructed, and avoid stimulant or sedative medications if prescribed.

GCS Reporting

GCS reports eye, verbal, and motor response. A total below 8 is associated with severe head injury/coma; 9-12 is moderate; above 13 is minor head trauma.

ICP Monitoring Purpose

Used for early identification and treatment of increased intracranial pressure, especially with coma or GCS 8 or lower.

ICP Range

Normal ICP is about 10-15 mm Hg; sustained elevation threatens cerebral circulation.

Monitoring System Care

Maintain a closed/sterile system, inspect insertion site, recalibrate per policy, and monitor neurologic status and waveforms.

Lumbar Puncture

CSF care

Lumbar puncture care protects the client before dural access and watches closely afterward for leak-related headache or puncture-site concerns.

Purpose

Withdraw CSF for analysis, reduce CSF pressure, instill contrast/air, or administer medication/chemotherapy into spinal fluid.

Preprocedure

Discuss risks/benefits, screen for increased ICP or bleeding risk, remove jewelry, have the client void, and position to flex the spine.

Postprocedure

Monitor puncture site and maintain prescribed bed rest to promote clotting and reduce post-lumbar puncture headache risk.

CSF Leak Headache

If headache occurs from CSF leakage, support flat positioning, hydration, prescribed pain medication, and possible epidural blood patch if persistent.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - MRI With Contrast

Active Learning Scenario

A client is scheduled for an MRI scan with contrast. Complete the Diagnostic Procedure template by defining the test and planning nursing care across the procedure.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
Procedure nameMRI uses magnetic fields to create multiple images of body structures.
PreprocedureRemove jewelry/metal, assess claustrophobia, ask about metal implants, and assess allergies when contrast is planned.
IntraprocedureStabilize the client's head and use MRI-compatible monitoring or oxygen equipment when needed.
PostprocedureMonitor for allergic reaction to contrast media if it was used.

Application Exercises

1

A client reports a throbbing headache when sitting upright after a lumbar puncture. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

  • A. Use the Glasgow Coma Scale as the priority response.
  • B. Assist the client to a supine position.
  • C. Administer prescribed opioid medication.
  • D. Encourage increased fluid intake.
  • E. Instruct deep breathing and coughing exercises.
B, C, D Flat positioning, hydration, and prescribed analgesia can relieve post-lumbar puncture headache from CSF leakage.
E Coughing can increase ICP and worsen the headache.
2

A client has a ventriculostomy for ICP monitoring after traumatic head injury. Which complication is directly related to the monitoring device?

  • A. Headache.
  • B. Infection.
  • C. Aphasia.
  • D. Hypertension.
B Infection is a major ventriculostomy risk, so strict asepsis and closed-system care are priorities.
3

A client opens eyes to voice, speaks incoherently/disoriented, and withdraws from pain. Which GCS score should the nurse document?

  • A. E2 + V3 + M5 = 10.
  • B. E3 + V4 + M4 = 11.
  • C. E4 + V5 + M6 = 15.
  • D. E2 + V2 + M4 = 8.
B Eye opening to voice is E3, incoherent/disoriented conversation is V4, and withdrawal from pain is M4.
4

Which client statements should the nurse report before cerebral angiography with contrast? Select all that apply.

  • A. "I think I might be pregnant."
  • B. "I take warfarin."
  • C. "I take antihypertensive medication."
  • D. "I am allergic to shrimp."
  • E. "I ate a light breakfast this morning."
A, B, D, E Pregnancy risk, anticoagulation, shellfish/contrast allergy concern, and food intake before prescribed NPO time all require follow-up.
C Antihypertensive medication alone is not the contraindication highlighted in this ATI item.

Suggested template type

Diagnostic Procedure: MRI with contrast, cerebral angiography, lumbar puncture, ICP monitoring, CT with contrast, or EEG. Worked AMS Templates will be linked after source-supported examples are built.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 4

Pain Management

Pain management begins with believing and reassessing the client's report. The nurse combines pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic strategies, uses functional goals, and watches closely for opioid sedation and respiratory depression.

TL;DR - Pain Is What the Client Says

Pain is subjective, so the client is the best source. Assess location, quality, intensity, timing, setting, associated manifestations, and aggravating/relieving factors. Treat undertreatment as a serious complication, and monitor opioids with both pain and sedation/respiratory assessments.

Pain Types

  • Acute: protective, temporary, resolves with healing.
  • Chronic: ongoing or recurrent, often longer than 3 months.
  • Nociceptive: tissue damage/inflammation; somatic or visceral.
  • Neuropathic: abnormal nerve processing; often burning, shooting, or pins-and-needles.

Safety Priorities

  • Premedicate before painful procedures when appropriate.
  • Only the client should press the PCA button unless a provider authorizes otherwise.
  • Sedation precedes respiratory depression; intervene early.

Pain Management Framework

Focused Pain Assessment

Subjective first

Pain assessment stays client-centered: believe the report, measure consistently, and connect the pain pattern to function and response.

Location

Where is the pain? Does it radiate? Ask the client to point to the area.

Quality

Sharp, dull, aching, burning, stabbing, throbbing, shooting, tight, tiring, or unbearable.

Measure

Use a consistent scale to rate current pain, best/worst pain, and response to interventions.

Timing

Onset, duration, frequency, constant vs. intermittent pattern.

Setting and Function

How pain affects sleep, work, movement, and ADLs; what the client is doing when pain occurs.

Associated and Modifying Factors

Fatigue, nausea, anxiety, depression, what worsens pain, and what relieves it.

Vital Sign Caution

Do not overtrust vital signs: acute pain can temporarily raise pulse, BP, and RR, but physiologic indicators can normalize even when pain persists.

Classifying Pain

Pick therapy

Classifying the pain helps match therapy, anticipate physiologic cues, and avoid undertreatment when vital signs look normal.

Acute

Protective, temporary, usually self-limiting, resolves with tissue healing. May show tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, diaphoresis, or muscle tension.

Chronic

Not protective; ongoing or recurrent, often beyond tissue healing or longer than 3 months. May have no vital sign change; can include depression, fatigue, decreased function, or disability.

Nociceptive

From tissue damage/inflammation outside the CNS/PNS; somatic or visceral. Often throbbing, aching, localized; can respond to nonopioids and opioids.

Neuropathic

From abnormal or damaged pain nerves. Often shooting, burning, intense, or pins-and-needles; adjuvant medications can help.

Breakthrough

Acute flare above the client's usual pain level. Requires additional relief beyond baseline chronic pain control.

Interventions and Medication Safety

Reassess

Effective pain care combines the client's functional goal with medication safety, planned reassessment, and early action for opioid oversedation.

Combined Strategies

Use both pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic strategies, considering the client's preferences and functional pain goal.

Premedication

Premedicate before painful care such as repositioning, wound care, or invasive diagnostic testing when appropriate.

Nonpharmacologic Support

Nonpharmacologic strategies can reduce stress and coping burden: mind-body practices, cognitive approaches, distraction, and other complementary approaches chosen by the client.

Nonopioids

Nonopioids are appropriate for mild to moderate pain and can be paired with opioids for more intense pain. Track total acetaminophen intake.

Opioid Monitoring

Opioids are appropriate for moderate to severe pain. Monitor constipation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, nausea/vomiting, sedation, and respiratory depression.

PCA Teaching

PCA provides small, frequent opioid doses with a lockout interval; the client should report inadequate relief rather than waiting until pain is severe.

Respiratory Depression Response

If respiratory rate is below 8/min and shallow or the client is difficult to arouse, stop the opioid, notify/act per protocol, and prepare naloxone as prescribed.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Types of Pain

Active Learning Scenario

A group of newly licensed nurses is reviewing pain types on a medical-surgical unit. Complete the Basic Concept template by defining the types and matching characteristics.

TypeDefinition/Characteristics
AcuteProtective and temporary; usually resolves with tissue healing; can produce tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, diaphoresis, muscle tension, grimacing, guarding, or moaning.
ChronicOngoing or frequently recurring; persists beyond healing or longer than 3 months; can reduce function and contribute to fatigue or depression.
NociceptiveArises from tissue damage or inflammation; can be somatic or visceral and can cause referred pain.
NeuropathicArises from abnormal or damaged nerves; can feel burning, shooting, intense, or like pins-and-needles.

Application Exercises

1

A client has mild acute pain after an ankle sprain. Which analgesic should the nurse expect?

  • A. Ketorolac.
  • B. Ketamine.
  • C. Meperidine.
  • D. Methadone.
A Ketorolac is an NSAID and fits mild acute inflammatory pain after a sprain.
2

A client with cancer takes extended-release opioids twice daily and reports an increase in localized aching over the last few days. How should the nurse document this increase?

  • A. Phantom limb pain.
  • B. Mixed pain.
  • C. Breakthrough pain.
  • D. Neuropathic pain.
C Breakthrough pain is an acute flare above the client's usual or baseline pain level.
3

A client is using morphine by PCA after abdominal surgery. Which statement shows correct understanding?

  • A. "I'll wait to use the device until it's absolutely necessary."
  • B. "I'll be careful about pushing the button so I don't get an overdose."
  • C. "I should tell the nurse if the pain doesn't stop after I use this device."
  • D. "I will ask my son to push the dose button when I am sleeping."
C The client should report inadequate pain control so the plan can be reevaluated.
D The client should be the one to press the PCA button unless a provider authorizes an exception.
4

Which statement about pain assessment should the nurse include when teaching a newly licensed nurse?

  • A. Most clients exaggerate pain.
  • B. Pain must have an identifiable source to justify opioids.
  • C. Objective data are essential to prove pain.
  • D. Pain is whatever the client says it is.
D Pain is subjective, and the client is the best source of pain information.
5

Which findings are adverse effects of opioid analgesics? Select all that apply.

  • A. Urinary incontinence.
  • B. Diarrhea.
  • C. Bradypnea.
  • D. Orthostatic hypotension.
  • E. Nausea.
C, D, E Opioids can cause respiratory depression, orthostatic hypotension, nausea/vomiting, sedation, urinary retention, and constipation.
A, B ATI highlights urinary retention and constipation, not urinary incontinence and diarrhea, as common opioid effects.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 5

Meningitis

Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges around the brain and spinal cord. ATI prioritizes early isolation, rapid infection treatment, neurologic protection, and complication surveillance because bacterial meningitis can progress quickly.

TL;DR - Isolate First

When meningitis is suspected, protect other people first with droplet precautions, then support antibiotics, fever control, low stimulation, and close neurologic monitoring. Watch for increased ICP, SIADH, septic shock, and septic emboli.

Classic Findings

  • Severe constant headache, stiff neck, photophobia, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and altered level of consciousness.
  • Kernig and Brudzinski findings can signal meningeal irritation.
  • Meningococcal meningitis can include a red macular rash.

Priority Nursing Moves

  • Initiate droplet precautions as soon as meningitis is suspected.
  • Decrease stimulation and keep the head of bed elevated about 30 degrees.
  • Avoid opioid masking of level-of-consciousness changes when ICP risk is present.

Meningitis Care Map

Types, Transmission, and Prevention

Infection control

Different causes change the urgency and prevention teaching, but suspected bacterial meningitis always raises infection-control priority.

Viral Meningitis

Viral meningitis is common and often resolves without specific treatment.

Fungal Meningitis

Fungal meningitis is associated with immunosuppression, including AIDS.

Bacterial Meningitis

Bacterial meningitis is contagious, has high mortality risk, and needs rapid care.

Hib Vaccine

Hib vaccination protects infants against one bacterial cause.

Pneumococcal Vaccine

Pneumococcal vaccination lowers respiratory and CNS infection risk in high-risk adults.

Meningococcal Vaccine

Meningococcal vaccine is recommended for adolescents and before communal living, such as college residence halls or military settings.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Recognize fast

Assessment starts with exposure and risk clues, then diagnostics confirm infection pattern and screen for complications.

Risk Factors

Risk factors include recent bacterial infection, immunosuppression, invasive procedures, skull fracture or penetrating injury, direct CSF contamination, and crowded living conditions.

CSF Analysis

CSF analysis from lumbar puncture is the definitive diagnostic procedure; bacterial CSF can appear cloudy with elevated WBC/protein, decreased glucose, and increased pressure.

Imaging

CT or MRI can be used to identify increased ICP or abscess.

Cultures and CBC

Culture and sensitivity from blood or other body fluids can guide early antimicrobial selection, and CBC can show elevated WBC count.

Nursing Care and Complications

Prevent spread + ICP

Nursing care pairs transmission prevention with neurologic protection and rapid escalation when infection or ICP worsens.

Droplet Precautions

Place in a private room and continue precautions per policy; bacterial cases can require ongoing isolation. Suspected meningitis can spread quickly to close contacts.

Neurologic Protection

Quiet room, reduced light, bed rest, head of bed about 30 degrees, seizure precautions, frequent neuro checks. Inflammation can raise ICP and trigger seizures.

Medication Support

Expect broad antibiotics until cultures return; use nonopioid fever/headache control and anticonvulsants if seizure/ICP risk is present. Antibiotics treat infection; nonopioids avoid masking level-of-consciousness changes.

Complication Surveillance

Monitor for decreased LOC, pupil changes, impaired extraocular movement, dilute blood/concentrated urine, shock, rash, extremity circulation changes, and coagulation changes. Meningitis can progress to increased ICP, SIADH, septic shock, septic emboli, DIC, stroke, gangrene, coma, or death.

Active Learning Scenario

Template PartStudy Fill-In

MedicationsCeftriaxone or cefotaxime with vancomycin for bacterial infection; acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever/headache; phenytoin if seizure risk is present.
ComplicationsIncreased ICP, SIADH, septic emboli, DIC, stroke, gangrene, coma, and death.

Application Exercises

1

A client reports severe headache and stiff neck, and assessment shows positive Kernig and Brudzinski findings. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Administer prescribed antibiotics.
  • B. Implement droplet precautions.
  • C. Initiate IV access.
  • D. Decrease bright lights.
B Suspected meningitis requires droplet precautions first to reduce transmission risk.
A, C, D These can be appropriate, but they do not come before preventing spread to others.
2

Which actions are used when assessing Brudzinski's sign? Select all that apply.

  • A. Place the client supine.
  • B. Flex the client's hip and knee.
  • C. Place hands behind the client's neck.
  • D. Bend the client's head toward the chest.
  • E. Straighten the flexed leg at the knee.
A, C, D Brudzinski assessment uses supine positioning, hand support behind the neck, and neck flexion toward the chest.
B, E Hip/knee flexion and leg extension fit Kernig assessment instead.
3

A client with meningitis is at risk for increased ICP. Which actions should the nurse plan? Select all that apply.

  • A. Implement seizure precautions.
  • B. Perform neurologic checks four times a day.
  • C. Administer morphine for neck and generalized pain.
  • D. Turn off room lights and television.
  • E. Monitor for impaired extraocular movements.
  • F. Encourage frequent coughing.
A, D, E Seizure precautions, low stimulation, and extraocular movement monitoring match increased ICP risk.
B, C, F Neuro checks should be more frequent than four times daily when ICP is a concern; opioids can mask LOC changes; coughing can increase ICP.
4

Which teaching about meningococcal vaccine should the nurse include?

  • A. It is primarily indicated to reduce respiratory infection.
  • B. It is administered in a four-dose infant series.
  • C. It is recommended for adolescents before starting college.
  • D. It is initially given at 2 months of age.
C ATI highlights meningococcal vaccination for adolescents before communal college living.
A, B, D These options describe pneumococcal or Hib vaccine patterns rather than MCV4 teaching.
5

Which actions belong in the plan of care for bacterial meningitis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Monitor for bradycardia.
  • B. Keep an emesis basin at the bedside.
  • C. Administer antipyretic medication.
  • D. Perform a skin assessment.
  • E. Keep the head of the bed flat.
B, C, D Nausea/vomiting, fever, and meningococcal rash surveillance are expected care priorities.
A, E Monitor for tachycardia, and elevate the head of bed about 30 degrees to support venous drainage and reduce ICP risk.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 6

Seizures and Epilepsy

Seizures are abrupt abnormal electrical discharges in the brain. Nursing care centers on injury prevention, airway and aspiration protection, accurate event documentation, medication adherence, and rapid treatment of status epilepticus.

TL;DR - Protect, Do Not Restrain

During a seizure, protect privacy and safety, turn the client to the side when possible, loosen restrictive clothing, and never restrain or force the jaw open. Afterward, keep the airway patent, assess, reorient, and document the episode.

Common Triggers

  • Overwhelming fatigue, excessive stress, hyperventilation, flashing lights, excess caffeine, acute alcohol use, and substance exposure.
  • Risk factors include head trauma, infection, stroke, metabolic problems, hypoxia, tumor, and abrupt AED discontinuation.
  • Older adults can develop new seizures related to cerebrovascular or cardiac disease.

Priority Follow-Up

  • Postictal priority is airway/aspiration protection in side-lying position.
  • Teach AEDs at the same time daily and periodic blood levels when prescribed.
  • Status epilepticus is prolonged or repeated seizure activity and requires emergency treatment.

Seizure Care Map

Seizure Patterns

Classify

Pattern recognition links what the nurse sees to the priority: protect safety, keep the airway clear, and document the event accurately.

Tonic-Clonic

Brief stiffening, loss of consciousness, then rhythmic jerking; breathing can pause or become irregular, and postictal confusion and sleepiness follow. Big safety and airway event.

Tonic, Clonic, Myoclonic, Atonic

Tonic = stiffening; clonic = rhythmic jerking; myoclonic = brief jerks or stiffening; atonic = sudden loss of muscle tone with fall risk. Name the movement pattern.

Complex Partial

Focal seizure with automatisms, possible blackout, and amnesia around the event. Lip smacking or picking at clothes is a clue.

Simple Partial

Focal seizure with preserved consciousness; can include unusual sensation, deja vu, autonomic changes, unilateral movement, pain, or smell. Awake but altered sensation/motor activity.

During and After a Seizure

Airway + injury

Care separates into immediate protection during activity and reassessment once the event ends.

Privacy and Fall Protection

Provide privacy, ease the client to the floor if standing, move furniture away, loosen clothing, and protect the head.

Airway Positioning

Position to keep the airway patent and turn the client to the side when possible.

Avoid Harmful Actions

Do not restrain, force open the jaw, insert an airway during seizure activity, or use padded tongue blades.

Postictal Assessment

Maintain side-lying position, check vital signs, assess for injury, and perform neurologic checks.

Reorientation and Recovery

Reorient and calm the client, allow rest as needed, and ask about aura or possible triggers.

Event Documentation

Document onset, duration, LOC, apnea, cyanosis, motor activity, incontinence, and postictal findings.

Medication, Procedures, and Long-Term Safety

Adherence

Long-term safety depends on consistent AED use, medication interaction review, device teaching when used, and practical restrictions that reduce injury.

AED Start and Monitoring

AED therapy often starts with one medication; blood levels help determine therapeutic range, adherence, and effectiveness.

Daily Adherence

Teach clients to take AEDs at the same time every day, report adverse effects, and keep routine dental care if gum overgrowth is a risk.

Phenytoin Review

Phenytoin can reduce oral contraceptive effectiveness and has important anticoagulant interactions, so medication review matters.

Vagal Nerve Stimulation

Vagal nerve stimulation can help some partial seizures; the client can hold a magnet over the implanted device at aura onset to abort or lessen a seizure.

Device Restrictions

Clients with vagal nerve stimulators should avoid MRI, ultrasound diathermy, microwave ovens, and shortwave radios per ATI teaching.

Identification and Access

Encourage medical identification, review state driving rules, and involve school/social/vocational resources when seizures affect access or functioning.

Application Exercises

1

A client with a seizure disorder says, "I am about to have a seizure." Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

  • A. Provide privacy.
  • B. Ease the client to the floor if standing.
  • C. Move furniture away from the client.
  • D. Loosen the client's clothing.
  • E. Protect the client's head with padding.
  • F. Restrain the client.
A, B, C, D, E These actions protect privacy, prevent injury, reduce restriction, and protect the head.
F Restraints increase injury risk and can worsen seizure activity.
2

A client has just experienced a generalized seizure. Which action should the nurse perform first?

  • A. Keep the client in a side-lying position.
  • B. Document the seizure duration.
  • C. Reorient the client to the environment.
  • D. Provide hygiene after incontinence.
A During the postictal phase, aspiration risk is the priority; side-lying positioning supports oral drainage and airway patency.
B, C, D These are appropriate after the airway and aspiration priority is addressed.
3

Which discharge teaching should the nurse include for a client taking phenytoin?

  • A. Consider taking an antacid with the medication.
  • B. Watch for receding gums.
  • C. Take the medication at the same time every day.
  • D. Provide urine samples to determine therapeutic levels.
C Taking phenytoin at the same time daily supports consistent therapeutic effect.
B, D Phenytoin can cause gum overgrowth, not receding gums; therapeutic levels are checked with blood testing.
4

Which trigger-factor teaching should the nurse include for a client with generalized seizures? Select all that apply.

  • A. Avoid overwhelming fatigue.
  • B. Remove caffeinated products from the diet.
  • C. Limit looking at flashing lights.
  • D. Perform vigorous aerobic exercise.
  • E. Limit episodes of hyperventilation.
  • F. Use aerosol hairspray freely.
A, B, C, E Fatigue, caffeine, flashing lights, and hyperventilation can trigger seizure activity.
D, F Vigorous physical activity and aerosol products can be triggers for some clients.
5

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client who received a vagal nerve stimulator?

  • A. It is safe to use microwaves that are 1,200 watts or less.
  • B. Avoid CT scans with contrast.
  • C. Place a magnet over the implanted device when an aura occurs.
  • D. Use ultrasound diathermy for pain management.
C ATI teaches that the client can hold a magnet over the stimulator at aura onset to reduce seizure activity.
A, B, D Avoid microwave exposure and ultrasound diathermy; ATI highlights avoiding MRI rather than CT contrast for the device.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 7

Parkinson's Disease

Parkinson's disease is a progressive motor disorder caused by decreased dopamine and relative acetylcholine dominance. Nursing care protects medication timing, swallowing, mobility, communication, cognition, and long-term family support.

TL;DR - Dopamine Down, Acetylcholine Dominates

Parkinson's disease produces tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability. Give medications on time, watch for swallowing and aspiration risk, support mobility while independence remains possible, and reassess cognition and mood as the disease advances.

Expected Findings

  • Pill-rolling tremor, slow shuffling or propulsive gait, stooped posture, and masklike expression.
  • Rigidity, bradykinesia or akinesia, slow monotonous speech, fatigue, and reduced manual dexterity.
  • Difficulty chewing/swallowing, drooling, dysarthria, mood changes, and possible dementia.

Priority Nursing Moves

  • Administer PD medications at prescribed times and monitor for wearing-off periods or dyskinesias.
  • Use swallowing precautions, small frequent meals, thickened/cold fluids when appropriate, and upright positioning.
  • Encourage active ROM, assistive devices, rest periods, and extra time for activities.

Parkinson's Disease Care Map

Pathophysiology and Stages

Motor decline

Frame Parkinson's disease by dopamine loss, acetylcholine dominance, and the staged shift from early independence to later nutrition, aspiration, skin, cognition, and caregiver priorities.

Core Problem

Degeneration of the substantia nigra lowers dopamine; acetylcholine overstimulates the basal ganglia. Treatment aims to raise dopamine effect or lower acetylcholine effect.

Stage I-II

Unilateral tremor appears first, then bilateral limb involvement with walking and balance difficulty. Encourage exercise, independence, and support resources early.

Stage III

Movement slows significantly with gait disturbance and postural instability. A walker or other assistive device can be needed for ambulation.

Stage IV-V

Rigidity/akinesia disrupt ADLs; later the client can no longer stand or walk and becomes dependent. Focus shifts toward nutrition, aspiration prevention, skin/safety, cognition, and caregiver support.

Mobility, Swallowing, and Communication

Function first

Function support is practical: protect swallowing and nutrition, preserve mobility, reduce falls, and support speech as motor control slows.

Swallowing Referral

Consult speech-language therapy for choking risk and dietitian support for semisolid foods or thickened liquids.

Nutrition Tracking

Track intake, encourage fluids, document weight at least weekly, and offer small frequent meals.

Eating Support

Use upright positioning, adaptive eating devices, cold/thick fluids when tolerated, and supplements between meals if weight is falling.

Mobility Support

Encourage active ROM, exercise such as yoga, assistive devices, and planned rest periods.

Fall Reduction

Teach the client to stop occasionally when walking to reduce propulsive gait and fall risk.

Communication

Encourage slow speech, frequent pauses, facial muscle exercises, alternate communication methods, and speech-language referral.

Medications, Procedures, and Complications

Timing matters

Medication timing protects function, while adverse-effect monitoring, procedure surveillance, swallowing precautions, and cognition checks reduce harm as the disease advances.

Levodopa and Carbidopa

Levodopa raises dopamine in the brain; carbidopa can reduce peripheral metabolism so more medication reaches the brain with fewer adverse effects.

Dopamine Agonists

Dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine, ropinirole, and pramipexole can cause orthostatic hypotension, dyskinesias, and hallucinations.

Anticholinergics

Benztropine and trihexyphenidyl can reduce tremor/rigidity but require monitoring for dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and acute confusion.

Entacapone

Entacapone can make more levodopa available; monitor dyskinesia/hyperkinesia, diarrhea, and expected dark urine.

MAO-B Inhibitors

MAO-B inhibitors can reduce wearing-off but require tyramine restriction and caution with sympathomimetics, meperidine, and fluoxetine.

Advanced Procedures

Advanced options include stereotactic pallidotomy/thalamotomy and deep brain stimulation; monitor postprocedure for neurologic change, bleeding, infection, or stroke-like findings.

Major Complications

Major complications include aspiration pneumonia and altered cognition; use swallowing precautions, suction standby when needed, a safe environment, and interprofessional planning.

Template PartStudy Fill-In

Application Exercises

1

A client displays manifestations of stage III Parkinson's disease. Which action should the nurse include?

  • A. Recommend a community support group.
  • B. Integrate a daily exercise routine.
  • C. Provide a walker for ambulation.
  • D. Perform all ADLs for the client.
C Stage III includes significant movement slowing and gait disturbance, so a walker supports safer ambulation.
A, B, D Support groups and exercise begin earlier; full ADL dependence is expected later, not stage III.
2

Which nutrition actions should the nurse include for stage IV Parkinson's disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Provide three large balanced meals daily.
  • B. Record diet and fluid intake daily.
  • C. Document weight every other week.
  • D. Offer cold fluids such as milkshakes.
  • E. Offer nutritional supplements between meals.
B, D, E Intake tracking, cold/thick fluids, and supplements support hydration and weight maintenance.
A, C Small frequent meals and at least weekly weights are preferred.
3

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client with a new prescription for bromocriptine?

  • A. Rise slowly when standing.
  • B. Expect urine to become dark-colored.
  • C. Avoid foods containing tyramine.
  • D. Report any skin discoloration.
A Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist and can cause orthostatic hypotension.
B, C, D Dark urine fits entacapone; tyramine restriction fits MAO-B inhibitors; skin discoloration fits amantadine.
4

Which findings are expected with Parkinson's disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Decreased vision.
  • B. Pill-rolling tremor of the fingers.
  • C. Shuffling gait.
  • D. Drooling.
  • E. Bilateral ankle edema.
  • F. Lack of facial expression.
B, C, D, F Pill-rolling tremor, shuffling gait, drooling, and masklike facial expression are ATI-supported findings.
A, E Decreased vision is not expected; ankle edema can be medication-related but is not a core expected finding.
5

A client with Parkinson's disease is starting to display bradykinesia. Which action is appropriate?

  • A. Teach the client to walk more quickly.
  • B. Complete passive range-of-motion exercises daily.
  • C. Place the client on a low-protein, low-calorie diet.
  • D. Give the client extra time to perform activities.
D Bradykinesia is slowed movement; extra time supports independence and safety.
A, B, C Teach the client to pause, encourage active ROM, and support adequate calories/protein rather than rushing or restricting intake.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 8

Alzheimer's Disease

Alzheimer's disease is a nonreversible dementia that progresses over years. Nursing care focuses on safety, structured routines, communication, cognitive support, caregiver education, medication monitoring, and planning for progressive decline.

TL;DR - Safety Plus Structure

Alzheimer's disease progresses from memory lapses to loss of ADLs, continence, swallowing, movement, and environmental awareness. Reduce injury and wandering risk, keep routines predictable, use short directions, and support caregivers before crisis points.

Stage Cues

  • Early: memory lapses, losing items, decreased concentration, difficulty with new names or tasks, but ADLs remain possible.
  • Middle: personal-history gaps, planning/money difficulty, personality or sleep changes, wandering, and possible incontinence.
  • Late: loss of conversation, ADL dependence, swallowing decline, immobility, infection risk, stupor, coma, and death.

Priority Nursing Moves

  • Keep the client away from stairs, exits, elevators, dangerous items, and environmental clutter.
  • Use a structured environment, short directions, consistency, repetition, and therapeutic touch.
  • Use reality orientation in earlier stages and validation therapy in later stages.

Alzheimer's Disease Care Map

Diagnosis, Risk, and Staging

Rule out + stage

Begin by recognizing dementia patterns, ruling out other causes, and pairing risk factors with staged cognitive assessment tools.

Dementia Pattern

Dementia involves multiple cognitive deficits that impair memory and can affect language, motor skills, and abstract thinking.

Diagnostic Limit

There is no single lab test or living diagnostic procedure that definitively diagnoses Alzheimer's disease; testing helps rule out other causes.

Evaluation Studies

MRI, CT/CAT, PET, EEG, and sometimes lumbar puncture can support evaluation when ruling out other causes.

Risk Factors

Risk factors include advanced age, family history, genetic predisposition, previous head injury, female sex, chemical imbalance, and environmental exposures such as herpes virus, metal, or toxic waste.

Assessment Tools

Assessment tools can include MMSE, set test using FACT, Short Blessed Test, or Clock Drawing Test.

Nursing Care: Cognition, Memory, and Behavior

Routine

Nursing care relies on structure, manageable stimulation, memory support, low-stimulation surroundings, and calm behavioral redirection.

Cognitive Stimulation

Offer walks, music, craft activities, and varied but manageable stimulation.

Structured Environment

Maintain a structured environment and introduce changes gradually.

Direction and Touch

Use calendars, short directions, consistency, repetition, and therapeutic touch.

Memory Training

Reminisce, use lists/rehearsal, and repeat the client's last statement to stimulate memory.

Overstimulation

Avoid overstimulation by reducing noise, clutter, and crowds.

Agitation

Reduce agitation with calm redirection, diversions, and toileting schedules.

Safety, Medications, and Family Planning

Caregiver support

Safety planning centers on wandering and falls, while medication teaching and caregiver planning anticipate progressive care needs.

Home Safety

Remove scatter rugs and clutter, improve stair lighting, install handrails, secure dangerous supplies, use hard-to-open locks/door alarms, lower the mattress if needed, and consider Safe Return enrollment. Wandering and falls are central risks.

Medication

Donepezil can slow progression and improve behavior/function for some clients; memantine can reduce deterioration and may be paired with donepezil. These do not cure AD.

Monitoring

Watch for frequent stools/upset stomach, dizziness, headache, lightheadedness, unsteady gait, and caution in asthma/COPD. Medication effects can worsen fall or respiratory risk.

Family Planning

Refer for support groups, social services, case management, adult day care, long-term care options, legal planning, advanced directives, guardianship, and caregiver respite. Care needs intensify over time.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Alzheimer's Disease

Active Learning Scenario

A charge nurse is preparing a program for assistive personnel about caring for clients who have Alzheimer's disease. Complete the System Disorder template by naming nursing care interventions.

Care AreaStudy Fill-In
Cognitive stimulationOffer walks, music, or crafts; keep structure; introduce changes slowly; use calendars; give short directions; be consistent and repetitive; use therapeutic touch.
Memory trainingReminisce about the past, help make lists and rehearse, and repeat the client's last statement to stimulate memory.
Safety and behaviorReduce clutter/noise, keep objects in consistent places, use calm redirection, monitor wandering, and match reality orientation or validation therapy to stage.

Application Exercises

1

Which statement by a partner indicates effective teaching about donepezil?

  • A. "This medication should increase my husband's appetite."
  • B. "This medication should help my husband sleep better."
  • C. "This medication should help my husband's daily function."
  • D. "This medication should increase my husband's energy level."
C Donepezil can slow progression and help improve behavior and daily function for some clients.
A, B, D ATI does not teach donepezil as an appetite, sleep, or energy medication.
2

Which intervention fits a client with moderate Alzheimer's disease in long-term care?

  • A. Use a gait belt for ambulation.
  • B. Thicken all liquids.
  • C. Provide protective undergarments.
  • D. Reorient the client to self and current events.
D Moderate Alzheimer's can require reorientation as cognitive function declines.
A, B, C Ambulation, swallowing, and persistent incontinence concerns are more characteristic of later-stage decline.
3

A client has disorientation, unsteady gait, and wandering. Which home safety measures should the nurse review? Select all that apply.

  • A. Remove floor rugs.
  • B. Have door locks that can be easily opened.
  • C. Provide increased lighting in stairwells.
  • D. Install handrails in the bathroom.
  • E. Place the mattress on the floor.
A, C, D, E Removing rugs, improving lighting, adding handrails, and lowering the mattress reduce fall and wandering-related injury risk.
B Easy-to-open locks increase the risk that a wandering client will leave and become lost.
4

A client with Alzheimer's disease falls frequently. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Keep the call light near the client.
  • B. Place the client in a room close to the nurses' station.
  • C. Encourage the client to ask for assistance.
  • D. Remind the client to walk with someone for support.
B Close observation near the nurses' station is the priority because the client might not remember to call or ask for help.
A, C, D These can help, but memory impairment makes them less reliable as the first safety action.
5

Which risk factors should the nurse include when teaching a family member about Alzheimer's disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Exposure to metal waste products.
  • B. Long-term estrogen therapy.
  • C. Sustained use of vitamin E.
  • D. Previous head injury.
  • E. History of herpes infection.
A, D, E ATI lists metal/toxic exposure, previous head injury, and herpes virus exposure among risk factors.
B, C Estrogen therapy is not taught as a risk factor here, and vitamin E use is not a listed AD risk factor.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 9

Brain Tumors

Brain tumors are space-occupying lesions that can interrupt CSF flow, raise intracranial pressure, create focal neurologic deficits, and require precise monitoring before and after biopsy, medication therapy, radiation, or craniotomy.

TL;DR - Space Occupying Means ICP Risk

For brain tumors, think location plus pressure. Supratentorial tumors tend to show headache, visual change, seizures, cognitive/personality change, nausea, and possible paralysis; infratentorial tumors often show cranial nerve, hearing, swallowing, eye movement, balance, and brainstem-related findings.

Assessment Clues

  • General findings can include dysarthria, dysphagia, vertigo, papilledema, hemiparesis, positive Romberg, positive Babinski, and cranial nerve dysfunction.
  • Increasing ICP is a priority pattern: change in level of consciousness, restlessness, unequal pupils, and headache.
  • Benign tumors do not metastasize, but location can still make a tumor life-threatening.

Care Priorities

  • Do not perform lumbar puncture when increasing ICP is suspected because herniation risk rises.
  • Avoid routine opioids when possible because they can reduce level of consciousness and depress respirations.
  • After craniotomy, monitor neurologic status, bleeding, seizure activity, positioning, and straining.

Brain Tumor Care Map

Classification, Location, and Clinical Pattern

Locate first

Start by separating origin, benign versus malignant behavior, and whether the tumor is above or below the tentorium.

Origin

Primary malignant tumors usually arise from neuroglial tissue; secondary malignant tumors are metastatic lesions from cancers elsewhere in the body. Metastatic disease changes goals of care and often makes treatment palliative.

Benign Tumors

Benign tumors often arise from meninges or cranial nerves, have clearer boundaries, and do not metastasize. They can still cause major harm by compression or cranial nerve impairment.

Supratentorial Pattern

Above the tentorium in the cerebral hemispheres; watch for morning headache, visual change, seizures, motor loss, cognition/personality change, nausea, and paralysis. Cerebral hemisphere pressure can present as focal or generalized neurologic change.

Infratentorial Pattern

Below the tentorium in the brainstem or cerebellum; watch hearing/ringing changes, facial droop, dysphagia, nystagmus, crossed eyes, ataxia, ANS dysfunction, and cranial nerve findings. Brainstem/cerebellar involvement threatens swallowing, airway, balance, and cranial nerve function.

Diagnostics and Medication Priorities

No LP with ICP

Diagnostic priorities define size, location, spread, and tissue pathology while medication priorities target swelling, ICP, seizures, stress-ulcer risk, and nausea.

Imaging and Biopsy

Imaging and angiographic studies help define tumor size, location, and spread; biopsy confirms cellular pathology when tissue diagnosis is needed.

LP and EEG

Lumbar puncture and EEG can provide information, but LP is avoided if the client has manifestations of increasing ICP.

Corticosteroids

Corticosteroids reduce cerebral edema and can improve headache or altered level of consciousness related to swelling.

Osmotic Diuretics

Osmotic diuretics can reduce brain fluid burden and help lower ICP.

Seizure and Stress-Ulcer Support

Anticonvulsants are used to prevent or control seizures; H2-antagonists help reduce stress-ulcer risk during high-stress treatment periods.

Antiemetics

Antiemetics can be used when nausea or vomiting is present from ICP, tumor location, or treatment.

Craniotomy, Positioning, and Complications

Post-op watch

Craniotomy care pairs preoperative teaching with postoperative neurologic surveillance, positioning, ICP precautions, and rapid reporting of decline.

Procedure Teaching

Explain the procedure, answer questions, and include the partner when possible to reduce miscommunication.

Preoperative Review

Review aspirin, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, alcohol, tobacco, and complementary therapy use according to provider instructions.

Preoperative Medications

Discuss advance directives and administer prescribed preoperative medications such as anxiolytics or muscle relaxants.

Postoperative Monitoring

Monitor vital signs, Glasgow Coma Scale, neurologic status, head dressing drainage, bleeding, and seizures.

Supratentorial Positioning

For supratentorial surgery, keep the head elevated 30 degrees and neutral; avoid neck/hip flexion and straining.

Infratentorial Positioning

For infratentorial surgery, side-lying/flat positioning and frequent turning can be prescribed early after surgery.

Complication Watch

Complications to recognize include SIADH, diabetes insipidus, increased ICP, hydrocephalus, postoperative bleeding, and seizures. Report new neurologic decline promptly.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Craniotomy for Brain Tumor

Active Learning Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has a brain tumor and will undergo craniotomy. Complete the Therapeutic Procedure template by connecting the procedure description with preoperative and postoperative interventions.

Template PartStudy Fill-In
DescriptionSurgical opening in the skull to expose brain tissue and remove all or part of a tumor.
Preoperative interventionsExplain the procedure, provide emotional support, give written teaching, include the partner when possible, review aspirin/complementary therapy use, discuss advance directives, and administer prescribed anxiety or muscle-relaxing medication.
Postoperative interventionsMonitor vital signs, neurologic status, Glasgow Coma Scale, bleeding, and seizures; keep the head elevated and neutral when prescribed; prevent straining that can increase ICP.

Application Exercises

1

After removal of an encapsulated acoustic tumor, which postoperative complications should the nurse monitor for? Select all that apply.

  • A. Increased intracranial pressure.
  • B. Hemorrhagic shock.
  • C. Hydrocephalus.
  • D. Hypoglycemia.
  • E. Seizures.
A, C, E Increased ICP, hydrocephalus, and seizures are priority complications after craniotomy.
B, D Hemorrhagic shock and hypoglycemia are not the expected postoperative concerns emphasized for this procedure.
2

A client just had a craniotomy for a supratentorial tumor and has a respiratory rate of 12/min. Which prescription should the nurse clarify?

  • A. Dexamethasone IV bolus.
  • B. Morphine sulfate IV bolus PRN for pain.
  • C. Ondansetron IV bolus PRN for nausea.
  • D. Phenytoin IV bolus.
B Morphine can depress respirations and level of consciousness, so clarification is needed with a low respiratory rate after craniotomy.
A, C, D Dexamethasone treats cerebral edema, ondansetron treats nausea, and phenytoin helps prevent seizures.
3

Which findings are expected with increased ICP? Select all that apply.

  • A. Disorientation to time and place.
  • B. Restlessness and irritability.
  • C. Unequal pupils.
  • D. ICP of 15 mm Hg.
  • E. Headache.
A, B, C, E Change in LOC, behavior change, unequal pupils, and headache fit increasing ICP.
D An ICP of 15 mm Hg is within the expected reference range.
4

Which teaching about dexamethasone is appropriate for a client who has an expanding brain tumor? Select all that apply.

  • A. It is used to reduce brain swelling.
  • B. It commonly causes low blood sugar.
  • C. Weight gain can occur.
  • D. It delays tumor growth.
  • E. Fluid retention can occur.
A, C, E Dexamethasone reduces cerebral edema and can cause weight gain and fluid retention.
B, D Hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia, is a concern; dexamethasone does not delay tumor growth.
5

A client with a benign brain tumor asks whether this type of tumor can occur elsewhere in the body. Which response is best?

  • A. It can spread to the breasts and kidneys.
  • B. It can develop in the gastrointestinal tract.
  • C. It is limited to brain tissue.
  • D. It probably started elsewhere and spread to the brain.
C Benign brain tumors develop from meninges or cranial nerves and do not metastasize.
A, B, D These describe metastasis or development outside the benign brain tumor pattern.
6

How should the nurse assess a positive Romberg sign?

  • A. Stroke the lateral sole of the foot.
  • B. Ask the client to blink both eyes.
  • C. Observe for facial drooping.
  • D. Have the client stand with eyes closed.
D A positive Romberg sign is loss of balance while standing erect with the eyes closed.
A, B, C These assess Babinski response or cranial nerve/facial movement findings, not Romberg balance.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 10

Multiple Sclerosis

Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune demyelinating disorder of the CNS. Nursing care focuses on recognizing relapse triggers and neurologic findings, preserving mobility and safety, managing bladder/bowel and visual changes, and teaching medication precautions.

TL;DR - Demyelination Causes Disconnected Signals

MS damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord, interrupting nerve impulse transmission. Expect relapses and remissions, fatigue, sensory changes, visual changes, dysarthria, dysphagia, spasticity, ataxia, bowel/bladder dysfunction, cognitive change, and heat-related worsening.

Trigger Watch

  • Relapses can be triggered by infection, stress, fatigue, pregnancy, injury, overexertion, cold-climate association, temperature extremes, and hot showers or baths.
  • Uhthoff's sign is temporary worsening of vision or neurologic function after exertion or heat exposure.
  • Diagnosis often takes time because early findings can be vague.

Care Priorities

  • Monitor vision, speech fatigue, swallowing, activity tolerance, skin integrity, cognition, and coping support.
  • Prevent fatigue and overheating; group care, plan rest, and stretch/exercise involved muscles within tolerance.
  • Teach bladder routines, infection prevention, assistive devices, and referral needs as function changes.

Multiple Sclerosis Care Map

Pathophysiology, Course, and Expected Findings

CNS myelin

Anchor the MS picture to CNS demyelination, relapse course, and function changes that can affect vision, swallowing, mobility, cognition, bowel, and bladder care.

Demyelination

MS is an autoimmune disorder affecting nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord; demyelination disrupts nerve impulse flow.

Plaque Injury

Plaques can form on damaged axons, causing permanent injury when the axon cannot regenerate.

Affected Areas

Commonly affected areas include the optic nerve, cerebrum, brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord.

Course

The most common course is relapsing-remitting; recovery after a relapse might not return the client to the previous baseline.

Expected Findings

Findings include fatigue, pain/paresthesia, diplopia or visual-field changes, tinnitus/vertigo, dysphagia, dysarthria, spasticity, ataxia, nystagmus, bowel/bladder dysfunction, cognitive changes, and sexual dysfunction.

Diagnostics and Nursing Care

Function support

Diagnostics identify plaques and inflammation patterns; nursing care turns those findings into bladder, vision, mobility, skin, and energy-conservation support.

CSF Analysis

CSF analysis can show elevated protein and a slight increase in WBCs.

MRI

MRI of the brain and spine is the key diagnostic study because it can show plaques.

Focused Assessment

Assessment must include vision, speech, swallowing, activity tolerance, skin, cognition, bowel, bladder, and mobility.

Bladder Routine

Encourage fluids and bladder routines to lower urinary tract infection risk; timed voiding or intermittent self-catheterization can be used when prescribed.

Vision Support

Use eye patches for diplopia and alternate eyes; teach scanning techniques for visual-field problems.

Safety and Energy

Reduce injury risk with a safe environment, wide-base walking, assistive devices, skin precautions, and energy conservation.

Medication Map

Relapse + symptoms

The medication map separates disease-modifying therapy, acute-exacerbation inflammation control, and symptom-specific support for spasticity, paresthesia, bowel, bladder, tremor, or ataxia.

Interferon Beta and Glatiramer

Disease-modifying therapy can reduce relapse frequency/duration. Interferon beta can cause flu-like manifestations; injectable therapy is often started early.

Oral Alternatives

Teriflunomide, fingolimod, and dimethyl fumarate are oral disease-modifying alternatives and are useful when injections are not tolerated or cause reactions.

Corticosteroids

Corticosteroids reduce inflammation during acute exacerbations. Monitor for infection risk, fluid/electrolyte changes, hyperglycemia, GI bleeding, and personality change.

Antispasmodics

Dantrolene, tizanidine, baclofen, and diazepam treat muscle spasticity. Report increased weakness or jaundice; avoid abrupt baclofen discontinuation; monitor liver risk with tizanidine or dantrolene.

Symptom Agents

Carbamazepine is used for paresthesia; docusate for constipation; propantheline for bladder dysfunction; propranolol/clonazepam for tremor or ataxia. Match medication teaching to the symptom being treated and watch for safety effects such as dizziness or weakness.

Which finding should the nurse expect for a client who has multiple sclerosis?

  • A. Fluctuations in blood pressure.
  • B. Loss of cognitive function.
  • C. Ineffective cough.
  • D. Drooping eyelids.

Which findings should the nurse expect during assessment of a client newly diagnosed with MS? Select all that apply.

  • A. Areas of paresthesia.
  • B. Involuntary eye movements.

  • B. This medication will help with bladder function.

  • D. This medication can cause dizziness.

Unit 2 · Neurologic Disorders · Chapter 11

Headaches

Headache care starts with distinguishing primary headaches from secondary headaches that need investigation. ATI emphasizes migraine and cluster patterns, trigger recognition, medication timing, comfort measures, and when neurologic imaging is needed.

TL;DR - Migraine Has Triggers, Cluster Has a Clock

Migraine headaches commonly bring unilateral throbbing pain, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, and possible aura. Cluster headaches are brief, intense, unilateral, nonthrobbing attacks that can occur 1 to 8 times daily with tearing, nasal congestion, eyelid changes, and pacing or rocking.

Red Flags

  • Secondary headaches are linked to an organic cause such as tumor or aneurysm and need further investigation.
  • Use neuroimaging for new-onset headaches in a client older than 50 years or when neurologic findings are present.
  • Report changes in headache intensity or new visual or neurologic disturbances.

Priority Moves

  • Maintain a cool, dark, quiet environment and elevate the head of the bed as desired.
  • Teach a headache diary to identify food, environment, hormone, sleep, stress, and medication triggers.
  • For cluster headache, high-flow oxygen at onset can provide rapid relief when prescribed.

Headache Care Map

Primary, Secondary, and Trigger Screening

Classify first

Start by sorting headache type and trigger pattern. The same screen points the learner toward secondary causes, medication overuse, lifestyle triggers, and teaching needs.

Primary Headaches

Primary headaches have no identifiable organic cause; migraine, tension-like, and cluster headaches fit this group.

Secondary Headaches

Secondary headaches are associated with an organic cause and warrant further medical management.

Common Triggers

Triggers include alcohol, allergies, intense odors, bright or flickering lights, medication overuse, fatigue, sleep deprivation, depression, anxiety, stress, hormone fluctuations, tyramine, MSG, nitrites, dairy, weather, and altitude changes.

Teaching Screen

Teach stress management, hand hygiene when cold-like symptoms are involved, safe use of over-the-counter medications, and provider review of herbal or supplement remedies.

Migraine Versus Cluster Pattern

Compare

Use the timing, associated findings, and behavior during pain to separate migraine patterns from cluster headache cycles.

Migraine With Aura

Prodrome can occur hours to days before pain; aura develops over minutes to an hour with neurologic or visual changes. Pain can become severe and throbbing with nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, or vertigo. Aura migraines often repeat the same manifestations each time.

Migraine Without Aura

Unilateral pulsating pain is aggravated by activity, often with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or vomiting, lasting 4 to 72 hr. Rest, low stimulation, and trigger avoidance matter.

Atypical Migraine

Status migrainous lasts longer than 72 hr; migrainous infarction includes persistent neurologic manifestations with possible ischemic findings on imaging. Duration and neurologic change raise urgency.

Cluster Headache

Intense unilateral nonthrobbing pain lasts 15 min to 3 hr and often occurs daily in cycles, with tearing, runny nose, nasal congestion, facial sweating, eyelid droop or edema, miosis, pallor/flushing, bradycardia, nausea, vomiting, and pacing or rocking. Spring/fall pattern and disrupted sleep-wake rhythm are high-yield cues.

Medication, Oxygen, and Comfort Teaching

Treat early

Medication teaching is anchored to timing: abort migraine early, prevent recurrent migraines when prescribed, and treat cluster headache at onset.

Abortive Timing

Abortive therapy is used during the aura or soon after headache onset; mild migraines can use NSAIDs, acetaminophen, or migraine-labeled anti-inflammatory combinations as prescribed.

Severe Migraine Options

Severe migraine therapy can include triptans, ergotamine preparations with caffeine, or other combination agents when prescribed.

Prevention

Preventive therapy can include NSAIDs with beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, beta-adrenergic blockers, antiepileptic medications, or onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine.

Pulse Checks

Teach pulse checks when beta-adrenergic blockers or calcium channel blockers are prescribed.

Cluster Oxygen

For cluster headache, oxygen at 12 L/min for 15 to 20 min at onset can relieve pain quickly; teach sitting position and home oxygen safety.

Comfort Strategies

Complementary strategies such as yoga, meditation, tai chi, exercise, biofeedback, massage, acupuncture, or acupressure can support relaxation and pain management.

1

Which food should a client with frequent migraine headaches avoid?

  • A. Baked salmon.
  • B. Salted cashews.

Which statement shows understanding of zolmitriptan teaching?

  • B. I should take it every day to prevent headaches.
  • C. I should expect facial flushing when I take it.
  • D. It will lower my sensitivity to food triggers.
C Zolmitriptan can cause facial flushing, tingling, and warmth.
A, B, D It constricts selected cranial blood vessels, is abortive rather than daily preventive therapy, and does not change food-trigger sensitivity.

Which findings are expected with cluster headaches? Select all that apply.

  • B. Altered sleep-wake cycle.
  • C. Headache approximately 1 to 8 times daily.
  • D. Dull, throbbing headache pain.
  • E. Nasal congestion and drainage.

Which discharge instruction should the nurse include for migraine headaches?

  • B. Increase physical activity during a headache.
  • C. Drink beverages with artificial sweeteners to prevent headaches.
  • D. Apply a cool cloth to the face during a headache.
D A cool cloth over the eyes or face can provide comfort and relieve pain.
A, B, C A quiet dark environment is preferred, activity can worsen pain, and artificial sweeteners can be a trigger.
5

Which question helps identify aura-type migraine headaches?

  • B. Is your headache accompanied by profuse facial sweating?
  • C. Does your headache occur on one side of your head?
  • D. Do you have the same manifestations each time the headache occurs?
D Aura-type migraines commonly have the same manifestations each time.
A, B, C Daily episodes and facial sweating fit cluster cues; unilateral pain can occur in cluster or common migraine and is less specific for aura.
