Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 20

Acute Respiratory Disorders

Acute respiratory disorders range from rhinitis and sinusitis to influenza and pneumonia, but the nursing priority stays steady: maintain airway patency, promote oxygenation, reduce transmission, and catch deterioration early.

TL;DR - Airway First, Infection Control Always

For acute respiratory disorders, prioritize airway clearance, oxygenation, hydration, rest, hand hygiene, cough etiquette, immunization, and cultures before antibiotics when pneumonia is suspected.

Upper Airway

  • Rhinitis causes rhinorrhea, congestion, sneezing, pruritus, watery eyes, sore throat, inflamed mucosa, and low-grade fever.
  • Sinusitis causes congestion, headache, facial pressure worse when leaning forward, cough, purulent or bloody drainage, and orbital/facial tenderness.
  • Decongestants can cause rebound congestion if used longer than 3 to 4 days.

Influenza and Pneumonia

  • Influenza prevention leans on yearly vaccination, hand hygiene, cough etiquette, and avoiding close contact during outbreaks.
  • Pneumonia in older adults can present vaguely, with confusion from hypoxia as a common manifestation.
  • For pneumonia, oxygen comes first when saturation is low, then sputum culture before antibiotics when possible.

Acute Respiratory Disorder Care Map

Risk, Rhinitis, and Sinusitis

Upper airway

Start with prevention and risk, then separate upper-airway symptom care from warning signs that suggest spread beyond the sinuses.

Prevention basics

Use hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, vaccination, allergen reduction, and smoking cessation to reduce acute respiratory disorders.

Risk cluster

Risk rises with very young or older age, lack of current influenza or pneumococcal immunization, tobacco smoke, substance use, chronic lung disease, immunocompromise, aspiration risk, immobility, impaired secretion clearance, and mechanical ventilation.

Rhinitis pattern

Rhinitis can be infectious or allergic and often overlaps with asthma or other allergy patterns.

Rhinitis care

Encourage 8 to 10 hr of rest, at least 2,000 mL/day of fluid if not contraindicated, humidification or steam, tissue disposal, and cough etiquette.

Rhinitis medications

Antihistamines, leukotriene inhibitors, mast cell stabilizers, decongestants, intranasal glucocorticoids, antipyretics, and antibiotics can be used depending on cause and symptoms.

Sinusitis care

Encourage steam, sinus irrigation, saline sprays, hot wet packs, fluids, rest, and correct nasal spray or irrigation technique.

Spread warning

Report severe headache, nuchal rigidity, or high fever because meningitis or encephalitis can occur if pathogens spread.

Influenza: Contagious Window and Prevention

Viral illness

Influenza care depends on timing: recognize the contagious window, start antivirals early when prescribed, and reinforce prevention habits.

Seasonal pattern

Seasonal influenza is highly contagious and commonly occurs in fall and winter.

Contagious window

Adults can transmit influenza from 24 hr before symptoms begin until about 5 days after onset.

Expected findings

Severe headache, muscle aches, chills, fatigue, weakness, fever, and cough can occur; severe diarrhea, cough, and hypoxia are emphasized for avian influenza patterns.

Hospital precautions

Use droplet and contact precautions for hospitalized clients with pandemic influenza.

Supportive monitoring

Monitor respiratory status, hydration, intake, and output; provide saline gargles and fluids as prescribed.

Antiviral timing

Begin prescribed antiviral therapy within 24 to 48 hr of symptom onset.

Prevention teaching

Teach annual influenza vaccination, hand hygiene, cough etiquette, increased fluids and rest if symptoms occur, and avoiding close contact or crowds during outbreaks.

Pneumonia: Assess, Culture, Oxygenate, Treat

Lower airway

For pneumonia, think in order: assess gas exchange, culture before antibiotics when possible, oxygenate, treat, and watch for complications.

Disease process

Pneumonia fills alveoli with inflammatory fluid or exudate and can be triggered by infection or aspiration.

Source pattern

Community-acquired pneumonia is common and can follow influenza; health care-associated pneumonia has higher mortality and can be more antibiotic-resistant.

Expected findings

Fever, chills, flushed face, diaphoresis, dyspnea, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, sputum, crackles, wheezes, cough, dull percussion, and low oxygen saturation can occur.

Older adult pattern

Older adults can have vague findings; confusion from hypoxia can be the most common manifestation.

Diagnostic monitoring

Obtain sputum culture before antibiotics when possible, and monitor CBC, ABGs, blood culture, electrolytes, chest x-ray, and pulse oximetry.

Airway support

Position in high-Fowler's unless contraindicated, encourage coughing or suctioning, administer oxygen, breathing treatments, and medications, and monitor skin under oxygen devices.

Recovery support

Encourage incentive spirometry, rest periods, nutrition, and 2 to 3 L/day of fluids if not contraindicated to thin secretions and support healing.

Antibiotic timing

Give antibiotics after cultures are obtained; monitor stool frequency and kidney function, especially in older adults receiving penicillins or cephalosporins.

Medication effects

Monitor bronchodilator and steroid effects, including albuterol tremor or tachycardia, ipratropium dry mouth or palpitations, theophylline toxicity, hyperglycemia, fluid retention, and poor wound healing.

Complications

Watch for atelectasis, bacteremia or sepsis, and ARDS when hypoxemia persists despite oxygen therapy.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Rhinitis

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse in a clinic is discussing health promotion and disease management with a client who has rhinitis.

Risk factors and findings

  • Risk factors include recent viral, bacterial, or influenza exposure; lack of current immunizations; allergens or environmental contaminants; tobacco smoke; substance use; foreign body; and immobility.
  • Expected findings include rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, purulent nasal drainage, sneezing, pruritus of the nose/throat/ears, watery eyes, sore dry throat, inflamed nasal mucosa, and low-grade fever.

Teaching and medications

  • Teach rest, increased fluids if not contraindicated, humidification or steamy air, tissue disposal, and cough etiquette.
  • Medication examples include brompheniramine/pseudoephedrine, cromolyn sodium, phenylephrine, and antipyretics as appropriate.

Application Exercises

1

Which clients are at increased risk for pneumonia? Select all that apply.

  • A. A client who has dysphagia.
  • B. A client who has AIDS.
  • C. A client vaccinated for pneumococcus and influenza 6 months ago.
  • D. A postoperative client who received local anesthesia.
  • E. A client with a closed head injury receiving mechanical ventilation.
  • F. A client who has myasthenia gravis.
A, B, E, F Dysphagia, immunocompromise, mechanical ventilation, and impaired secretion clearance or muscle weakness increase pneumonia risk.
C, D Recent vaccination lowers risk, and local anesthesia is not the same risk pattern as general anesthesia, immobility, or ventilation.
2

A client awakens disoriented and reports chills and pleuritic chest pain. Which action is the nurse's priority?

  • A. Obtain baseline vital signs and oxygen saturation.
  • B. Obtain a sputum culture.
  • C. Obtain a complete history.
  • D. Provide a pneumococcal vaccine.
A The first priority is assessment, including oxygenation, to determine immediate respiratory risk.
B, C, D Culture, history, and vaccination can matter, but the nurse first assesses current status and oxygenation.
3

A client with pneumonia has RR 30/min, HR 100/min, and SaO2 91% on room air. In what order should the nurse act?

  • A. Administer antibiotics.
  • B. Administer oxygen therapy.
  • C. Obtain a sputum culture.
  • D. Teach yearly influenza vaccination.
B, C, A, D Use ABCs first: oxygenate, obtain sputum culture before antibiotics, administer antibiotics, then provide prevention teaching.
Why not antibiotics first? A culture should be collected before antibiotics when possible, but oxygenation is the immediate priority.
4

Which assessment technique helps identify sinusitis manifestations?

  • A. Percussion of posterior lung lobes.
  • B. Auscultation of the trachea.
  • C. Inspection of the conjunctiva.
  • D. Palpation of the orbital areas.
D Sinusitis can cause tenderness over the orbital, frontal, and facial areas.
A, B, C These techniques fit other assessments, not the focused sinus tenderness check.
5

Which statement shows correct influenza teaching?

  • A. "I should wash my hands after blowing my nose to prevent spreading the virus."
  • B. "I should avoid drinking fluids if symptoms develop."
  • C. "I need a flu shot every 2 years."
  • D. "I should cover my mouth with my hand when I sneeze."
A Hand hygiene reduces transmission of influenza viruses.
B, C, D Fluids should increase if tolerated, influenza vaccination is yearly, and sneezing into the elbow/shoulder or tissue avoids contaminating hands.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

System Disorder and Medication: rhinitis, sinusitis, influenza, pneumonia, aspiration risk, atelectasis, ARDS, antiviral timing, decongestant rebound precautions, antibiotics after cultures, bronchodilator effects, and glucocorticoid monitoring. Worked AMS Templates will be linked after source-supported examples are built.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 21

Asthma

Asthma is intermittent, reversible airway obstruction driven by inflammation, hyperresponsiveness, bronchoconstriction, mucosal edema, and mucus production. The nurse's job is to read airflow decline early and match rescue versus prevention therapy.

TL;DR - Rescue Fast, Prevent Daily, Escalate Early

Asthma worsens when wheezing, retractions, tachycardia, low SaO2, or rising PaCO2 appear. Use short-acting beta2 agonists for rapid relief, anti-inflammatory therapy for prevention, peak flow zones for self-management, and prepare for intubation if respiratory failure or status asthmaticus develops.

Trigger Control

  • Promote smoking cessation, infection prevention, influenza/pneumonia vaccines, and protective masks or ventilation in dusty or particle-heavy environments.
  • Teach avoidance of cold air shifts, humidity changes, pollutants, strong odors, seasonal/perennial allergens, stress, aspirin/NSAIDs, beta-blockers, cholinergics, detergents, cleaners, sinusitis/postnasal drip, and viral infections when relevant.
  • Exercise is part of therapy, but some clients need premedication before activity.

Red Flags

  • Early ABGs can show low PaO2 with low PaCO2 from hyperventilation; later high PaCO2 signals fatigue and worsening ventilation.
  • Status asthmaticus is life-threatening and can be unresponsive to usual treatment.
  • For severe obstruction, prepare for emergency intubation and give prescribed IV fluids, oxygen, bronchodilators, epinephrine, and systemic steroids.

Asthma Care Map

Assess Severity and Identify Triggers

Airflow obstruction

Start by classifying symptom frequency, then connect triggers, age-related reserve, and assessment cues to the current severity.

Classification

Asthma is classified by symptom frequency: mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, or severe persistent.

Risk factors

Family history, smoking, secondhand smoke, environmental allergies, chemical irritants or dust, GERD, and age-related loss of pulmonary reserve increase risk.

Older adult risks

Older adults have decreased pulmonary reserve, more infection susceptibility, and reduced beta-adrenergic receptor sensitivity, which can blunt response to beta agonists.

Expected findings

Dyspnea, chest tightness, anxiety, coughing, wheezing, mucus production, accessory muscle use, prolonged exhalation, low SaO2, and increased chest diameter can occur.

History questions

Ask about onset, duration, triggers, medication changes, relief medications, other medications, and self-care used during current and prior exacerbations.

Declining status

Wheezing, sternal retractions, tachycardia, worsening oxygenation, and increased work of breathing show declining status.

Diagnostics and Acute Nursing Care

Priority response

Diagnostics clarify severity and treatment response, but acute care should reduce work of breathing while monitoring oxygenation closely.

ABGs

ABGs can show hypoxemia, hypocarbia early in an attack, and hypercarbia later in an attack.

Sputum culture

Sputum culture can identify infection when bacteria are present.

PFTs

PFTs are the most accurate test for diagnosing asthma and severity; FEV1 can drop below expected values, and improvement after bronchodilator therapy supports asthma diagnosis.

Chest x-ray

Chest x-ray can show structural changes over time.

Position and access

Position in high-Fowler's, administer prescribed oxygen and medications, and initiate or maintain IV access.

Monitoring

Monitor heart rhythm, respiratory effort, symmetry, SaO2, and lung sounds.

Anxiety and mobility

Stay calm and reassuring because anxiety can worsen air hunger. Provide rest periods and safe walking paths for older adults with dyspnea.

Infection prevention

Encourage prompt treatment of infections and appropriate immunizations.

Medication Logic: Rescue Versus Prevention

Pharmacology

Medication logic hinges on timing: rescue medications relieve acute obstruction, while prevention medications reduce inflammation and future attacks.

Short-acting beta2 agonists

Albuterol provides rapid relief for acute manifestations and can prevent exercise-induced asthma.

Anticholinergics

Ipratropium supports bronchodilation and decreases secretions; monitor dry mouth and heart rate.

Theophylline

Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range and is used only when other treatments are ineffective; monitor levels and toxicity signs such as tachycardia, nausea, and diarrhea.

Long-acting beta2 agonists

Salmeterol is for prevention, not rescue at attack onset.

Anti-inflammatory classes

Corticosteroids, leukotriene antagonists, mast cell stabilizers, and monoclonal antibodies decrease airway inflammation and are used for prophylaxis.

Adverse-effect watch

Monitor for decreased immune function, poor wound healing, hyperglycemia, fluid retention, weight gain, mouth or throat lesions, and anaphylaxis with omalizumab.

Prednisone teaching

Teach prednisone with food, hydration, black or tarry stool reporting, hand and mouth care, infection avoidance, and no abrupt discontinuation.

Inhaler order

If separate inhaled bronchodilator and anti-inflammatory agents are both prescribed at the same time, give the bronchodilator first to improve absorption of the anti-inflammatory medication.

Complications: Respiratory Failure and Status Asthmaticus

Escalation

Escalation focuses on persistent hypoxemia, rising ventilatory fatigue, and airway obstruction that no longer responds to usual treatment.

Respiratory failure risk

Persistent hypoxemia from asthma can progress to respiratory failure.

Failure monitoring

Monitor oxygenation and acid-base balance closely.

Ventilation escalation

Prepare for intubation and mechanical ventilation when ventilation or oxygenation cannot be maintained.

Status asthmaticus

Status asthmaticus is a life-threatening airway obstruction episode that can be unresponsive to common treatment.

Arrest warning cues

Extreme wheezing, labored breathing, accessory muscle use, distended neck veins, and risk for cardiac or respiratory arrest can occur.

Emergency treatment

Prepare for emergency intubation and administer prescribed IV fluids, oxygen, bronchodilators, epinephrine, and systemic steroids.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Prednisone for Asthma

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is caring for a client who has asthma and a prescription for prednisone.

Nursing interventions

  • Monitor for decreased immune function and delayed wound healing.
  • Monitor blood glucose for hyperglycemia.
  • Observe for fluid retention and weight gain.
  • Inspect the mouth and throat for aphthous lesions.

Client teaching

  • Take prednisone with food to reduce GI distress.
  • Report black, tarry stools.
  • Maintain hydration, hand hygiene, and mouth care.
  • Do not stop glucocorticoids suddenly without provider guidance.

Application Exercises

1

A client is having an acute asthma attack. Which findings indicate declining respiratory status? Select all that apply.

  • A. SaO2 95%.
  • B. Wheezing.
  • C. Retraction of sternal muscles.
  • D. Pink mucous membranes.
  • E. Tachycardia.
B, C, E Wheezing, sternal retractions, and tachycardia indicate airway narrowing, increased work of breathing, and decreased oxygenation.
A, D SaO2 95% and pink mucous membranes are expected findings, not signs of decline.
2

A client with asthma has SaO2 91%, audible wheezes, and accessory muscle use. Which class of medication should the nurse expect to administer?

  • A. Antibiotic.
  • B. Beta-blocker.
  • C. Antiviral.
  • D. Beta2 agonist.
D A beta2 agonist rapidly dilates bronchioles to relieve wheezing and open the airway.
A, B, C Antibiotics treat bacterial infection, antivirals treat viral infection, and beta-blockers can worsen bronchospasm risk.
3

Which statement by a client taking prednisone for asthma shows correct teaching?

  • A. "I will decrease my fluid intake while taking this medication."
  • B. "I will expect to have black, tarry stools."
  • C. "I will take my medication with meals."
  • D. "I will monitor for weight loss while taking this medication."
C Prednisone should be taken with food to reduce GI distress.
A, B, D Fluids are encouraged if not contraindicated, black/tarry stools should be reported, and fluid retention/weight gain can occur.
4

Which factor should the nurse identify as an asthma risk factor?

  • A. Sex.
  • B. Environmental allergies.
  • C. Alcohol use.
  • D. History of diabetes.
B Environmental allergies are associated with asthma and can coexist with allergic rhinitis or skin manifestations.
A, C, D Sex, alcohol use, and diabetes history are not listed asthma risk factors in this ATI source section.
5

Which client statement shows correct understanding of a bronchodilator?

  • A. "This medication can decrease my immune response."
  • B. "I take this medication to prevent asthma attacks."
  • C. "I need to take this medication with food."
  • D. "This medication has a slow onset to treat my symptoms."
B Bronchodilators can prevent attacks and rapidly relieve bronchospasm depending on the agent.
A, C, D Decreased immune response and food-with-dose teaching fit anti-inflammatory agents; bronchodilators have a fast onset for acute manifestations.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 22

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

COPD is irreversible airflow limitation from emphysema, chronic bronchitis, or both. Care centers on controlled oxygen, secretion clearance, nutrition, breathing techniques, medication safety, infection prevention, and support for long-term lifestyle change.

TL;DR - Clear Secretions, Controlled Oxygen, Conserve Energy

COPD clients need high-Fowler's positioning, effective coughing or suctioning, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, prescribed oxygen usually targeting 88% to 92%, high-calorie nutrition, fluids to thin secretions, pursed-lip breathing, and infection prevention.

Recognize COPD

  • Emphysema destroys alveoli, reduces gas-exchange surface area, traps air, and causes CO2 retention and respiratory acidosis.
  • Chronic bronchitis is chronic bronchial and bronchiolar inflammation from long-term irritant exposure.
  • Smoking is the primary risk factor; also assess age, AAT deficiency, and environmental pollution exposure.

Prevent Deterioration

  • Administer oxygen as prescribed and monitor closely; clients with chronic CO2 retention can require lower-flow oxygen.
  • Teach pursed-lip breathing: breathe in through the nose and exhale slowly through pursed lips without puffing the cheeks.
  • Report infection concerns early and maintain influenza and pneumonia immunizations.

COPD Care Map

Pathophysiology, Risk, and Findings

Irreversible obstruction

Start by separating the chronic obstruction pattern from the assessment cues. COPD affects ventilation, gas exchange, nutrition demand, and long-term perfusion.

COPD pattern

COPD includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis; most clients with emphysema also have chronic bronchitis.

Emphysema

Emphysema causes loss of elasticity, hyperinflation, alveolar destruction, decreased gas-exchange surface area, CO2 retention, and respiratory acidosis.

Chronic bronchitis

Chronic bronchitis is inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles from chronic irritant exposure.

Age pattern

COPD usually affects middle-age to older adults.

Common findings

Chronic dyspnea, exertional dyspnea, productive morning cough, hypoxemia, crackles, wheezes, rapid shallow respirations, accessory muscle use, irregular breathing, and decreased oxygen saturation can occur.

Emphysema clues

Barrel chest, hyperresonance from trapped air, thin extremities, and enlarged neck muscles can appear.

Late cues

Late or advanced findings include clubbing, pallor or cyanosis, and dependent edema from right-sided heart failure.

Exacerbation cue

During acute exacerbations, respiratory rate can reach 40 to 50/min.

Diagnostics and Core Nursing Care

Controlled support

Diagnostics trend chronic hypoxemia and airflow limitation, while nursing care supports ventilation without overshooting oxygen goals.

Hematocrit

Increased hematocrit can reflect chronic low oxygenation.

Infection workup

Sputum cultures and WBC counts help diagnose acute respiratory infection.

ABGs

ABGs can show hypoxemia and hypercarbia.

PFTs

PFTs classify COPD severity with FEV/FVC comparisons; as COPD advances, the ratio decreases.

Imaging and AAT

Chest x-ray can show hyperinflation and flattened diaphragm in late emphysema, and AAT levels assess for deficiency.

Airway support

Position in high-Fowler's, encourage effective coughing or suction, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, and medication or breathing treatments.

Oxygen target

Administer oxygen as prescribed; in many COPD cases, maintain oxygen saturation between 88% and 92%. Monitor skin under oxygen devices.

Nutrition and conditioning

Promote nutrition because work of breathing raises caloric demand; encourage soft, high-calorie foods, rest, hydration to thin secretions if not contraindicated, and self-paced walking with stops for dyspnea.

Breathing Techniques and Medication Safety

Self-management

Self-management blends breathing techniques, secretion clearance, and medication-specific monitoring.

Diaphragmatic breathing

Lie supine with knees bent, place a hand over the abdomen for resistance, and verify the hand rises and falls with breathing.

Pursed-lip breathing

Form lips as if whistling, inhale through the nose, exhale slowly through pursed lips, and do not puff the cheeks.

Secretion and expansion tools

Positive expiratory pressure devices help loosen secretions by vibration during exhalation. Incentive spirometry promotes lung expansion: seal lips around the mouthpiece, inhale deeply, and hold for 3 to 5 seconds.

Albuterol

Albuterol gives rapid bronchodilation; monitor tremors and tachycardia.

Ipratropium

Ipratropium decreases pulmonary secretions and helps prevent bronchospasm; monitor dry mouth, heart rate, palpitations, headache, and blurred vision.

Theophylline

Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range; monitor levels and toxicity signs such as tachycardia, nausea, and diarrhea.

Anti-inflammatory agents

Corticosteroids and other anti-inflammatory agents decrease airway inflammation; monitor immune function, wound healing, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, fluid retention, weight gain, mouth lesions, and black or tarry stools.

Mucolytics

Mucolytics help thin secretions and include nebulized and oral options.

Complications and Discharge Teaching

Long-term care

Long-term COPD care watches for infection and cor pulmonale while teaching the routines that protect breathing capacity at home.

Respiratory infection

Respiratory infection can occur from increased mucus and poor oxygenation; monitor oxygenation, WBC, CRP, SaO2, temperature, and infection symptoms.

Cor pulmonale

Cor pulmonale occurs when air trapping, airway collapse, and stiff alveoli increase pulmonary pressure and right-sided workload.

Right-sided findings

Manifestations include low oxygenation, cyanosis, enlarged tender liver, distended neck veins, and dependent edema.

Complication monitoring

Monitor respiratory status, GI disturbances, heart rate and rhythm, and fluid balance; administer oxygen and prescribed medications.

Daily teaching

Eat high-calorie foods, rest as needed, practice hand hygiene, take inhaled and oral medications as prescribed, and stop smoking if needed.

Prevention and oxygen safety

Obtain influenza and pneumonia immunizations, use oxygen as prescribed, and keep others from smoking near oxygen because of flammability.

When to report

Report unusual findings or infection concerns early. Portable oxygen and home services can support independence rather than confine the client to the house.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Ipratropium for COPD

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is reviewing discharge instructions for a client who has a new prescription for ipratropium.

Nursing interventions

  • Observe for dry mouth while taking ipratropium.
  • Monitor heart rate because palpitations can indicate toxicity.
  • Assess for headache or blurred vision and reinforce reporting these findings.

Client teaching

  • Suck on hard candies to moisten dry mouth.
  • Increase fluid intake if not contraindicated.
  • Use the medication as prescribed to prevent bronchospasm and support bronchodilation.

Application Exercises

1

Which statement by a client with COPD taking albuterol shows correct teaching?

  • A. "This medication can increase my blood sugar levels."
  • B. "This medication can decrease my immune response."
  • C. "I can have an increase in my heart rate while taking this medication."
  • D. "I can have mouth sores while taking this medication."
C Albuterol is a bronchodilator and can cause tachycardia.
A, B, D Hyperglycemia, decreased immune response, and mouth sores are more associated with anti-inflammatory agents such as corticosteroids.
2

Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for after an initial prednisone dose for COPD? Select all that apply.

  • A. Hypokalemia.
  • B. Tachycardia.
  • C. Fluid retention.
  • D. Nausea.
  • E. Black, tarry stools.
A, C, E Prednisone can cause hypokalemia, fluid retention, and GI bleeding signs such as black/tarry stools.
B, D Tachycardia and nausea are more closely tied to bronchodilator adverse effects in this source comparison.
3

A client with COPD is anxious about continuous oxygen limiting the ability to leave home. Which response should the nurse make?

  • A. "There are portable oxygen delivery systems that you can take with you."
  • B. "You can remove the oxygen while you are out and reapply it at home."
  • C. "You probably will not be able to go out as much as before."
  • D. "Home health services will come to you so you will not need to go out."
A Portable oxygen systems support mobility and help reduce anxiety about leaving home.
B, C, D Oxygen should be used as prescribed, and teaching should support independence with rest periods rather than unnecessarily limiting activity.
4

Which statement shows correct incentive spirometer teaching?

  • A. "I will place the adapter on my finger to read my oxygen level."
  • B. "I will lie on my back with my knees bent."
  • C. "I will rest my hand over my abdomen to create resistance."
  • D. "I will take in a deep breath and hold it before exhaling."
D Incentive spirometry requires a tight seal, deep inhalation, and a brief breath hold to promote lung expansion.
A, B, C Finger adapter describes pulse oximetry, and the supine/knee-bent hand-on-abdomen instructions describe diaphragmatic breathing.
5

Which instruction should the nurse include when teaching pursed-lip breathing?

  • A. "Take quick breaths when inhaling."
  • B. "Place your hand over your stomach."
  • C. "Take a deep breath in through your nose."
  • D. "Puff your cheeks when exhaling."
C Pursed-lip breathing starts with a slow, deep inhalation through the nose and a controlled exhalation through pursed lips.
A, B, D Breaths should be slow and deep, hand-on-abdomen belongs to diaphragmatic breathing, and cheek puffing decreases effective exhalation.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 23

Tuberculosis

Tuberculosis is an airborne infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It can remain latent for years, become active when host defenses weaken, and requires strict transmission control plus long-course combination therapy.

TL;DR - Airborne Isolation, Multi-Drug Therapy, Full Course

Think TB when a client has prolonged cough, weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, or risk exposure. Use airborne precautions in care settings, collect early-morning sputum specimens, teach medication adherence for months, and monitor for hepatotoxicity, neurotoxicity, vision changes, and resistant disease.

Transmission Control

  • TB spreads through airborne particles and needs a negative-airflow room in the hospital.
  • Wear an N95 or powered air-purifying respirator when caring for a hospitalized client with TB.
  • If transport is required, place a surgical mask on the client and use the shortest, least busy route.

Therapy Logic

  • Treatment typically starts with multiple antitubercular medications to reduce resistance.
  • Sputum cultures every 2 to 4 weeks help show treatment response.
  • Clients are no longer considered infectious after three consecutive negative sputum cultures.

Tuberculosis Care Map

Transmission, Latency, and Screening

Airborne infection

Start by separating exposure, latency, active disease, and public-health follow-through. TB can stay contained for years, then become active or spread beyond the lungs.

Tubercle formation

After inhalation, the body can wall off the TB organism in the lung, producing a tubercle visible on imaging.

Latent infection

Only some exposed clients develop active disease; latent infection can remain dormant for years.

Spread pattern

TB primarily affects the lungs but can spread through the blood to other organs.

Infectiousness trend

Transmission risk decreases after 2 to 3 weeks of effective antitubercular therapy.

Who to screen

Screen close contacts, family members, high-risk communities, clients born outside the United States, migrant workers, and clients living in high-risk areas.

When to suspect TB

Consider TB with persistent cough, chest pain, weakness, weight loss, anorexia, hemoptysis, dyspnea, fever, night sweats, or chills.

Public-health priority

Completion of treatment is a public-health priority because incomplete therapy promotes resistant TB.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Detect active versus latent

Use risk and symptom duration to suspect TB, then diagnostics help separate latent infection from active disease and drug resistance.

Risk cluster

Risk increases with close contact with untreated TB, homelessness or low socioeconomic status, crowded or poorly ventilated housing, advanced age, recent endemic travel, immigration from higher-incidence areas, substance use, immunocompromise, and high-risk health care activities.

Expected findings

Cough lasting longer than 3 weeks, purulent or blood-streaked sputum, fatigue, lethargy, weight loss, anorexia, afternoon low-grade fever, and night sweats can occur.

Older adult pattern

Older adults can show atypical findings such as altered mentation, behavior change, fever, anorexia, and weight loss.

NAAT

Nucleic acid amplification testing detects TB organisms in respiratory secretions and can screen for rifampin resistance quickly.

QuantiFERON-TB Gold

QuantiFERON-TB Gold supports diagnosis of latent or active infection and is useful when Mantoux results might be unreliable.

Smear and culture

Acid-fast bacilli smear suggests active infection, but culture confirms Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Sputum collection

Collect three early-morning sputum specimens using PPE and negative-airflow precautions.

Mantoux reading

Mantoux testing is read in 48 to 72 hr; induration thresholds vary by immune status, and a positive result does not by itself confirm active disease.

Nursing Care and Precautions

Protect others

Care focuses on oxygenation, airborne containment, medication adherence, and support systems that help the client finish therapy.

Oxygen support

Administer heated, humidified oxygen as prescribed.

Airborne precautions

Implement airborne precautions and place the hospitalized client in a negative-airflow room.

Respirator and barriers

Use an N95 or powered air-purifying respirator; add barrier protection if hands or clothing can be contaminated.

Cough hygiene

Teach coughing and sputum expectoration into tissues that the client disposes into bags or no-touch receptacles.

Medication adherence

Administer prescribed medications exactly as ordered.

Nutrition support

Promote adequate fluids and calories and encourage protein, iron, vitamin C, and B-vitamin intake.

Access support

Arrange social services or community clinic follow-up if medication access or monitoring is at risk.

Antitubercular Medication Safety

Resistance prevention

Medication safety centers on combination therapy, full-course completion, liver monitoring, vision checks, and resistance prevention.

Initial combination

A common initial regimen combines isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

Completion teaching

Teach that medications are not interchangeable and the full prescribed course must be completed.

Isoniazid

Isoniazid is taken on an empty stomach; monitor liver function and signs of hepatotoxicity or peripheral neurotoxicity. Pyridoxine can be prescribed to reduce neurotoxicity risk.

Rifampin

Rifampin can turn urine and other secretions orange and can reduce oral contraceptive effectiveness.

Pyrazinamide

Pyrazinamide can cause hepatotoxicity and joint problems; monitor liver enzymes and teach fluids if not contraindicated.

Ethambutol

Ethambutol requires baseline and ongoing visual acuity and color discrimination checks; report vision changes immediately.

Streptomycin and alcohol

Streptomycin is reserved for multidrug-resistant TB because of toxicity risk; monitor hearing and renal status. Avoid alcohol with hepatotoxic TB medications.

Home Teaching and Complications

Follow-through

Home management is common, but it only works when exposure follow-up, infection-control habits, sputum monitoring, and complication awareness stay consistent.

Family exposure

TB is often managed at home; family members have usually already been exposed, but they still need testing.

Full duration

Continue therapy for the full prescribed duration, which can extend longer for multidrug-resistant disease.

Home infection control

Use hand hygiene, cover coughs and sneezes, dispose contaminated tissues in plastic bags, and wear a mask in public while active TB is infectious.

Noninfectious benchmark

Continue follow-up and sputum monitoring until three consecutive negative cultures confirm noninfectious status.

Miliary TB

Miliary TB occurs when the organism enters the bloodstream and spreads to multiple organs.

Neurologic warning

Possible complications include life-threatening neurologic findings such as headache, neck stiffness, and drowsiness.

Pericarditis warning

Pericarditis can cause dyspnea, neck vein distention, pleuritic pain, and hypotension from impaired cardiac filling. Treatment follows the same core approach as pulmonary TB.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Tuberculosis

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is caring for a client who has tuberculosis and is completing a system disorder template.

Pathophysiology

  • TB is an airborne infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • The organism can be contained in lung tissue, lie dormant, later become active, and spread outside the lungs through the blood.

Nursing care and complication

  • Administer humidified oxygen, prescribed medications, and nutrition support.
  • Prevent spread with airborne precautions, negative-airflow placement, N95 or powered respirator use, and masked transport if needed.
  • Teach safe tissue disposal and cough hygiene.
  • Monitor for miliary TB, including neurologic findings or pericarditis manifestations.

Application Exercises

1

A home health nurse is reinforcing teaching for a client with active TB who takes isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Which statements show understanding? Select all that apply.

  • A. "If I run out of one medication, I can substitute another TB medication."
  • B. "I will wash my hands each time I cough."
  • C. "I will wear a mask when I am in a public area."
  • D. "I will not need more sputum samples after medication starts."
  • E. "I can return to crowded public settings as soon as I start therapy."
B, C Hand hygiene and masking in public reduce airborne transmission while active TB remains infectious.
A, D, E TB medications are not interchangeable, sputum cultures continue every 2 to 4 weeks, and crowded settings should still be avoided while the client is infectious.
2

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client receiving TB treatment?

  • A. "The medication regimen is usually finished in 4 months."
  • B. "Sputum samples are needed every 2 to 4 weeks to monitor response."
  • C. "You will need to stay hospitalized for the entire treatment course."
  • D. "You must wear a mask at all times, including at home alone."
B Ongoing sputum cultures help monitor therapy and infectious status.
A, C, D TB therapy usually lasts many months, is often managed at home, and masking is focused on public exposure or contact while active disease is infectious.
3

A client begins ethambutol for TB. Which instruction is most important?

  • A. "Expect urine and body secretions to look orange."
  • B. "Take pyridoxine each day to prevent tingling."
  • C. "Report any change in vision immediately."
  • D. "Take this medication only after a large meal."
C Ethambutol can cause ocular toxicity, so vision changes require immediate reporting.
A, B, D Orange secretions are linked to rifampin, pyridoxine is paired with isoniazid, and the source does not identify a required large-meal instruction for ethambutol.
4

A client who is newly prescribed isoniazid asks what adverse finding to report. Which response should the nurse give?

  • A. "Orange urine is expected with this medication."
  • B. "Painful joints are the priority adverse effect."
  • C. "Report tingling in your hands or feet."
  • D. "Vision changes are the expected dose-limiting effect."
C Isoniazid can cause peripheral neurotoxicity; pyridoxine is often used to reduce this risk.
A, B, D Orange secretions are associated with rifampin, joint problems with pyrazinamide or rifampin teaching, and vision changes with ethambutol.
5

Which manifestations should the nurse include when teaching a community group about TB? Select all that apply.

  • A. Persistent cough.
  • B. Weight gain.
  • C. Fatigue.
  • D. Night sweats.
  • E. Purulent sputum.
A, C, D, E TB commonly causes persistent cough, fatigue, night sweats, and purulent or blood-streaked sputum.
B Weight loss and anorexia, not weight gain, are expected TB findings.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

System Disorder and Medication: tuberculosis, latent TB, active TB, airborne precautions, Mantoux testing, sputum culture collection, isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin, miliary TB, and TB home teaching. Worked AMS Templates will be linked after source-supported examples are built.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 24

Pulmonary Embolism

Pulmonary embolism is a medical emergency caused by a solid, gas, or liquid blockage in the pulmonary vasculature. Rapid oxygenation, clot control, diagnostic confirmation, and bleeding surveillance drive safe care.

TL;DR - Oxygen First, Control Clots, Watch Bleeding

PE can present with sudden chest pressure, dyspnea, air hunger, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, low oxygen saturation, pleural friction rub, petechiae, or anxiety. Prioritize oxygen and high-Fowler's positioning, maintain IV access, prepare anticoagulant or thrombolytic therapy, and monitor closely for hemorrhage.

Risk Control

  • Prevent DVT with mobility, leg exercises, compression stockings, hydration, and avoidance of prolonged sitting.
  • Risk increases with immobility, obesity, tobacco use, estrogen therapy, pregnancy, orthopedic surgery, central lines, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, long-bone fracture, cancer, trauma, septicemia, and advanced age.
  • Older adults can decompensate quickly because pulmonary reserve is lower.

Priority Response

  • Use ABC priority: oxygenation comes before diagnostics or anticoagulants when acute dyspnea is present.
  • MDCTA is the criterion standard when available; V/Q scan can be used when contrast is contraindicated.
  • Anticoagulants prevent clot extension; thrombolytics dissolve clot but carry major bleeding risk.

Pulmonary Embolism Care Map

Risk and Presentation

Medical emergency

Start by recognizing what is blocking pulmonary blood flow, then match the sudden respiratory and perfusion cues to the emergency pattern.

Most common source

Most pulmonary emboli originate from venous thromboembolism.

Other emboli

Fat, air, infection-related thrombus, amniotic fluid, tumor, bone marrow, or foreign material can also obstruct pulmonary circulation.

Perfusion effect

A large embolus impairs pulmonary blood flow and worsens tissue hypoxia.

Subjective cues

Anxiety, impending doom, sudden chest pressure, inspiratory pain, chest wall tenderness, dyspnea, air hunger, cough, and hemoptysis can occur.

Physical cues

Pleurisy, pleural friction rub, tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, crackles, S3/S4, diaphoresis, low-grade fever, low SaO2, cyanosis, petechiae over the chest or axillae, distended neck veins, and syncope can appear.

Diagnostics and Priority Nursing Care

Oxygenation first

Oxygenation comes first. Diagnostics clarify the clot burden, but bedside care should stabilize breathing and perfusion while the workup proceeds.

ABG trend

Early ABGs can show low PaCO2 from hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis; worsening hypoxemia can progress to respiratory and metabolic acidosis.

D-dimer

D-dimer rises when clot formation and fibrin breakdown are present.

Imaging map

MDCTA is the criterion standard when available. V/Q scanning can detect PE when contrast allergy limits imaging, pulmonary angiography can detect PE when MDCTA is unavailable but is invasive and higher risk than V/Q scanning, and chest x-ray can support the picture with findings such as diaphragm elevation or pleural effusion.

Ventilation support

Administer oxygen and position in high-Fowler's to maximize ventilation.

Access and medication

Initiate and maintain IV access and administer prescribed medications.

Respiratory assessment

Assess respiratory status at least every 30 min, including lung sounds, respiratory rate, rhythm, ease, skin color, capillary refill, and tracheal position.

Cardiac and neuro cues

Compare arm blood pressures, palpate pulse quality, monitor for dysrhythmias, inspect for petechiae, check for neck vein distention, provide emotional support, and monitor level of consciousness and mental status.

Medication and Procedure Safety

Clot control

Medication and procedure questions usually test one pairing: clot control must be balanced with bleeding surveillance and postprocedure monitoring.

Anticoagulants

Heparin, enoxaparin, and warfarin help prevent the existing clot from enlarging and reduce new clot formation.

Lab surveillance

Monitor PT/INR for warfarin, aPTT for heparin, CBC, and signs of thrombocytopenia, anemia, or hemorrhage.

Direct oral agents

Direct factor Xa inhibitors such as rivaroxaban, apixaban, and fondaparinux require bleeding surveillance. Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor; assess for bleeding and blood loss.

Thrombolytics

Alteplase, reteplase, and tenecteplase dissolve clots but are contraindicated with high bleeding-risk conditions such as active bleeding, recent surgery or trauma, uncontrolled hypertension, pregnancy, history of stroke, or peptic ulcer disease.

Consults and removal

Consult cardiology, pulmonary, respiratory, and radiology services as indicated. Embolectomy surgically removes an embolus; prepare with NPO status and informed consent.

Filter and postprocedure checks

A vena cava filter can prevent additional emboli from reaching the pulmonary vasculature. After invasive procedures, monitor vital signs, SaO2, incision drainage, and pain.

Prevention, Teaching, and Complications

Bleeding watch

Teaching targets recurrence prevention, while complication surveillance focuses on falling cardiac output and bleeding from clot-control therapy.

Daily prevention

Encourage smoking cessation, walking, physical activity, compression stockings, avoiding leg crossing, and avoiding prolonged immobility.

Travel prevention

During travel, stand or walk about 5 min each hour, remain hydrated, wear support stockings, and perform ankle pump exercises.

Warfarin and bleeding teaching

Keep vitamin K intake consistent, follow PT/INR monitoring instructions, expect regular blood draws, use soft toothbrushes and electric razors, perform daily skin and mouth checks, and avoid aspirin products unless prescribed.

Decreased cardiac output

Hypotension, tachycardia, cyanosis, neck vein distention, syncope, S3/S4, low urine output, and dysrhythmias can occur.

Perfusion support

Maintain IV access, monitor urine output, ECG, and pulmonary pressures, and administer prescribed fluids, inotropes, or vasodilators.

Hemorrhage watch

Assess injection and surgical sites, CBC, PT/aPTT/INR, stool, urine, emesis, abdominal girth, and abdominal or flank pain. Keep the appropriate reversal agent available when ordered or required by facility protocol.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Pulmonary Embolism

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is caring for a client who has a pulmonary embolism and is completing a system disorder template.

Pathophysiology and care

  • A PE occurs when a substance enters venous circulation and blocks pulmonary blood flow; DVT is the most common source.
  • Administer oxygen as prescribed and place the client in high-Fowler's.
  • Maintain IV access, administer prescribed medications, provide emotional support, and monitor mental status.

Medication examples

  • Anticoagulants: enoxaparin, heparin, and warfarin.
  • Thrombolytics: alteplase, reteplase, and tenecteplase.
  • Monitor closely for bleeding with either medication class.

Application Exercises

1

Which clients are at increased risk for pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.

  • A. A client with a BMI of 30.
  • B. A postmenopausal client not receiving estrogen therapy.
  • C. A client with a fractured femur.
  • D. A marathon runner with no other risk factors.
  • E. A client with chronic atrial fibrillation.
A, C, E Obesity, long-bone fracture, and turbulent cardiac flow such as atrial fibrillation increase clot or embolus risk.
B, D Decreased estrogen after menopause alone is not the risk factor identified here, and regular running generally supports circulation.
2

Which assessment findings should the nurse expect with pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.

  • A. Bradypnea.
  • B. Pleural friction rub.
  • C. Hypertension.
  • D. Petechiae.
  • E. Tachycardia.
B, D, E Pleural friction rub, petechiae, and tachycardia are expected PE findings.
A, C PE is associated with tachypnea and hypotension rather than bradypnea and hypertension.
3

A client has acute dyspnea, diaphoresis, anxiety, heart rate 117/min, respirations 38/min, temperature 38.4 C (101.2 F), and blood pressure 100/54 mm Hg. Which action is priority?

  • A. Notify the provider.
  • B. Start prescribed IV heparin.
  • C. Administer oxygen therapy.
  • D. Prepare the client for CT scanning.
C Using ABC priority, oxygenation is the first action for acute respiratory distress.
A, B, D Notification, anticoagulation, and imaging are important, but oxygenation is the immediate priority.
4

A client with PE has a new heparin prescription. Which client statement needs immediate follow-up before therapy starts?

  • A. "I am allergic to morphine."
  • B. "I take antacids several times a day for my ulcer."
  • C. "I had a clot in my leg several years ago."
  • D. "It hurts when I take a deep breath."
B Peptic ulcer disease increases bleeding concern with heparin and should be reported before therapy.
A, C, D These findings matter to the plan of care, but they are not the immediate anticoagulation safety concern.
5

Which finding is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy for PE?

  • A. Hip arthroplasty 2 weeks ago.
  • B. Elevated sedimentation rate.
  • C. Exercise-induced asthma 1 week ago.
  • D. Elevated platelet count.
A Recent major surgery creates a high hemorrhage risk and is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy.
B, C, D These are not the thrombolytic contraindications emphasized by the PE source.

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 25

Pneumothorax, Hemothorax, and Flail Chest

Pneumothorax, hemothorax, and flail chest are respiratory emergencies that reduce lung expansion and gas exchange. The nurse watches for distress, supports oxygenation, prepares for decompression or chest tube therapy, and prevents respiratory failure.

TL;DR - Re-Expand the Lung, Relieve Pressure, Watch the Tube

Chest trauma and pleural-space air or blood can rapidly impair ventilation. Prioritize oxygenation, recognize tension signs such as tracheal deviation and worsening distress, prepare for needle decompression or chest tube insertion when indicated, and monitor drainage, pain, oxygenation, and infection signs.

Spot the Emergency

  • Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space causing lung collapse.
  • Hemothorax is blood in the pleural space.
  • Tension pneumothorax traps air under pressure, compresses lung and heart structures, reduces venous return, and can be fatal without rapid treatment.

Do First

  • Administer oxygen and position to maximize ventilation.
  • Prepare emergency decompression for a spontaneous or tension pneumothorax when respiratory function is threatened.
  • After chest tube placement, monitor drainage, system function, dressing, vital signs, SaO2, ABGs, CBC, and chest x-ray results.

Pleural Injury Care Map

Pathophysiology and Assessment

Pleural space emergency

Start by sorting the pleural-space problem, then match the assessment cues to the amount of lung collapse, blood loss, or chest wall instability.

Pneumothorax

Air or gas in the pleural space collapses lung tissue.

Tension pneumothorax

Air enters during inspiration and cannot escape on expiration, increasing pleural pressure and shifting mediastinal structures.

Hemothorax

Blood accumulates in the pleural space.

Spontaneous pneumothorax

A small bleb can rupture without trauma.

Flail chest

At least two neighboring ribs sustain multiple fractures, creating unstable chest wall movement and impaired expansion.

Risk cluster

Blunt or penetrating chest trauma, a closed or occluded chest tube, older adult pulmonary reserve loss, and COPD increase risk.

General distress

Expected findings include anxiety, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, cyanosis, dyspnea, and accessory muscle use.

Pneumothorax clues

Reduced or absent breath sounds, asymmetrical movement, hyperresonance, subcutaneous emphysema, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side can occur if tension develops.

Hemothorax clue

Dull percussion can be heard over the affected side.

Diagnostics and Initial Nursing Care

Stabilize breathing

Stabilize ventilation while diagnostics confirm the pleural injury and trend the client's response to treatment.

ABGs

ABGs can show hypoxemia when PaO2 is less than expected.

Chest x-ray

Chest x-ray confirms pneumothorax or hemothorax.

Thoracentesis role

Thoracentesis can help confirm hemothorax; ensure consent, position the client at the bedside, transport specimens, and monitor vital signs, SaO2, and the insertion site.

Thoracentesis teaching

Teach the client to remain still and avoid moving, coughing, or deep breathing during the procedure.

Priority positioning

Administer oxygen therapy and position in high-Fowler's to maximize ventilation.

Ongoing monitoring

Auscultate heart and lung sounds, monitor vital signs every 4 hr or more often when unstable, check ABGs, SaO2, CBC, and chest x-ray results, monitor chest tube drainage, administer prescribed medications, and provide emotional support.

Medication and Chest Tube Safety

Pain and tube management

Pair pain and anxiety control with respiratory surveillance, then use chest tube checks to confirm the pleural space is decompressing safely.

Benzodiazepines

Lorazepam or midazolam can decrease anxiety, but monitor for hypotension, respiratory distress, amnesia, and paradoxical effects.

Opioids

Morphine and fentanyl treat moderate to severe pain but can cause respiratory depression, sedation, euphoria, hypotension, bradypnea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, and fluid retention.

Opioid hold cue

Use opioids cautiously for clients who have asthma or emphysema. If respirations are 12/min or less in a client receiving opioids, stop the medication and notify the provider immediately.

Chest tube purpose

Chest tubes drain air, fluid, or blood, re-establish negative pressure, support lung expansion, and restore intrapleural pressure.

Before insertion

Obtain consent, gather supplies, monitor status, and administer pain medication.

After insertion and teaching

Monitor vital signs, SaO2, drainage, tube placement, drainage system function, and dressing. Teach deep breathing, coughing, incentive spirometry, rest periods, hand hygiene, vaccinations, smoking cessation if applicable, and follow-up for fever, cough, breathing difficulty, sharp chest pain, or upper respiratory infection.

Flail Chest

Paradoxical movement

Recognize paradoxical movement quickly, then support gas exchange while pain control and ventilation needs are addressed.

Mechanism

Multiple rib fractures from blunt trauma or CPR can create a free-floating chest wall segment.

Movement pattern

The affected segment moves inward with inspiration and outward with expiration.

Expected findings

Unequal chest expansion, paradoxical chest movement, tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnea, cyanosis, anxiety, and chest pain can occur.

Monitor oxygenation

Administer humidified oxygen, monitor vital signs and SaO2, review pulmonary function findings, serial chest x-rays, and ABGs, and assess lung sounds, color, and capillary refill.

Promote expansion

Use positioning and deep breathing to promote expansion.

Severe injury support

Mechanical ventilation can be required, often using positive pressure to stabilize the flail segment. Administer pain medication, prescribed IV fluids, and suction the trachea or endotracheal tube as needed.

Complications

Perfusion and ventilation

Complications cluster around impaired perfusion and impaired ventilation, so the warning signs should be checked together.

Decreased cardiac output

Rising intrathoracic pressure can reduce the amount of blood pumped by the heart, and hypotension can develop as cardiac output falls.

Perfusion response

Administer prescribed IV fluids or blood products, monitor heart rate and rhythm, and monitor intake/output including chest tube drainage.

Respiratory failure

Lung collapse can produce inadequate gas exchange. Prepare for mechanical ventilation if oxygenation or ventilation cannot be maintained, continue frequent respiratory assessment, and escalate new distress quickly.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Hemothorax

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is teaching a newly licensed nurse about care for a client who has a hemothorax.

Description and nursing care

  • Hemothorax is blood accumulation in the pleural space.
  • Administer oxygen therapy and position in high-Fowler's.
  • Monitor ABGs, SaO2, CBC, chest x-ray findings, heart and lung sounds, vital signs, and chest tube drainage.
  • Document ventilator settings hourly if the client is ventilated.
  • Provide emotional support and encourage prompt care for infection manifestations.

Medication examples

  • Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam or midazolam can reduce anxiety.
  • Opioid agonists such as morphine sulfate or fentanyl can treat moderate to severe pain.
  • Monitor respiratory status closely when sedatives or opioids are used.

Application Exercises

1

A nurse assesses a client after a gunshot wound to the chest. Which findings should the nurse monitor for to detect pneumothorax? Select all that apply.

  • A. Tachypnea.
  • B. Tracheal deviation.
  • C. Bradycardia.
  • D. Decreased accessory muscle use.
  • E. Pleuritic pain.
A, B, E Pneumothorax can cause tachypnea, tracheal deviation as pressure rises, and pleuritic pain.
C, D Tachycardia and increased accessory muscle use are more consistent with respiratory distress from pneumothorax.
2

A client develops a spontaneous pneumothorax with respiratory compromise. Which action should the nurse perform first?

  • A. Assess pain intensity.
  • B. Obtain a large-bore needle for decompression.
  • C. Administer lorazepam.
  • D. Prepare for chest tube insertion.
B Using ABC priority, restoring respiratory function with decompression is the first action when tension or severe compromise is present.
A, C, D Pain control, anxiety management, and chest tube preparation are important, but decompression comes first when breathing is threatened.
3

A client with COPD is discharged after pneumothorax treatment. Which instruction should the nurse include?

  • A. "Notify your provider if you experience expected weakness."
  • B. "You should be able to return to work in 1 week."
  • C. "Wear a mask in crowded places because of the pneumothorax."
  • D. "Notify your provider if you develop a productive cough."
D A productive or persistent cough can indicate infection and should be reported promptly.
A, B, C Weakness can be expected, recovery can be lengthy, and mask use is not required solely because of pneumothorax.
4

A client has multiple rib fractures and flail chest. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

  • A. Bradycardia.
  • B. Cyanosis.
  • C. Hypotension.
  • D. Dyspnea.
  • E. Paradoxical chest movement.
B, C, D, E Flail chest can cause cyanosis, hypotension, dyspnea, and paradoxical chest wall movement.
A Tachycardia, not bradycardia, is expected with inadequate oxygenation and distress.
5

A client receiving opioid analgesia after a hemothorax has a respiratory rate of 10/min. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Continue the dose because sedation is expected.
  • B. Stop the medication and notify the provider.
  • C. Encourage the client to use a PCA button more often.
  • D. Place the client flat to improve venous return.
B Opioids can cause respiratory depression; respirations of 12/min or less require stopping the medication and notifying the provider.
A, C, D Continued opioid dosing or more PCA use can worsen respiratory depression, and high-Fowler's positioning is used to maximize ventilation.

Suggested template type

Unit 3 · Respiratory Disorders · Chapter 26

Respiratory Failure

Respiratory failure includes acute respiratory failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and severe acute respiratory syndrome. Care centers on oxygenation, ventilation, airway protection, medication safety, infection prevention, and early recognition of ventilator complications.

TL;DR - Oxygenate, Ventilate, Prevent Collapse

Respiratory failure is confirmed and trended with ABGs and oxygenation findings. Maintain a patent airway, oxygenate before suctioning, use mechanical ventilation with PEEP or CPAP when needed, monitor for pneumothorax and tube complications, and pair paralysis with sedation and analgesia.

Recognize Failure

  • ARF can be ventilatory failure, oxygenation failure, or both.
  • ARDS involves inflammatory injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane, fluid-filled lung spaces, reduced surfactant, and severe hypoxemia.
  • SARS is a coronavirus-related pulmonary infection spread by respiratory droplets.

Protect the Airway

  • Assess respiratory status at least hourly and more often when unstable.
  • Use PEEP or CPAP to prevent alveolar collapse when prescribed.
  • Monitor for high-pressure alarms, tube displacement, aspiration pneumonia, infection, barotrauma, and decreased cardiac output.

Respiratory Failure Care Map

Types and Risk Factors

ARF, ARDS, SARS

Start by sorting the failure pattern, then attach the risk cluster. The pattern explains whether the main problem is ventilation, oxygenation, or both.

Ventilatory failure

Lung or chest wall mechanics, respiratory muscle impairment, diaphragm dysfunction, or respiratory control center problems reduce ventilation.

Oxygenation failure

Poor pulmonary perfusion, pulmonary edema, pneumonia, or gas-exchange membrane changes reduce oxygen transfer.

Combined failure

Gas exchange is poor and carbon dioxide is retained, causing deeper hypoxemia. Older adults can decompensate quickly because pulmonary reserve is lower.

ARF risk cluster

COPD, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, flail chest, ARDS, asthma, pulmonary edema, lung fibrosis, neuromuscular disorders, spinal cord injury, stroke, elevated intracranial pressure, pneumonia, hypoventilation, shock, low hemoglobin, carbon monoxide poisoning, high altitude, and smoke inhalation increase ARF risk.

ARDS and SARS risk cluster

ARDS can follow shock, DIC, aspiration, pulmonary emboli, pneumonia, sepsis, near-drowning, trauma, multiple blood transfusions, CNS damage, smoke or toxic gas inhalation, and drug toxicity. SARS risk increases after exposure to an infected person or immunocompromised status.

Assessment and Diagnostics

ABG-driven

Use assessment cues to suspect failure, then use ABGs and imaging to confirm the pattern and trend response to support.

Bedside danger cues

Shortness of breath, dyspnea, orthopnea, rapid shallow breathing, retractions, adventitious sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, dysrhythmias, confusion, lethargy, and cyanotic, mottled, or dusky skin or mucous membranes point toward worsening oxygenation.

ARF pattern

ARF can show dyspnea, orthopnea, cyanosis, pallor, hypoxemia, tachycardia, confusion, irritability, agitation, restlessness, hypercarbia, and SaO2 less than 90%.

ARDS pattern

ARDS can show dyspnea, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with crackles, reduced lung compliance, dense bilateral infiltrates, and severe hypoxemia despite 100% oxygen.

Confirm and trend

ABGs confirm and monitor ARF, ARDS, and SARS. Respiratory failure criteria include PaO2 less than expected with oxygen saturation less than 90% on room air, or PaCO2 greater than expected with acidemia.

Imaging and monitoring

Chest x-ray can show pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, diffuse infiltrates, white-out or ground-glass ARDS appearance, or SARS infiltrates. ECG helps rule out cardiac involvement, and hemodynamic monitoring supports fluid management because pulmonary capillary wedge pressure in ARDS is usually low or within expected range.

Airway, Ventilation, and Supportive Care

Prevent hypoxemia

Protect gas exchange first. Then build the supportive routine around infection prevention, nutrition, aspiration prevention, and communication.

Airway and ventilation

Maintain a patent airway, monitor respiratory status every hour and more often as needed, and use mechanical ventilation with PEEP or CPAP when prescribed to prevent alveolar collapse during expiration.

Suctioning and monitoring

Oxygenate before suctioning to prevent worsening hypoxemia. Suction as needed, document sputum color, amount, and consistency, obtain ABGs as prescribed and after ventilator setting changes, and use continuous ECG monitoring during hypoxemia-risk moments such as repositioning and suctioning.

Pressure risk

Monitor for pneumothorax because high PEEP can collapse the lungs.

Infection prevention

Use hand hygiene, appropriate suctioning technique, oral care every 2 hr and as needed, and protective clothing when indicated.

Nutrition and aspiration

Assess bowel sounds, monitor elimination, daily weights, and intake/output, and support prescribed enteral or parenteral feedings. For enteral feedings, elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees and confirm NG tube placement before feeding.

Communication support

Provide emotional support and alternative communication tools such as a dry erase board, pen, or paper.

Medication Safety

Sedation and paralysis

Medication questions often test the pairing: anxiety, pain, sedation, inflammation, paralysis, and infection all require different monitoring.

Benzodiazepines

Lorazepam or midazolam can reduce anxiety, resistance to ventilation, and oxygen consumption. Monitor respirations when the client is not mechanically ventilated, blood pressure, and SaO2.

Propofol

Propofol sedates intubated and ventilated clients. Monitor ECG, blood pressure, sedation level, and hypotension, and remember that propofol has no analgesic action.

Opioids

Morphine or fentanyl can manage pain. Monitor respirations, blood pressure, heart rate, SaO2, ABGs, pain response, and have naloxone and resuscitation equipment available for severe respiratory depression when the client is not ventilated.

Corticosteroids

Corticosteroids reduce inflammation. Taper gradually, give with antiulcer protection as prescribed, monitor weight, blood pressure, glucose, and electrolytes, and teach oral doses with food.

Neuromuscular blockers

Vecuronium, atracurium, or rocuronium facilitate ventilation and decrease oxygen consumption but do not sedate or relieve pain. Give pain medication and sedatives with them, monitor ECG, blood pressure, and muscle strength, keep reversal medications and resuscitation equipment available, and explain that paralysis is medication-induced.

Antibiotic readiness

When antibiotics are prescribed for identified organisms, culture sputum before the first dose and monitor hypersensitivity, IV site, renal function, and coagulopathy.

Ventilation Procedures and Complications

Tube and pressure risks

For procedures, think before, after, and complication surveillance. The highest-yield risks are tube position, aspiration, pressure injury to the lungs, and reduced cardiac output.

Before intubation

Oxygenate with 100% oxygen, assist ventilation with a manual resuscitation bag and face mask, and keep emergency equipment ready.

After intubation

Confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide, bilateral lung sounds, symmetrical chest movement, and chest x-ray findings. Secure the endotracheal tube and assess the balloon cuff for leaks periodically.

PEEP and kinetic therapy

PEEP applies pressure at the end of expiration to keep alveoli expanded, increase oxygenation, and improve lung expansion. Kinetic therapy rotates the client laterally to reduce atelectasis and improve ventilation; increase rotation gradually and stop if distress develops.

Tube surveillance

Endotracheal tube trauma can injure the trachea or vocal cords, and long-term ventilation can require tracheostomy. Check tube position every 1 to 2 hr and after movement, transfer, or turning; assess lung sounds, SaO2, and chest movement.

Aspiration and alarms

Prevent aspiration pneumonia by checking cuff leaks, suction contents, and NG tube placement. A high-pressure alarm can signal a blocked tube or pneumothorax; suction secretions or insert an oral airway if biting is causing obstruction.

Pressure complications

PEEP can increase intrathoracic pressure, reduce venous return and cardiac output, cause hypotension, and lower urine output; monitor intake/output, weight, and hydration. Positive-pressure ventilation can cause barotrauma such as pneumothorax or subcutaneous emphysema.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse reviews the plan of care for a client who has ARDS.

Risk factors

  • ARDS can follow aspiration, pulmonary emboli, pneumonia, other pulmonary infections, sepsis, near-drowning, trauma, CNS damage, smoke or toxic gas inhalation, and drug toxicity.
  • Localized lung injury or systemic problems can trigger the inflammatory process.

Oxygenation care and complications

  • Maintain a patent airway, monitor respiratory status, suction as needed, assess lung sounds, document sputum, and oxygenate before suctioning.
  • Use mechanical ventilation and PEEP as prescribed, monitor for pneumothorax, obtain ABGs after ventilator setting changes, and maintain continuous ECG monitoring.
  • Watch for endotracheal tube trauma, aspiration pneumonia, infection, blocked or displaced tube, increased intrathoracic pressure, decreased cardiac output, and barotrauma.

Application Exercises

1

A client after a motor-vehicle crash has absent breath sounds in the left lower lobe, dyspnea, heart rate 124/min, respirations 38/min, temperature 38.6 C (101.4 F), and SaO2 92% on room air. Which action is priority?

  • A. Obtain a chest x-ray.
  • B. Prepare for chest tube insertion.
  • C. Administer oxygen through a high-flow mask.
  • D. Initiate IV access.
C Using ABC priority, oxygenation is first because the client has dyspnea and decreased lung sounds.
A, B, D Imaging, chest tube preparation, and IV access are important but follow immediate oxygenation.
2

A nurse teaches a newly licensed nurse about vecuronium for a client with ARDS. Which statement shows understanding?

  • A. "This medication treats infection."
  • B. "This medication facilitates ventilation."
  • C. "This medication decreases inflammation."
  • D. "This medication reduces anxiety."
B Vecuronium is a neuromuscular blocker used to facilitate ventilation and decrease oxygen consumption.
A, C, D Antibiotics treat infection, corticosteroids reduce inflammation, and benzodiazepines reduce anxiety.
3

Which clients are at risk for ARDS? Select all that apply.

  • A. A client after a near-drowning event.
  • B. A client after coronary artery bypass graft surgery.
  • C. A client with hemoglobin 15.1 mg/dL.
  • D. A client with dysphagia.
  • E. A client with acute drug toxicity.
A, B, D, E Near-drowning, chest trauma or major surgery, aspiration risk from dysphagia, and drug toxicity increase ARDS risk.
C Hemoglobin 15.1 mg/dL is within the expected range; low hemoglobin is the risk concern.
4

Which actions should the nurse include for a client who has severe acute respiratory syndrome? Select all that apply.

  • A. Administer antibiotics as the primary SARS treatment.
  • B. Provide supplemental oxygen.
  • C. Administer antiviral medications proven to treat SARS.
  • D. Administer bronchodilators as prescribed.
  • E. Maintain ventilatory support when needed.
B, D, E SARS care can include oxygen, bronchodilators, and ventilatory support for severe hypoxemia or airway compromise.
A, C Antibiotics treat bacterial infection, and the source notes no effective antiviral medication for SARS.
5

A client receives vecuronium during mechanical ventilation. Which medications should the nurse anticipate administering with it? Select all that apply.

  • A. Fentanyl.
  • B. Furosemide.
  • C. Midazolam.
  • D. Famotidine.
  • E. Dexamethasone.
A, C Neuromuscular blockers do not provide analgesia or sedation, so pain medication and a sedative are given with them.
B, D, E These medications can have other uses, but they do not provide the needed analgesia and sedation pairing for paralysis.

Suggested template type
