Unit 4 · Cardiovascular Disorders · Chapter 34

Inflammatory Disorders

Cardiac inflammatory disorders can involve the pericardium, myocardium, or endocardium and can destroy healthy tissue if infection or inflammation is not controlled. Nursing priorities are early infection treatment, rhythm and oxygenation monitoring, medication safety, antibiotic adherence, and rapid recognition of cardiac tamponade.

TL;DR - Treat Infection, Rest the Heart, Watch Tamponade

Pericarditis pain worsens with inspiration, coughing, or swallowing and improves when sitting forward; myocarditis can cause tachycardia, dysrhythmias, and cardiomegaly; rheumatic endocarditis follows untreated streptococcal pharyngitis; infective endocarditis can show fever, murmur, petechiae, positive blood cultures, and splinter hemorrhages. Tamponade is the emergency to catch fast.

Prevent

  • Treat streptococcal infections early to prevent rheumatic fever.
  • Use prophylactic antibiotics for at-risk cardiac defects when prescribed.
  • Keep influenza and pneumonia immunizations current to lower myocarditis-related infection risk.

Escalate

  • Notify the provider for ECG changes, fever, heart-failure findings, or tamponade manifestations.
  • Cardiac tamponade can cause dyspnea, dizziness, chest tightness, restlessness, pulsus paradoxus, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, and JVD.
  • Prepare for pericardiocentesis when tamponade is suspected.

Inflammatory Cardiac Disorder Care Map

Disorder Patterns

Layer of the heart

Pericarditis pattern

Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium and commonly follows respiratory infection, MI, or systemic connective-tissue disease flare.

Pericarditis findings

Pericarditis findings include chest pressure or pain worsened by inspiration, coughing, or swallowing; friction rub at the left lower sternal border; shortness of breath; and relief when sitting and leaning forward.

Myocarditis pattern

Myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium from infection or systemic inflammatory disease.

Myocarditis findings

Myocarditis findings include tachycardia, murmur, lung friction rub, cardiomegaly, chest pain, and dysrhythmias.

Rheumatic endocarditis

Rheumatic endocarditis follows group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis and can cause fever, chest pain, joint pain, tachycardia, shortness of breath, rash, friction rub, murmur, and muscle spasms.

Infective endocarditis

Infective endocarditis is infection of the endocardium from organisms such as staphylococci, streptococci, or fungi.

Endocarditis risk

Risk is higher with structural cardiac malformations, cardiac devices, prosthetic valves, IV substance use, and invasive procedures that cause bacteremia.

Endocarditis findings

Findings include fever, flu-like symptoms, murmur, petechiae, positive blood cultures, and splinter hemorrhages.

Diagnostics and Nursing Care

Infection and rhythm

Blood cultures

Blood cultures can identify bacterial infection and guide antimicrobial therapy.

Inflammation labs

WBC elevation can suggest bacterial infection, and elevated ESR/CRP supports systemic inflammation.

Cardiac enzymes

Cardiac enzymes can be elevated with pericarditis.

ECG and echocardiography

ECG can show heart block with rheumatic fever or widespread ST elevation with pericarditis; echocardiography can show inflamed layers or pericardial effusion.

Auscultation and oxygenation

Auscultate for murmur or friction rub and review ABGs, oxygen saturation, and chest x-ray results.

Oxygen and rhythm monitoring

Administer oxygen, monitor vital signs and fever, monitor ECG, and report changes.

Tamponade and failure surveillance

Monitor for cardiac tamponade and heart failure.

Infection and comfort care

Obtain throat cultures when indicated, administer antibiotics and antipyretics, assess pain, give pain medication, encourage bed rest, and support coping.

Medications and Procedures

Treat cause

Penicillin safety

Penicillin treats infection; monitor for rash, hives, electrolyte levels, and kidney function, and teach GI distress reporting.

NSAID safety

NSAIDs such as ibuprofen treat fever and inflammation with pericarditis; avoid in peptic ulcer disease and monitor GI effects, platelets, liver function, and kidney function.

Prednisone safety

Prednisone treats inflammation; use low doses, monitor blood pressure, electrolytes, blood glucose, and impaired healing, and teach not to stop abruptly.

Amphotericin B

Amphotericin B treats fungal infection; monitor liver and kidney function.

Pericardiocentesis purpose

Pericardiocentesis aspirates pericardial fluid and can send fluid for culture and sensitivity.

Post-pericardiocentesis monitoring

After pericardiocentesis, monitor for recurrence of tamponade.

Endocarditis procedures

In infective endocarditis, procedures can include valve debridement, abscess drainage, or congenital shunt repair.

Procedure follow-up

Monitor after procedures for bleeding, infection, and altered cardiac output.

Cardiac Tamponade

Emergency

Tamponade cause

Tamponade can result from fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac.

Tamponade findings

Findings include dyspnea, dizziness, chest tightness, increasing restlessness, pulsus paradoxus, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, and jugular venous distention.

Hemodynamic pattern

Hemodynamic monitoring can show similar elevated intracardiac and pulmonary artery plateau pressures.

Immediate response

Notify the provider immediately and support blood pressure with IV fluids as prescribed.

Confirm diagnosis

Obtain chest x-ray or echocardiogram to confirm the diagnosis.

Prepare pericardiocentesis

Prepare for pericardiocentesis, including consent, supplies, and prescribed medications.

Postprocedure surveillance

Monitor hemodynamics, rhythm changes, and recurrence of findings after the procedure.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Myocarditis Discharge Teaching

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse reviews discharge teaching with a client who has myocarditis.

Referral resources

  • Home health can support postoperative care and home IV antibiotic therapy.
  • Pharmaceutical services can provide IV therapy supplies and medications.
  • Rehabilitation services can help monitor and gradually increase activity.

Home actions

  • Rest as needed and take medications as prescribed.
  • Wash hands, maintain good oral hygiene, and avoid crowded areas to reduce infection risk.
  • Learn IV antibiotic administration and management if prescribed for home therapy.
  • Participate in tobacco-use cessation if applicable.

Application Exercises

1

Which finding should the nurse expect in a client who has pericarditis?

  • A. Petechiae.
  • B. Murmur.
  • C. Rash.
  • D. Friction rub.
D A pericardial friction rub is expected with pericarditis.
A, B, C Petechiae point toward endocarditis, murmur toward myocarditis or endocarditis, and rash toward rheumatic endocarditis.
2

Which client is at risk for developing rheumatic endocarditis?

  • A. Older adult with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
  • B. Child with streptococcal pharyngitis.
  • C. Middle-aged adult with lupus erythematosus.
  • D. Young adult who recently received a body tattoo.
B Streptococcal pharyngitis can progress to rheumatic fever, which can lead to rheumatic endocarditis.
A, C, D COPD and lupus are not the specific rheumatic-endocarditis risk unless rheumatic fever occurs; tattooing increases infective endocarditis risk.
3

A client has been taking long-term NSAID therapy for pericarditis. Which laboratory finding should the nurse report?

  • A. Platelets 100,000/mm3.
  • B. Serum glucose 110 mg/dL.
  • C. Serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL.
  • D. ALT 30 IU/L.
A Long-term NSAID therapy can lower platelets; 100,000/mm3 is outside expected range and should be reported.
B, C, D The listed glucose, creatinine, and ALT values are within expected ranges for this item.
4

Splinter hemorrhages under the nail beds plus fever are associated with which disorder?

  • A. Infective endocarditis.
  • B. Pericarditis.
  • C. Myocarditis.
  • D. Rheumatic endocarditis.
A Fever and splinter hemorrhages are classic manifestations of infective endocarditis.
B, C, D Pericarditis is associated with chest pain/friction rub, myocarditis with rapid heart rate, and rheumatic endocarditis with joint pain and preceding streptococcal infection.
5

Which laboratory test helps confirm suspected rheumatic endocarditis?

  • A. Arterial blood gases.
  • B. Serum albumin.
  • C. Liver enzymes.
  • D. Throat culture.
D Throat culture can identify streptococcal infection, the leading cause of rheumatic endocarditis.
A, B, C ABGs, albumin, and liver enzymes can support broader assessment but do not confirm the streptococcal source.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular Disorders · Chapter 35

Peripheral Vascular Diseases

Peripheral vascular disorders disrupt blood flow through arteries or veins. Nursing priorities are comparing pulses and skin findings, improving arterial perfusion without injury, preventing venous stasis, using anticoagulants safely, and escalating symptoms of graft occlusion, compartment syndrome, or pulmonary embolism.

TL;DR - Compare Pulses, Keep Blood Moving, Protect the Limb

PAD is an arterial inflow problem: expect claudication, cool/pale skin, weak pulses, delayed capillary refill, and dependent rubor. Venous disease is a return problem: expect edema, heaviness, stasis changes, ulcers near the ankle, and DVT risk. Do not massage a suspected DVT, do not use direct heat on ischemic legs, and report sudden dyspnea or chest pain as possible pulmonary embolism.

Arterial

  • PAD commonly results from atherosclerotic narrowing in lower-extremity arteries.
  • Leg pain improves with rest or a dependent position because gravity helps perfusion.
  • After arterial procedures, bleeding and pulse changes are priority checks.

Venous

  • Venous stasis, vessel injury, and hypercoagulability drive VTE risk.
  • Compression stockings go on before dependent edema builds.
  • Heparin, warfarin, thrombolytics, and newer anticoagulants require bleeding surveillance.

Peripheral Vascular Disease Care Map

Peripheral Arterial Disease

Arterial perfusion

PAD pattern

PAD decreases blood flow below an arterial obstruction, most often in lower extremities affected by atherosclerosis.

Risk factors

Risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, smoking, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history, older age, and female sex.

Ischemic pain pattern

Intermittent claudication, foot pain while in bed, and relief when legs are dependent point toward impaired arterial flow.

Assessment findings

Assessment findings include femoral or aortic bruit, delayed toe capillary refill, weak or absent pulses, hair loss, dry scaly skin, thick nails, cool cyanotic skin, elevation pallor, dependent rubor, muscle atrophy, ulcers, and possible gangrene.

Walking plan

Build collateral circulation with gradual walking: walk to pain, rest, then walk a little farther.

Promote vasodilation

Promote vasodilation with warmth, insulated socks, and avoidance of cold, stress, caffeine, nicotine, and tobacco.

Avoid direct heat

Avoid direct heat because decreased sensation increases burn risk.

Avoid flow restriction

Avoid crossing legs, restrictive clothing, and raising legs above heart level when arterial flow is poor.

Arterial Diagnostics and Procedures

Pulse first

Arteriography

Arteriography visualizes decreased arterial flow and can lead directly to angioplasty or stent placement.

Exercise tolerance testing

Exercise tolerance testing compares pulse volumes and pressures before and after exertion to evaluate claudication.

Flow comparison studies

Plethysmography and segmental systolic blood pressure measurements compare upper and lower extremity flow patterns.

Ankle-brachial index

An ankle-brachial index below the expected range supports a PAD diagnosis.

Puncture-site checks

After arteriography or angioplasty, watch the puncture site for bleeding and reassess distal pulses.

Postprocedure limb care

After angioplasty or atherectomy, keep the treated limb straight during prescribed bed rest and monitor vital signs, pulses, and capillary refill.

Anticoagulation and antiplatelets

Anticoagulation can be used during procedures and antiplatelet therapy can follow.

Bypass surgery checks

For arterial bypass surgery, compare color, temperature, sensation, capillary refill, and marked pulse sites with the other limb.

Arterial Procedure Complications

Save the limb

Graft occlusion findings

Graft occlusion can present with decreased or absent pulses, increased pain, and changed extremity color or temperature.

Occlusion response

Notify the surgeon promptly for occlusion findings and prepare for possible thrombectomy, thrombolytic therapy, platelet inhibitor therapy, or combined treatment.

Wound surveillance

Use sterile technique for surgical dressing changes and monitor for warmth, tenderness, erythema, edema, induration, or purulent drainage.

Bypass teaching

Teach loose clothing, no leg crossing, limited hip and knee bending, wound care, smoking avoidance, and careful foot care.

Escalate early symptoms

Escalate tingling, numbness, worsening pain, edema, pain with passive motion, or unequal pulses.

Limb-threat pattern

Use the limb-threat pattern of pain, pressure, paralysis, paresthesia, pallor, and pulselessness.

Early warning

Paresthesia is often an early warning sign.

Prevent tissue injury

Loosen dressings and prepare for fasciotomy if ordered to prevent further tissue injury.

Venous Disorders

Return flow

VTE pattern

VTE develops from stasis, vessel injury, or hypercoagulability and can progress to pulmonary embolism.

VTE risk

Risk is increased by major lower-body surgery, heart failure, immobility, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, active cancer, central venous access, dialysis access, inflammatory bowel disease, and inherited clotting disorders.

DVT findings

DVT can be silent or cause calf or groin pain, tenderness, sudden edema, warmth, induration, and increasing limb circumference.

Embolus warning

Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain can indicate embolus movement to the lungs.

Venous insufficiency pattern

Venous insufficiency results from valve damage and prolonged venous hypertension, causing pooling, edema, tissue injury, and stasis ulcers.

Venous findings

Venous findings include heaviness after standing, brown ankle-to-calf discoloration, edema, and ulcers commonly near the ankle.

Varicose vein risk

Varicose veins are enlarged superficial tortuous veins often associated with prolonged standing, pregnancy, obesity, age, and family history.

Varicosity symptoms

Clients can report aching, cramping, pain after sitting, and itching.

Venous Care, Medications, and Ulcers

Prevent emboli

Venous diagnostics

D-dimer can support suspicion of clot formation; venous duplex ultrasound, Doppler flow study, plethysmography, venogram, or MRI can help evaluate suspected DVT.

Mobility after anticoagulation

After anticoagulation is started, encourage ambulation and foot dorsiflexion/plantar flexion exercises.

DVT limb care

Elevate legs intermittently while in bed, avoid pillows under the knees, apply warm moist compresses if prescribed, and do not massage the affected limb.

Mechanical prevention

Compression or antiembolism stockings and an inferior vena cava filter can be used when indicated.

Unfractionated heparin

Unfractionated heparin requires aPTT monitoring, platelet monitoring for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, bleeding surveillance, and available protamine sulfate.

Enoxaparin teaching

Enoxaparin can be used for prevention or treatment of DVT; teach bleeding precautions for home injections.

Warfarin safety

Warfarin overlaps with heparin until therapeutic effect develops; monitor PT/INR, keep vitamin K intake consistent, and keep vitamin K available for excessive bleeding.

Thrombolytic and direct inhibitor safety

Thrombolytic therapy dissolves an existing clot and requires close bleeding monitoring; direct thrombin inhibitors have specific reversal considerations and are avoided with renal insufficiency.

Venous ulcer risk

Venous ulcers are chronic, hard to heal, often recur, and can lead to severe limb outcomes.

Wound specialist support

Coordinate long-term wound care with wound specialists and nutrition support.

Prescribed ulcer treatments

Use prescribed dressings, debridement agents, antibiotics, and pain control.

Nutrition for healing

Support healing with diet high in protein, iron, zinc, and vitamins A and C.

Pulmonary embolism findings

Recognize sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, restlessness, apprehension, cough, hemoptysis, tachypnea, crackles, tachycardia, diaphoresis, low-grade fever, and falling oxygen saturation.

Immediate PE response

Notify the provider immediately, reassure the client, and position for comfort with the head of bed elevated.

PE preparation

Prepare for oxygen therapy, arterial blood gases, ongoing assessment, and prescribed anticoagulation.

Rapid response priority

Rapid response matters because pulmonary blood flow obstruction can become fatal.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Peripheral Arterial Disease Poster

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse prepares community teaching about PAD for a health fair.

Alteration and risks

  • Explain PAD as reduced lower-extremity arterial flow from progressive arterial wall thickening and plaque formation.
  • Include risk factors such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, smoking, obesity, inactivity, family history, older age, and female sex.

Findings and teaching

  • Include bruit, delayed capillary refill, weak pulses, hair loss, dry mottled skin, thick nails, cool cyanotic skin, elevation pallor, dependent rubor, muscle atrophy, ulcers, and gangrene risk.
  • Teach no leg crossing, no restrictive garments, elevation only to reduce swelling but not above heart level, warmth without direct heat, and avoidance of cold, stress, caffeine, nicotine, and tobacco.

Application Exercises

1

A client with chronic venous insufficiency has thigh-high compression stockings prescribed. Which action is best?

  • A. Apply the stockings before getting out of bed in the morning.
  • B. Roll the stockings down if they feel tight behind the knees.
  • C. Remove the stockings for long rest periods during the day.
  • D. Elevate the legs briefly while the stockings are already in place.
A Applying stockings before dependent edema develops supports venous return and reduces venous stasis.
B, C, D Rolling stockings restricts circulation, daytime removal reduces support, and elevation is most useful before application when swelling is minimal.
2

Which assessment finding is most consistent with chronic PAD rather than venous stasis?

  • A. Brown discoloration around the ankles.
  • B. Edema of the ankles and feet.
  • C. Pallor with elevation and rubor when dependent.
  • D. Ulceration near the medial malleolus.
C Elevation pallor with dependent rubor reflects impaired arterial perfusion.
A, B, D Ankle discoloration, edema, and medial-malleolus ulcers fit venous insufficiency patterns.
3

Which instruction belongs in teaching for severe PAD?

  • A. Apply direct heat to the legs for comfort.
  • B. Elevate the legs above heart level whenever resting.
  • C. Keep legs in a dependent position if rest pain occurs.
  • D. Wear tight insulated socks to improve warmth.
C A dependent position can improve arterial blood flow to the feet and relieve ischemic discomfort.
A, B, D Direct heat can burn poorly sensate tissue, high elevation worsens arterial flow, and tight socks restrict circulation.
4

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client taking clopidogrel? Select all that apply.

  • A. Report black, tarry stools.
  • B. Avoid herbal supplements unless approved.
  • C. Take the medication only when leg pain occurs.
  • D. Expect routine weekly PT testing.
  • E. Limit vitamin K foods every day.
A, B Clopidogrel increases bleeding risk; GI bleeding and herb interactions such as garlic, ginger, ginkgo, and ginseng require caution.
C, D, E Clopidogrel is taken routinely, while PT/INR monitoring and vitamin K consistency are warfarin priorities.
5

A client with DVT receives IV heparin and has just started warfarin. How should the nurse explain the overlap?

  • A. "Both medications are needed until warfarin reaches its therapeutic effect."
  • B. "The heparin prescription was likely an error once warfarin was started."
  • C. "Two anticoagulants are required because your clot is now larger."
  • D. "Only one of these medicines is actually treating the DVT."
A Warfarin takes several days to affect clotting factors, so heparin continues until warfarin becomes therapeutic.
B, C, D The overlap is intentional, not evidence of an error or clot enlargement; both medications can be part of DVT treatment.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular Disorders · Chapter 36

Hypertension

Hypertension is often quiet until target organs are damaged. Nursing priorities are accurate blood-pressure confirmation, lifestyle risk reduction, medication teaching, electrolyte and kidney monitoring, and urgent response to hypertensive crisis.

TL;DR - Confirm Pressure, Reduce Risk, Protect Organs

Hypertension is persistent elevation of systolic or diastolic pressure and can damage the heart, brain, eyes, kidneys, and peripheral vessels. Most clients have essential hypertension without one known cause; secondary hypertension comes from another condition or medication. Teach lifestyle change, safe position changes with antihypertensives, medication adherence even when asymptomatic, and emergency care for crisis findings.

Find

  • When pressure is elevated, check both arms and compare sitting and standing readings.
  • Clients can have few findings; morning headache, flushing, dizziness, fainting, visual changes, retinal changes, and nocturia can occur.
  • Labs do not diagnose hypertension but help identify secondary causes and organ damage.

Treat

  • Lifestyle care includes sodium and fat reduction, DASH eating, exercise, weight management, smoking cessation, alcohol limits, and stress reduction.
  • Medication classes require pulse, blood pressure, potassium, kidney, and adverse-effect monitoring.
  • Hypertensive crisis requires IV therapy, frequent blood pressure checks, neurologic assessment, and ECG monitoring.

Hypertension Care Map

Definition, Regulation, and Risk

Often silent

Hypertension definition

Hypertension in adults is persistent elevation of systolic or diastolic blood pressure across repeated assessments.

Essential hypertension

Essential hypertension has no single known cause and accounts for most cases.

Secondary hypertension

Secondary hypertension is linked to conditions such as kidney disease, adrenal disorders, neurologic disorders, pregnancy, or medications such as estrogen, steroids, and sympathomimetics.

Target-organ risk

Untreated hypertension increases risk for target-organ damage, including left ventricular hypertrophy.

Modifiable risks

Modifiable risks include sodium excess, physical inactivity, obesity, high alcohol intake, smoking, hyperlipidemia, and stress.

Nonmodifiable risks

Family history, age over 60, postmenopausal status, and African American ancestry increase essential hypertension risk.

Risk-reduction support

Support BMI management, diabetes glucose control, caffeine and alcohol limits, stress management, smoking cessation, aerobic exercise, and sodium/fat limits.

Blood pressure regulation

Blood pressure regulation involves baroreceptors, body-fluid volume control, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and vascular autoregulation.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Confirm and screen

Routine screening

Many clients have few or no manifestations, so routine screening matters.

Possible findings

Possible findings include morning headache, facial flushing, dizziness, fainting, retinal changes, visual disturbances, and nocturia.

Confirm elevated readings

If a reading is elevated, assess both arms and compare sitting and standing readings.

Blood pressure classifications

Current classifications include elevated blood pressure, stage I hypertension, and stage II hypertension based on systolic and diastolic thresholds.

Lab limits

No lab test diagnoses hypertension by itself.

Kidney involvement

BUN and creatinine help identify kidney involvement or kidney-related secondary hypertension.

Corticoid studies

Corticoid studies can point toward Cushing-related hypertension.

Vascular and cardiac screening

Glucose and cholesterol studies identify vascular risk contributors; ECG and chest x-ray can show left ventricular strain or cardiomegaly.

Medication Priorities

Monitor potassium

Thiazide and loop diuretics

Thiazide diuretics reduce water and sodium reabsorption and increase potassium loss; loop diuretics also increase potassium excretion.

Potassium-sparing diuretics

Potassium-sparing diuretics can cause hyperkalemia, so monitor potassium and teach clients to avoid potassium-heavy salt substitutes unless prescribed.

Diuretic adverse effects

Watch for muscle weakness, irregular pulse, dehydration, hyponatremia, and potassium imbalance.

Calcium-channel blockers

Calcium-channel blockers promote vasodilation; monitor blood pressure and pulse, change positions slowly, use caution with heart failure, avoid grapefruit juice, and teach constipation management with verapamil.

ACE inhibitors

ACE inhibitors block conversion to angiotensin II; monitor blood pressure, pulse, edema, kidney complications, persistent cough, and angioedema.

ARBs

ARBs block angiotensin II receptor effects and can be useful when ACE-inhibitor cough occurs; teach slow position changes and reporting swelling of the lips or face.

Potassium precautions

ARBs and aldosterone-receptor antagonists can increase potassium, so monitor levels and avoid potassium supplements or potassium-rich salt substitutes unless prescribed.

Aldosterone-receptor antagonists

Aldosterone-receptor antagonists also require kidney function, sodium, potassium, and triglyceride monitoring.

Beta blockers

Beta blockers slow heart rate and lower blood pressure; monitor blood pressure and pulse.

Avoid abrupt beta-blocker stop

Teach not to stop beta blockers abruptly because rebound hypertension can occur.

Masked hypoglycemia

Beta blockers can mask tachycardia from hypoglycemia, so clients with diabetes need alternate hypoglycemia cues.

Orthostatic hypotension

Central alpha2 agonists and alpha-adrenergic antagonists can cause orthostatic hypotension; dose timing and slow position changes reduce injury risk.

Fall risk

Antihypertensive effects can increase fall risk, especially when getting out of bed, driving, or using stairs.

Follow-up visits

Keep provider appointments to monitor effect and electrolyte balance.

Adherence when asymptomatic

Take medications as prescribed even when no symptoms are present.

Report adverse findings

Report pulse changes, irregular pulse, edema, cough, angioedema, or severe dizziness promptly.

Lifestyle Plan and Hypertensive Crisis

Prevent emergency

Limit sodium and fats

Limit sodium, saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol.

DASH pattern

The DASH pattern emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy foods.

Blood-pressure control habits

Alcohol limits, weight reduction, regular aerobic exercise, smoking cessation support, and stress reduction all support blood-pressure control.

Salt substitute caution

Monitor for hyperkalemia if salt substitutes are used, especially with potassium-sparing therapy.

Crisis findings

Hypertensive crisis can follow missed medication therapy and can present with severe headache, very high pressure, blurred vision, dizziness, disorientation, and epistaxis.

IV antihypertensives

Administer prescribed IV antihypertensives such as nitroprusside, nicardipine, or labetalol.

Controlled reduction

The initial goal is controlled reduction, not sudden normalization.

Crisis monitoring

Monitor blood pressure every 5 to 15 min during IV therapy, assess neurologic status, and monitor ECG.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Community Hypertension Teaching

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse prepares a community education presentation about hypertension.

Diagnosis and risks

  • Explain essential hypertension as high blood pressure without one known cause.
  • Explain secondary hypertension as high blood pressure related to another disorder or medication.
  • Include primary risks such as family history, sodium excess, inactivity, obesity, alcohol intake, smoking, hyperlipidemia, stress, older age, and postmenopausal status.
  • Include secondary causes such as kidney disease, Cushing disease, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, brain tumors, encephalitis, and medications such as estrogen, steroids, and sympathomimetics.

Findings

  • Teach that clients can have few or no symptoms.
  • Possible subjective findings include morning headache, dizziness, fainting, visual changes, nocturia, and facial flushing.
  • Objective teaching should include blood pressure categories and the need to confirm elevated readings using proper technique.
  • Encourage learners to connect hypertension with target-organ protection, not just a number on the cuff.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings increase a client's risk for hypertension? Select all that apply.

  • A. Eating high-sodium movie-theater popcorn.
  • B. Drinking a large amount of beer each day.
  • C. Walking briskly every day.
  • D. Choosing low-fat dairy products.
  • E. Using massage for stress reduction.
A, B High sodium/fat intake and excessive alcohol intake increase hypertension risk.
C, D, E Regular exercise, low-fat foods, and stress management help lower risk.
2

A client with type 2 diabetes and hypertension reports a second hypoglycemic episode in 2 weeks. Which medication data should the nurse report?

  • A. Takes metoprolol daily.
  • B. Uses psyllium as a fiber laxative.
  • C. Drinks skim milk as a bedtime snack.
  • D. Drinks grapefruit juice with breakfast.
A Beta blockers such as metoprolol can mask tachycardia, an important warning sign of hypoglycemia.
B, C, D Psyllium is not the hypoglycemia concern here; skim milk can raise glucose; grapefruit juice interacts with some medications but is not the reason to report recurrent masked hypoglycemia.
3

A client arrives with very high blood pressure, severe headache, and double vision after running out of diltiazem. What should the nurse do first?

  • A. Obtain IV access and prepare for IV antihypertensive therapy.
  • B. Teach the client not to stop antihypertensive medication abruptly.
  • C. Request financial assistance referral for medication access.
  • D. Give acetaminophen for the headache.
A The immediate threat is hypertensive crisis with neurologic symptoms, so rapid IV access and prescribed IV therapy are priority.
B, C, D Teaching, financial support, and pain relief matter after the life-threatening pressure is addressed.
4

Which statement shows understanding of spironolactone teaching for hypertension?

  • A. "I will report changes in my heart rate."
  • B. "I should replace table salt with a potassium salt substitute."
  • C. "I should eat extra bananas and potatoes every day."
  • D. "I can reduce the dose when headaches stop."
A Pulse or rhythm changes can signal potassium imbalance and should be reported.
B, C, D Spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia, so potassium salt substitutes and high-potassium intake require caution; antihypertensives should not be self-reduced.
5

When should a client take once-daily furosemide for hypertension?

  • A. In the morning.
  • B. Right after lunch.
  • C. Right before dinner.
  • D. At bedtime.
A Morning dosing places peak diuretic effect during waking hours and reduces sleep disruption from urination.
B, C, D Later dosing increases the chance that diuresis will interrupt rest or sleep.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular Disorders · Chapter 37

Hemodynamic Shock

Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion that can rapidly progress to organ failure. Nursing priorities are early recognition, oxygenation, IV access, hemodynamic support, cause-specific treatment, and escalation before compensatory mechanisms fail.

TL;DR - Oxygen First, Restore Perfusion, Treat the Cause

All shock types threaten cellular oxygen delivery, but treatment depends on the cause: pump failure, volume loss, mechanical obstruction, or distributive vasodilation. Watch for altered mentation, cool or flushed skin patterns, tachypnea, weak pulses, narrowed pulse pressure, decreased urine output, and worsening hypoxia. In hypovolemic shock, replace volume before vasopressors.

Recognize

  • Early shock can be subtle; older adults can decompensate quickly due to reduced compensatory response.
  • Shock progresses from cellular-level injury to compensation, failed compensation, and irreversible failure.
  • Seizures, tachypnea greater than 40/min, weak thready pulse, and oliguria are late-danger signals.

Respond

  • Continuous airway and vital-sign monitoring comes first.
  • Use high-flow oxygen unless the client needs COPD-adjusted oxygen support.
  • Maintain IV access, support hemodynamics, and prepare for ICU, surgery, specialty care, or diagnostics.

Hemodynamic Shock Care Map

Types, Causes, and Stages

Cause drives care

Start by naming the shock pattern. The category tells you whether the first move is to support the pump, replace volume, remove an obstruction, or reverse vasodilation/permeability.

Cardiogenic - pump failure

The heart cannot move blood forward well enough to meet tissue oxygen needs.

Common causes include MI, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, dysrhythmia, and valve rupture or stenosis.

Hypovolemic - volume loss

Major intravascular volume loss leaves too little circulating volume for adequate preload and perfusion.

Common causes include dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, hemorrhage, surgery, trauma, burns, and DKA.

Obstructive - blocked flow

A noncardiac blockage or pressure problem prevents normal filling or pumping.

Common causes include pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, aortic dissection, and pulmonary artery obstruction.

Distributive - maldistributed flow

Massive vasodilation and capillary permeability changes reduce effective perfusion.

Neurogenic, septic, and anaphylactic shock are distributive patterns.

After the category, identify the stage. The stage tells you whether the body is still compensating or has moved into failing compensation.

Progression stages

Initial: cellular-level injury begins before obvious vital-sign changes.

Compensatory: the body attempts to restore cardiac output, perfusion, and oxygenation.

Progressive: compensatory mechanisms are failing.

Refractory: total-body failure has become irreversible.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Perfusion clues

Expected findings

Subjective findings can include chest pain, lethargy, somnolence, restlessness, anxiety, dyspnea, diaphoresis, thirst, weakness, nausea, and constipation.

Physical findings can include hypoxia, tachypnea, cool moist skin, pallor, cyanosis, mottling, wheezing, decreased blood pressure, narrowed pulse pressure, postural hypotension, tachycardia, weak thready pulse, and low urine output.

Anaphylactic shock can include angioedema and initially flushed skin.

Septic and anaphylactic shock can initially show warm or flushed skin before later poor perfusion appears.

Tests and monitoring

ABGs can reflect poor tissue oxygenation and acid-base deterioration.

Lactic acid rises when cells shift toward anaerobic metabolism.

Cardiac enzymes, BNP, Hgb/Hct, cultures, coagulation tests, glucose, and electrolytes help match treatment to cause.

Arterial lines and pulmonary artery catheters support continuous pressure, cardiac output, and medication titration decisions.

Priority Nursing Care

ABCs and perfusion

Immediate actions

Monitor oxygenation status, vital signs, continuous cardiac rhythm, level of consciousness, urine output, skin findings, capillary refill, and turgor.

Report urine output below the expected shock threshold promptly.

Provide high-flow oxygen for most clients and prepare for intubation if needed.

Maintain patent IV access and place hypotensive clients flat with legs elevated unless contraindicated.

Escalation

Notify rapid response and the provider for status changes.

Have resuscitation equipment available for transport or procedures.

Prepare for ICU transfer, surgery, specialty unit care, or diagnostic testing.

Explain procedures and findings to reduce fear for the client and family.

Medication Priorities

Titrate closely

Perfusion support

Inotropes such as milrinone and dobutamine improve contraction and cardiac output; give by continuous infusion with hemodynamic monitoring.

Vasopressors such as dopamine and norepinephrine can improve contraction and vascular tone; titrate to parameters, monitor urine output, and use central access to reduce extravasation risk.

Vasopressin increases systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure; monitor hemodynamics and urine output.

Crystalloids, colloids, or blood products replace volume in hypovolemic shock before vasopressors are used.

Cause-specific medications

Epinephrine is rapid-acting and priority for anaphylactic airway compromise; monitor blood pressure, pulse, and cardiac output.

Diphenhydramine can be secondary support for urticaria or angioedema, but it can worsen hypotension or sedation.

Broad IV antibiotics are urgent in septic shock after cultures when possible; monitor kidney function, coagulopathy, hypersensitivity, and IV site integrity.

Nitroprusside can reduce afterload/preload in cardiogenic shock; use continuous arterial pressure monitoring and protect the solution from light.

Procedures and Complications

Prevent failure

Procedures

Intubation and mechanical ventilation support oxygenation; preoxygenate, assist ventilation, keep suction and resuscitation equipment ready, and confirm tube placement with assessment and imaging.

PEEP keeps alveoli open to improve oxygenation and lung expansion.

Needle decompression and chest tube insertion relieve tension pneumothorax causing obstructive shock.

Pericardiocentesis drains fluid causing tamponade and obstructive shock; additional procedures can still be needed.

Complications

MODS follows inadequate oxygenation and perfusion; lungs often fail first, but kidney, heart, and GI failure can follow.

Support organ function with ventilation, inotropic support, clotting factors, dialysis, or other prescribed measures.

DIC can complicate septic shock with widespread microclotting followed by bleeding risk.

Monitor bleeding from mucous membranes, venipuncture sites, gums, IV sites, and central/arterial lines.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Shock Review for New Nurses

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse educator reviews shock care with newly hired nurses.

Risk factors by type

  • Cardiogenic: MI, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, dysrhythmia, valve rupture, or stenosis.
  • Hypovolemic: fluid loss, vomiting, diarrhea, or blood loss.
  • Obstructive: great-vessel blockage, pulmonary artery obstruction, PE, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or aortic dissection.
  • Distributive: gram-negative sepsis, neurogenic loss of sympathetic tone, or allergen-triggered anaphylaxis.

Expected findings

  • Blood pressure can decrease with narrowed pulse pressure and postural hypotension.
  • Pulse is often rapid and weak, though distributive shock can feel bounding early.
  • Respirations can become rapid with hypoxia and hypocarbia.
  • Urine output decreases as perfusion falls.

Application Exercises

1

An afterload-reducing medication is prescribed for which shock pattern?

  • A. Cardiogenic shock.
  • B. Obstructive shock.
  • C. Hypovolemic shock.
  • D. Distributive shock.
A Reducing afterload can help a failing heart pump more effectively in cardiogenic shock.
B, C, D Obstructive shock needs the obstruction corrected, hypovolemic shock needs volume replacement, and distributive shock already has reduced vascular tone.
2

Which intervention is priority for septic shock?

  • A. Administer antibiotic therapy.
  • B. Maintain fluid volume with IV infusions.
  • C. Monitor hemodynamic readings.
  • D. Administer a vasopressor.
A Eliminating the infectious cause reduces endotoxin/mediator-driven vasodilation and is the key priority.
B, C, D Fluids, monitoring, and vasopressors support perfusion, but they do not treat the source of sepsis.
3

A client has wheezing and tongue swelling after allergen exposure. Which medication should the nurse anticipate first?

  • A. Epinephrine.
  • B. Diphenhydramine.
  • C. Methylprednisolone.
  • D. Dobutamine.
A Epinephrine is rapid-acting and supports airway, breathing, and circulation in anaphylactic shock.
B, C, D Antihistamines and steroids can follow, and dobutamine supports cardiac output when indicated but is not the first anaphylaxis airway medication.
4

Which findings can occur in shock? Select all that apply.

  • A. Respiratory rate 42/min.
  • B. Weak, thready pulse.
  • C. Seizure activity.
  • D. Heart rate 60/min.
  • E. Increased urine output.
A, B, C Tachypnea, weak thready pulse, and seizure activity can reflect worsening oxygenation and perfusion.
D, E Tachycardia and decreased urine output are expected shock patterns.
5

Which client is at risk for obstructive shock?

  • A. A client with pulmonary arterial stenosis.
  • B. A client with vomiting and diarrhea for several days.
  • C. A client with a gram-negative bacterial infection.
  • D. A client with occasional premature ventricular contractions.
A Obstructive shock occurs when a noncardiac obstruction interferes with cardiac pumping.
B, C, D Vomiting and diarrhea point toward hypovolemic shock, gram-negative infection toward septic shock, and dysrhythmias toward cardiogenic risk.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular Disorders · Chapter 38

Aneurysms

Aneurysms are weakened, dilated arterial segments that can rupture or dissect. Nursing priorities are blood pressure control, rupture recognition, avoiding palpation of suspected abdominal masses, distal perfusion checks, renal perfusion monitoring, and postoperative graft surveillance.

TL;DR - Control Pressure, Do Not Palpate, Watch the Graft

AAA can cause constant abdominal gnawing, low back pain, bruit, or a pulsating mass that should not be palpated. Thoracic aneurysm commonly causes severe back pain plus cough, dyspnea, hoarseness, or dysphagia. Dissection causes sudden tearing or ripping pain with shock findings. After repair, report pulse changes, cool or cyanotic extremities, severe pain, abdominal distention, or low urine output.

Prevent

  • Promote smoking cessation, healthy weight, healthy diet, physical activity, and blood pressure control.
  • Uncontrolled hypertension, atherosclerosis, tobacco use, hyperlipidemia, family history, male sex, trauma, syphilis history, and aging vessel changes increase risk.
  • All aneurysms can become life-threatening and need medical attention.

Escalate

  • Rupture requires simultaneous resuscitation and immediate repair.
  • Emergency care focuses on controlled systolic pressure reduction and circulation support.
  • Graft thrombus can send emboli downstream, so distal pulse/color/temperature and urine output matter.

Aneurysm Care Map

Definition, Types, and Risk

Weak arterial wall

Forms

An aneurysm is a weakened, widened, or ballooned section of artery.

Saccular aneurysms affect one side of the vessel wall.

Fusiform aneurysms involve the full vessel circumference.

Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters the artery wall after an intimal tear, often associated with hypertension.

Risk factors

Atherosclerosis is the most common cause.

Other risks include uncontrolled hypertension, tobacco use, hyperlipidemia, family history, male sex, blunt trauma, syphilis history, and age-related loss of arterial elasticity.

Older adults are more vulnerable to aneurysm development and have higher mortality when rupture occurs.

Prevention teaching centers on blood pressure control, tobacco cessation, healthy activity, and healthy weight.

Findings and Diagnostics

Pain pattern

Findings

Clients can be asymptomatic at first.

AAA findings can include constant abdominal gnawing, low back pain, abdominal bruit, elevated blood pressure, and a pulsating abdominal mass that should not be palpated.

Thoracic aneurysm can cause severe back pain, hoarseness, cough, shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, and decreased urine output from shock.

Aortic dissection can cause sudden tearing, ripping, or stabbing abdominal/back pain with diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, faintness, apprehension, weak or absent peripheral pulses, neurologic deficits, hypotension, tachycardia, and oliguria.

Diagnostics

X-ray can detect an aneurysm.

CT and ultrasonography assess aneurysm size and location and can be repeated to monitor progression.

TEE helps diagnose thoracic aneurysm and aortic dissection.

Monitor ABGs, oxygen saturation, electrolytes, CBC findings, hemodynamic readings, and hourly urine output.

Nursing Care and Medications

Pressure control

Monitoring

Take vital signs frequently until stable, then continue close monitoring for blood pressure increases.

Assess onset, quality, duration, and severity of pain.

Assess extremity temperature, circulation, and range of motion.

Continuously monitor cardiac rhythm, hemodynamics, oxygenation, labs, and urine output; output above the expected renal-perfusion threshold supports adequate kidney perfusion.

Medications

Emergency treatment prioritizes systolic blood pressure reduction into the prescribed range.

Long-term care keeps systolic pressure within the provider-set maintenance goal to reduce rupture risk.

Antihypertensive therapy often uses more than one class, such as beta blockers and calcium-channel blockers.

Administer oxygen, IV fluids, and other medications as prescribed while maintaining IV access.

Repair and Postoperative Priorities

Distal perfusion

Procedures

AAA resection removes the aneurysm and places a synthetic graft; elective repair is used for large AAAs and emergency repair for rupture.

Percutaneous repair places an endovascular stent graft and can shorten the postoperative course.

Thoracic repair resembles major thoracic or open-heart surgery and can require cardiopulmonary bypass.

Thoracic repair requires close respiratory monitoring because distress is common after this procedure.

Postoperative care

Monitor arterial pressure, rhythm, hemodynamics, and evidence of graft occlusion or rupture.

Check distal pulses and circulation frequently, and keep the head of bed below the flexion limit ordered for graft protection.

Maintain blood pressure within prescribed parameters: prolonged hypotension can promote graft clotting, and severe hypertension can cause leak or rupture at the suture line.

Monitor kidney perfusion, lung sounds, bowel sounds, abdominal distention, infection, thromboembolism prevention, and femoral insertion sites after endovascular repair.

Complications and Teaching

Rupture watch

Complications

Rupture is a life-threatening emergency with massive hemorrhage, shock, and death risk.

Treatment of rupture requires resuscitation and immediate surgical repair at the same time.

A thrombus can form inside the aneurysm, dislodge, and block distal arteries.

Distal ischemia can appear as pulse changes, coolness, white or blue skin, severe pain, abdominal distention, or low urine output.

Discharge teaching

Take blood pressure medications as prescribed and stay within provider-set parameters.

Keep CT or ultrasound follow-up visits to monitor aneurysm size if managed nonsurgically.

Report wound redness, edema, drainage, fever, abdominal fullness or pain, chest or back pain, dyspnea, cough, dysphagia, or hoarseness immediately.

Avoid strenuous activity and heavy lifting after surgery as prescribed; support wound healing with low-fat, high-protein nutrition and vitamins/minerals as directed.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Aneurysm Nursing In-Service

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse manager prepares an in-service on caring for clients who have aneurysms.

Risk and diagnostics

  • Risk factors include atherosclerosis, uncontrolled hypertension, tobacco use, hyperlipidemia, family history, male sex, trauma, syphilis history, and age-related arterial changes.
  • Diagnostic support can include x-ray, CT, ultrasonography, and transesophageal echocardiography.

Nursing care

  • Monitor vital signs, pain characteristics, extremity circulation, range of motion, cardiac rhythm, hemodynamics, ABGs, oxygen saturation, electrolytes, CBC, and hourly urine output.
  • Administer oxygen, maintain IV access, give medications as prescribed, and escalate signs of rupture, dissection, or graft occlusion immediately.

Application Exercises

1

A client with a possible dissecting abdominal aortic aneurysm reports severe pain and fullness. Which action is priority?

  • A. Administer prescribed IV fluids.
  • B. Administer prescribed pain medication.
  • C. Provide a warm environment.
  • D. Initiate a 12-lead ECG.
A Circulation is the priority because leaking or rupture can rapidly cause inadequate circulating volume.
B, C, D Pain relief, warmth, and ECG assessment can be appropriate after immediate circulatory support is addressed.
2

Which findings can occur with thoracic aortic aneurysm? Select all that apply.

  • A. Cough.
  • B. Shortness of breath.
  • C. Difficulty swallowing.
  • D. Diaphoresis.
  • E. Upper chest pain as the classic finding.
A, B, C Thoracic aneurysm can cause cough, dyspnea, and dysphagia from pressure on nearby structures.
D, E Diaphoresis fits dissection/shock, and severe back pain is the more expected thoracic pain pattern.
3

Which postoperative interventions belong in care after endovascular aneurysm stent graft placement? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assess pedal pulses.
  • B. Monitor for increased pain below the graft.
  • C. Check the femoral site for bleeding.
  • D. Maintain high-Fowler's position continuously.
  • E. Report urine output of 60 mL/hr.
A, B, C Distal pulses, new pain below the graft, and femoral-site bleeding help detect occlusion, rupture, bleeding, or thrombus formation.
D, E Excess hip flexion can stress the graft; urine output of 60 mL/hr is expected rather than reportable.
4

A client asks what can cause an aneurysm to rupture. Which response is best?

  • A. "Hypertension increases pressure against the weakened arterial wall."
  • B. "Rupture occurs because the artery becomes thin and flexible."
  • C. "A bruit is the main reason rupture occurs."
  • D. "Abdominal enlargement causes the aneurysm to rupture."
A Hypertension raises pressure within the diseased artery and increases rupture risk.
B, C, D Loss of elasticity contributes to aneurysm formation, bruit is a finding, and abdominal distention can result from rupture rather than cause it.
5

Which finding supports suspected occlusion of an abdominal aortic graft?

  • A. Irregular cyanotic areas and tenderness in the lower extremities.
  • B. Bounding pedal pulses bilaterally.
  • C. Increased urine output.
  • D. Decreased abdominal girth.
A Distal cyanosis, tenderness, and decreased pulses can occur when graft thrombus blocks blood flow.
B, C, D Weak or absent pulses, decreased urine output, and increasing abdominal girth would be more concerning patterns.

Unit 5 · Hematologic Disorders · Chapter 39

Hematologic Diagnostic Procedures

Hematologic diagnostics use blood and bone marrow findings to identify anemia, infection, clotting problems, malignancy, treatment response, and bleeding risk. Nursing priorities are correct specimen handling, timely reporting of abnormal results, anticoagulation monitoring, and bleeding/infection prevention after bone marrow biopsy.

TL;DR - Read the CBC, Time the Coags, Protect the Biopsy Site

CBC trends show oxygen-carrying capacity, infection/inflammation patterns, and platelet-related bleeding risk. Coagulation tests guide heparin, warfarin, DIC, and clot-risk decisions. Bone marrow biopsy requires consent, prone or side-lying positioning, sterile technique, local anesthesia/sedation teaching, pressure afterward, bed rest, and clear instructions to report bleeding or infection.

Blood tests

  • CBC includes RBC, WBC, MCV, MCH, Hgb, and Hct.
  • Platelets help explain bleeding risk, malignancy patterns, hemorrhage, leukemia, and splenic involvement.
  • PT/INR, aPTT, D-dimer, fibrinogen, and fibrin degradation products help evaluate anticoagulation and coagulation disorders.

Bone marrow

  • Biopsy evaluates marrow function and helps diagnose blood disorders, infection, leukemia, lymphoma staging, and other cancers.
  • Older adults are at higher sedation risk; kidney function matters when analgesics or sedatives are used.
  • Postprocedure priorities are pressure, sterile dressing, bed rest, ice, and bleeding/infection monitoring.

Hematologic Diagnostics Care Map

Blood Collection and CBC Interpretation

Trend the cells

Specimen basics

Use standard precautions when collecting and handling blood specimens.

For coagulation studies, draw specimens at the ordered time and send them promptly.

Preliminary hematologic results are usually available before final reporting; abnormal results require provider notification for follow-up.

Anticoagulant dose changes are based on lab results and the prescription.

Cell patterns

Low RBC, Hgb, or Hct can support anemia, hemorrhage, or kidney disease.

High RBC, Hgb, or Hct can reflect erythrocytosis, polycythemia vera, COPD, or severe dehydration.

WBC elevation points toward infection or inflammation; decreased WBCs can occur with immunosuppression or autoimmune disease.

MCV/MCH help distinguish macrocytic patterns such as megaloblastic anemia from microcytic patterns such as iron deficiency anemia.

Coagulation, Iron, and Platelet Clues

Bleed or clot

Iron and platelets

Low iron can reflect iron deficiency, chronic blood loss, or inadequate intake; high iron can point toward iron excess, liver disorder, hemochromatosis, or lead toxicity.

High TIBC can support iron deficiency anemia or polycythemia vera; low TIBC can occur with malnutrition, cirrhosis, or pernicious anemia.

Increased platelets can occur with malignancy, polycythemia vera, or rheumatoid arthritis.

Decreased platelets can occur with enlarged spleen, hemorrhage, or leukemia.

Coagulation

aPTT monitors heparin therapy and can increase with vitamin K deficiency, DIC, liver disease, or heparin administration.

PT/INR monitor warfarin effect; therapeutic warfarin goals are higher than the usual INR range.

A negative D-dimer can help rule out PE or DVT in the appropriate clinical setting; a positive result can occur with DIC or malignancy.

Low fibrinogen or elevated fibrin degradation products can support serious clotting/fibrinolysis problems such as DIC or massive trauma effects.

Bone Marrow Aspiration/Biopsy

Diagnostic procedure

Before and during

Confirm informed consent and explain the procedure.

Position the client prone or side-lying to expose the iliac crest.

Teach that local anesthetic is used and that pressure, brief pain, and a crunching sound can occur as the needle enters bone.

Administer sedative medication if prescribed, cleanse the site, maintain sterile supplies, and assist the provider.

Afterward

Apply pressure and a sterile dressing to the biopsy site.

Keep the client on bed rest for the prescribed 30 to 60 min window to reduce bleeding risk.

Use ice to limit bleeding and bruising and mild analgesics for discomfort as prescribed.

Avoid aspirin and other medications that affect clotting unless the provider directs otherwise.

Biopsy Complications and Teaching

Bleeding/infection

Complications

Infection can occur at the aspiration site.

Bleeding can occur from the biopsy site.

Monitor for fever, increased WBCs, pain, swelling, drainage, or continued bleeding.

Report bleeding immediately and apply a pressure dressing as directed.

Home teaching

Check the biopsy site daily.

Keep the dressing clean, dry, and intact.

Report excessive bleeding or evidence of infection to the provider.

Return for suture removal in the prescribed 7 to 10 day window if sutures were placed.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Bone Marrow Biopsy

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse cares for a client scheduled for bone marrow biopsy.

Pre/intra/post

  • Pre: verify consent, position prone or side-lying, and explain pressure/brief pain expectations.
  • Intra: administer prescribed sedation, maintain sterile technique, cleanse the site, and assist the provider.
  • Post: apply pressure and sterile dressing, monitor bleeding/infection, use ice, and give mild analgesics while avoiding clot-affecting medications.

Complications and teaching

  • Potential complications include bleeding, infection, and higher sedation risk for older adults.
  • Teach daily site checks, clean/dry dressing care, reporting excessive bleeding or infection, and suture removal follow-up if needed.

Application Exercises

1

Which laboratory result supports suspected anemia?

  • A. Hgb 10 g/dL.
  • B. Iron 90 mcg/dL.
  • C. RBC 6.5 million/uL.
  • D. WBC 4,800/mm3.
A A hemoglobin of 10 g/dL is below the expected range and supports anemia.
B, C, D Iron 90 mcg/dL is expected, a high RBC count does not fit anemia, and WBC count does not diagnose anemia.
2

A client taking warfarin has an INR of 1.1. What should the nurse anticipate?

  • A. The dose may need to be increased.
  • B. The client is at high risk for bleeding from excessive anticoagulation.
  • C. The aPTT is the better test for dose adjustment.
  • D. A negative D-dimer determines the warfarin dose.
A INR 1.1 is expected for someone not taking warfarin but is subtherapeutic for usual warfarin anticoagulation goals.
B, C, D Bleeding risk rises with excessive PT/INR elevation; aPTT monitors heparin, and D-dimer does not guide warfarin dosing.
3

Which statement shows understanding of bone marrow biopsy teaching?

  • A. "I will stay in bed for about 30 to 60 min afterward."
  • B. "I will be flat on my back during the procedure."
  • C. "This test identifies which antibiotic treats infection."
  • D. "I will receive general anesthesia."
A Bed rest after the biopsy helps reduce bleeding risk.
B, C, D The client is positioned prone or side-lying; culture/sensitivity identifies antibiotics; local anesthesia with possible sedation is expected.
4

Which result is most useful when the provider wants to help rule out PE or DVT?

  • A. Negative D-dimer.
  • B. Low fibrinogen.
  • C. Elevated TIBC.
  • D. Decreased MCV.
A A negative D-dimer can help rule out pulmonary embolus or deep-vein thrombosis in the appropriate clinical context.
B, C, D Fibrinogen supports coagulation assessment, while TIBC/MCV support anemia pattern assessment.
5

Which post-biopsy finding should the nurse report promptly?

  • A. Continued bleeding from the biopsy site.
  • B. Mild discomfort relieved by prescribed analgesic.
  • C. Dressing remaining clean and dry.
  • D. Client resting during the prescribed bed-rest period.
A Bleeding is a potential complication and should be reported immediately while pressure is applied as directed.
B, C, D Mild discomfort, an intact dressing, and bed rest are expected postprocedure findings/actions.

Unit 5 · Hematologic Disorders · Chapter 40

Blood and Blood Product Transfusions

Blood and blood products replace lost volume, oxygen-carrying capacity, clotting factors, proteins, or platelets. Nursing priorities are compatibility verification, correct product/solution/tubing, first-15-to-30-minute reaction surveillance, older-adult overload prevention, and rapid response to transfusion reactions.

TL;DR - Match the Blood, Stay for the Start, Stop for Reaction

Before transfusion, verify the order, consent, labs, history of reactions, type/crossmatch or ABO compatibility, blood appearance, client ID, and product ID with the required nurse check. Prime blood tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride only and never add medication to blood. Most severe reactions happen early, so stay with the client at the start and stop the transfusion for suspected reaction.

Products

  • Packed RBCs treat blood loss, anemia, and kidney-failure-related needs.
  • FFP supports coagulation factor deficiency; platelets support thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction.
  • Cryoprecipitate can support hemophilia A, and albumin can support burns or hypoproteinemia.

Reactions

  • Acute hemolytic reaction can occur after a very small volume and can become life-threatening.
  • Febrile reaction includes temperature rise, chills, flushing, hypotension, and tachycardia.
  • Allergic, bacterial, and circulatory-overload reactions require different medication and positioning priorities.

Blood Product Transfusion Care Map

Products, Types, and Indications

Choose the component

Transfusion types

Standard donation uses compatible donor blood.

Autologous donation stores the client's own blood for anticipated future transfusion and is used only for that client.

Autologous donation can begin weeks before elective surgery and continue weekly if Hgb and Hct remain stable.

Intraoperative blood salvage collects, filters, and reinfuses sterile blood lost during a procedure within the ordered time window.

Products

Packed RBCs are used for excessive blood loss, significant anemia with findings, and kidney failure.

FFP is used for coagulation factor deficiencies, such as hemophilia-related replacement needs.

Platelets are used for thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction; platelets do not need ABO matching.

Cryoprecipitate can support hemophilia A, and albumin can support burns or hypoproteinemia.

Safe Administration

Verify twice

Before

Review labs and the prescription for the specific product.

Explain the procedure, obtain consent if required, assess reaction history, and obtain compatibility samples such as type and crossmatch.

Use large-bore IV access for most clients and inspect blood for discoloration, cloudiness, or excessive bubbles.

Follow the required two-person check for client identity, product identity, compatibility, and expiration.

During and after

Prime blood tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride only and use filtered blood tubing.

Initiate the transfusion within the prescribed time after obtaining the product to reduce bacterial-growth risk.

Remain with the client for the initial 15 to 30 min and monitor vital signs and infusion rate per policy.

At completion, obtain vital signs, dispose of the administration set per policy, complete documentation, and record the client's response.

Special Products and Older Adults

Fragile clients

Product-specific care

Platelets are fragile, require immediate infusion after arrival, and use special filtered short tubing.

FFP is infused as soon as thawed while clotting factors remain active and requires ABO compatibility.

WBC transfusions are uncommon because reaction risk is high; amphotericin B timing must be separated from WBC transfusion.

Washed RBCs can be used for clients with prior transfusion reactions or hematopoietic stem cell transplant history.

Older adults

Assess kidney function, fluid status, and circulation before transfusion.

Older adults are at increased risk for fluid overload, especially with cardiac or renal dysfunction.

Check vital signs every 15 min throughout transfusion for older adults to detect overload or reaction.

Use the prescribed smaller-gauge approach and avoid unnecessary concurrent IV fluids during transfusion.

Transfusion Reactions

Stop first

Hemolytic, febrile, allergic

Acute hemolytic reaction can occur immediately from incompatible blood; findings include chills, fever, low back pain, tachycardia, flushing, hypotension, chest tightness, tachypnea, nausea, anxiety, hemoglobinuria, and impending doom.

For acute hemolytic reaction, stop the transfusion, remove blood tubing, start 0.9% sodium chloride with new tubing, monitor vital signs/fluid status, and send the bag/tubing for testing.

Febrile reaction commonly occurs within 2 hr and can include chills, temperature rise, flushing, hypotension, and tachycardia; stop transfusion, give antipyretic, and start normal saline with new tubing.

Allergic reaction can occur during or within 24 hr; mild symptoms include itching, urticaria, and flushing, while anaphylaxis can cause bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, hypotension, and shock.

Bacterial and overload

Bacterial reaction can occur during or after transfusion from contaminated blood products and can cause wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, cyanosis, hypotension, and shock.

For bacterial reaction, stop transfusion, give antibiotics and 0.9% sodium chloride with new tubing, and send blood culture specimens.

Circulatory overload can occur any time when the rate is too rapid for the client; findings include crackles, dyspnea, cough, anxiety, JVD, and tachycardia progressing toward pulmonary edema.

For overload, slow or stop the transfusion, position upright with feet lower than the heart, and administer oxygen, diuretics, and morphine as prescribed.

Active Learning Scenario

Nursing Skill - Suspected Transfusion Reaction

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse plans care for a client who develops findings during a blood transfusion.

Reaction timing and medications

  • Acute hemolytic can be immediate; febrile commonly occurs within 2 hr; allergic occurs during or within 24 hr; bacterial occurs during or several hours after; overload can occur any time.
  • Medication support can include antipyretics for febrile reaction, diphenhydramine for mild allergic reaction, epinephrine/corticosteroids/vasopressors/oxygen for anaphylaxis, antibiotics for bacterial reaction, and diuretics/morphine for overload.

Core actions

  • Stop the transfusion for suspected reaction and maintain IV access with 0.9% sodium chloride using new tubing.
  • Remove blood tubing when indicated, monitor vital signs and fluid status, send blood products/tubing or cultures as prescribed, and notify the provider.
  • Use upright positioning with feet lower than heart for overload and feet-elevated low head positioning for hypotensive allergic reaction support as prescribed.

Application Exercises

1

During the first 15 min of packed RBC transfusion, what is the priority assessment?

  • A. Acute hemolytic reaction.
  • B. Whether consent has been obtained.
  • C. Whether the procedure was explained.
  • D. Blood culture results.
A Acute hemolytic reaction can occur early, even after a very small volume of blood product.
B, C, D Consent and explanation occur before starting; cultures are obtained if bacterial reaction is suspected.
2

Which actions are appropriate for a suspected allergic transfusion reaction? Select all that apply.

  • A. Stop the transfusion.
  • B. Maintain IV access with 0.9% sodium chloride using new tubing.
  • C. Administer diphenhydramine as prescribed.
  • D. Monitor for hypertension as the expected shock pattern.
  • E. Place the client upright with feet dependent for hypotension.
A, B, C Stop the blood, keep access open with normal saline/new tubing, and give prescribed antihistamine for mild allergic findings.
D, E Hypotension is the concern; feet-dependent upright positioning is used for overload rather than allergic hypotension.
3

Which findings suggest febrile transfusion reaction? Select all that apply.

  • A. Tachycardia after transfusion starts.
  • B. Flushed appearance.
  • C. Itching.
  • D. Hypertension.
  • E. No meaningful temperature change.
A, B Tachycardia and flushing can occur with febrile reaction, along with chills, hypotension, and temperature rise.
C, D, E Itching points toward allergic reaction; hypotension and temperature rise are expected febrile clues.
4

Which teaching is correct for a client requesting autologous donation before elective surgery?

  • A. "You can donate weekly if your Hgb and Hct remain stable."
  • B. "Your brother's donated blood counts as autologous blood."
  • C. "Unused autologous blood can be used for other clients."
  • D. "You should wait until the week of surgery to begin donation."
A Autologous donation uses the client's own blood and can occur weekly before surgery if blood values remain stable.
B, C, D Donor blood from someone else is not autologous, autologous blood is for that client only, and donation begins weeks before surgery.
5

Which action by a newly licensed nurse shows understanding when transfusing an older adult?

  • A. Obtains vital signs every 15 min throughout the transfusion.
  • B. Verifies blood compatibility with assistive personnel.
  • C. Administers dextrose-containing IV fluid with the blood.
  • D. Chooses an 18-gauge catheter because it is always required for older adults.
A Frequent vital signs help detect fluid overload or transfusion reaction in older adult clients.
B, C, D Verification requires qualified licensed staff, blood runs with 0.9% sodium chloride only, and older adults should not receive an unnecessarily large catheter.

Unit 5 · Hematologic Disorders · Chapter 41

Anemias

Anemia means the client has too little circulating red cell oxygen-carrying capacity. Think: identify the cause, restore the missing component, protect activity tolerance, and watch for cardiac strain.

TL;DR · Anemia

Low RBCs, low hemoglobin, or both reduce oxygen delivery. Prioritize oxygenation, fall prevention, energy conservation, occult blood screening when bleeding is possible, and correct medication teaching for iron, epoetin alfa, vitamin B12, and folic acid.

Most testable clues

  • Expected findings include fatigue, shortness of breath with exertion, tachycardia, palpitations, pallor, dizziness or syncope, and cold sensitivity.
  • Iron-deficiency clues include microcytic/hypochromic indices, low iron stores, elevated TIBC, and possible spoon-shaped nails.
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency can add a smooth sore tongue, paresthesias, and balance changes.

Priority nursing frame

  • Assist with ambulation when dizziness is likely, monitor oxygen saturation, and schedule rest periods.
  • Teach iron with vitamin C and away from milk when possible; stools can become green-black.
  • Monitor hemoglobin/hematocrit closely with epoetin alfa and watch for rising blood pressure or rapid hemoglobin increase.

Core Concepts

Anemia Pattern Recognition

ATI source-authored

Anemia is a sign of an underlying problem: blood loss, inadequate red cell production, increased red cell destruction, or deficiency of iron, folate, vitamin B12, or erythropoietin. The practical bedside question is whether the client can deliver enough oxygen to tissues.

Causes and risks

Blood loss can be acute or chronic from trauma, heavy menstrual bleeding, GI bleeding, surgery, or hemorrhage.

Rapid growth or demand states such as pregnancy, adolescence, and infection can increase need.

Hemolysis can occur with sickle-cell disease, G6PD deficiency, immune destruction, transfusion reactions, mechanical valves, or bypass exposure.

Malabsorption or poor intake can cause iron, folate, or vitamin B12 deficiency; older adults are at risk, and GI bleeding should be considered.

Bone-marrow suppression or aplastic anemia decreases RBCs and can also decrease platelets and WBCs.

Assessment and labs

Ask about fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, cold sensitivity, headache, irritability, dizziness, syncope, numbness, tingling, and sickle-cell pain or hypoxia.

Inspect nail beds and mucous membranes for pallor; spoon-shaped nails support iron-deficiency anemia.

Use CBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and RBC indices to sort size and hemoglobin concentration.

Low serum iron with elevated TIBC supports iron-deficiency anemia; ferritin reflects total iron stores.

Hgb electrophoresis and sickle-cell testing support hemoglobinopathy workups; bone-marrow testing supports aplastic anemia diagnosis.

Medication and Replacement Teaching

High-yield teaching

Iron and epoetin

Oral iron restores iron stores needed for hemoglobin and oxygen transport; severe anemia can require parenteral iron using Z-track technique.

Teach clients to take oral iron between meals if tolerated and pair it with vitamin C to improve absorption.

Milk decreases iron absorption; dark green to black stools can occur during iron therapy.

Epoetin alfa stimulates RBC production; monitor blood pressure plus hemoglobin and hematocrit twice weekly until targets are reached.

A rapid hemoglobin rise increases cardiovascular risk, so trend values rather than treating the number in isolation.

Vitamin B12 and folate

Vitamin B12 is needed for folate activation and DNA production; pernicious anemia or loss of intrinsic factor requires non-oral replacement routes.

Clients who lack intrinsic factor after gastric surgery need lifelong vitamin B12 replacement, commonly monthly injections; nasal therapy can be an option.

Do not assume oral B12 or dietary B12 will correct deficiency when intrinsic factor is absent.

Folic acid supports production of new RBCs and can be given orally or parenterally.

Large folic acid doses can mask vitamin B12 deficiency and can turn urine dark yellow.

Complication Watch: Heart Failure

Oxygen delivery

When hematocrit is low, the heart works harder to deliver oxygen, which can lead to tachycardia, palpitations, and heart failure. Nursing care focuses on oxygen as prescribed, oxygen saturation, cardiac rhythm, daily weight, transfusion when prescribed, and antianemia or cardiac medications as ordered.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Community Teaching for Anemia

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse educator is preparing a community session about anemia risk, manifestations, and testing.

Pathophysiology to include

  • Anemia can result from blood loss, decreased RBC production, increased RBC destruction, or deficiency of iron, folate, erythropoietin, or vitamin B12.
  • Reduced hemoglobin or RBC count lowers oxygen-carrying capacity, so tissue oxygenation becomes the central care concern.
  • Iron-deficiency patterns can reflect intake problems in pregnancy, adolescence, and menstruation, or blood loss in older adults and males.

Findings and TIBC

  • Expected findings include exertional shortness of breath, fatigue, tachycardia, palpitations, dizziness, syncope, pallor, nail changes, and cold sensitivity.
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency can add a bright sore tongue, paresthesias, and balance concerns.
  • TIBC indirectly reflects transferrin; low iron with high TIBC supports iron-deficiency anemia.

Application Exercises

1

A client has hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, hematocrit 21.5%, fatigue, and dizziness with standing. Which nursing actions fit this pattern? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assist the client with ambulation.
  • B. Monitor oxygen saturation.
  • C. Screen stool for occult blood if GI bleeding is possible.
  • D. Plan rest periods through the day.
  • E. Encourage prolonged uninterrupted activity to rebuild endurance quickly.
A, B, C, D Severe anemia increases fall risk, lowers oxygen-carrying capacity, can reflect occult blood loss, and causes fatigue that requires energy conservation.
E Activity should be paced; pushing endurance during symptomatic anemia can worsen oxygen demand and dizziness.
2

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client starting ferrous sulfate?

  • A. Take it with vitamin C when possible.
  • B. Take it with milk to increase absorption.
  • C. Expect stools to become bright red.
  • D. Stop after 14 days when symptoms improve.
A Vitamin C increases oral iron absorption.
B, C, D Milk decreases absorption, stools can become green-black, and therapy usually continues long enough to restore hemoglobin and stores.
3

A client had a gastrectomy. Which discharge teaching about vitamin B12 is appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Lifelong monthly injections can be required.
  • B. Daily nasal cyanocobalamin can be an option.
  • C. Oral B12 will be reliably absorbed because the stomach was removed.
  • D. Dietary animal protein alone will correct the deficiency.
  • E. The issue is loss of intrinsic factor needed for absorption.
A, B, E Lack of intrinsic factor after gastric surgery requires a route that bypasses the absorption problem, often lifelong injection or nasal therapy.
C, D Oral or dietary B12 is not reliable when intrinsic factor is absent.
4

Which integumentary finding is consistent with anemia?

  • A. Spoon-shaped nails.
  • B. Yellow mucous membranes.
  • C. Shiny hairless legs.
  • D. Absent skin turgor.
A Nail deformities, including spoon-shaped nails, can occur with anemia.
B, C, D Yellow membranes suggest jaundice, shiny hairless legs suggest peripheral vascular disease, and absent turgor fits dehydration.
5

A client asks how epoetin alfa therapy will be monitored. What should the nurse review?

  • A. Hemoglobin and hematocrit checks twice weekly until target values are reached.
  • B. Weekly erythrocyte sedimentation rate checks.
  • C. No blood pressure monitoring unless headache develops.
  • D. Therapy works by increasing folic acid production.
A Epoetin alfa requires hemoglobin and hematocrit trending, and blood pressure should also be monitored.
B, C, D ESR is not the monitoring focus, blood pressure can increase, and epoetin alfa stimulates RBC production rather than folic acid production.
