Unit 5 · Hematologic Disorders · Chapter 42

Coagulation Disorders

Coagulation disorders can look like bleeding, clotting, or both at the same time. The nurse watches the skin, gums, urine, incisions, brain, kidneys, extremities, labs, and hemodynamics together.

TL;DR · Coagulation Disorders

DIC is the big two-direction problem: clotting and bleeding happen together as clotting factors are consumed. Monitor for bleeding, microemboli, organ failure, low platelets/fibrinogen, prolonged clotting times, and increased fibrin breakdown markers.

Disorders to separate

  • ITP: autoimmune platelet destruction with normal platelet production and hemorrhage risk.
  • TTP: abnormal platelet clumping in capillaries, leaving too few circulating platelets and risking kidney, cardiac, and neurologic injury.
  • HIT: immune-mediated platelet drop after heparin exposure, especially prolonged unfractionated heparin.
  • DIC: microclots and hemorrhage at the same time, with organ ischemia risk.

Nursing priorities

  • Trend vital signs, hemodynamic status, clotting labs, and signs of intracranial bleed or organ failure.
  • Protect from injury, avoid NSAIDs, avoid needles when possible, and teach avoidance of Valsalva.
  • For DIC, correct the underlying cause, replace volume and clotting components, and monitor for microemboli.

Core Concepts

Bleeding Plus Clotting Risk

ATI source-authored

Coagulopathy means clotting does not work as expected. It can come from platelet problems, clotting factor problems, autoimmune processes, blood loss, heparin exposure, or widespread microclot formation that consumes clotting resources.

Risk pattern

ITP is associated with autoimmune platelet destruction and can follow viral or autoimmune triggers.

TTP involves platelet clumping in capillaries, which can cause ischemic complications and leave too few platelets circulating.

HIT risk increases with heparin exposure, especially unfractionated heparin and therapy longer than 1 week.

DIC can follow sepsis, cardiopulmonary arrest, trauma, hemorrhage, burns, obstetric complications, malignancy, or severe allergic reaction.

Expected findings

Bleeding can appear as epistaxis, gum bleeding, oozing from incisions, petechiae, ecchymoses, hematuria, or prolonged bleeding after venipuncture.

Shock or poor perfusion cues include tachycardia, hypotension, diaphoresis, and respiratory distress.

Microemboli can cause organ failure, decreased level of consciousness, oliguria, pain, and cyanotic nail beds.

HIT can present with lower-extremity redness, pain, warmth, and swelling due to thrombotic complications.

Labs and Immediate Care

DIC focus

Lab pattern

Hemoglobin can decrease with bleeding disorders such as DIC and ITP.

Platelets decrease in DIC, TTP, and ITP; decreased platelets and decreased fibrinogen point to depleted clotting factors in DIC.

PT, PTT, and thrombin time increase in DIC because clotting is delayed.

Fibrin split products and D-dimer rise in DIC as clots are broken down.

Blood typing and crossmatch can be needed because replacement of blood products may be part of care.

Care bundle

Assess and correct the underlying cause first, then prevent organ damage from microemboli and replace clotting components as prescribed.

Monitor vital signs, hemodynamic status, clotting labs, oxygenation, organ function, and neurologic status.

Administer fluid volume replacement, blood, platelets, and other clotting products as prescribed; monitor for transfusion complications.

Use bleeding precautions, protect from injury, avoid NSAIDs, avoid needles when possible, and teach the client to avoid Valsalva.

Heparin can be prescribed in DIC to reduce microclot formation and preserve clotting factors.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - DIC Plan of Care

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is developing care for a client who has disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Assess and trend

  • Monitor for microemboli such as cyanotic nail beds and pain.
  • Assess vital signs and hemodynamic status frequently.
  • Watch for organ failure and intracranial bleeding, including oliguria and decreased level of consciousness.
  • Monitor clotting factors and coagulation labs closely.

Prevent harm

  • Administer fluids, blood, platelets, and clotting products as prescribed.
  • Give supplemental oxygen and monitor response.
  • Avoid NSAIDs and unnecessary needles; use bleeding precautions and injury prevention.
  • Teach the client to avoid Valsalva because of cerebral hemorrhage risk.

Application Exercises

1

Which lab results support depleted clotting factors in DIC? Select all that apply.

  • A. Platelets 100,000/mm3.
  • B. Fibrinogen 120 mg/dL.
  • C. Increased fibrin split products.
  • D. Increased D-dimer.
  • E. Normal clotting times with no bleeding.
A, B, C, D DIC consumes platelets and fibrinogen and increases fibrin breakdown markers such as fibrin split products and D-dimer.
E DIC is associated with delayed clotting and bleeding risk, not normal clotting with no bleeding.
2

Which physical finding should the nurse expect with suspected DIC?

  • A. Epistaxis.
  • B. Bradycardia.
  • C. Hypertension.
  • D. Dry mouth as the defining sign.
A Unexpected bleeding from the nose or gums is consistent with DIC.
B, C, D DIC more often raises concern for tachycardia, hypotension, bleeding, and perfusion problems.
3

A client who has ITP develops cyanotic nail beds. What is the nurse's priority interpretation?

  • A. Possible small-vessel clotting requiring prompt reporting.
  • B. Expected bruising that can be documented at end of shift.
  • C. Normal finding after platelet destruction.
  • D. Finding that rules out microvascular ischemia.
A Cyanotic nail beds can signal microvascular clotting and should be reported promptly to prevent ischemic injury.
B, C, D Petechiae and bruising suggest impaired clotting, but cyanosis points to a more urgent perfusion problem.
4

Which medication might be prescribed in DIC to decrease microclot formation?

  • A. Heparin.
  • B. Vitamin K.
  • C. Simvastatin.
  • D. A routine antihistamine.
A Heparin can be used in DIC to decrease microclot formation and reduce consumption of clotting factors.
B, C, D Vitamin K promotes coagulation, simvastatin treats hyperlipidemia, and antihistamines are not the DIC microclot treatment.
5

Which history increases concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?

  • A. Heparin therapy for more than 1 week.
  • B. Warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation.
  • C. Placental abruption.
  • D. Folic acid deficiency.
A HIT is associated with heparin exposure, especially therapy lasting longer than 1 week.
B, C, D Placental abruption is a DIC risk; warfarin therapy and folic acid deficiency do not define HIT risk.

Unit 6 · Fluid/Electrolyte/Acid-Base Imbalances · Chapter 43

Fluid Imbalances

Fluid imbalance questions are usually asking one thing: is the client short on circulating volume, overloaded with volume, or shifting toward pulmonary edema or shock?

TL;DR · Fluid Balance

Hypovolemia looks dry and poorly perfused: tachycardia, thready pulse, orthostatic hypotension, oliguria, concentrated urine, poor skin turgor, dizziness, confusion, and fall risk. Hypervolemia looks overloaded: weight gain, edema, crackles, dyspnea, bounding pulse, hypertension, JVD, and pulmonary edema risk.

Fluid deficit

  • Common causes include vomiting, diarrhea, NG suction, sweating without replacement, diuretics, kidney disease, burns, hemorrhage, poor intake, fever, DKA, diabetes insipidus, and osmotic diuresis.
  • Labs can show increased hematocrit, increased BUN, high urine specific gravity, high sodium with dehydration, and increased blood osmolality.
  • Care centers on rehydration, I&O, orthostatic vital signs, mentation, gait stability, weights during replacement, and slow position changes.

Fluid excess

  • Common causes include heart failure, kidney disease, cirrhosis, excessive fluids, burns, corticosteroids, stress, hyperaldosteronism, SIADH, and excessive hypotonic fluids.
  • One kilogram of weight change in 24 hr roughly equals 1 L of fluid gain or loss.
  • Care centers on I&O, daily weight, lung sounds, edema, sodium/fluid restrictions, diuretic monitoring, Fowler's positioning, skin protection, and electrolyte trends.

Core Concepts

Fluid Compartments and Imbalance Types

ATI source-authored

Body fluid balance depends on volume, osmolality, electrolyte composition, and pH. Intracellular fluid holds about two thirds of body water, while extracellular fluid includes intravascular, interstitial, and transcellular fluid.

Deficit language

Dehydration is lack of body fluid from low intake or excess loss.

Hypovolemia, or isotonic dehydration, is loss of both water and electrolytes with decreased circulating volume.

Relative dehydration involves movement of water from plasma into interstitial space.

Older adults are hit harder because of decreased skin elasticity, kidney concentrating ability, muscle mass, and thirst response.

Excess language

Overhydration is too much fluid from excess intake or ineffective removal.

Fluid overload can dilute blood components and make values appear lower.

Hypervolemia is excess water plus electrolytes, often from impaired regulation or sodium-driven water retention.

Clients with fluid overload are at risk for pulmonary edema and heart failure.

Fluid Volume Deficit

Dry and underfilled

Assessment pattern

Vital signs can show hypothermia, tachycardia, thready pulse, hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, tachypnea, hypoxia, and decreased central venous pressure.

Neurologic and functional cues include dizziness, syncope, confusion, weakness, fatigue, and gait instability.

GI and renal cues include thirst, dry furrowed tongue, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, acute weight loss, and oliguria.

Skin and perfusion cues include diminished capillary refill, cool clammy skin, sunken eyes, flat neck veins, poor turgor, tenting, and diaphoresis.

Care priorities

Provide oral or IV rehydration, monitor I&O, and trend orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate.

Watch mentation because confusion can signal worsening imbalance.

Monitor weight every 8 hr during fluid replacement.

Use fall precautions: assess gait, encourage call light use, and help the client change positions slowly.

If hypovolemic shock develops, stay with the unstable client, give oxygen, monitor vital signs frequently, and prepare for crystalloids, colloids, vasoactive medications, and hemodynamic monitoring as prescribed.

Fluid Volume Excess

Wet and overloaded

Assessment pattern

Vital signs can show tachycardia, bounding pulse, hypertension, tachypnea, and increased central venous pressure.

Respiratory cues include crackles, cough, dyspnea, and possible pulmonary congestion on chest x-ray.

Other findings include peripheral edema, weight gain, distended neck veins, ascites, weakness, visual changes, paresthesias, altered level of consciousness, and seizures with severe sudden water excess.

Labs can show decreased hematocrit, hemoglobin, blood osmolarity, urine sodium, urine specific gravity, and BUN from dilution.

Care priorities

Monitor I&O, daily weight, breath sounds, peripheral edema, serum sodium, and serum potassium.

Maintain prescribed sodium restriction and fluid restriction; ask about over-the-counter products because some contain sodium.

Position in semi-Fowler's or Fowler's and reposition to protect edematous skin.

Use pressure-reducing support and inspect bony prominences.

Teach daily weights and provider notification for 1- to 2-lb gain in 24 hr or 3-lb gain in 1 week.

Complication Watch: Pulmonary Edema

Fluid in lungs

Severe fluid overload can progress to pulmonary edema. Watch for anxiety, tachycardia, increased vein distention, premature ventricular contractions, dyspnea at rest, restlessness, lethargy, change in level of consciousness, ascending crackles, and frothy pink-tinged sputum. Position in high-Fowler's, give oxygen or positive airway pressure as prescribed, and prepare for possible intubation, diuretics, nitrates, and morphine if blood pressure supports them.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Fluid Volume Excess Plan

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is planning care for a client who is experiencing fluid volume excess.

Assess and trend

  • Check ABGs, oxygen saturation, CBC, and chest x-ray results as prescribed.
  • Obtain daily weight, monitor intake and output, and document edema location such as pretibial, sacral, or periorbital.
  • Monitor vital signs, heart rhythm, and lung sounds for crackles.
  • Watch for dyspnea, altered level of consciousness, and worsening pulmonary congestion.

Reduce overload

  • Position in semi-Fowler's to Fowler's as tolerated and give supplemental oxygen as prescribed.
  • Reduce IV flow rate as prescribed and administer diuretics as ordered.
  • Limit fluid and sodium intake as prescribed.
  • Reposition at least every 2 hr and support dependent extremities to reduce edema-related skin injury.

Application Exercises

1

A client reports vomiting and weakness, has dry mucous membranes, and has blood pressure 102/64 mm Hg. Which findings support fluid volume deficit? Select all that apply.

  • A. Decreased skin turgor.
  • B. Concentrated urine.
  • C. Bradycardia.
  • D. Low-grade fever.
  • E. Tachypnea.
A, B, D, E Fluid deficit can cause poor turgor, concentrated urine, low-grade fever, and tachypnea as the body compensates.
C Tachycardia, not bradycardia, is expected as the body attempts to maintain blood pressure.
2

An older adult gained 5 lb in 48 hr. Which findings should the nurse expect with fluid volume excess? Select all that apply.

  • A. Dyspnea.
  • B. Edema.
  • C. Bradycardia.
  • D. Hypertension.
  • E. Weakness.
A, B, D, E Excess volume can produce dyspnea, edema, hypertension, and weakness from increased workload and retained fluid.
C Fluid excess is associated with tachycardia and bounding pulses, not bradycardia.
3

Which finding is expected in dehydration?

  • A. Moist skin.
  • B. Distended neck veins.
  • C. Increased urinary output.
  • D. Tachycardia.
D Tachycardia helps maintain blood pressure when circulating volume drops.
A, B, C Moist skin, distended neck veins, and increased urinary output fit fluid excess more than dehydration.
4

A long-term care client is weak, confused, dizzy when standing, and has a low-grade fever. Which action is best?

  • A. Initiate fluid restriction.
  • B. Check for peripheral edema first.
  • C. Encourage unassisted ambulation.
  • D. Monitor for orthostatic hypotension.
D Dizziness with dehydration cues requires orthostatic blood pressure monitoring and fall precautions.
A, B, C Fluids are usually offered for dehydration, edema points to excess, and unassisted ambulation increases fall risk.
5

Which finding requires urgent pulmonary edema action in a client with severe fluid overload?

  • A. Frothy pink-tinged sputum with dyspnea at rest.
  • B. Dry furrowed tongue and oliguria.
  • C. Flat neck veins and poor skin turgor.
  • D. Concentrated urine after vomiting.
A Frothy pink-tinged sputum and dyspnea at rest signal pulmonary edema; position high-Fowler's and support oxygenation.
B, C, D These cues point toward fluid deficit or dehydration rather than pulmonary edema from overload.

Unit 6 · Fluid/Electrolyte/Acid-Base Imbalances · Chapter 44

Electrolyte Imbalances

Electrolyte imbalance questions are high-risk because small shifts can change brain function, muscle strength, breathing, and cardiac rhythm.

TL;DR · Electrolyte Safety

Sodium drives water shifts and neurologic risk. Potassium drives muscle, respiratory, and cardiac risk. Calcium and magnesium imbalances can look neuromuscular first, then become seizure, dysrhythmia, or respiratory problems.

Sodium

  • Hyponatremia is sodium loss or water gain; water shifts into cells and can cause headache, confusion, lethargy, weakness, seizures, respiratory compromise, and coma.
  • Sodium replacement must be controlled; rapid correction increases neurologic injury risk.
  • Hypernatremia pulls water out of cells and can cause thirst, dry mucous membranes, restlessness, irritability, twitching, weakness, seizures, coma, and cardiac/endocrine concerns.

Potassium

  • Hypokalemia: weak/thready pulse, orthostatic hypotension, confusion, flattened T waves, U waves, constipation, abdominal distention, weakness, shallow breathing, and digoxin toxicity risk.
  • IV potassium is never given by bolus, IM, or subcutaneous route; monitor urine output and cardiac rhythm.
  • Hyperkalemia: slow irregular pulse, hypotension, weakness, paresthesias, diarrhea, oliguria, peaked T waves, widened QRS, and cardiac arrest risk.

Core Concepts

Electrolyte Pattern Recognition

ATI source-authored

Electrolytes are charged particles in body fluids. Differences between intracellular and extracellular concentrations maintain cell excitability and nerve impulse transmission. Ill and older adult clients are at higher risk for imbalance, and plasma labs do not directly measure electrolyte levels inside cells.

High-risk relationships

Sodium is the major extracellular cation and strongly influences water movement, fluid retention, fluid excretion, and movement between body spaces.

Potassium is the major intracellular cation and supports nerve impulses, cardiac tissue, lung tissue, skeletal muscle, cell metabolism, and acid-base balance.

Potassium and sodium have reciprocal actions, so GI losses, tap water enemas, diuretics, and fluid shifts can affect both.

Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia are especially testable because of neuromuscular excitability, seizure risk, and dysrhythmia risk.

Safety priorities

Trend level of consciousness, seizure risk, airway, respiratory effort, vital signs, I&O, and daily weight.

Use continuous cardiac monitoring when potassium is abnormal or dysrhythmia risk is present.

Report abnormal findings promptly and avoid rapid correction of sodium or unsafe potassium administration.

Coordinate nephrology, respiratory services, nutrition, and cardiology consults when replacement, oxygenation, diet, dialysis, or dysrhythmias are concerns.

Sodium Imbalances

Water follows sodium

Hyponatremia

Risk factors include sweating, diuretics, GI wound drainage, NG suction, low aldosterone, kidney disease, NPO status, low-sodium diet, hypotonic fluid excess, heart failure, kidney failure, SIADH, anticonvulsants, SSRIs, desmopressin, and older-adult chronic illness.

Expected findings include headache, confusion, lethargy, fatigue, muscle weakness, decreased DTRs, seizures, lightheadedness, dizziness, increased GI motility, cramping, and nausea.

Care includes sodium-containing foods or fluids when tolerated, lactated Ringer's or 0.9% saline as prescribed, water restriction if overloaded, I&O, daily weight, vital signs, and level of consciousness.

Severe hyponatremia can lead to coma, seizures, and respiratory arrest; use airway support and seizure precautions.

Hypernatremia

Risk factors include kidney failure, Cushing's syndrome, aldosteronism, glucocorticosteroids, excess sodium intake, water deprivation, hypertonic tube feedings without water, diabetes insipidus, heatstroke, hyperventilation, watery stools, burns, and excessive sweating.

Expected findings include thirst, hyperthermia, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, restlessness, irritability, twitching, weakness, decreased or absent DTRs, seizures, coma, dry mucous membranes, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and diarrhea.

Care includes level of consciousness, safety, vital signs, heart rhythm, lung sounds, oral hygiene, I&O, provider notification for inadequate output, water intake, sodium restriction, and loop diuretics if kidney excretion is poor.

Severe hypernatremia can cause seizures, convulsions, and death; maintain airway, monitor vital signs, use seizure precautions, and trend level of consciousness.

Potassium Imbalances

Cardiac rhythm risk

Hypokalemia

Risk factors include diuretics, digitalis, corticosteroids, aldosterone excess, Cushing's syndrome, vomiting, diarrhea, NG suction, laxative overuse, repeated tap water enemas, NPO status, kidney disease, alkalosis, insulin effects, TPN, water intoxication, and older-adult diuretic/laxative use.

Expected findings include decreased blood pressure, thready pulse, orthostatic hypotension, altered mental status, anxiety, lethargy, confusion, flattened T waves, prominent U waves, ST depression, prolonged PR interval, hypoactive bowel sounds, constipation, abdominal distention, weakness, reduced DTRs, and shallow breathing.

Replacement safety: never give potassium IV bolus, IM, or subcutaneous; monitor urine output, rhythm, respirations, oxygen saturation, bowel sounds, hand grasps, DTRs, and phlebitis with IV replacement.

Hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk and can lead to respiratory failure or cardiac arrest.

Hyperkalemia

Risk factors include kidney failure, ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, salt substitutes, high-potassium intake, rapid replacement, RBC transfusions, adrenal insufficiency, decreased insulin, acidosis, tissue damage, sepsis, trauma, surgery, fever, and myocardial infarction.

Expected findings include slow irregular pulse, hypotension, restlessness, irritability, weakness that can progress to ascending flaccid paralysis, paresthesias, diarrhea, hyperactive bowel sounds, oliguria, peaked T waves, widened QRS, PVCs, ventricular fibrillation, heart block, and asystole.

Immediate care includes stopping potassium infusions and supplements, keeping IV access, promoting potassium restriction, monitoring I&O and potassium level, and monitoring for hypokalemia while therapies lower potassium.

Severe hyperkalemia can require calcium gluconate, dextrose with regular insulin, sodium bicarbonate for acidosis, loop diuretics if kidney function is adequate, sodium polystyrene sulfonate, beta-2 agonists, patiromer, or dialysis.

Hypocalcemia and Hypomagnesemia

Neuromuscular clues

Hypocalcemia

Risk factors include low intake, lactose intolerance, malabsorption, diarrhea, steatorrhea, low vitamin D, end-stage kidney disease, wound drainage, alkalosis, pancreatitis, hyperphosphatemia, calcium chelators, and parathyroid removal or damage.

Tetany is the key manifestation; early clues include paresthesias of fingers and lips, muscle twitches, painful spasms, hyperactive DTRs, seizures, positive Chvostek's sign, and positive Trousseau's sign.

Cardiac concerns include prolonged QT/ST interval, torsades risk, decreased myocardial contractility, decreased heart rate, and hypotension when severe.

Care includes calcium and vitamin D replacement as prescribed, seizure and fall precautions, quiet low-stimulation environment, emergency equipment, and high-calcium foods.

Hypomagnesemia

Risk factors include celiac disease, Crohn's disease, malnutrition, alcohol use, diarrhea, steatorrhea, chronic laxatives, citrate from blood products, myocardial infarction, heart failure, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and medications such as aminoglycosides, cisplatin, cyclosporine, and amphotericin B.

Expected findings include increased blood pressure or dysrhythmias, PVCs, flat or inverted T waves, ST depression, prolonged PR, widened QRS, hyperactive DTRs, paresthesias, tetany, seizures, positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, constipation, distention, paralytic ileus, depressed mood, apathy, or agitation.

Care includes correcting concurrent electrolyte imbalances, magnesium-rich foods, stopping magnesium-depleting medications, oral replacement for mild cases, IV magnesium sulfate by pump for severe cases, and hourly DTR monitoring during IV therapy.

Low magnesium predisposes clients taking digitalis to toxicity; calcium gluconate should be available to reverse hypermagnesemia.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Hypokalemia Care

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is caring for a client who has hypokalemia and is completing a system disorder template.

Nursing care

  • Report abnormal findings, replace potassium as prescribed, and encourage potassium-rich foods when oral intake is appropriate.
  • Never administer potassium by IV bolus, IM, or subcutaneous route; use safe IV rates and assess for phlebitis.
  • Monitor urine output, respirations, oxygen saturation, cardiac rhythm, level of consciousness, bowel sounds, abdominal distention, muscle strength, and DTRs.
  • Monitor clients receiving digoxin because hypokalemia increases toxicity risk.

Team, teaching, complications

  • Consult nephrology for electrolyte/fluid management, respiratory services for oxygen support, nutrition for potassium-rich food choices, and cardiology for dysrhythmias.
  • Teach potassium-rich foods and prevention of potassium loss by avoiding excessive diuretics and laxatives.
  • Watch for respiratory failure and cardiac arrest.

Application Exercises

1

A client has sodium 133 mEq/L and potassium 3.4 mEq/L. Which treatment can cause this pattern?

  • A. Three tap water enemas.
  • B. 0.9% sodium chloride at 50 mL/hr.
  • C. Dextrose 5% with 0.45% sodium chloride and potassium at 80 mL/hr.
  • D. Antibiotic therapy.
A Repeated tap water enemas can dilute solutes and lower sodium and potassium.
B, C, D These do not match the source pattern for simultaneous low sodium and low potassium.
2

A client's potassium is 5.4 mEq/L. Which manifestation should the nurse assess for first?

  • A. ECG changes.
  • B. Constipation.
  • C. Polyuria.
  • D. Paresthesia as the only concern.
A Hyperkalemia can cause dangerous dysrhythmias, so ECG changes are a priority.
B, C, D Constipation and polyuria fit hypokalemia; paresthesia can occur, but cardiac rhythm risk is the priority.
3

A client has an NG tube to low intermittent suction. Which electrolyte imbalance should the nurse monitor for?

  • A. Hypercalcemia.
  • B. Hyponatremia.
  • C. Hyperphosphatemia.
  • D. Hyperkalemia.
B NG losses are isotonic and contain sodium, so hyponatremia is a concern.
A, C, D The source pattern does not point to increased calcium, phosphate, or potassium from NG suction.
4

Which condition is associated with hyperkalemia?

  • A. Diabetic ketoacidosis.
  • B. Heart failure causing low sodium.
  • C. Cushing's syndrome causing high sodium.
  • D. Thyroidectomy causing low calcium.
A Acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis can shift potassium out of cells and is associated with hyperkalemia.
B, C, D These options point to other electrolyte patterns rather than hyperkalemia.
5

How should the nurse assess for Chvostek's sign?

  • A. Inflate a blood pressure cuff on the arm.
  • B. Auscultate over the carotid artery.
  • C. Tap lightly on the cheek over the facial nerve.
  • D. Ask the client to flex the neck forward.
C Chvostek's sign is elicited by tapping over the facial nerve and watching for facial twitching.
A, B, D Cuff inflation assesses Trousseau's sign; the other actions assess different findings.

Unit 6 · Fluid/Electrolyte/Acid-Base Imbalances · Chapter 45

Acid-Base Imbalances

Acid-base questions are ABG pattern questions plus cause recognition. Read pH first, decide respiratory versus metabolic from PaCO2 or HCO3, then ask whether the lungs or kidneys are compensating.

TL;DR · ABG Pattern

pH below 7.35 is acidosis; pH above 7.45 is alkalosis. PaCO2 points to respiratory problems, HCO3 points to metabolic problems. Treat the cause, support oxygenation/airway, and watch for convulsions, coma, and respiratory arrest.

Respiratory

  • Respiratory acidosis is hypoventilation: CO2 rises from poor ventilation, obstruction, chest expansion problems, pulmonary blockage, neurologic weakness, respiratory depression, or inadequate mechanical ventilation.
  • Respiratory alkalosis is hyperventilation: CO2 falls from anxiety, fear, intracerebral trauma, salicylate toxicity, excessive mechanical ventilation, hypoxemia, shock, high altitude, or early asthma/pneumonia.
  • Nursing care focuses on oxygen, airway, gas exchange, breathing techniques, ventilatory support, bronchodilators, mucolytics, anxiety reduction, and rebreathing techniques when appropriate.

Metabolic

  • Metabolic acidosis is low bicarbonate or excess hydrogen: DKA, starvation, lactic acidosis, aspirin or alcohol toxicity, kidney failure, severe lung problems, pancreatitis, liver failure, or diarrhea.
  • Metabolic alkalosis is high bicarbonate or acid loss: antacids, blood transfusions, TPN, sodium bicarbonate, prolonged vomiting, NG suction, potassium depletion, diuretics, laxatives, Cushing's syndrome, and hyperaldosteronism.
  • Care varies by cause: insulin for DKA, rehydration and antidiarrheals for GI bicarbonate loss, antiemetics/fluids/electrolytes for gastric losses, and sodium bicarbonate when prescribed for low bicarbonate.

Core Concepts

Buffers, Compensation, and ABG Reading

ATI source-authored

Acid-base balance reflects hydrogen ion control. The lungs regulate CO2, the kidneys regulate bicarbonate, and ABGs are used to evaluate the balance. Small hydrogen changes can create major changes in cellular function.

Buffer systems

Chemical and protein buffers respond first by binding or releasing hydrogen ions.

Respiratory buffers respond by changing rate and depth of respirations to control CO2 and hydrogen ion levels.

Kidney buffers are slower but longer-lasting; kidneys reabsorb, excrete, or produce bicarbonate based on hydrogen ion needs.

Full compensation brings pH back into 7.35 to 7.45; partial compensation improves but does not normalize pH.

ABG steps

Step 1: look at pH. Less than 7.35 is acidosis; greater than 7.45 is alkalosis.

Step 2: look at PaCO2 and HCO3 together. PaCO2 outside 35 to 45 mm Hg points respiratory; HCO3 outside 22 to 26 mEq/L points metabolic.

Step 3: combine the pH name with the respiratory or metabolic source.

Step 4: check PaO2 and SaO2 for hypoxia.

Step 5: decide compensation: uncompensated has abnormal pH plus one abnormal driver, partial has abnormal pH plus both PaCO2 and HCO3 abnormal, full has normal pH with both PaCO2 and HCO3 abnormal.

Respiratory Acid-Base Patterns

CO2 problem

Respiratory acidosis

Hypoventilation increases CO2 and causes acidosis.

Causes include respiratory depressants, neurologic conditions affecting respiratory effort, muscle weakness, pneumothorax, hemothorax, flail chest, obesity, sleep apnea, airway obstruction, pulmonary embolus, ARDS, chest trauma, drowning, pulmonary edema, and inadequate ventilation settings.

Expected findings include early tachycardia and hypertension, then bradycardia and hypotension as acidosis worsens.

Other cues include dysrhythmias, anxiety, irritability, confusion, lethargy, possible coma, ineffective shallow rapid breathing, and pale or cyanotic skin.

Respiratory alkalosis

Hyperventilation decreases CO2 and causes alkalosis.

Causes include anxiety, fear, intracerebral trauma, salicylate toxicity, excessive mechanical ventilation, asphyxiation, high altitude, shock, early asthma, and early pneumonia.

Expected findings include tachypnea, rapid deep breathing, inability to concentrate, numbness, tingling, tinnitus, possible loss of consciousness, tachycardia, and atrial or ventricular dysrhythmias.

Care includes oxygen therapy, anxiety reduction, and rebreathing techniques when clinically appropriate.

Metabolic Acid-Base Patterns

HCO3 problem

Metabolic acidosis

Metabolic acidosis reflects decreased bicarbonate and increased hydrogen concentration.

Causes include DKA, starvation, lactic acidosis from heavy exercise/seizures/hypoxia, aspirin or alcohol toxicity, kidney failure, severe lung problems, low bicarbonate production, pancreatitis, liver failure, and diarrhea.

Expected findings include dysrhythmias, bradycardia, weak peripheral pulses, hypotension, tachypnea, headache, drowsiness, confusion, Kussmaul respirations, and warm dry pink skin.

Complications include convulsions, coma, and respiratory arrest.

Metabolic alkalosis

Metabolic alkalosis reflects increased bicarbonate and decreased hydrogen concentration.

Causes include antacids, base administration through blood products/TPN/sodium bicarbonate, gastric acid loss from vomiting or NG suction, and potassium depletion from diuretics, laxatives, Cushing's syndrome, or hyperaldosteronism.

Expected findings include tachycardia, normal or low blood pressure, atrial tachycardia or ventricular dysrhythmias, numbness, tingling, tetany, weakness, hyperreflexia, confusion, convulsions, and ineffective breathing from depressed skeletal muscles.

Care varies by cause: antiemetics, fluids, electrolyte replacement, and stopping the causative agent when potassium depletion drives the pattern.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Metabolic Acidosis

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is caring for a client with liver cancer whose ABGs reveal metabolic acidosis.

Risk factors to include

  • Excess hydrogen production can occur with DKA, starvation, lactic acidosis, seizure activity, hypoxia, aspirin toxicity, and alcohol toxicity.
  • Hydrogen elimination can be impaired by kidney failure or severe lung problems.
  • Bicarbonate production or retention can be reduced by kidney failure, pancreatitis, impaired liver or pancreatic function, liver failure, and diarrhea.

Care and complications

  • If DKA is the cause, administer insulin as prescribed.
  • If GI bicarbonate loss is the cause, give antidiarrheals and rehydration as prescribed.
  • If bicarbonate is low, administer sodium bicarbonate as prescribed.
  • Use seizure precautions and prepare life-support interventions if convulsions, coma, or respiratory arrest occur.

Application Exercises

1

A client is found with an empty aspirin bottle, confusion, lethargy, and deep rapid respirations. Which ABG pattern fits aspirin toxicity?

  • A. pH 7.68, PaCO2 38, HCO3 28.
  • B. pH 7.48, PaCO2 28, HCO3 23.
  • C. pH 6.98, PaCO2 30, HCO3 18.
  • D. pH 7.58, PaCO2 38, HCO3 29.
C Aspirin toxicity can cause metabolic acidosis: low pH with low bicarbonate.
A, B, D These patterns point to alkalosis rather than metabolic acidosis.
2

A client has a pneumothorax with chest pain and difficulty breathing. Which ABG pattern is expected?

  • A. pH 7.06, PaCO2 52, HCO3 24.
  • B. pH 7.42, PaCO2 38, HCO3 23.
  • C. pH 6.98, PaCO2 30, HCO3 18.
  • D. pH 7.58, PaCO2 38, HCO3 29.
A Pneumothorax can cause hypoventilation and CO2 retention, producing respiratory acidosis.
B, C, D These indicate homeostasis, metabolic acidosis, or metabolic alkalosis rather than respiratory acidosis.
3

A client has vomited for 24 hr. Which acid-base imbalance should the nurse anticipate?

  • A. Respiratory acidosis.
  • B. Respiratory alkalosis.
  • C. Metabolic acidosis.
  • D. Metabolic alkalosis.
D Prolonged vomiting causes loss of gastric acid and increased bicarbonate, producing metabolic alkalosis.
A, B, C Vomiting does not primarily create a respiratory pattern or bicarbonate-loss acidosis.
4

Which statement shows correct understanding of metabolic acidosis?

  • A. "It can occur with diabetic ketoacidosis."
  • B. "It occurs from myasthenia gravis."
  • C. "It is the expected pattern in asthma."
  • D. "It is caused by cancer itself."
A DKA produces excess hydrogen ions and is associated with metabolic acidosis.
B, C, D Myasthenia gravis and asthma are respiratory-acidosis risk contexts; cancer alone is not the specific source pattern.
5

A client with pancreatitis has metabolic acidosis. Which findings are expected? Select all that apply.

  • A. Tachycardia.
  • B. Hypertension.
  • C. Bounding pulses.
  • D. Hyperreflexia.
  • E. Dysrhythmia.
  • F. Tachypnea.
E, F Dysrhythmia and tachypnea are expected with metabolic acidosis.
A, B, C, D Tachycardia/hypertension/bounding pulses fit respiratory acidosis patterns; hyperreflexia fits metabolic alkalosis.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 46

Gastrointestinal Diagnostic Procedures

GI diagnostics test either contents, blood/urine markers, direct visualization, or contrast flow. The nursing pattern is preparation, medication and diet restrictions, airway after sedation, bleeding/perforation monitoring, and contrast elimination.

TL;DR · GI Diagnostics

For endoscopy, verify consent, allergies, labs, history, medication restrictions, bowel prep, and NPO status. After sedation or topical throat anesthesia, airway comes first and fluids wait until gag reflex returns. For barium studies, push fluids afterward and watch for white stools until contrast clears.

Labs and stool

  • AST, ALT, ALP, bilirubin, and albumin support liver evaluation; amylase/lipase support pancreatic evaluation; alpha-fetoprotein and ammonia support liver-related concerns.
  • Urine bilirubin/urobilinogen can support liver or biliary tract disorder evaluation.
  • FOBT screens for occult blood and colon cancer risk; stool samples can test for ova, parasites, bacteria, C. difficile, and DNA changes.

Scopes and contrast

  • Colonoscopy uses bowel prep, clear liquids, NPO after midnight, medication restrictions, moderate sedation, left-side/knees-to-chest positioning, and postprocedure bleeding/perforation checks.
  • EGD and ERCP require airway/respiratory monitoring and no oral fluids until gag reflex returns.
  • GI series use barium/contrast to define anatomic or functional abnormalities; barium enema comes before upper GI studies when both are ordered.

Core Concepts

Blood, Urine, and Stool Testing

ATI source-authored

GI diagnostic testing often starts with noninvasive samples. Explain what is being collected, how results will be given, and which foods or medications can interfere with results.

Liver and biliary markers

Liver function testing includes AST, ALT, ALP, bilirubin, and albumin.

Other GI-related blood tests include amylase, lipase, alpha-fetoprotein, and ammonia.

Elevated AST/ALT can occur with hepatitis or cirrhosis; elevated ALP can indicate liver damage.

Amylase and lipase elevations occur with pancreatitis; low albumin can indicate hepatic disease; elevated ammonia occurs with liver disease.

Urine bilirubin/urobilinogen supports suspected liver or biliary tract disorder evaluation.

FOBT and stool samples

FOBT is used for possible GI bleeding and can screen for colon cancer.

Guaiac card testing commonly requires three samples; positive repeated findings support GI bleeding.

Clients can need medication restrictions such as anticoagulants, NSAIDs, or aspirin before testing.

Diet restrictions can include avoiding vitamin C-rich foods, red meat, chicken, and fish before sample collection.

Stool studies can identify ova/parasites, C. difficile after broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, and DNA changes associated with colorectal cancer risk.

Endoscopy Preparation and Recovery

Airway first after sedation

Preprocedure checks

Verify understanding, signed consent, vital signs, allergies, baseline labs, and relevant diagnostic results.

Review medical history, cognitive status, support system, recent food or fluid intake, medication restrictions, recent barium/contrast studies, and fluid/electrolyte status.

Ensure bowel prep and NPO instructions were followed; inadequate preparation can cancel or delay the exam.

Teach medication, food, and bowel-prep instructions clearly before the day of the procedure.

Postprocedure priorities

Monitor vital signs and respiratory status, and maintain an open airway until the client is awake.

After EGD or ERCP, withhold fluids until the gag reflex returns.

Notify the provider for bleeding, abdominal or chest pain, signs of infection, respiratory compromise, or severe pain suggesting perforation.

Teach no driving or equipment use for 12 to 18 hr after sedated endoscopy.

Teach throat lozenges for persistent sore throat or hoarse voice after upper endoscopy if allowed.

Procedure Map

What each test sees

Scopes

Colonoscopy visualizes the rectum through ascending colon with a flexible scope through the anus; moderate sedation is common, and postprocedure flatus can occur from air instillation.

EGD visualizes the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum, can identify bleeding or gastric lesions, and can treat or dilate some findings.

ERCP passes through the mouth into the biliary tree through the duodenum, then contrast and x-rays visualize biliary ducts, gallbladder, liver, and pancreas.

M2A capsule endoscopy visualizes the small bowel over about 8 hr; the client swallows the capsule and later returns the recorder.

Sigmoidoscopy visualizes the anus, rectum, and sigmoid colon; sedation is not required, and the client lies on the left side.

GI series

GI series use radiographic imaging with or without contrast to define anatomic or functional abnormalities.

Upper GI imaging uses swallowed barium; small bowel follow-through traces barium through the small intestine.

Barium enema places contrast through the rectum into the colon and should be scheduled before upper GI studies when both are needed.

After barium, increase fluid intake, monitor elimination of contrast, and use laxatives as prescribed.

Teach that stools can be white for 24 to 72 hr and to report abdominal fullness, pain, constipation/retention, diarrhea with weakness, or delayed return to brown stool.

Complication Watch

Sedation, bleeding, aspiration, perforation

Oversedation

Difficult to arouse, poor respiratory effort, hypoxemia, tachycardia, and abnormal blood pressure. Assess airway first, give oxygen, monitor vital signs, call for help, and prepare antidotes as prescribed.

Hemorrhage

Bleeding, cool clammy skin, hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, and tachypnea. Assess the site, trend vital signs, monitor hemoglobin/hematocrit, and notify the provider immediately.

Aspiration

Dyspnea, tachypnea, adventitious breath sounds, tachycardia, and fever. Keep NPO until gag reflex returns, ensure awake/alert status before oral intake, encourage deep breathing/coughing, and notify the provider if gag reflex return is delayed.

Perforation

Chest or abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distention. Monitor diagnostics for infection such as elevated WBC and report unexpected findings.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Gastrointestinal Series

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario: A nurse is teaching a client who will undergo a gastrointestinal series of x-rays.

Description and indications

  • Radiographic images define anatomic or functional abnormalities of the esophagus, stomach, and intestinal tract.
  • An upper GI study uses swallowed radiopaque barium; a barium enema instills barium into the rectum and colon.
  • Indications include gastric ulcers, peristaltic disorders, tumors, varices, intestinal enlargement, and intestinal constriction.
  • Manifestations leading to testing include abdominal pain, altered elimination patterns, and GI bleeding.

Teaching points

  • Follow food and fluid restrictions for bowel preparation.
  • Additional radiographs might be needed over the next 24 hr when the small intestine is being visualized.
  • Increase fluids after the procedure if allowed and monitor elimination of contrast.
  • Report constipation or retained contrast, diarrhea with weakness, abdominal fullness, pain, or delayed return to brown stool.

Application Exercises

1

Which teaching belongs with polyethylene glycol bowel prep before colonoscopy?

  • A. Check with the provider about taking current medications during the prep.
  • B. Eat a normal diet until the bowel prep starts.
  • C. Expect the prep to start working the day after all of it is consumed.
  • D. Stop drinking the prep as soon as stool begins to pass.
A Polyethylene glycol can reduce absorption of some medications, so the client should check medication instructions with the provider.
B, C, D Clear liquids are used before prep, action begins within hours, and the full prescribed amount should be consumed.
2

A client is difficult to arouse after EGD. What is the priority action?

  • A. Assess the airway.
  • B. Allow the client to sleep.
  • C. Prepare an antidote before assessing.
  • D. Review preprocedure labs first.
A Airway is the priority after sedation when the client is difficult to arouse.
B, C, D Rest, reversal medication, and lab review can matter, but airway assessment comes first.
3

Which client statement shows understanding of a fecal occult blood test requiring three mailed specimens?

  • A. "I will keep taking warfarin while I complete the tests."
  • B. "I do not need any diet changes before collection."
  • C. "This test checks for parasites in my bowel."
  • D. "This is an easy way to screen for colon cancer."
D FOBT is used as a screening procedure for colon cancer and occult GI bleeding.
A, B, C Anticoagulants and certain foods can interfere, and ova/parasite testing is a different stool test.
4

Which teaching is appropriate before sigmoidoscopy? Select all that apply.

  • A. Increased flatus can occur after the procedure.
  • B. NPO status is maintained before the procedure.
  • C. Conscious sedation is routinely used.
  • D. Repositioning occurs throughout the procedure.
  • E. Fluid intake is limited the day after the procedure.
A, B Air instillation can increase flatus, and the client is NPO after midnight before the procedure.
C, D, E Sedation is not indicated, the client lies on the left side, and fluids are encouraged afterward if allowed.
5

A client has a suspected tumor of the jejunum. Which tests should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

  • A. Blood alpha-fetoprotein.
  • B. ERCP.
  • C. GI x-ray with contrast.
  • D. Small bowel capsule endoscopy.
  • E. Colonoscopy.
C, D Contrast GI imaging and capsule endoscopy can visualize the small bowel, including the jejunum.
A, B, E Alpha-fetoprotein supports liver cancer evaluation, ERCP evaluates biliary/pancreatic structures, and colonoscopy visualizes the colon.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 47

Gastrointestinal Therapeutic Procedures

GI therapeutic procedures are safety-heavy: protect nutrition, prevent aspiration and infection, watch fluid shifts, and teach the client how to manage a changed GI pathway after discharge.

TL;DR · Therapeutic Procedure Safety

Enteral feedings require placement and aspiration precautions. TPN requires sterile central-line care, glucose monitoring, and no abrupt rate changes. Paracentesis can improve breathing but can cause hypovolemia or perforation. Bariatric and ostomy care depend on early complication recognition plus very concrete discharge teaching.

Nutrition support

  • Use enteral feedings when the GI tract works but the client cannot safely swallow or meet calorie/protein needs.
  • Watch enteral feeding complications: overfeeding, diarrhea, aspiration pneumonia, and refeeding syndrome.
  • Use TPN when the client cannot absorb or meet nutrition needs enterally; protect the central line and monitor glucose, weight, I&O, and infection cues.

Procedure watch points

  • Paracentesis: have the client void, position upright, record baseline weight/girth/vitals, then monitor leakage, fever, I&O, mental status, and hypovolemia.
  • NG decompression: verify tube/suction function, include drainage and flushes in I&O, assess bowel sounds/girth/flatus, and maintain NPO status.
  • Ostomy care: a healthy stoma is pink or red and moist; report pale, bluish, purple, black, dry, or obstructed findings.

Core Concepts

Enteral Feedings and TPN

ATI source-authored

Enteral feeding priorities

Indications include inability to eat because of a medical condition, aspiration risk or swallowing difficulty, and increased metabolic demand from cancer therapy, burns, or sepsis.

Malnutrition cues include decreased prealbumin and decreased transferrin or total iron-binding capacity.

Overfeeding can cause abdominal distention, nausea, and vomiting; follow facility policy for residual checks and rate changes.

Diarrhea requires slowing the rate, notifying the provider, involving the dietitian, protecting skin, and evaluating for C. difficile when diarrhea persists or is foul-smelling.

Aspiration prevention includes confirming tube placement before feedings and keeping the head of bed at least 30 degrees during feedings and for at least 1 hr afterward.

TPN priorities

TPN is hypertonic complete nutrition, usually through a central line; PPN is less hypertonic, short-term, and given through a large peripheral vein.

Use TPN for impaired absorption, prolonged recovery, hypermetabolic states, chronic malnutrition, severe burns, short bowel syndrome, diffuse peritonitis, chronic pancreatitis, or gastric paresis.

Obtain daily labs including electrolytes; pharmacy customizes the solution based on current needs.

Never abruptly stop TPN or speed it up to catch up; abrupt rate changes can cause major blood glucose shifts.

Check capillary glucose frequently early in therapy, use sterile technique, change tubing and bag every 24 hr, and do not use the TPN line for other fluids or medications.

Paracentesis and NG Decompression

Procedure care

Paracentesis

Therapeutic paracentesis drains ascitic fluid to relieve abdominal pressure and improve lung expansion.

Preprocedure care includes consent, labs, baseline vital signs, weight, abdominal girth, bladder emptying, and upright positioning.

Postprocedure care includes pressure and dressing to the site, repeat vital signs/weight/girth, I&O, temperature monitoring, and documentation of fluid amount and appearance.

Teach low-sodium diet, avoidance of alcohol, puncture-site monitoring, slow position changes, and reporting mental-status changes.

Complications include hypovolemia from protein-rich fluid removal and bowel perforation, which can present with fever.

NG decompression

NG decompression relieves abdominal distention in mechanical or functional intestinal obstruction.

Presentation can include vomiting that progresses toward fecal material, absent or high-pitched bowel sounds, colicky abdominal pain, distention, and hiccups.

Maintain tube and suction function, include flushes and drainage in I&O, assess bowel sounds, abdominal girth, and return of flatus.

Monitor for tube displacement: decreased drainage, nausea, vomiting, and increasing distention.

Keep the client NPO, provide oral and nares care, and monitor electrolytes and hematocrit.

Bariatric Surgery Care

Therapeutic procedure

Bariatric procedures are used when nonsurgical weight-loss efforts have failed and usually require BMI greater than 40, or greater than 35 with comorbidities. Procedures can be restrictive, malabsorptive, or a combination.

Procedure comparison

Adjustable gastric band restricts stomach volume with a band near the proximal stomach.

Sleeve gastrectomy removes a large portion of the stomach, including tissue that secretes ghrelin.

Vertical-banded gastroplasty creates a smaller pouch with staples.

Roux-en-Y gastric bypass restricts stomach volume and bypasses the duodenum and much of the stomach to reduce absorption.

Postoperative priorities

Report anastomosis leak cues immediately: increasing back, shoulder, or abdominal pain; restlessness; tachycardia; or oliguria.

Do not reposition an NG tube after bariatric surgery because it can disrupt sutures.

Monitor airway, oxygen saturation, bowel sounds, abdominal girth, I&O, dumping syndrome, skin integrity, thromboembolism, and peritonitis risk.

Initial fluids can be as little as 30 mL at a time, then volume and frequency increase as prescribed.

Teach six small meals, limited early liquids or pureed foods, daily walking, vitamin/mineral supplements, and lifelong avoidance of overeating.

Ostomy Care

Discharge teaching

Type and output

Ileostomy drains from the ileum; output is frequent and liquid because the large intestine is bypassed.

Ascending colostomy output is more liquid, transverse colostomy output becomes more formed, and sigmoid colostomy output can become near-normal stool.

New ileostomies carry higher risk for fluid and electrolyte imbalance.

Empty the pouch when it is one-third to one-half full.

Stoma and skin

Assess visual ability, manual dexterity, cognition, culture, support systems, and wound-ostomy nurse needs before surgery.

The stoma should be pink or red and moist; pale, bluish, purple, black, or dry findings need urgent follow-up.

Protect peristomal skin with correct appliance fit, barriers, creams, and leakage checks.

Monitor for obstruction: abdominal pain, hypoactive or absent bowel sounds, distention, nausea, vomiting, and output changes.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Bariatric Surgery

Active Learning Scenario

Description and interventions

  • Restrictive procedures decrease stomach capacity; malabsorptive procedures bypass portions of the GI tract to decrease nutrient absorption.
  • Discuss weight, eating behaviors, and required lifestyle changes before surgery.
  • Arrange bariatric equipment and lifting support to protect the client and staff.
  • Monitor for anastomosis leak, respiratory compromise, bowel-sound changes, abdominal girth changes, and NG function if present.

Client education

  • Fluids resume in very small amounts and gradually increase.
  • Food resumes as small, frequent meals; early volume can be limited to liquids or pureed foods.
  • Daily walking, protein intake, nutrient-dense foods, and vitamin/mineral supplements support long-term safety.
  • Overeating can enlarge the surgical pouch and contribute to weight regain.

Application Exercises

1

A client develops a fever after paracentesis. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

  • A. Bowel perforation.
  • B. Bladder perforation.
  • C. Expected albumin shift.
  • D. Normal postprocedure response.
A Fever after paracentesis can indicate bowel perforation and needs prompt follow-up.
B, C, D Decreased urine output suggests bladder injury; pallor/hypotension suggest hypovolemia. Fever is not an expected finding.
2

Which actions belong in the plan of care for a client receiving TPN? Select all that apply.

  • A. Check capillary blood glucose as prescribed.
  • B. Give routine medications through the TPN tubing.
  • C. Monitor vital signs during the shift.
  • D. Change the TPN tubing every 24 hr.
  • E. Increase the rate to catch up if the infusion is behind.
A, C, D TPN care includes glucose checks, vital sign monitoring, and 24-hr tubing/bag changes to reduce metabolic and infection risks.
B, E Do not use the TPN line for other medications or abruptly change the infusion rate.
3

A paracentesis site is leaking clear, pale-yellow fluid. What should the nurse do?

  • A. Apply a dry sterile dressing.
  • B. Leave the site open to air.
  • C. Place the client flat.
  • D. Increase oral fluids immediately.
A A dry sterile dressing contains drainage and allows continued assessment.
B, C, D The site should be protected, the head of bed is usually elevated for lung expansion, and fluid replacement follows orders and assessment.
4

Which finding is expected for a new transverse colostomy?

  • A. A black, dry stoma.
  • B. A pink, moist stoma.
  • C. An appliance emptied only when full.
  • D. No mucus or blood in the first 2 to 3 days.
B A healthy stoma should be pink or red and moist.
A, C, D Black or dry suggests ischemia, the pouch is emptied before it is full, and early mucus or blood can occur after surgery.
5

A TPN bag has been hanging for 24 hr and still contains solution. What is the nurse's priority action?

  • A. Remove it and hang a new bag.
  • B. Continue the bag until empty.
  • C. Increase the rate to finish within the hour.
  • D. Stop TPN and leave the line saline locked.
A TPN bags should not hang longer than 24 hr because infection risk increases.
B, C, D Continuing the bag, catching up by increasing the rate, or abruptly stopping TPN creates safety risks.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 48

Esophageal Disorders

Esophageal questions tend to split into reflux teaching versus variceal bleeding emergencies. For GERD and hiatal hernia, reduce reflux triggers; for bleeding varices, think airway, circulation, bleeding control, and portal-pressure therapy.

TL;DR · Esophageal Safety

GERD and hiatal hernia care centers on lifestyle changes, acid reduction, diagnostic testing, and aspiration prevention. Esophageal varices can be silent until bleeding, then become a shock risk requiring large-bore IV access, blood preparation, vasoactive therapy, endoscopic treatment, and airway vigilance.

GERD and hiatal hernia

  • GERD occurs when gastric contents and enzymes reflux into the esophagus and irritate tissue.
  • Common triggers include high-fat/fried foods, chocolate, caffeine, peppermint, spicy foods, tomatoes, citrus, alcohol, tight clothing, bending, lying flat, and late meals.
  • Hiatal hernia manifestations are worse after meals and can include heartburn, reflux, chest pain, dysphagia, belching, fullness, and breathlessness.

Varices

  • Esophageal varices develop from portal hypertension, usually related to cirrhosis.
  • Bleeding cues include hematemesis, melena, deterioration in mental/physical status, shock, hypotension, tachycardia, and cool clammy skin.
  • Care includes large-bore IV access, vital signs, hematocrit monitoring, type and cross-match, bleeding surveillance, and support for endoscopic or shunt therapy.

Core Concepts

GERD Recognition and Care

ATI source-authored

GERD results from excessive reflux caused by incompetent lower esophageal sphincter function, pyloric stenosis, hiatal hernia, increased intra-abdominal or intragastric pressure, or motility problems. Untreated GERD can contribute to esophagitis, Barrett's epithelium, and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Risk and findings

Risk factors include obesity, older age, sleep apnea, NG tube, pregnancy, stress, hiatal hernia, lying flat, tight clothing, bending at the waist, and medications that relax the LES.

Food and beverage triggers include fatty/fried foods, chocolate, caffeine, peppermint, spicy foods, tomatoes, citrus fruits, and alcohol.

Expected findings include dyspepsia, regurgitation, pyrosis, painful swallowing, radiating neck/jaw/back pain, pain after eating, throat irritation, chronic cough, laryngitis, hypersalivation, bitter taste, flatus, and burping.

Pain often worsens with bending, straining, or lying down and improves with water, upright position, or antacids.

Diagnostics and medications

EGD can show tissue damage, esophagitis, strictures, Barrett's epithelium, and high-grade dysplasia; withhold oral intake until gag response returns.

Esophageal pH monitoring is the most accurate GERD diagnostic method; the client records foods, symptoms, and activity during testing.

Manometry measures LES pressure and esophageal peristalsis; barium swallow can identify hiatal hernia, strictures, or structural abnormalities.

Medications include PPIs, antacids, H2-receptor antagonists, and metoclopramide; monitor for adverse effects and separate antacids from other medications when needed.

Hiatal Hernia

Reflux teaching

A hiatal hernia is protrusion of part or all of the stomach through the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. Sliding hernia moves the gastroesophageal junction above the diaphragm; paraesophageal hernia moves part of the fundus above the diaphragm while the junction remains below it.

Expected findings

Sliding hernia can cause heartburn, reflux, chest pain, dysphagia, and belching.

Paraesophageal hernia can cause fullness after eating, breathlessness or suffocation sensation, chest pain, and worse symptoms when reclining.

Assessment can show pharyngitis and inspiratory or expiratory wheezing.

Complications include volvulus, obstruction, strangulation, and iron-deficiency anemia from gastric mucosal bleeding.

Care and teaching

Avoid late meals, reflux-trigger foods, tight abdominal clothing, straining, and excessive vigorous exercise.

Maintain healthy weight, exercise regularly, and elevate the head of the bed on blocks.

Barium swallow, EGD, and chest CT with contrast can help evaluate the esophagus and stomach; follow contrast precautions and encourage fluids when prescribed after IV contrast.

Fundoplication reinforces the LES; teach soft diet, avoiding carbonated beverages, ambulation, avoiding heavy lifting, and splinting the incision when coughing or moving.

Esophageal Varices

Bleeding emergency

Risk and recognition

Varices are fragile swollen veins in the lower esophagus that occur from portal hypertension, usually due to cirrhosis.

Risk factors include portal hypertension, alcoholic cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, and older-adult vulnerability from decreased immune/liver function and cardiac disorders.

Clients can have no symptoms until bleeding begins; bleeding cues include hematemesis, melena, and general physical or mental deterioration.

Bleeding can be triggered by Valsalva, heavy lifting, coughing, sneezing, and alcohol consumption.

Emergency care

If bleeding is suspected, establish large-bore IV access, monitor vital signs and hematocrit, type and cross-match blood, and monitor overt and occult bleeding.

Propranolol can reduce portal pressure prophylactically but is not for active hemorrhage.

Vasopressin constricts esophageal and proximal gastric veins; avoid in coronary artery disease unless specifically protected by the ordered regimen, and monitor for fluid retention and hyponatremia.

Octreotide can decrease bleeding from varices without lowering blood pressure.

Variceal Procedures and Complications

Risk reduction

Endoscopic variceal ligation

Endoscopic variceal ligation bands the varices to stop circulation, causing necrosis and sloughing; it reduces rebleeding and mortality.

Endoscopic sclerotherapy

Endoscopic sclerotherapy injects a sclerosing agent into varices, causing thrombosis; complications include bleeding, perforation, aspiration pneumonia, and stricture.

TIPS

TIPS can rapidly lower portal pressure when endoscopic and pharmacologic measures do not control bleeding; monitor for bleeding, sepsis, heart failure, organ perforation, and liver failure.

Balloon tamponade

Balloon tamponade is rare and temporary; tube migration can obstruct the airway, aspiration is possible, clients are often intubated, and tissue necrosis risk increases if left in place too long.

Hypovolemic shock

Hypovolemic shock from variceal hemorrhage requires close monitoring of vital signs, Hgb/Hct, coagulation studies, replacement of losses, and support for procedures that stop bleeding.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

Active Learning Scenario

Risk factors

  • Obesity, older age, sleep apnea, pregnancy, stress, hiatal hernia, and lying flat.
  • Foods and beverages that relax the LES: fatty/fried foods, chocolate, caffeine, peppermint, spicy foods, tomatoes, citrus, and alcohol.
  • Bending at the waist, tight clothing, and medications such as theophylline, nitrates, calcium channel blockers, anticholinergics, and NSAIDs.

Expected findings

  • Dyspepsia after eating and regurgitation.
  • Throat irritation, chronic cough, laryngitis, hypersalivation, and bitter taste.
  • Chest pain from esophageal spasm, increased flatus, and burping.
  • Pain relieved by drinking water, sitting upright, or taking antacids.

Application Exercises

1

Which medications should the nurse expect for a client with newly diagnosed GERD? Select all that apply.

  • A. Antacids.
  • B. Histamine2-receptor antagonists.
  • C. Opioid analgesics.
  • D. Fiber laxatives.
  • E. Proton pump inhibitors.
A, B, E Antacids, H2-receptor antagonists, and PPIs reduce acid exposure and irritation from reflux.
C, D Opioids and fiber laxatives are not GERD treatments.
2

A client is actively bleeding from esophageal varices. Which medication should the nurse anticipate?

  • A. Propranolol.
  • B. Metoclopramide.
  • C. Famotidine.
  • D. Vasopressin.
D Vasopressin constricts blood vessels and can be used to treat active variceal bleeding.
A, B, C Propranolol is prophylactic rather than for active bleeding; metoclopramide and famotidine do not control variceal hemorrhage.
3

Which finding is expected in GERD?

  • A. Absence of saliva.
  • B. Painful swallowing.
  • C. Sweet taste in the mouth.
  • D. Absence of burping.
B Painful swallowing can occur from esophageal inflammation or stricture.
A, C, D GERD can cause hypersalivation, bitter taste, and increased burping.
4

Which statement indicates understanding of hiatal hernia teaching?

  • A. "I can take my medications with soda."
  • B. "Peppermint tea can increase my indigestion."
  • C. "An abdominal binder will limit my symptoms."
  • D. "Hot chocolate at bedtime can help me sleep."
B Peppermint can decrease LES pressure and worsen reflux symptoms.
A, C, D Carbonation, tight abdominal pressure, chocolate, and bedtime intake can worsen reflux.
5

Which discharge statement shows understanding after fundoplication?

  • A. "I will lower my recliner after meals."
  • B. "I will eat three large meals daily."
  • C. "I will elevate the head of my bed on blocks."
  • D. "I will eat within 1 hr before bedtime."
C Elevating the head of the bed helps limit reflux after fundoplication.
A, B, D The client should remain upright after meals, avoid large meals, and avoid food close to bedtime.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 49

Peptic Ulcer Disease

Peptic ulcer disease questions center on mucosal erosion, H. pylori therapy, bleeding/perforation recognition, and post-gastric-surgery teaching. Separate gastric versus duodenal pain patterns, then prioritize shock and peritonitis cues.

TL;DR · Ulcer Risk and Rescue

Most peptic ulcers are linked to H. pylori, but NSAIDs, corticosteroids, severe physiologic stress, alcohol, chronic disease, and hypersecretory conditions matter too. Bleeding or perforation is an emergency: look for hematemesis, melena, boardlike abdomen, rebound tenderness, shock, and falling hemoglobin.

Pattern recognition

  • Gastric ulcer pain usually occurs 30 to 60 min after meals, is worsened by food, and can be associated with weight loss and hematemesis.
  • Duodenal ulcer pain usually occurs 1.5 to 3 hr after meals or at night, is often relieved by food or antacids, and can be associated with melena.
  • Stress ulcers occur after major physiologic stress such as burns, shock, severe sepsis, multiple trauma, head injury, or critical illness.

Care priorities

  • Test for H. pylori with gastric samples, urea breath testing, serologic testing, or stool antigen testing as ordered.
  • EGD confirms ulcers, evaluates treatment response, obtains gastric samples, and can treat bleeding.
  • Teach full medication adherence, NSAID/alcohol avoidance, smoking cessation, stress reduction, and reporting coffee-ground emesis or black stools.

Core Concepts

Peptic Ulcer Patterns

ATI source-authored

A peptic ulcer is erosion of the stomach, esophageal, or duodenal mucosa. When the mucosal barrier is eroded enough to expose tissue to acid and pepsin, bleeding and perforation can occur.

Risk factors

H. pylori: H. pylori infection is a major cause and can be transmitted through food, water, or body fluids.

Medication and stress risks: NSAIDs, corticosteroids, severe stress, family tendency, type O blood, excess alcohol, chronic pulmonary or kidney disease, and pernicious anemia increase risk.

Hypersecretion: Hypersecretory states, pancreatic gastrin-secreting tumors, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome increase acid exposure.

Health promotion: Health promotion includes limiting alcohol and caffeine, stopping tobacco use, stress management, avoiding NSAIDs when indicated, balanced diet, and regular exercise.

Expected findings

Dyspepsia: Dyspepsia can feel like heartburn, bloating, nausea, uncomfortable fullness, or hunger.

Pain pattern: Pain is often dull, gnawing, or burning at the midepigastrium or back.

Assessment: Assessment can show epigastric tenderness, abdominal distention, hematemesis, melena, and weight loss.

Ulcer timing: Gastric ulcers are classically worsened by food; duodenal ulcers are classically relieved by food or antacids.

Diagnostics and Medications

Treatment map

Diagnostics

H. pylori testing: H. pylori can be evaluated through gastric samples collected during endoscopy, urea breath testing, serologic testing, or stool antigen testing.

Bleeding labs: Hemoglobin, hematocrit, and stool occult blood help evaluate bleeding.

EGD: EGD provides definitive diagnosis, permits biopsy or H. pylori sampling, can be repeated to evaluate treatment, and can treat bleeding with interventions such as epinephrine or coagulation.

Post-EGD care: For EGD, monitor vital signs after sedation, keep the client NPO until gag reflex returns, and report pain, bleeding, or fever that can signal perforation.

Medications

H. pylori regimen: H. pylori therapy uses a combination regimen that can include metronidazole, amoxicillin, clarithromycin, tetracycline, acid suppression, and mucosal protection.

H2-receptor antagonists: H2-receptor antagonists decrease gastric acid and can be used with antibiotics for H. pylori or to prevent stress ulcers.

PPIs: PPIs strongly suppress acid production; teach not to crush sustained-release or enteric-coated forms and to avoid alcohol and NSAIDs.

Antacids: Antacids neutralize acid but can reduce absorption of other medications, so separate them from other oral drugs.

Mucosal protection: Sucralfate coats the ulcer; bismuth subsalicylate helps prevent H. pylori adherence but can darken stools and should not be combined with aspirin products without guidance.

Surgery and Complications

Emergency cues

Procedures

Surgery indications: Surgery can be needed for ulcers that do not heal with medical therapy, hemorrhage, perforation, or obstruction.

Gastrectomy or antrectomy: Gastrectomy removes all or part of the stomach; antrectomy removes the lower stomach.

Billroth II: Billroth II removes the lower stomach and connects the remaining stomach to the jejunum.

Vagotomy and pyloroplasty: Vagotomy cuts vagal stimulation to reduce gastric acid; pyloroplasty enlarges the gastric outlet to improve emptying.

Postoperative care: After surgery, monitor incision, lung expansion, NG drainage, bowel sounds, diet tolerance, and do not reposition or irrigate the NG tube without provider direction.

Complications

Perforation: Perforation causes sudden severe epigastric pain that can spread across the abdomen and radiate to the shoulder, plus rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness, hypotension, and tachycardia.

Bleeding: Bleeding can present with hematemesis, melena, shock findings, dizziness, confusion, and decreased hemoglobin.

Priority care: Priority care includes frequent pain/vital assessment, oxygen or ventilatory support as needed, two large-bore IVs, blood/fluid replacement, NG tube, lavage as prescribed, and preparation for endoscopic or surgical intervention.

Pyloric obstruction: Pyloric obstruction causes fullness, distention, nausea after eating, and vomiting of undigested food; prepare for NG decompression and fluid/electrolyte monitoring.

Dumping Syndrome and Pernicious Anemia

Post-gastrectomy teaching

Pernicious anemia

Cause and findings: Pernicious anemia can occur when intrinsic factor production is impaired; manifestations include pallor, glossitis, fatigue, and paresthesias.

Replacement: Lifelong monthly vitamin B12 injections can be required.

Dumping syndrome

Mechanism: Dumping syndrome occurs after gastric surgery when rapid gastric emptying shifts fluid into the abdomen and triggers vasomotor and GI symptoms after meals.

Early dumping: Early dumping can include fullness, weakness, diaphoresis, palpitations, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Late dumping: Late dumping can reflect glucose and insulin shifts, causing shakiness, anxiety, confusion, sweating, tachycardia, and palpitations.

Teaching: Teaching includes small frequent meals, high-protein/high-fat/low-fiber/moderate-to-low-carbohydrate intake, limiting fluids with meals, avoiding milk and concentrated sugars, and lying down after meals when symptoms occur.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Peptic Ulcer Disease

Active Learning Scenario

Alteration and prevention

  • Peptic ulcer disease is mucosal erosion of the stomach or duodenum with risk for bleeding and perforation.
  • Types include gastric, duodenal, and stress ulcers.
  • Prevention teaching includes moderate alcohol intake, tobacco cessation, stress management, NSAID avoidance when indicated, and limiting caffeine-containing beverages.

Risk factors

  • H. pylori infection.
  • NSAID or corticosteroid use.
  • Severe physiologic stress or hypersecretory conditions.
  • Type O blood, excess alcohol, chronic pulmonary or kidney disease, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings should the nurse expect with suspected peptic ulcer perforation? Select all that apply.

  • A. Boardlike abdomen.
  • B. Tachycardia.
  • C. Hypertension.
  • D. Circumoral cyanosis.
  • E. Rebound tenderness.
A, B, E Perforation can produce rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness, tachycardia, hypotension, and shock.
C, D Hypotension is expected with shock; circumoral cyanosis is not a key perforation finding.
2

Which teaching is appropriate for dumping syndrome after gastric surgery?

  • A. Eat three moderate meals daily.
  • B. Drink a full glass of water with each meal.
  • C. Choose a milk-based bedtime snack.
  • D. Increase protein intake.
D A high-protein, high-fat, low-fiber, low- to moderate-carbohydrate pattern helps reduce dumping symptoms.
A, B, C Use small frequent meals, limit liquids around meals, and avoid milk and concentrated sugars if they trigger symptoms.
3

Which statement shows understanding of H. pylori treatment?

  • A. "I should keep taking corticosteroids to heal the ulcer."
  • B. "A CT scan is the usual way to recheck treatment."
  • C. "I will take a combination of medications."
  • D. "A throat swab confirms whether the bacteria is gone."
C H. pylori treatment uses combination therapy, often antibiotics plus acid suppression or mucosal protection.
A, B, D Corticosteroids increase risk; EGD or H. pylori testing is used, not routine CT or throat swab.
4

Which findings fit a gastric ulcer? Select all that apply.

  • A. Pain relieved by eating.
  • B. Pain commonly waking the client at night.
  • C. Bloating or uncomfortable fullness.
  • D. Pain 30 to 60 min after eating.
  • E. Epigastric tenderness.
C, D, E Gastric ulcers commonly cause dyspepsia, post-meal pain, and epigastric tenderness.
A, B Pain relieved by food and night pain are more typical of duodenal ulcers.
5

Which teaching should be included for esomeprazole prescribed for a duodenal ulcer? Select all that apply.

  • A. Take it before a meal as directed.
  • B. Limit NSAID use.
  • C. Expect skin flushing.
  • D. Increase fiber because this drug requires it.
  • E. Crush or chew the capsule before swallowing.
A, B PPIs are taken before meals as directed, and NSAIDs should be limited because they can worsen ulcer risk.
C, D, E Skin flushing and required fiber increase are not expected teaching points, and sustained-release/enteric-coated forms should not be crushed or chewed.
