Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 50

Acute and Chronic Gastritis

Gastritis is a mucosal protection problem. Think COX/prostaglandin protection versus irritants, then distinguish sudden bleeding-prone acute gastritis from chronic gastritis that can injure parietal cells and cause pernicious anemia.

TL;DR · Mucosal Protection

Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining. Acute gastritis is sudden and can bleed; chronic gastritis develops slowly and can damage parietal cells, reducing intrinsic factor and causing pernicious anemia. Monitor I&O, electrolytes, bleeding cues, anemia cues, and medication safety.

Types and risks

  • Nonerosive gastritis is often associated with H. pylori infection.
  • Erosive gastritis is linked to NSAIDs, alcohol use disorder, and radiation therapy.
  • Risk factors include H. pylori exposure, NSAIDs/corticosteroids, alcohol, bile reflux, older age, radiation, tobacco, caffeine, stress, contaminated food/water, and autoimmune disease.

Care priorities

  • Assess abdominal discomfort, nausea/vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, bloating, hematemesis, occult blood, coffee-ground emesis, melena, and anemia cues.
  • Support fluids, electrolytes, small frequent meals, food-trigger identification, stress reduction, and avoidance of alcohol, caffeine, tobacco, NSAIDs, and irritating foods.
  • Escalate severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood, continuous vomiting, black stools, dehydration, or gastric outlet obstruction cues.

Core Concepts

Gastritis Patterns and Findings

ATI source-authored

COX supports gastric mucosal protection by helping produce prostaglandins, decreasing acid, increasing bicarbonate and protective mucus, and supporting submucosal blood flow. Gastritis develops when irritation and acid injury overwhelm that protection.

Type comparison

Acute gastritis: Acute gastritis has sudden onset, short duration, and can cause gastric bleeding when severe.

Severe acute injury: Severe acute gastritis from caustic irritants can cause tissue necrosis, perforation, scarring, and pyloric stenosis.

Chronic gastritis: Chronic gastritis can be related to autoimmune disease, H. pylori, or pernicious anemia.

Long-term damage: Long-term mucosal damage can cause erosive gastritis, ulceration, and increased stomach cancer risk.

Assessment cues

Expected findings: Expected findings include dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort, indigestion, headache, hiccups, upper abdominal pain or burning, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, bloating, distention, and weight loss.

Bleeding cues: Bleeding cues include hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, black tarry stools, occult blood, and gastric hemorrhage.

Anemia cues: Anemia cues include tachycardia, hypotension, fatigue, shortness of breath, pallor, lightheadedness, dizziness, and chest pain.

Timing: Acute gastritis manifestations can appear quickly.

Diagnostics and Nursing Care

Risk reduction

Testing

CBC and H. pylori: CBC evaluates anemia; blood/stool antibody or antigen testing and C13 urea breath testing can evaluate H. pylori.

Upper endoscopy: Upper endoscopy visualizes the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum and can permit biopsy, cauterization, polyp removal, dilation, or diagnosis.

Endoscopy teaching: Endoscopy teaching includes NPO status before the procedure, ride home after sedation, possible sore throat, and urgent reporting of chest/abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, or distention.

Nursing care

Fluid balance: Monitor fluid intake, urine output, and electrolytes because vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss.

IV fluids: Administer IV fluids as prescribed.

Meals and triggers: Help identify food triggers, provide small frequent meals, and encourage slow eating.

Avoidance teaching: Teach avoidance of alcohol, caffeine, tobacco, NSAIDs, and foods that irritate the stomach.

Ongoing monitoring: Monitor for gastric bleeding and anemia findings.

Medication Map

Pharm safety

Acid suppression

H2-receptor antagonists: H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine, cimetidine, and nizatidine decrease acid output; separate antacids by about 1 hr, monitor for neutropenia/hypotension, and give IV forms slowly.

PPIs: PPIs such as omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole, pantoprazole, and esomeprazole block acid production at the proton pump; do not crush enteric-coated or sustained-release forms.

Buffering and mucosal protection

Antacids: Antacids such as aluminum hydroxide or magnesium/aluminum combinations increase gastric pH; avoid in severe kidney disease, monitor constipation or diarrhea patterns, and separate from other oral medications.

Misoprostol: Misoprostol replaces prostaglandin effect, supports mucosal protection, and can be used with NSAIDs to prevent mucosal damage; it can cause abdominal pain and diarrhea and is contraindicated when pregnancy is possible.

Sucralfate: Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over mucosa and should be taken on an empty stomach; avoid smoking and alcohol and continue therapy even when symptoms improve.

H. pylori antibiotics

Combination therapy: H. pylori antibiotics can include clarithromycin, amoxicillin, tetracycline, and metronidazole; take the full regimen and report persistent diarrhea.

Complications

Escalation cues

Bleeding and obstruction

Gastric bleeding: Gastric bleeding can occur when inflammation extends deeply or chronic erosive gastritis bleeds slowly or profusely.

Bleeding care: Care includes vital signs, airway monitoring, fluid and blood replacement, CBC and clotting studies, NG lavage when indicated, and IV acid-reducing medications as prescribed.

Gastric outlet obstruction: Gastric outlet obstruction can follow deep inflammation and causes continuous vomiting, bloating, nausea, chloride loss, metabolic alkalosis, and severe fluid/electrolyte depletion.

Obstruction care: Prepare for NG decompression, diagnostic endoscopy, and fluid/electrolyte replacement when obstruction is suspected.

Dehydration, anemia, dumping

Dehydration: Vomiting or diarrhea can cause dehydration; monitor I&O, electrolytes, and need for IV fluids.

Pernicious anemia: Chronic gastritis can damage parietal cells, reduce intrinsic factor, impair vitamin B12 absorption, and cause pernicious anemia requiring monthly B12 injections.

Dumping syndrome: Dumping syndrome after gastric surgery causes fullness, weakness, dizziness, palpitations, sweating, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea after eating.

Dumping teaching: Teach lying down after meals, small meals, limited liquids with meals, high-protein/high-fat/low-to-moderate-carbohydrate intake, and octreotide self-injection if prescribed.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Acute and Chronic Gastritis

Active Learning Scenario

Alteration and pathophysiology

  • Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining from mucosal irritation.
  • Acute gastritis is sudden, shorter in duration, and can bleed.
  • Chronic gastritis develops more slowly and can damage parietal cells, causing pernicious anemia.
  • Gastric acid can overwhelm COX-1 supported mucosal prostaglandin protection, eroding mucosa and increasing ulcer and stomach cancer risk.

Risk factors

  • Bacterial infection such as H. pylori, Salmonella, Streptococci, Staphylococci, or E. coli.
  • Family history of H. pylori, prolonged NSAID or corticosteroid use, alcohol use, bile reflux, and autoimmune disease.
  • Advanced age, radiation therapy, smoking, caffeine, excessive stress, and exposure to contaminated food or water.

Application Exercises

1

A client with chronic gastritis asks about pernicious anemia. Which teaching is correct?

  • A. It occurs because acid-producing cells make too much intrinsic factor.
  • B. Monthly vitamin B12 injections can be needed.
  • C. Vitamin K is the primary replacement therapy.
  • D. It is caused by increased intrinsic factor production.
B Chronic gastritis can damage parietal cells, decrease intrinsic factor, and require monthly vitamin B12 injections.
A, C, D The issue is decreased intrinsic factor and impaired B12 absorption, not vitamin K deficiency or excess intrinsic factor.
2

Which discharge teaching fits aluminum hydroxide therapy?

  • A. Take it with meals only.
  • B. Expect diarrhea as the main adverse effect.
  • C. Separate it from other oral medications by about 1 hr.
  • D. Follow a low-fiber diet.
C Antacids can reduce absorption of other oral medications, so spacing is important.
A, B, D Aluminum antacids are taken on an empty stomach in this source context, can cause constipation, and do not require low-fiber intake.
3

Which interventions belong in the plan for acute gastritis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Evaluate intake and output.
  • B. Monitor electrolyte reports.
  • C. Provide three large meals daily.
  • D. Use ibuprofen routinely for pain.
  • E. Observe stool characteristics.
A, B, E I&O, electrolytes, and stool assessment help detect dehydration, electrolyte loss, and bleeding.
C, D Small frequent meals are preferred, and NSAIDs can worsen gastric irritation.
4

Which client statement indicates correct understanding of famotidine?

  • A. "This medicine coats my stomach lining."
  • B. "This should stop pain immediately after the first dose."
  • C. "I can take it at bedtime as prescribed."
  • D. "I only need to watch for nosebleeds."
C Famotidine can be taken at bedtime to suppress nocturnal acid production.
A, B, D Sucralfate coats mucosa, pain relief can take time, and the client should monitor for GI bleeding cues.
5

A client with chronic gastritis is scheduled for selective vagotomy. What is the goal of the procedure?

  • A. Increase gastric emptying into the duodenum.
  • B. Decrease gastric acid secretion.
  • C. Increase gastric mucus production.
  • D. Increase hydrogen/potassium ATPase activity.
B Selective vagotomy decreases vagal stimulation to reduce gastric acid secretion.
A, C, D Pyloroplasty affects gastric emptying; prostaglandin therapy supports mucosal protection; PPIs block the proton pump.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 51

Noninflammatory Bowel Disorders

Noninflammatory bowel disorder questions often ask you to separate functional bowel-pattern problems from mechanical emergencies. IBS is trigger and symptom management; obstruction is fluid, electrolyte, decompression, and surgery readiness.

TL;DR · Bowel Pattern vs Obstruction

IBS causes chronic bowel-pattern change without inflammatory labs. Hernia becomes urgent when irreducible or strangulated. Small-bowel obstruction causes vomiting, dehydration, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis; large-bowel obstruction causes marked lower distention and can cause metabolic acidosis.

IBS and hernia

  • IBS triggers include stress, large high-fat meals, caffeine, alcohol, and food intolerances such as dairy or wheat.
  • IBS care includes stress reduction, high-fiber/fluid intake, food diary use, and avoiding irritating foods and fluids.
  • Hernia becomes dangerous when bowel cannot be reduced or blood supply is compromised, causing obstruction, necrosis, and perforation risk.

Obstruction

  • Mechanical obstruction is blockage by adhesions, tumors, fecal impaction, hernia, volvulus, intussusception, fibrosis, or strictures.
  • Nonmechanical obstruction is decreased peristalsis from surgery, spinal injury, vascular problems, hypokalemia, peritonitis, or sepsis.
  • Care focuses on NPO/bowel rest, NG decompression, I&O, electrolytes, oral care, semi-Fowler's positioning, and surgery preparation when mechanical obstruction is suspected.

Core Concepts

Hernia and IBS

ATI source-authored

Hernia safety

Bowel herniation: Bowel herniation occurs when bowel displaces through weakened abdominal muscle into another area.

Incisional risk: Incisional hernias can follow poor incision healing from malnutrition, infection, or obesity.

Irreducible hernia: Irreducible hernia requires immediate surgical evaluation.

Strangulated hernia: Strangulated hernia cuts off blood supply and can cause obstruction, necrosis, perforation, abdominal distention, tachycardia, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fever.

Postoperative teaching: Postoperative teaching includes avoiding cough/strain/heavy lifting for 2 to 3 weeks, preventing constipation, and reporting redness or swelling.

IBS care

Pattern: IBS causes chronic diarrhea, constipation, bloating, and abdominal pain without expected inflammatory lab changes.

Expected findings: Expected findings include cramping, left-lower-quadrant pain with bowel pattern change, nausea, anorexia, bloating, belching, diarrhea or constipation, abnormal bowel sounds, incomplete defecation sensation, and mucus in stools.

Hydrogen breath testing: Hydrogen breath testing can evaluate malabsorption, impaired digestion, or bacterial overgrowth; the client remains NPO except sips of water before the test.

Teaching: Teach food diary use, stress reduction, avoidance of triggers, 2 to 3 L fluid/day, and about 30 to 40 g/day of fiber as tolerated.

IBS Medication Teaching

Medication safety

Diarrhea-predominant IBS

Loperamide: Loperamide decreases peristalsis and increases bulk for diarrhea-predominant IBS; it can cause drowsiness and is discontinued if there is no response after 48 hr.

Constipation-predominant IBS

Psyllium: Psyllium is a bulk-forming laxative; discontinue for abdominal cramping, rectal bleeding, or vomiting and monitor for electrolyte imbalance.

Lubiprostone and linaclotide: Lubiprostone and linaclotide increase intestinal fluid/motility for constipation-predominant IBS; lubiprostone is taken with food and water, and linaclotide is taken before breakfast.

Alosetron safety

Use restrictions: Alosetron can be used only in selected females with severe IBS-D resistant to usual therapy; it is contraindicated with bowel obstruction, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, impaired intestinal circulation, or thrombophlebitis.

Report immediately: Alosetron teaching includes reporting constipation, fever, increasing abdominal pain, fatigue, dark urine, bloody diarrhea, or rectal bleeding because ischemic colitis can occur.

Intestinal Obstruction Patterns

Mechanical vs nonmechanical

Mechanical obstruction

Causes: Mechanical obstruction can result from adhesions, tumors, fecal impaction, endometriosis/fibrosis, Crohn's strictures, radiation strictures, hernia, volvulus, or intussusception.

Small-bowel pattern: Small-bowel obstruction often causes severe fluid/electrolyte imbalance, metabolic alkalosis, epigastric or upper abdominal distention, visible peristaltic waves, and sudden projectile vomiting with fecal odor.

Large-bowel pattern: Large-bowel obstruction often causes significant lower abdominal distention, intermittent cramping, infrequent vomiting, diarrhea or ribbon-like stools around impaction, and possible metabolic acidosis.

Nonmechanical obstruction

Paralytic ileus: Nonmechanical obstruction, or paralytic ileus, comes from decreased peristalsis.

Risk factors: Risk factors include bowel manipulation during surgery, spinal fracture, vascular insufficiency, mesenteric emboli, hypokalemia, peritonitis, and sepsis.

Findings: Findings include vague diffuse constant pain, significant abdominal distention, and frequent vomiting.

Common obstruction cues: Common obstruction cues include inability to pass stool or flatus for more than 8 hr despite urge, abdominal distention, high-pitched sounds above the obstruction, hypoactive sounds below it, or absent sounds later.

Obstruction Care and Complications

Priority nursing

Care and procedures

Diagnostics: Diagnostics include flat/upright abdominal x-rays, endoscopy, and CT scan.

Nonmechanical care: Nonmechanical obstruction care includes NPO, bowel rest, bowel sound assessment, oral hygiene, IV fluids and electrolytes, pain management after diagnosis, ambulation, and semi-Fowler's position.

Mechanical care: Mechanical obstruction care includes surgery preparation and withholding intake until peristalsis returns.

NG decompression: NG decompression requires intermittent suction, patency/placement checks, irrigation as prescribed, gastric output monitoring, nasal skin checks, oral care every 2 hr, weights, vital signs, skin assessment, and I&O.

Complications

Dehydration: Small-bowel obstruction can cause dehydration from persistent vomiting; monitor hematocrit, BUN, orthostatic vitals, skin/mucosa, urine output, and specific gravity.

Hypokalemia: Monitor potassium closely because vomiting can cause hypokalemia and dysrhythmia risk.

Metabolic alkalosis: Metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss can cause hypoventilation, confusion, and hypercarbia.

Metabolic acidosis: Large-bowel obstruction can cause metabolic acidosis with deep rapid respirations, confusion, hypotension, and flushed skin.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Bowel Obstruction

Active Learning Scenario

Risk factors and findings

  • Mechanical risks include adhesions, tumors, fibrosis, strictures, volvulus, intussusception, hernia, and fecal impaction.
  • Nonmechanical risks include decreased peristalsis from neurogenic or vascular problems, electrolyte imbalance, and inflammatory responses.
  • Small-bowel obstruction causes severe fluid/electrolyte imbalance, metabolic alkalosis, and profuse projectile vomiting with fecal odor.
  • Large-bowel obstruction causes significant distention, infrequent vomiting, diarrhea or ribbon-like stools around impaction, and possible metabolic acidosis.

Diagnostics

  • Flat plate and upright abdominal x-rays evaluate free air and gas patterns.
  • Endoscopy can determine the cause of obstruction.
  • CT scan can identify the cause and exact location.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings should be reported for a client with small-bowel obstruction? Select all that apply.

  • A. Emesis before NG tube insertion.
  • B. Urine specific gravity 1.040.
  • C. Hematocrit 60%.
  • D. Potassium 3.0 mEq/L.
  • E. WBC 10,000/mm3.
B, C, D High urine specific gravity and hematocrit suggest dehydration; low potassium from vomiting can cause dysrhythmias and needs replacement.
A, E Emesis is expected with small-bowel obstruction, and this WBC is within the expected reference range.
2

Which actions belong in care for small-bowel obstruction with an NG tube? Select all that apply.

  • A. Document NG drainage as output.
  • B. Irrigate the NG tube every 8 hr.
  • C. Assess bowel sounds.
  • D. Provide oral hygiene every 2 hr.
  • E. Monitor NG tube placement.
A, C, D, E NG output guides fluid replacement, bowel sounds track resolution, oral care improves comfort, and placement checks help prevent aspiration and worsening distention.
B The source specifies irrigation every 4 hr or as prescribed, not every 8 hr.
3

Which findings fit small-bowel obstruction from adhesions? Select all that apply.

  • A. Large emesis with fecal odor.
  • B. Spasmodic abdominal pain.
  • C. High-pitched bowel sounds.
  • D. Flat abdomen with rebound tenderness.
  • E. Metabolic acidosis.
A, B, C Small-bowel obstruction can cause fecal-smelling projectile vomiting, abdominal pain, and high-pitched bowel sounds.
D, E Distention is expected, and small-bowel obstruction more commonly causes metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss.
4

Which finding suggests large-bowel obstruction from fecal impaction?

  • A. One bowel movement yesterday.
  • B. Small frequent liquid stools.
  • C. Passing flatus.
  • D. One episode of vomiting this morning.
B Small frequent liquid stools can pass around a fecal impaction.
A, C, D These do not best indicate large-bowel obstruction due to impaction; frequent vomiting fits small-bowel obstruction more strongly.
5

Which discharge instruction should the nurse include for IBS?

  • A. Keep a food diary to identify triggers.
  • B. Limit fiber to 15 to 20 g/day.
  • C. Eat three moderate to large meals daily.
  • D. Limit fluid intake to 1 L/day.
A A food diary helps identify triggers and tailor the diet to prevent exacerbations.
B, C, D IBS teaching includes increasing fiber to about 30 to 40 g/day, small frequent meals, and 2 to 3 L/day fluid intake as tolerated.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 52

Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease asks you to compare ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, and diverticulitis, then protect nutrition, hydration, electrolytes, infection risk, and perforation/peritonitis safety.

TL;DR · IBD and Diverticulitis

Ulcerative colitis usually starts in the rectum/rectosigmoid colon with bloody mucus/pus stools and LLQ cramping. Crohn's often affects the distal ileum, can involve all bowel layers, and causes fistulas, malabsorption, and RLQ cramping. Diverticulitis is infected/inflamed diverticula and can perforate.

Compare patterns

  • Ulcerative colitis can involve mucosa/submucosa, produce 15 to 20 liquid stools/day, and increase colon cancer risk.
  • Crohn's can affect mouth to anus, creates sporadic full-thickness lesions, and commonly causes fistulas.
  • Diverticulitis causes acute LLQ pain, fever, chills, tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, distention, and occult blood risk.

Priority care

  • Monitor I&O, weight, dehydration, potassium and other electrolytes, albumin, Hgb/Hct, WBC, ESR/CRP, and stool blood.
  • Teach small frequent high-protein, high-calorie, low-fiber meals during active disease, no caffeine/alcohol, vitamin/iron supplementation, and emergency care for obstruction or perforation cues.
  • Peritonitis is life-threatening: boardlike abdomen, rebound tenderness, fever, tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, and older-adult confusion need rapid escalation.

Core Concepts

Disease Map

ATI source-authored

Acute inflammatory disorders

Appendicitis: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, often from obstruction by a fecalith; adolescents and young adults are at increased risk.

Peritonitis: Peritonitis is inflammation/infection of the peritoneum after puncture, GI rupture, or peritoneal dialysis infection.

Gastroenteritis: Gastroenteritis is stomach and small-intestine inflammation triggered by bacterial or viral infection; vomiting and watery stools increase fluid/electrolyte and nutrition risk.

Chronic inflammatory disorders

Ulcerative colitis: Ulcerative colitis produces edema/inflammation primarily in the rectum and rectosigmoid colon and can extend through the colon in severe cases.

Crohn's disease: Crohn's disease produces inflammation and ulceration often at the distal ileum, can involve the entire GI tract, and can affect all bowel layers.

Diverticulitis: Diverticulitis is inflammation/infection caused when bacteria, food, or fecal matter becomes trapped in diverticula.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Pattern recognition

Expected findings

Ulcerative colitis: Ulcerative colitis: LLQ cramping, anorexia, weight loss, fever, 15 to 20 liquid stools/day, mucus/blood/pus in stool, rectal bleeding, distention, tenderness, and high-pitched bowel sounds.

Crohn's disease: Crohn's disease: RLQ cramping, anorexia, weight loss, fever, loose stools with mucus or pus, steatorrhea, distention, tenderness, and high-pitched bowel sounds.

Diverticulitis: Diverticulitis: acute LLQ abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, chills, tachycardia, and abdominal distention.

Shared labs: UC, Crohn's, and diverticulitis can have decreased Hgb/Hct, increased ESR/WBC, positive occult blood, and fluid/electrolyte changes.

Diagnostics

Magnetic resonance enterography: Magnetic resonance enterography can be used for IBD; the client remains NPO beforehand and might drink contrast.

Ulcerative colitis: Ulcerative colitis can be diagnosed by sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy; CT or MRI can identify abscesses.

Crohn's disease: Crohn's diagnostics include endoscopy, capsule endoscopy, proctosigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy/sigmoidoscopy, ultrasound, x-ray, and CT scan for bowel thickening.

Barium enema: Barium enema can help distinguish ulcerative colitis and show diverticulosis, but it is contraindicated with diverticulitis due to perforation risk.

Care and Medication Safety

Inflammation control

Nursing care

Teaching: Teach the usual course of the disease, medication therapy, vitamins, food-trigger identification, and colonoscopy monitoring because colon cancer risk increases.

Monitoring: Monitor potassium and other electrolytes, I&O, dehydration, weight, and stool count.

Active UC/Crohn's nutrition: During active UC/Crohn's, teach high-protein, high-calorie, low-fiber intake, small frequent meals, caffeine/alcohol avoidance, multivitamin with iron, protein supplements, and weekly weights.

Severe diverticulitis: Severe diverticulitis can require hospitalization, NPO status, NG suction, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, and opioid analgesics.

Medication map

Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine reduces intestinal mucosal inflammation; monitor CBC, kidney and hepatic function, and teach full water intake, sun avoidance, folic acid, and reporting sore throat/rash/bruising/fever.

5-ASA options: Mesalamine, balsalazide, and olsalazine are nonsulfonamide 5-ASA options; monitor kidney toxicity and report headache or GI problems.

Corticosteroids: Corticosteroids induce remission but are not long-term therapy; taper slowly, monitor BP/electrolytes/glucose, and report infection or fluid retention.

Immunosuppressants and immunomodulators: Immunosuppressants and immunomodulators increase infection/bleeding risk; monitor CBC, liver enzymes, coagulation studies, pancreatitis, neutropenia, and possible TB reactivation.

Antidiarrheals: Antidiarrheals reduce stool frequency but can precipitate toxic megacolon; monitor fever, hypotension, distention, and decreased bowel sounds.

Procedures and Complications

Escalation cues

Procedures

Surgery indications: Surgery is considered when medical therapy fails or complications occur, such as bowel perforation or colon cancer.

Procedure types: Ulcerative colitis surgery can include colectomy with or without ileostomy; Crohn's procedures can include stricturoplasty or fistula repair; diverticulitis can require colon resection with or without colostomy.

Stoma planning: When a stoma is planned, collaborate with an enterostomal therapy nurse; after ileostomy, output can reach 1,000 mL/day, so fluid-volume deficit prevention matters.

Complications

Peritonitis cues: Peritonitis cues include rigid boardlike abdomen, abdominal distention, nausea/vomiting, rebound tenderness, tachycardia, fever, and older-adult confusion.

Complication risks: Complications include bleeding, fluid/electrolyte imbalance, peritonitis, abscess/fistula formation, and toxic megacolon.

Toxic megacolon: Toxic megacolon requires NG suction, IV fluids/electrolytes, antibiotics/corticosteroids as prescribed, and surgery preparation if no improvement occurs within 72 hr.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Diverticulitis

Active Learning Scenario

Pathophysiology and findings

  • Diverticulitis is inflammation and infection of bowel mucosa when bacteria or fecal material becomes trapped in diverticula.
  • Risk factors include older age and male sex.
  • Expected findings can include decreased hemoglobin/hematocrit and stool positive for occult blood.
  • Diagnostics can include abdominal x-ray, CT scan, colonoscopy, and sigmoidoscopy when clinically appropriate.

Diet teaching

  • Use clear liquids until manifestations subside.
  • Advance to low-fiber foods once solid foods are tolerated.
  • Slowly advance to a high-fiber diet after inflammation resolves.
  • Avoid seeds or indigestible material such as nuts, popcorn, and seeds; avoid alcohol and limit fat intake.

Application Exercises

1

Which blood laboratory results should increase during an acute Crohn's exacerbation? Select all that apply.

  • A. Hematocrit.
  • B. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
  • C. WBC count.
  • D. Folic acid.
  • E. Albumin.
B, C ESR and WBC increase with inflammation and active disease.
A, D, E Hematocrit can decrease with chronic blood loss, and folic acid/albumin can decrease with malabsorption.
2

A client taking prednisone for IBD reports several findings. Which is the priority?

  • A. Difficulty sleeping.
  • B. Glucose in the urine.
  • C. Elevated body temperature.
  • D. Weight gain over 6 months.
C Prednisone can cause immunosuppression, so fever or other infection cues are the priority.
A, B, D Insomnia, hyperglycemia, and fluid-related weight gain can occur, but infection risk is the immediate priority.
3

Which sulfasalazine teaching should the nurse include?

  • A. Take it 2 hr after eating.
  • B. Stop it if skin or urine turns yellow-orange.
  • C. Notify the provider for a sore throat.
  • D. Expect black stools.
C Sore throat can signal infection or blood dyscrasia and should be reported.
A, B, D Take after meals with water; yellow-orange discoloration can be harmless; black stools can indicate GI bleeding and are not expected.
4

Which discharge instruction fits Crohn's disease nutrition teaching?

  • A. Decrease calorie-dense foods.
  • B. Use canned protein supplements.
  • C. Increase high-fiber foods during exacerbation.
  • D. Eat high-residue foods.
B High-protein supplements can support nutrition when Crohn's causes malabsorption and weight loss.
A, C, D High-calorie/high-protein and low-fiber/low-residue intake is recommended during active inflammation.
5

Which statement shows understanding of ulcerative colitis teaching?

  • A. "I will limit fiber in my diet during active symptoms."
  • B. "I will restrict fluids with meals."
  • C. "I will switch from coffee to black tea."
  • D. "I will choose cold foods when my stomach is upset."
A Low-fiber foods can reduce bowel stimulation during active ulcerative colitis.
B, C, D Fluid restriction with meals is dumping-syndrome teaching, caffeine can worsen diarrhea/cramping, and cold foods can increase motility.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 53

Cholecystitis and Cholelithiasis

Gallbladder disease is about blocked bile flow: recognize biliary colic, obstructed duct findings, atypical older-adult presentations, and post-procedure drainage or bile-leak red flags.

TL;DR · Biliary Obstruction

Cholecystitis is gallbladder-wall inflammation, usually from gallstones obstructing the cystic or common bile duct. Think RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder, pain after high-fat foods, nausea/vomiting, fever, and obstructed-bile cues such as jaundice, dark urine, clay stools, steatorrhea, and pruritus.

Recognize

  • Risk is higher with female sex, estrogen therapy or some oral contraceptives, obesity/high cholesterol, older age, type 2 diabetes, Crohn's disease, rapid weight loss, and some ancestry patterns.
  • Murphy's sign is pain with deep inspiration during right subcostal palpation; Blumberg's sign is rebound tenderness.
  • Older adults might have no pain or fever; delirium or localized tenderness can be the first clue.

Act

  • Use labs and imaging to separate inflammation, duct obstruction, liver involvement, and pancreatic involvement.
  • Manage pain with prescribed analgesics; bile acids can dissolve cholesterol stones gradually but are not acute pain relief.
  • After cholecystectomy, monitor drainage, bile-leak findings, bile peritonitis, infection, and return of stool color.

Core Concepts

Disease Map

ATI source-authored

Pathophysiology

Cholecystitis: Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder wall, most often when gallstones obstruct bile flow from the gallbladder toward the duodenum.

Cholelithiasis: Cholelithiasis means stones are present in the gallbladder; stones form when bile or cholesterol precipitates.

Obstruction: Obstruction can back up bile, inflame the gallbladder, obstruct the pancreatic duct, cause pancreatitis, or progress to rupture and secondary peritonitis.

Prevention and risk

Health promotion: Health promotion includes a low-fat diet with HDL-supporting foods, regular exercise, and no smoking.

Common risk factors: Common risk factors include female sex, estrogen exposure, obesity, high cholesterol, genetics, older age, type 2 diabetes, Crohn's disease, low-calorie liquid protein diets, and rapid weight loss.

Older adults: Older adults can present atypically, so mental-status change or localized tenderness deserves attention even without classic pain or fever.

Assessment and Diagnostics

Obstruction cues

Expected findings

Pain: Classic pain is sharp RUQ pain that can radiate to the right shoulder.

Biliary colic: Biliary colic after high-fat foods can cause intense pain, tachycardia, pallor, diaphoresis, nausea, and vomiting.

Other findings: Other findings include Murphy's sign, rebound tenderness, dyspepsia, belching, flatulence, and fever.

Obstructed bile flow: Chronic or obstructed bile flow can cause jaundice, icterus, clay-colored stools, steatorrhea, dark urine, and pruritus.

Testing logic

Inflammation: WBC elevation supports inflammation.

Bilirubin: Direct, indirect, and total bilirubin can rise when a bile duct is obstructed.

Pancreatic or liver involvement: Amylase and lipase can rise with pancreatic involvement; AST, LDH, and ALP can rise with liver dysfunction or common bile duct obstruction.

Imaging: Ultrasound visualizes gallstones and common bile duct dilation; CT or x-ray can show calcified stones or an enlarged gallbladder.

Biliary procedures: HIDA evaluates biliary patency; ERCP can visualize the duct and remove stones with sphincterotomy; MRCP helps determine cause with MRI plus contrast.

Medications and Procedures

Pain and stone removal

Pain control and bile acids

Acute biliary pain: Prescribed opioids such as morphine or hydromorphone are preferred for acute biliary pain; ketorolac can be used for mild to moderate pain, with GI bleeding monitoring.

Bile acids: Bile acids such as chenodiol or ursodiol gradually dissolve cholesterol-based stones. Use caution with liver disorders or varices, report abdominal pain/diarrhea/vomiting, and expect therapy to be limited to about 2 years with ultrasound monitoring during the first year.

Stone removal and surgery

Lithotripsy: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy can break small cholesterol stones in selected nonsurgical candidates; teach that repeated treatments and procedural pain from spasms or stone movement can occur.

Cholecystectomy: Cholecystectomy can be laparoscopic, minimally invasive through a natural orifice, or open. Laparoscopic discharge is often within 24 hr; open surgery can require a longer stay.

Drain and T-tube care

Open procedure drains: Open procedures can include a Jackson-Pratt drain or T-tube. Monitor amount, color, skin condition, bile leakage, infection, stool color, and food response.

T-tube priorities: If a T-tube is present, report absent drainage with nausea and pain, clamp before and after meals if prescribed, and monitor for bile peritonitis: pain, fever, and jaundice.

Postoperative Teaching and Complications

Safety priorities

Postoperative teaching

Laparoscopic surgery: After laparoscopic surgery, ambulate frequently to decrease free-air pain under the right clavicle, shoulder, or scapula.

Bile leak cues: Report pain, vomiting, or abdominal distention because these can indicate a bile leak.

Open approach: For an open approach, resume activity gradually, avoid heavy lifting for 4 to 6 weeks, shower instead of bathing until tubes are removed, and report sudden drainage increase, foul odor, pain, fever, or jaundice.

Diet teaching: Diet teaching includes low-fat foods, reduced dairy, avoiding fried foods/chocolate/nuts/gravies and gas-forming foods, small frequent meals, weight reduction if indicated, and prescribed fat-soluble vitamins or bile salts.

Complications

Bile duct obstruction: Bile duct obstruction can lead to ischemia, gangrene, rupture, abscess, or peritonitis with rigid boardlike abdomen and guarding.

Bile peritonitis: Bile peritonitis is rare but dangerous; pain, fever, and jaundice require immediate reporting.

Postcholecystectomy syndrome: Postcholecystectomy syndrome means pain or nausea resembling prior gallbladder disease continues or returns and might require further diagnostic workup.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Gallbladder Disease

Active Learning Scenario

Risk factors

  • Female sex, estrogen therapy, and some oral contraceptives.
  • Obesity, high-fat or low-calorie liquid protein diets, and rapid weight loss.
  • Genetic predisposition, age over 60, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and Native American or Mexican American ethnicity.

Findings and prevention

  • Expected findings include RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder, pain with right subcostal palpation, high-fat meal pain with nausea/vomiting, dyspepsia, belching, flatulence, fever, jaundice, clay stools, steatorrhea, dark urine, and pruritus.
  • Prevention teaching includes regular exercise, tobacco cessation, and a low-fat diet with HDL-supporting foods such as seafood, nuts, and olive oil.

Application Exercises

1

Which discharge instructions should the nurse include after laparoscopic cholecystectomy? Select all that apply.

  • A. Resume the prescribed diet after discharge.
  • B. Clean puncture sites with mild soap and water.
  • C. Remove adhesive strips after 24 hr.
  • D. Report nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
  • E. Avoid showering for 1 week.
A, B, D Diet can usually resume as directed, puncture sites are cleansed gently, and nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain can signal a complication.
C, E Adhesive strips should fall off naturally, and bathing/showering instructions depend on the approach and provider directions.
2

Which history finding is a risk factor for cholecystitis?

  • A. Obesity.
  • B. Male sex.
  • C. Low triglyceride level.
  • D. Slow weight gain over 10 years.
A Obesity and impaired fat metabolism increase risk for gallbladder disease.
B, C, D Female sex, increased cholesterol/triglyceride patterns, and rapid weight loss are stronger ATI-supported risks.
3

Which teaching belongs in preoperative preparation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy?

  • A. "You might feel shoulder pain after surgery."
  • B. "A Jackson-Pratt drain is expected with every laparoscopic case."
  • C. "Walking should be limited for 1 to 2 weeks."
  • D. "The scope is passed through the rectum for this approach."
A Free air after laparoscopic surgery can cause shoulder, clavicle, or scapular pain, and ambulation helps.
B, C, D Drains are more associated with open or complicated cases, ambulation is encouraged, and rectal entry refers to selected NOTES procedures.
4

Which teaching should be included for chenodiol?

  • A. It relieves acute biliary pain within minutes.
  • B. It gradually dissolves cholesterol gallstones.
  • C. It requires thyroid testing every 6 months.
  • D. It is first-line therapy for clients with liver disorders and varices.
B Bile acid therapy gradually dissolves cholesterol-based gallstones and can be limited to long-term monitored therapy.
A, C, D Acute biliary pain requires analgesics, ultrasound monitoring is used, and liver conditions or varices require caution.
5

Which laboratory result supports suspected cholelithiasis with duct obstruction?

  • A. Direct bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL.
  • B. WBC 9,000/mm3.
  • C. Amylase within the expected range.
  • D. Alkaline phosphatase below the expected range.
A Bilirubin can increase when a bile duct is obstructed.
B, C, D WBC can rise with inflammation, amylase can rise with pancreatic involvement, and ALP can rise with common bile duct obstruction.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 54

Pancreatitis

Pancreatitis is premature activation of digestive enzymes that injure the pancreas; priority care rests the pancreas, protects volume/electrolytes, controls pain, and catches necrosis or organ failure early.

TL;DR · Pancreatic Autodigestion

Acute pancreatitis presents with severe constant knifelike or boring epigastric/LUQ pain that can radiate to the back, left flank, or left shoulder. Pain worsens lying down and improves somewhat with fetal position or sitting upright and leaning forward.

Recognize

  • Major risks include biliary tract disease, alcohol use disorder, ERCP complications, GI surgery, metabolic disturbances, kidney failure/transplant, trauma, penetrating ulcer, medication toxicity, viral infections, and smoking.
  • Findings can include nausea/vomiting, weight loss, jaundice, decreased bowel sounds, ascites, hyperglycemia cues, flank ecchymosis, periumbilical discoloration, and hypocalcemia tetany.
  • High amylase and lipase support pancreatic cell injury; high glucose reflects decreased insulin production.

Act

  • Rest the pancreas: NPO until pain-free, antiemetics, NG decompression if severe vomiting or ileus, and nutrition support for severe disease.
  • Use comfort positioning, prescribed analgesics, glucose monitoring/insulin, hydration monitoring, IV fluids, and electrolyte replacement.
  • Escalate for hypovolemia, infection or pseudocyst/abscess, diabetes, lung complications, DIC, and multi-system organ failure.

Core Concepts

Pathophysiology and Assessment

ATI source-authored

Disease map

Autodigestion: Pancreatitis is autodigestion of the pancreas after digestive enzymes activate too early, before reaching the intestines.

Inflammation: Inflammation can obstruct ducts, increase pressure, rupture ducts, and release enzymes into pancreatic tissue, causing inflammation, necrosis, and hemorrhage.

Acute and chronic disease: Acute disease ranges from mild inflammation to necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis. Chronic disease is progressive inflammation and fibrosis and can be calcifying, obstructive, autoimmune, idiopathic, or hereditary.

Assessment pattern

Pain: Pain is sudden, severe, boring, and epigastric; it can radiate to the back, left flank, or left shoulder.

Positioning: Pain worsens when lying down and improves somewhat in fetal position or sitting upright and bending forward.

Expected findings: Expected findings include nausea, vomiting, weight loss, jaundice, absent or decreased bowel sounds, warm moist skin, fruity breath, ascites, and tetany.

Bruising patterns: Flank ecchymosis and bluish-gray periumbilical discoloration are concerning bruising patterns from enzyme-related tissue injury.

Labs, Imaging, and Nursing Care

Rest the pancreas

Diagnostics

Amylase: Blood amylase rises early and can remain elevated for several days; prolonged elevation can suggest abscess or pseudocyst.

Lipase and urine amylase: Blood lipase rises more slowly and remains elevated longer than amylase; urine amylase can remain elevated after serum levels.

Associated labs: WBC and ESR can rise; platelets, calcium, and magnesium can fall; liver enzymes and bilirubin can rise with biliary dysfunction; glucose can rise from reduced insulin production.

CT scan: CT scan with contrast is a reliable diagnostic test for acute pancreatitis.

Nursing care

Pancreatic rest: Keep the client NPO until pain-free; severe disease can require enteral or parenteral nutrition.

Diet progression: Resume bland, high-protein, low-fat foods with no stimulants such as caffeine; use small frequent meals.

Symptom control: Administer antiemetics, use NG decompression for severe vomiting or paralytic ileus, and reinforce no alcohol, no smoking, and stress limitation.

Monitoring: Position for comfort, administer prescribed analgesics, monitor glucose/insulin need, track hydration with orthostatic BP, I&O, and labs, and replace IV fluids/electrolytes as prescribed.

Medications and Procedures

Pain, acid, enzymes

Pain and infection control

Pain medication: Morphine or hydromorphone can be prescribed for acute pain; ketorolac can be used for mild to moderate pain. Meperidine is discouraged because seizure risk is a concern, especially in older adults.

Imipenem: Imipenem can be indicated for acute necrotizing pancreatitis; monitor for infection and seizures.

Acid and enzyme support

Acid reduction: Cimetidine reduces gastric acid secretion; teach separation from antacids by 1 hr. Omeprazole also reduces acid; monitor magnesium.

Pancrelipase: Pancrelipase helps digest fats and proteins with meals and snacks. Teach a full glass of water, no chewing, mouth rinsing/lip wiping to prevent irritation, and sprinkling capsule contents only on nonprotein foods if needed.

Procedures and interprofessional care

Procedures: Procedures can include ERCP for gallstone-related sphincter opening, cholecystectomy for cholecystitis/gallstones, sphincterotomy, endoscopic necrosectomy or NOTES for necrotic tissue, and pancreaticojejunostomy to reroute pancreatic drainage.

Interprofessional care: Interprofessional care can include dietary referral, home health for nutrition/wound care/ADLs, and substance-use support when alcohol use disorder contributes.

Complications

Escalation cues

Fluid and infection

Hypovolemia: Hypovolemia can occur from third spacing and can progress to shock; monitor electrolytes, hypotension, tachycardia, and replace fluids/electrolytes as prescribed.

Pseudocyst or abscess: Pancreatic pseudocyst or abscess can occur when fluid leaks from a damaged duct; watch for fever, epigastric mass, nausea, vomiting, and jaundice.

Drainage: If drainage is present, maintain the sump tube and protect surrounding skin from corrosive enzymes.

Systemic complications

Diabetes mellitus: Destruction of pancreatic beta cells can cause type 1 diabetes mellitus, requiring glucose monitoring, insulin, and long-term diabetes teaching.

Pulmonary complications: Left lung effusion and atelectasis can precipitate pneumonia, especially in older adults; monitor hypoxia and provide ventilatory support as needed.

DIC and organ failure: Necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis can trigger DIC and multi-system organ failure; monitor coagulation, bleeding, respiratory distress, jaundice, oliguria, and other organ-failure cues.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Pancreatitis

Active Learning Scenario

Classic presentation and labs

  • Classic presentation is severe constant knifelike pain in the LUQ or midepigastric area that can radiate to the back.
  • Expected labs include increased blood amylase and lipase, increased urine amylase, increased WBC, decreased calcium and magnesium, increased liver enzymes/bilirubin with biliary dysfunction, and increased glucose.

Nursing care

  • Maintain NPO status until pain-free, and provide prescribed parenteral or jejunal nutrition when needed.
  • Maintain NG decompression for severe vomiting or paralytic ileus.
  • Restart with bland high-protein, low-fat foods without caffeine; plan small frequent meals.
  • Administer antiemetics, limit stress, provide pain management, and reinforce no alcohol or smoking.

Application Exercises

1

Which laboratory finding should the nurse expect with acute pancreatitis?

  • A. Decreased blood lipase.
  • B. Decreased blood amylase.
  • C. Increased blood calcium.
  • D. Increased blood glucose.
D Pancreatic injury can decrease insulin production, causing increased glucose.
A, B, C Lipase and amylase increase with pancreatic cell injury; calcium can decrease due to fat necrosis.
2

Which action should the nurse take when administering pancrelipase?

  • A. Offer a full glass of water after administration.
  • B. Have the client chew the medication before swallowing.
  • C. Give it 30 min before meals only.
  • D. Sprinkle capsule contents on peanut butter.
A Pancrelipase teaching includes drinking a full glass of water after taking the medication.
B, C, D Do not chew it; take it with every meal and snack; if sprinkling contents, use nonprotein foods rather than peanut butter.
3

Which pain description is most consistent with pancreatitis?

  • A. RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder.
  • B. Pain relieved by defecation.
  • C. Epigastric pain radiating to the left shoulder.
  • D. Pain that improves when lying flat.
C Pancreatitis can cause severe boring epigastric pain radiating to the back, left flank, or left shoulder.
A, B, D RUQ to right shoulder fits gallbladder disease; relief with defecation fits IBS patterns; pancreatitis is worse lying down.
4

Which assessment finding is a manifestation of pancreatitis?

  • A. Gray-blue discoloration around the umbilicus.
  • B. Hyperactive bowel sounds.
  • C. Generalized cyanosis.
  • D. Wheezing in the lower lung fields.
A Bluish-gray periumbilical discoloration can occur with pancreatitis.
B, C, D Bowel sounds are more often decreased/absent; jaundice and diminished breath sounds/dyspnea are more expected than cyanosis or wheezing.
5

Which nutrition statements show correct pancreatitis teaching? Select all that apply.

  • A. "I will eat small frequent meals."
  • B. "I will choose bland, easy-to-digest foods."
  • C. "I will use skim milk when cooking."
  • D. "I will drink regular cola with meals."
  • E. "I will avoid alcohol."
A, B, C, E Small frequent bland low-fat meals and no alcohol support pancreatic rest and prevent recurrence.
D Regular cola contains caffeine; stimulant-free intake is recommended.

Unit 7 · Gastrointestinal Disorders · Chapter 55

Hepatitis and Cirrhosis

Liver disorders ask you to connect transmission and inflammation with declining liver function: impaired detoxification, bleeding risk, ascites, varices, encephalopathy, and transplant complications.

TL;DR · Liver Inflammation to Failure

Hepatitis inflames liver cells; cirrhosis permanently scars the liver after chronic injury. Watch the pattern: jaundice/dark urine/clay stools in hepatitis, then cirrhosis findings such as ascites, varices, bleeding, low albumin, prolonged PT/INR, high ammonia, asterixis, and fetor hepaticus.

Hepatitis priorities

  • HAV and HEV are fecal-oral; HBV and HCV are bloodborne; HDV occurs with HBV coinfection.
  • Use vaccines, infection control, safe injection practice, hand hygiene, and travel food/water precautions to prevent transmission.
  • ALT/AST and bilirubin rise with hepatitis; disease-specific antibodies or viral tests identify the type.

Cirrhosis priorities

  • Monitor respiratory effort, skin integrity, fluid volume excess, neurologic changes, nutrition, GI bleeding, and pain.
  • Use diuretics, beta blockers, lactulose, and nonabsorbable antibiotics as prescribed; give other liver-metabolized medications sparingly.
  • Escalate encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, transplant rejection, infection, clotting problems, hepatic complications, and acute kidney injury.

Core Concepts

Hepatitis Map

ATI source-authored

Transmission and risk

Inflammation: Hepatitis is liver-cell inflammation from viral, toxic, medication, chemical, alcohol, or secondary viral causes; it can be acute or chronic.

Fecal-oral spread: HAV and HEV spread by fecal-oral exposure, including contaminated food or water and contact with infected stool.

Blood and body fluid spread: HBV spreads through blood and sexual or perinatal exposure; HCV spreads through blood, contaminated needles/equipment, organ or blood-product exposure, and sexual contact.

HDV: HDV occurs as coinfection with HBV and shares blood/sexual exposure risks.

Prevention

Vaccination and precautions: Follow vaccination recommendations and CDC infection-control precautions.

Injection safety: Use safe injection practices: aseptic preparation, sterile single-use needles/syringes, single-dose vials when possible, and needleless systems or safety caps.

Hand hygiene: Use proper hand hygiene before food preparation/eating and after toileting or diaper care.

Travel precautions: When traveling in underdeveloped areas, drink purified water and avoid shared utensils and linens.

Hepatitis Assessment and Care

Transmission control

Findings and labs

Expected findings: Expected findings include exposure history, fatigue, decreased appetite with nausea, abdominal pain, joint pain, fever, vomiting, dark urine, clay-colored stools, and jaundice.

Liver labs: ALT, AST, bilirubin, and sometimes ALP rise with hepatitis.

HAV, HBV, and HCV: Anti-HAV identifies hepatitis A; HBsAg identifies infectious hepatitis B; anti-HCV, EIA, and HCV RNA PCR support hepatitis C diagnosis.

HDV and HEV: Anti-HDV and anti-HEV support hepatitis D and E identification.

Care and medications

Home care: Most clients receive home care unless acutely ill; use indicated precautions and teach home transmission prevention.

Nutrition: After nausea and anorexia improve, provide high-carbohydrate, high-calorie, moderate-fat, moderate-protein nutrition with small frequent meals.

Hepatic rest: Promote hepatic rest: give only necessary medications, avoid alcohol, and limit activity.

Virus-specific care: HAV postexposure protection can include immunization or immunoglobulin for selected clients. Acute HBV and HEV receive supportive care; chronic HBV uses antivirals; HCV treatment can use combination antiviral therapy.

Cirrhosis Map

Scarring and portal pressure

Pathophysiology and risks

Scarring: Cirrhosis is extensive permanent scarring after necrotic injury or chronic inflammation; fibrotic tissue replaces functioning liver tissue.

Flow obstruction: Scarring and nodules can obstruct bile channels and normal hepatic blood flow, causing jaundice and portal-pressure complications.

Types: Types include postnecrotic cirrhosis, Laennec's cirrhosis from chronic alcohol use disorder, and biliary cirrhosis from chronic obstruction or autoimmune disease.

Risk factors: Risk factors include alcohol use disorder, chronic HBV/HCV/HDV, autoimmune hepatitis, fatty liver disease, medications/substances/toxins/infections, chronic biliary obstruction, and severe right-sided heart failure.

Expected findings

General findings: General findings include fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain/distention, severe pruritus, and confusion or difficulty thinking.

Neurologic signs: Neurologic signs include cognitive change, altered sleep-wake pattern, personality or mood changes, asterixis, and fetor hepaticus.

Portal and bleeding findings: Portal and bleeding findings include varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, splenomegaly with thrombocytopenia, ascites, dependent edema, petechiae, ecchymoses, nosebleeds, hematemesis, and melena.

Skin findings: Skin findings include jaundice, icterus, palmar erythema, and spider angiomas.

Cirrhosis Labs, Diagnostics, and Care

Function loss

Testing logic

Enzymes: Liver enzymes can be elevated early; ALT and AST can normalize when damaged liver cells can no longer mount an inflammatory response. ALP increases with intrahepatic biliary obstruction.

Synthesis and excretion: Bilirubin rises because the liver cannot excrete it. Total protein and albumin decrease from reduced hepatic synthesis.

Bleeding profile: RBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelets decrease; PT/INR prolongs due to decreased prothrombin synthesis.

Ammonia and kidney function: Ammonia rises when the liver cannot convert ammonia to urea; creatinine can rise when advanced liver disease impairs kidney function.

Diagnostics: Ultrasound, x-ray, CT, MRI, liver biopsy, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy help identify ascites, organ enlargement, obstruction, masses, disease progression, and varices.

Nursing care

Respiratory support: Monitor oxygen saturation and respiratory distress; elevate the head of bed or use a chair position to ease breathing when ascites or plasma volume excess impairs effort.

Skin protection: Protect skin from pressure and scratching; cold-water washing and lotion can reduce pruritus discomfort.

Monitoring: Track strict I&O, daily weights, ascites, peripheral edema, abdominal girth over the largest area, vital signs, pain, GI bleeding, and neurologic deterioration.

Nutrition: Nutrition commonly includes high-carbohydrate, high-protein, moderate-fat, low-sodium intake with thiamine, folate, multivitamins, and small frequent meals; protein restriction can be needed with encephalopathy.

Procedures and Complications

Escalation cues

Procedures

Paracentesis: Paracentesis relieves ascites. Before the procedure, explain, witness consent, obtain vital signs and weight, and have the client void; afterward, monitor vital signs, bed rest, fluid amount/color, lab specimen, puncture site drainage, and weight.

Variceal procedures: Varices can be banded or sclerosed endoscopically; banding lowers hemorrhage risk. Severe portal hypertension/ascites can require TIPS or surgical shunting.

Liver transplantation: Liver transplantation requires multidisciplinary care and transplant eligibility; severe cardiac/respiratory disease, metastatic malignant liver cancer, or active alcohol/substance use disorder can exclude candidacy.

After transplant: After transplant, monitor acute graft rejection: tachycardia, fever, RUQ pain, changed bile color or more jaundice, and increased ALT/AST. Also monitor infection, clotting problems, hepatic complications, and acute kidney injury.

Complications

Hepatic encephalopathy: Hepatic encephalopathy occurs when ammonia and other toxins reach the brain. Give lactulose as prescribed, monitor potassium because diarrhea can cause hypokalemia, assess LOC/orientation, and report asterixis or fetor hepaticus.

Esophageal varices: Esophageal varices are fragile collateral vessels from portal hypertension. Monitor bleeding, hemoglobin, and vital signs; assist with lavage, balloon tamponade, transfusion, ligation/sclerotherapy, or shunting as prescribed.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Liver Biopsy

Active Learning Scenario

Description and nursing actions

  • A liver biopsy collects a liver tissue sample for diagnostic testing using a needle inserted between the right lower ribs into the liver.
  • Preprocedure: explain the procedure, witness informed consent, verify fasting since midnight, and administer prescribed medication.
  • Intraprocedure: position supine with RUQ exposed, support relaxation, have the client exhale and hold during needle insertion, resume breathing after removal, and apply pressure.
  • Postprocedure: position right side-lying for several hours, monitor vital signs, assess abdominal pain, and check the puncture site for bleeding.

Potential complications

  • Bleeding.
  • Bile peritonitis.
  • Pneumothorax.

Application Exercises

1

Which plan-of-care action fits a client who has hepatitis B with ascites?

  • A. Initiate contact precautions.
  • B. Weigh the client weekly.
  • C. Measure abdominal girth at the base of the ribcage.
  • D. Provide a high-calorie, high-carbohydrate diet.
D Hepatitis nutrition emphasizes high-calorie, high-carbohydrate intake after nausea and anorexia improve.
A, B, C HBV is bloodborne and standard precautions are generally used; fluid status needs daily weights and abdominal girth measured over the largest part of the abdomen.
2

Which laboratory finding supports a new diagnosis of hepatitis C?

  • A. Presence of immunoglobulin G antibodies.
  • B. Positive enzyme immunoassay test.
  • C. AST 35 units/L.
  • D. ALT 15 units/L.
B An EIA can detect antigens or antibodies associated with hepatitis C infection.
A, C, D IgG fits hepatitis A history, and AST/ALT are expected to be elevated rather than within reference range.
3

Which findings indicate hepatic encephalopathy in advanced cirrhosis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Change in orientation.
  • B. Asterixis.
  • C. Ascites.
  • D. Fetor hepaticus.
  • E. Anorexia.
A, B, D Orientation changes, asterixis, and fruity/musty breath odor indicate worsening encephalopathy.
C, E Ascites and anorexia occur with liver dysfunction but are not the specific encephalopathy indicators in this item.
4

Which medications can the nurse expect for a client who has cirrhosis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Diuretic.
  • B. Beta-blocking agent.
  • C. Opioid analgesic.
  • D. Lactulose.
  • E. Sedative.
A, B, D Diuretics reduce excess fluid, beta blockers help prevent variceal bleeding, and lactulose promotes ammonia excretion.
C, E Opioids and sedatives are liver-metabolized and used sparingly or avoided when possible in cirrhosis.
5

Which home-care teaching should be included for hepatitis B? Select all that apply.

  • A. Limit physical activity.
  • B. Avoid alcohol.
  • C. Take acetaminophen for comfort.
  • D. Wear a mask in public places.
  • E. Eat small frequent meals.
A, B, E Activity limitation, alcohol avoidance, and small frequent meals support hepatic rest and nutrition.
C, D Acetaminophen is metabolized in the liver and should be avoided unless specifically approved; masks do not prevent bloodborne HBV transmission.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 56

Renal Diagnostic Procedures

Renal diagnostics hinge on kidney function, contrast safety, infection monitoring, bleeding risk, and protecting clients whose renal reserve is already limited.

TL;DR · Contrast, Catheters, and Kidney Function

Creatinine is the kidney-specific red flag, BUN can rise from kidney disease and other stressors, and urinalysis points toward infection or metabolic problems. For procedures, separate noncontrast tests from contrast studies, then watch for kidney injury, bleeding, infection, and urinary obstruction.

Lab logic

  • Blood creatinine rises with kidney disease; at least substantial kidney function loss can be present before it elevates.
  • BUN reflects urea nitrogen from protein breakdown and can rise with dehydration, infection, chemotherapy, steroid therapy, damaged tissue reabsorption, or kidney disease.
  • Urinalysis can detect glucose, ketones, protein, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, sediment, RBCs, and other clues; culture and sensitivity identifies the organism and antibiotic options.

Procedure safety

  • Contrast procedures increase acute kidney injury risk, especially for older adults, dehydration, prior renal insufficiency, and nephrotoxic medication use.
  • Kidney biopsy requires coagulation review and postprocedure monitoring for hemorrhage, hematuria, dressing changes, Hgb/Hct, and pain.
  • Cystoscopy and retrograde studies require infection/bleeding monitoring, urine-output checks, pink-tinged urine teaching, and catheter irrigation if clots reduce output.

Core Concepts

Renal Laboratory Map

ATI source-authored

Blood and urine tests

Creatinine: Blood creatinine comes from protein and muscle breakdown; kidney disease is the condition that raises it.

BUN: BUN comes from protein breakdown in the liver and renal excretion of urea nitrogen; liver failure can lower BUN even when kidney failure is also present.

Urinalysis: Urinalysis evaluates urine color, clarity, concentration/dilution, specific gravity, pH, drug metabolites, glucose, ketones, protein, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, sediment, and RBCs.

24-hr urine: A 24-hr urine collection can measure creatinine, urea nitrogen, electrolytes, catecholamines, and proteins; 24-hr creatinine clearance estimates GFR.

Collection teaching

Urinalysis timing: Use an early-morning specimen when a more concentrated urinalysis sample is needed.

24-hr start: For a 24-hr urine collection, discard the first voided specimen and record that time as the collection start.

Storage: Refrigerate the collection or keep it on ice.

Culture trigger: If leukocyte esterase and nitrites are positive, obtain a clean-catch urine specimen for culture and sensitivity.

Imaging and Contrast Safety

Risk reduction

Noncontrast and cross-sectional imaging

KUB x-ray: KUB x-ray visualizes kidneys, ureters, and bladder and can detect calculi, strictures, calcium deposits, or obstructions; no contrast is used.

CT: CT gives three-dimensional renal/urinary images and can use iodine-based contrast; contrast can cause acute kidney injury.

MRI: MRI requires the client to lie still and is not used when metal implants can be affected by the magnet.

Ultrasound: Ultrasound images kidney size, ureters, bladder, masses, cysts, calculi, and lower urinary tract obstruction and is an alternative to excretory urography.

Excretory urography

Preprocedure: Excretory urography uses iodine contrast to detect obstruction, masses, and kidney size; before it, encourage fluids the day before, bowel cleanse, NPO after midnight, assess iodine/seafood/egg/milk/chocolate allergy and asthma, check BUN/creatinine, and withhold metformin for 24 hr.

Postprocedure: After excretory urography, give IV or oral fluids to flush contrast, check BUN/creatinine before restarting metformin, and monitor for contrast-related kidney injury.

Instrumentation and Biopsy

Bleeding and infection

Catheter-based studies

VCUG: VCUG uses catheter-instilled contrast to image the bladder/ureters and determine whether urine refluxes into the ureters; contrast does not reach blood or kidneys and is not nephrotoxic.

After VCUG: After VCUG, monitor for infection, encourage fluids to dilute urine and reduce burning, and report urine output below 30 mL/hr when pelvic or urethral trauma is suspected.

Cystoscopy/cystourethroscopy: Cystoscopy/cystourethroscopy evaluates bladder-wall abnormalities or ureter/urethral occlusion; preprocedure care includes NPO after midnight and bowel preparation as prescribed.

After cystoscopy: After cystoscopy, monitor vital signs and urine output, document urine color, encourage oral fluids, and irrigate with 0.9% sodium chloride if clots or decreased/absent urine output occur.

Biopsy and renal scan

Kidney biopsy: Kidney biopsy removes tissue for cytology/histology; preprocedure care includes coagulation review and NPO status, and postprocedure care includes vital signs, dressing/urine assessment, Hgb/Hct review, and analgesia.

Priority complication: Hemorrhage is the priority kidney biopsy complication.

Renal scan: Renal scan evaluates renal blood flow and estimates GFR after IV radioactive material; if captopril is used, monitor blood pressure and orthostatic hypotension.

After renal scan: Increase fluids after renal scan if hypotension occurs and to promote radioisotope excretion; the radioisotope is not nephrotoxic.

Gerontological Considerations

Lower reserve

Renal reserve

Aging changes: Kidney size, function, blood-flow adaptability, and GFR decrease with aging.

Comorbid conditions: Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and heart failure can further affect GFR.

Contrast and medication risk: Older adults are more vulnerable to kidney injury from contrast media and medications due to decreased kidney size, blood flow, and GFR.

Urinary pattern changes

Tubular and outlet changes: Tubular changes can cause urgency and nocturnal polyuria; short urethra and weak urinary sphincter can increase incontinence and UTI risk in women, and enlarged prostate can cause retention and infection in men.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Cystoscopy with Retrograde Pyelogram

Active Learning Scenario

Description and indications

  • Cystoscopy is instrumentation into the urinary tract to inspect the bladder wall.
  • Retrograde pyelogram injects media into the ureters to inspect the ureters and kidney pelvis.
  • Cystoscopy can identify bladder-wall cysts, tumors, or stones.
  • Retrograde pyelogram can identify ureter or renal pelvis obstruction and structural disorders such as strictures, stones, or masses.

Nursing interventions

  • Preprocedure: keep the client NPO after midnight and administer a laxative the night before if prescribed.
  • Postprocedure: monitor vital signs, encourage oral fluids to reduce burning, and document urine color.
  • If a urinary catheter is present, irrigate with 0.9% sodium chloride for active bleeding, clots, or decreased/absent urine output.

Application Exercises

1

Which teaching should the nurse include for an x-ray of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder?

  • A. "You will receive contrast dye."
  • B. "An enema is required before the procedure."
  • C. "You will lie prone during the procedure."
  • D. "The procedure can determine whether you have a kidney stone."
D A KUB can identify renal calculi, strictures, calcium deposits, and urinary obstructions.
A, B, C KUB does not use contrast, does not require bowel prep for this ATI item, and is performed supine.
2

Which kidney biopsy complication creates the greatest risk?

  • A. Infection.
  • B. Hemorrhage.
  • C. Hematuria.
  • D. Pain.
B Hemorrhage is the priority risk after kidney biopsy because clotting at the puncture site can fail.
A, C, D Infection, hematuria, and pain can occur, but hemorrhage is the greatest risk.
3

Which actions belong before excretory urography for a client with type 2 diabetes mellitus? Select all that apply.

  • A. Identify seafood allergy.
  • B. Withhold metformin for 24 hr.
  • C. Administer an enema as prescribed.
  • D. Obtain a blood coagulation profile.
  • E. Assess for asthma.
A, B, C, E Contrast allergy risk, metformin-related lactic acidosis risk, bowel cleansing, and asthma risk should be addressed.
D Coagulation studies are a priority before kidney biopsy, not excretory urography.
4

A client received captopril during a renal scan. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Assess for hypertension.
  • B. Restrict fluid intake.
  • C. Monitor for orthostatic hypotension.
  • D. Encourage early ambulation.
C Captopril can cause orthostatic hypotension during or after a renal scan.
A, B, D Monitor for hypotension, increase fluids if needed, and protect from falls.
5

Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Repeat the test early tomorrow.
  • B. Start a 24-hr urine collection for creatinine clearance.
  • C. Obtain a clean-catch urine specimen for culture and sensitivity.
  • D. Insert an indwelling catheter for specimen collection.
C Culture and sensitivity identifies the organism and antibiotic most likely to treat the UTI.
A, B, D Repeating the urinalysis will not change the result, creatinine clearance assesses kidney function, and catheterization is reserved for clients who cannot empty the bladder.
