Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 57

Hemodialysis and Peritoneal Dialysis

Dialysis sustains life by removing fluid, electrolytes, and waste, but it does not restore kidney function or replace hormonal kidney roles. Safety depends on access protection, fluid shifts, infection prevention, and complication recognition.

TL;DR · Hemodynamics vs Peritoneal Filtering

Hemodialysis moves blood through a dialyzer and needs vascular access; peritoneal dialysis instills hypertonic dialysate into the abdomen and uses the peritoneum as the membrane. Hemodialysis priorities are access patency, bleeding, hypotension, and disequilibrium. Peritoneal priorities are asepsis, cloudy outflow, glucose absorption, protein loss, and inflow/outflow problems.

Hemodialysis

  • Indications include renal insufficiency, AKI, CKD, medication or illicit drug toxicity, persistent hyperkalemia, and diuretic-resistant hypervolemia.
  • Before dialysis, assess access bruit/thrill, distal circulation, labs, vital signs, weight, and medications to hold.
  • After dialysis, compare weights, check labs/vitals, assess bleeding/infection, and monitor hypovolemia and disequilibrium syndrome.

Peritoneal dialysis

  • Use surgical asepsis, warm dialysate without a microwave, monitor inflow/outflow, and keep the outflow bag below the abdomen.
  • Clear light-yellow outflow is expected; cloudy or opaque effluent is the earliest peritonitis cue.
  • Monitor blood glucose, protein loss, access leakage/infection, respiratory distress, abdominal pain, and poor dialysate flow.

Core Concepts

Dialysis Map

ATI source-authored

Functions

Core purpose: Dialysis removes excess fluid and electrolytes, restores acid-base balance, eliminates waste products, and supports internal homeostasis through osmosis, diffusion, and ultrafiltration.

Limits: Dialysis can sustain life in AKI or CKD but does not replace kidney hormonal function.

Client presentations: Client presentations can include fluid volume changes, electrolyte or pH imbalance, nitrogenous waste buildup, fluid overload, neurologic changes, bleeding, and uremia.

Compare modalities

Hemodialysis: Hemodialysis shunts blood from the body through a dialyzer and back to circulation and requires vascular access.

Peritoneal dialysis: Peritoneal dialysis instills hypertonic dialysate into the peritoneal cavity, allows dwell time, then drains fluid containing waste products.

Peritoneal dialysis fit: Peritoneal dialysis requires an intact peritoneal membrane and is often used for older adults or clients who cannot tolerate anticoagulation, have difficult vascular access, chronic infections, instability, or chronic disease burdens.

Hemodialysis Care

Access and fluid shifts

Before and during

Access assessment: Check informed consent, use temporary access until a long-term device is available, and assess AV fistula or graft bruit, thrill, distal pulses, and circulation.

Access protection: Avoid blood pressure, injections, venipuncture, or IV catheters on the access arm; elevate the extremity after AV fistula creation to reduce swelling.

Preprocedure checks: Assess vital signs, BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, hematocrit, and weight; discuss which dialyzable or blood-pressure-lowering medications to hold until after dialysis.

During dialysis: During dialysis, monitor for circuit clotting, air in tubing, dialysate temperature issues, ultrafiltration regulation, hypotension, cramping, vomiting, access-site bleeding, contamination, and coagulation status.

After and teaching

Fluid removed: Compare pre- and postprocedure weights to estimate fluid removed; 1 L fluid equals about 1 kg or 2.2 lb.

Postprocedure monitoring: Monitor vitals, BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, hematocrit, bleeding, infection, hypovolemia, muscle cramps, headache, and disequilibrium findings.

Bleeding risk: Avoid invasive procedures for several hours after dialysis because anticoagulation increases bleeding risk.

Access teaching: Teach access protection: report bleeding longer than 30 min, absent thrill/bruit, or infection cues; avoid heavy lifting, constriction, sleeping on the access arm, and venipuncture or BP on that arm.

Diet teaching: Diet teaching includes folate replacement, high-folate foods, increased protein compared with predialysis restriction, and continued sodium, potassium, and phosphorus limits as prescribed.

Hemodialysis Complications

Unexpected responses

Access and infection

Access clotting or infection: Use surgical asepsis during cannulation, avoid compression, avoid BP/venipuncture on the access arm, assess thrill/bruit, inspect redness/swelling/drainage, and monitor fever.

Bloodborne infection risk: Frequent blood access raises HIV and hepatitis B/C transmission risk; use sterile equipment, skin antisepsis, and standard precautions.

Fluid-shift complications

Disequilibrium syndrome: Disequilibrium syndrome occurs when BUN and circulating volume drop too quickly, causing cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure; watch for nausea, vomiting, LOC change, seizures, and agitation.

Disequilibrium prevention: For disequilibrium risk, use a slow exchange rate for older adults or first-time hemodialysis and administer prescribed anticonvulsants or barbiturates if needed.

Hypotension: Hypotension can result from antihypertensives and rapid fluid removal; replace volume carefully, slow the exchange rate, lower the head of bed, and discontinue dialysis for severe unresponsive hypotension.

Anemia

Blood loss and folate removal: Anemia can worsen from blood loss and folate removal; erythropoietin, Hgb/RBC monitoring, hypotension/tachycardia monitoring, and transfusion can be used as prescribed.

Peritoneal Dialysis Care

Asepsis and outflow

Before and during

Readiness: Assess dry weight, vital signs, electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, and glucose; determine whether the client can self-perform dialysis and maintain sterile technique.

Initial monitoring: Monitor initial hospital dialysis vital signs frequently and monitor blood glucose because dialysate contains glucose.

Outflow: Record inflow compared with outflow; expected outflow is clear, light yellow, and equal to or greater than inflow.

Dialysate handling: Warm dialysate before instillation, but do not use a microwave; follow prescribed infusion, dwell, and outflow timing.

Asepsis and flow: Maintain surgical asepsis at the catheter site and when accessing the catheter; keep the outflow bag below the abdomen and reposition for poor flow.

Teaching and complications

Expected sensations: Teach that fullness can occur during dwell and initial infusion discomfort can happen.

Exchange patterns: CAPD occurs daily with exchanges across the day; CCPD and APD use nighttime cycling patterns with prescribed dwell timing.

Infection monitoring: Monitor for infection: fever, bloody/cloudy/frothy dialysate, drainage, redness, swelling, or cloudy opaque effluent.

Complication cues: Watch respiratory distress, abdominal pain, insufficient outflow, discolored outflow, wet access-site dressing, catheter leakage, and exit-site infection.

Home support: Support home access care, careful adherence, medication/supplement use, local support resources, and body-image concerns from bloating.

Peritoneal Dialysis Complications

Flow and metabolic safety

Infection

Peritonitis: Maintain surgical asepsis, monitor fever, pain, purulent drainage, redness, swelling, and cloudy or discolored drained dialysate, and teach strict sterile exchange technique.

Access-site infection: Access-site infection can result from dialysate leakage and can progress to peritonitis; assess wetness, leakage, tugging, twisting, redness, swelling, drainage, and fever.

Metabolic effects

Protein loss: Protein loss occurs when dialysis removes protein along with fluid and waste; increase dietary protein over predialysis restrictions and monitor albumin.

Hyperglycemia: Hyperglycemia can occur because glucose is absorbed from hypertonic dialysate; monitor glucose, administer insulin as prescribed, and follow the provider's diet plan.

Hyperlipidemia: Hyperlipidemia can occur with long-term therapy and contribute to hypertension; administer antilipemic medications and antihypertensives as prescribed.

Poor inflow or outflow

Flow troubleshooting: Poor inflow or outflow can be caused by tubing obstruction/twisting, constipation, positioning, fibrin clot, or catheter displacement; reposition, check clamps/kinks, milk tubing for fibrin clots as prescribed, and prevent constipation.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Peritoneal Dialysis

Active Learning Scenario

Description and complications

  • Peritoneal dialysis instills hypertonic dialysate into the peritoneal cavity, allows prescribed dwell time, and drains fluid containing waste products.
  • Potential complications include peritonitis, protein loss, hyperglycemia, and poor dialysate inflow or outflow.

Nursing actions

  • Peritonitis: maintain surgical asepsis and monitor outflow color, pain, and fever.
  • Protein loss: increase dietary protein and monitor albumin.
  • Hyperglycemia: monitor blood glucose and administer insulin as prescribed.
  • Poor flow: reposition, milk tubing for fibrin clots if prescribed, check for kinks or closed clamps, and prevent constipation with diet and stool softeners.

Application Exercises

1

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client beginning hemodialysis?

  • A. Hemodialysis restores kidney function.
  • B. Hemodialysis replaces hormonal kidney function.
  • C. Hemodialysis allows an unrestricted diet.
  • D. Hemodialysis returns balance to blood electrolytes.
D Hemodialysis removes excess electrolytes, fluid, and waste and helps restore acid-base balance.
A, B, C Dialysis sustains life but does not restore kidney function, replace hormonal function, or remove renal diet restrictions.
2

Which actions should the nurse take before initiating hemodialysis for acute kidney injury? Select all that apply.

  • A. Review current medications.
  • B. Assess the AV fistula for bruit.
  • C. Measure the client's weight.
  • D. Check blood electrolytes.
  • E. Use the access site for venipuncture.
A, B, C, D Medication review, access patency, baseline weight, and electrolyte assessment are preprocedure priorities.
E Never use the access site area for venipuncture because compression can damage or collapse vascular access.
3

Which interventions should be included after hemodialysis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Check BUN and blood creatinine.
  • B. Administer medications withheld before dialysis as appropriate.
  • C. Observe for hypovolemia.
  • D. Assess the access site for bleeding.
  • E. Measure blood pressure on the arm with AV access.
A, B, C, D Postdialysis care includes lab review, medication timing, hypovolemia monitoring, and bleeding assessment because heparin is used.
E Blood pressure is never measured on the access extremity because compression can harm the fistula or graft.
4

A client develops disequilibrium syndrome after hemodialysis. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Administer an opioid medication.
  • B. Monitor for hypertension.
  • C. Assess level of consciousness.
  • D. Increase the dialysis exchange rate.
C Disequilibrium can increase intracranial pressure, so decreased level of consciousness is a priority assessment.
A, B, D Opioids can worsen status, hypotension is more expected, and the dialysis exchange rate should be decreased rather than increased.
5

Which actions should be included for peritoneal dialysis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Monitor blood glucose levels.
  • B. Report cloudy dialysate return.
  • C. Warm dialysate in a microwave oven.
  • D. Assess for shortness of breath.
  • E. Check the access-site dressing for wetness.
  • F. Maintain medical asepsis when accessing the catheter site.
A, B, D, E Dialysate contains glucose, cloudy outflow suggests infection, respiratory distress can mean intolerance of dialysate volume, and wet dressings suggest leakage.
C, F Do not microwave dialysate, and use surgical rather than medical asepsis for catheter access.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 58

Kidney Transplant

Kidney transplant improves quality of life for eligible clients with end-stage kidney disease, but success depends on donor matching, lifelong immunosuppression, infection prevention, urine-output surveillance, and rapid rejection recognition.

TL;DR · Graft Perfusion and Rejection Watch

After kidney transplant, urine output is the pulse of the graft. Report urine output below 30 mL/hr, abrupt output decrease, fever, hypertension, transplant-site pain, bloody drainage, oliguria/anuria, fluid retention, or infection cues immediately.

Before transplant

  • Donor matching includes ABO compatibility and histocompatibility, including human leukocytic antigen and minor antigens.
  • Living related donors with matching tissue type have the greatest graft-survival chance.
  • Risk rises with very young or older age, advanced cardiac disease, active cancer, chemical dependency, chronic infection, coagulopathy, morbid obesity, diabetes, chronic pulmonary disease, and untreated GI disease.

After transplant

  • Monitor vital signs, hourly I&O, urine appearance, daily urinalysis, daily weight, electrolytes, infection, rejection, bleeding, and fluid balance.
  • Replace hourly urine output with IV fluids as prescribed and maintain catheter drainage/CBI to protect the graft from clot obstruction.
  • Teach strict medication adherence, infection reporting, grapefruit avoidance with cyclosporine, activity progression, and avoiding contact sports.

Core Concepts

End-Stage Kidney Disease and Candidacy

ATI source-authored

ESKD indicators

Indications: Indications include anuria, proteinuria, marked azotemia, severe electrolyte imbalance such as hyperkalemia or hypernatremia, fluid-volume excess with heart failure or pulmonary edema, and uremic lung.

Expected findings: Expected findings can include anorexia, fatigue, numbness/tingling, shortness of breath, dry itchy skin, metallic taste, muscle cramping, decreased attention span, seizures, tremor, heart failure, edema, dyspnea, distended neck veins, anemia, vomiting, hypertension, dysrhythmias, pallor, bruising, halitosis, and diminished or dark urine.

Labs: Labs can show proteinuria, hematuria, elevated BUN/creatinine, decreased GFR, decreased Hgb/Hct, elevated potassium/phosphorus, sodium changes, and metabolic acidosis.

Matching and risk

Donor sources: Donors can be living, non-heart-beating, or cadaver donors; donor kidneys must be adequately perfused to remain viable.

Matching: Recipient and donor tissue matching includes ABO compatibility and histocompatibility testing.

Risk factors: Risks that increase transplant surgery, immunosuppression, or rejection complications include age younger than 2 or older than 70, advanced untreatable cardiac disease, active cancer, chemical dependency, chronic infections such as HIV or hepatitis B/C, coagulopathies, immune disorders, morbid obesity, diabetes mellitus, chronic pulmonary disease, and untreated peptic ulcer disease.

Preprocedure Priorities

Readiness and immunosuppression

Surgery readiness

Dialysis timing: Dialysis is usually performed within 24 hr of surgery.

Preoperative labs: Preoperative labs include blood chemistry, CBC/differential, bleeding times, urine culture, blood type, and crossmatch.

Medication preparation

Preoperative medications: Prescribed preoperative medications can include prophylactic antibiotics and immunosuppression.

Immunosuppression roles: Corticosteroids decrease the inflammatory immune response; cyclosporine and azathioprine prevent donor-kidney rejection; mTOR inhibitors interrupt T-cell signaling; everolimus helps prevent B- and T-cell activation; basiliximab or daclizumab bind T cells to decrease activation.

Teaching readiness

Preprocedure teaching: Teaching includes mental/emotional preparation, transplant-team roles, lifelong immunosuppression adherence, smoking cessation, and blood pressure/glucose control.

Postprocedure Monitoring

Protect the graft

Early monitoring

Vital signs: Assess vital signs frequently at first, then per protocol, and keep blood pressure within prescribed parameters.

Urine output: Assess I&O at least hourly; urine output should stay above 30 mL/hr.

Output decrease: Report oliguria below 30 mL/hr and abrupt urine-output decrease because these can indicate rejection, tissue injury, renal artery thrombosis, or urinary obstruction.

Urine appearance: Assess urine appearance and odor hourly; urine can be pink/bloody at first and gradually clear over days to weeks.

Daily surveillance: Monitor daily urinalysis, daily weight, fluid/electrolyte imbalance, infection, rejection cues, and surgical dressing bleeding.

Fluid, catheter, and medication care

Fluid replacement: Administer IV fluids as prescribed, often replacing hourly urine output; transition to oral fluids when bowel function returns and fluids are tolerated.

Catheter drainage: Maintain the large indwelling urinary catheter to dependent bedside drainage and use continuous bladder irrigation as prescribed to prevent clot obstruction that could injure the graft.

Catheter removal: Remove the urinary catheter as soon as possible to reduce infection risk.

Oliguria or diuresis: Oliguria can require prescribed diuretics or dialysis until kidney function is satisfactory; excessive diuresis can cause hypovolemia, hypotension, and reduced graft blood flow.

Medications and follow-up: Administer immunosuppressive medications, antibiotics, stool softeners, and follow-up/counseling referrals as prescribed.

Client Teaching

Lifelong safety

Infection and medication adherence

Infection reporting: Report infection findings such as fever, incisional drainage, redness, fatigue, discomfort, or mental-status change.

Medication adherence: Adhere to immunosuppressive therapy and other prescribed medications.

Diet and supplement precautions

Prednisone teaching: When taking prednisone, avoid concentrated sugars or carbohydrates as prescribed for glycemic control.

Magnesium: Magnesium supplements can be needed because cyclosporine can reduce magnesium levels.

Grapefruit: Avoid grapefruit with cyclosporine because it can raise cyclosporine blood levels.

Activity protection

Activity teaching: Avoid contact sports that could injure the transplanted kidney and increase activity as tolerated.

Complications

Report rapidly

Rejection and ischemia

Hyperacute rejection: Hyperacute rejection occurs within 48 hr and is not reversible; fever, hypertension, and transplant-site pain require immediate treatment, often donor-kidney removal.

Acute rejection: Acute rejection occurs from 1 week to 2 years and can cause oliguria, anuria, low-grade fever, hypertension, tenderness over the transplanted kidney, lethargy, azotemia, and fluid retention; treatment uses increased immunosuppression.

Chronic rejection: Chronic rejection develops gradually over months to years with returning azotemia, fluid retention, electrolyte imbalance, and fatigue; conservative monitoring continues until dialysis is required.

Ischemia: Ischemia can occur when transplanting is delayed after harvesting; monitor urine output, creatinine, and BUN, report output below 30 mL/hr, assist with dialysis, and prepare for biopsy to distinguish ischemia from rejection.

Vascular and infection risks

Renal artery stenosis: Renal artery stenosis can occur from surgical anastomosis scarring; report hypertension, bruit over the anastomosis, oliguria, and elevated BUN/creatinine.

Thrombosis: Thrombosis can form in a major graft vessel; sudden urine-output decrease requires emergency escalation and possible transplant nephrectomy.

Infection risk: Infection is a major first-year morbidity and mortality cause, and immunosuppression can make early signs subtle.

Infection control: Prioritize infection control with frequent hand hygiene, avoiding crowds or communicable illness exposure, possible mask use in public when indicated, and rapid reporting of localized or systemic infection.

Active Learning Scenario

Nursing Skill - Post-Transplant Urinary Catheter Care

Active Learning Scenario

Indications and complications

  • Indications include hourly urine-output monitoring and monitoring urine color/clots.
  • Potential complications include oliguria, infection from the indwelling urinary catheter, and blood clot formation.

Nursing interventions

  • Regulate IV fluids according to urinary output as prescribed.
  • Keep the drainage bag lower than the client for gravity drainage.
  • Remove the indwelling catheter within a few days after the procedure when prescribed.
  • Implement continuous bladder irrigation as prescribed to remove clots that could obstruct drainage and damage the donor kidney.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings should the nurse expect with end-stage kidney disease? Select all that apply.

  • A. Anuria.
  • B. Marked azotemia.
  • C. Crackles in the lungs.
  • D. Increased calcium level.
  • E. Proteinuria.
A, B, C, E ESKD can cause anuria, elevated BUN/creatinine, pulmonary edema with crackles, and proteinuria.
D Calcium tends to decrease as phosphate rises in end-stage kidney disease.
2

Which postoperative actions should the nurse include after kidney transplant? Select all that apply.

  • A. Obtain daily weights.
  • B. Assess dressings for bloody drainage.
  • C. Replace hourly urine output with IV fluids as prescribed.
  • D. Expect oliguria during the first 4 hr.
  • E. Monitor blood electrolytes.
A, B, C, E Daily weights, dressing checks, urine-output replacement, and electrolyte monitoring protect fluid status and graft function.
D Oliguria can indicate ischemia, acute kidney injury, rejection, or hypovolemia and should be reported.
3

Which cyclosporine teaching should the nurse include after kidney transplant?

  • A. Decrease protein-rich foods.
  • B. Take the medication with grapefruit juice.
  • C. Report a sore throat to the provider.
  • D. Expect skin to turn yellow.
C Cyclosporine causes immunosuppression, so infection cues such as sore throat should be reported.
A, B, D Protein supports healing, grapefruit raises cyclosporine levels, and jaundice should be reported as possible hepatotoxicity rather than expected.
4

Which findings increase kidney transplantation surgery risk? Select all that apply.

  • A. Age older than 70 years.
  • B. BMI of 41.
  • C. Insulin-requiring diabetes mellitus.
  • D. Past history of lymphoma.
  • E. Blood pressure averaging 120/70 mm Hg.
A, B, C, D Older age, morbid obesity, diabetes, and cancer history increase risk from surgery, lifelong immunosuppression, or rejection.
E This blood pressure is within expected range and is not the increased-risk finding in this item.
5

Which rejection teaching should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

  • A. Hyperacute rejection can require immediate donor-kidney removal.
  • B. Dialysis is the primary treatment for hyperacute rejection.
  • C. Fever can occur with acute rejection.
  • D. Fluid retention can occur with acute rejection.
  • E. Increased immunosuppression treats chronic rejection.
A, C, D Hyperacute rejection can require immediate graft removal; fever and fluid retention can occur with acute rejection.
B, E Dialysis is conservative support for chronic failure progression, and increased immunosuppression treats acute rejection rather than chronic rejection.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 59

Polycystic Kidney Disease, Acute Kidney Injury, and Chronic Kidney Disease

Kidney failure questions usually turn on time course, perfusion, obstruction, nephrotoxins, fluid balance, potassium, and whether the client needs urgent stabilization, dialysis planning, or long-term disease management.

TL;DR · Perfusion, Potassium, and Progression

For AKI, identify the cause and protect perfusion fast. For CKD, trend GFR, BUN/creatinine, potassium, phosphorus, anemia, fluid overload, and uremia. For PKD, blood pressure control and infection/stone surveillance are the priority cues.

AKI test logic

  • Prerenal AKI points to low perfusion from hypovolemia, shock, low cardiac output, sepsis, renal vascular obstruction, or medication effects.
  • Intrarenal AKI points to direct nephron damage from ischemia, trauma, nephrotoxins, transfusion reaction, infection, vasculitis, or glomerulonephritis.
  • Postrenal AKI points to obstruction such as stones, tumors, bladder atony, prostate enlargement, urethral stricture, or spinal cord disorder.

CKD/PKD test logic

  • CKD is progressive and irreversible; stage 4 means severe GFR reduction, and stage 5 means kidney failure/end-stage kidney disease.
  • CKD safety centers on renal diet, fluid restriction when prescribed, nephrotoxin avoidance, dialysis/transplant planning, anemia treatment, and potassium/phosphate control.
  • PKD is hereditary; watch for hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, hematuria/cloudy urine, stones, constipation, cyst infection or rupture, and progressive kidney failure.

Core Concepts

Acute Kidney Injury

ATI source-authored

Phases and classes

Definition: AKI is abrupt renal-function loss after kidney blood flow or kidney tissue is compromised.

Phases: Phases move from onset, to oliguria, to diuresis, to recovery; recovery can take months.

Severity: Severity is staged by creatinine rise and urine-output decline; severe AKI includes marked creatinine elevation or very low urine output for many hours.

Expected findings: Expected findings are often waste buildup and output changes, but cardiovascular, respiratory, neurologic, integumentary, and renal findings can all appear.

Findings and diagnostics

Assessment: Assess for hypertension, fluid overload, edema, dysrhythmias from hyperkalemia, crackles, decreased oxygenation, shortness of breath, hematuria, lethargy, twitching, seizures, dry skin, and dry mucous membranes.

Labs: Trend BUN, creatinine, urine specific gravity, electrolytes, hematocrit, urinalysis sediment, and ABGs for metabolic acidosis.

Imaging: Imaging can include KUB, ultrasound, CT without contrast, MRI, or nuclear medicine studies when obstruction, perfusion, or anatomy must be evaluated.

Biopsy: Kidney biopsy can be used when the AKI cause remains unclear or immune disease/reversibility must be evaluated.

Nursing care

Monitoring: Correct the underlying cause, monitor hemodynamics, and track strict intake/output, daily weights, edema, heart failure cues, pulmonary edema cues, fever, infection, urine particles or blood, and ECG changes.

Nephrotoxin caution: Avoid or reduce nephrotoxic medications when possible and use contrast cautiously; report flank pain, nausea, vomiting, urine-stream changes, or difficulty starting urine.

Diet and fluids: Restrict fluids and electrolytes such as potassium, phosphate, sodium, or magnesium when prescribed, and individualize protein support to the client's phase and catabolic state.

Renal support: Prepare for continuous renal replacement therapy, hemodialysis, or peritoneal dialysis when kidney function and complications require renal support.

Medication logic

IV fluids: IV fluids can restore kidney perfusion or replace losses during the diuretic phase when prescribed.

Diuretics: Diuretics can be prescribed to promote urine formation and fluid removal when appropriate.

Potassium and acid-base: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate, sorbitol, insulin/dextrose, calcium, or sodium bicarbonate can be used for potassium or severe acid-base problems as prescribed.

Phosphate binders: Phosphate-binding agents can be used when phosphate rises.

Chronic Kidney Disease

Progressive and irreversible

Risk and staging

Progression: CKD can remain quiet until physiologic stress or advancing nephron loss makes manifestations visible.

Older adult risk: Older adults are at higher risk because functioning nephrons and GFR decline with age; dehydration risk rises with bed rest, confusion, poor thirst, or poor water access.

Risk factors: Risk factors include AKI, diabetes mellitus, chronic glomerulonephritis, nephrotoxic medications or chemicals, hypertension, autoimmune disease, PKD, renal artery stenosis, and recurrent severe infections.

Stages: Stage 1 has minimal damage with expected-range GFR; stage 3 is moderate GFR decrease; stage 4 is severe GFR decrease; stage 5 is kidney failure/end-stage kidney disease.

Expected findings

Neurologic and uremic cues: Assess for nausea, fatigue, lethargy, leg movements, depression, hiccups, reduced attention, slurred speech, tremors, ataxia, seizures, coma, and uremic breath.

Fluid overload: Fluid overload can cause jugular distention, sacral/ocular/peripheral edema, hypertension, heart failure, crackles, pleural friction rub, frothy pink sputum, and dysrhythmias from hyperkalemia.

Systemic findings: Anemia, bruising, GI bleeding, mouth/throat ulcers, vomiting, fragile bones, protein/blood/particles in urine, pruritus, yellow skin cast, and uremic frost can occur.

Labs: Labs can show hematuria, proteinuria, low specific gravity, rising creatinine/BUN, low sodium/calcium, high potassium/phosphorus/magnesium, and low hemoglobin/hematocrit from reduced erythropoietin.

Daily care

Monitoring: Monitor urinary pattern, blood pressure, weight, vascular access or peritoneal dialysis sites, medication/herb history, skin integrity, activity tolerance, and injury risk.

Diet and fluids: Control protein intake based on CKD stage and dialysis plan; restrict sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, and fluids when prescribed.

Teaching: Teach daily weight and blood pressure tracking, renal diet adherence, prescribed fluid limits, dialysis instructions, rest periods, skin-breakdown reporting, and avoidance of magnesium-containing antacids.

Long-term support: Dialysis and kidney transplantation can sustain life but are not cures for CKD.

Medication cautions

Nephrotoxin caution: Avoid nephrotoxic antimicrobials, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and IV contrast unless the provider determines they are necessary.

Digoxin: Digoxin doses can need reduction because CKD slows excretion; monitor digoxin and potassium levels and toxicity cues.

Sodium polystyrene: Sodium polystyrene increases potassium elimination but adds sodium, so monitor for fluid retention and hypertension.

Anemia and phosphate: Epoetin alfa and iron support anemia management; calcium carbonate binds dietary phosphate and can cause constipation.

Loop diuretics: Loop diuretics can remove excess fluid, but avoid giving them to clients with end-stage kidney disease unless specifically prescribed.

Polycystic Kidney Disease

Hereditary cyst disorder

Assessment

Definition: PKD is hereditary and causes multiple fluid-filled renal cysts that replace healthy kidney tissue.

Forms: The autosomal dominant form is most common and usually becomes clinically apparent in adulthood; the recessive form is present at birth.

Expected findings: Expected findings include family history, anxiety or guilt, abdominal/flank pain, headaches, hypertension from renal ischemia, enlarged abdominal girth, constipation, hematuria/cloudy urine, stones, hyponatremia, nocturia, and progressive kidney failure.

Pain pattern: Dull pain can suggest kidney enlargement or cyst infection; sharp pain can suggest ruptured cyst or renal lithiasis.

Testing: Testing can include urinalysis, BUN/creatinine/creatinine clearance trends, ultrasound, CT, or MRI.

Care priorities

Blood pressure: Blood pressure control is the priority nursing focus; teach the client and family to measure and record blood pressure and daily weights.

Pain: Use prescribed pain medication and nonpharmacologic strategies; use NSAIDs cautiously in kidney disease.

Infection prevention: Prevent infection by administering prescribed antibiotics and monitoring creatinine and urine output for nephrotoxicity.

Bowel regularity: Support bowel regularity with allowed fluids, fiber, ambulation, bowel assessment, and stool softeners as prescribed.

Teaching: Teach daily blood pressure and weight monitoring, low-sodium diet adherence, elevated temperature reporting, and reporting urine or bowel-pattern changes.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - CKD Medication Safety

Active Learning Scenario

Medication purpose

  • Digoxin increases myocardial contractility and supports cardiac output.
  • Sodium polystyrene promotes potassium elimination.
  • Calcium carbonate binds phosphate in food to reduce phosphate absorption.
  • Furosemide promotes diuresis of excess fluid when kidney function and provider direction support its use.

Nursing interventions

  • With digoxin, monitor digoxin level, potassium level, and toxicity cues such as nausea, vomiting, anorexia, or visual changes.
  • With sodium polystyrene, monitor for hypokalemia and restrict sodium intake as prescribed.
  • With furosemide, monitor intake/output and blood pressure, and avoid use in end-stage kidney disease unless specifically prescribed.
  • Across CKD medication administration, screen for nephrotoxic agents and anticipate renal-dose adjustments.

Application Exercises

1

A client has prerenal AKI after abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, urine output of 60 mL over 2 hr, and blood pressure of 92/58 mm Hg. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?

  • A. Prepare for CT with contrast.
  • B. Administer nitroprusside.
  • C. Prepare for a prescribed fluid challenge.
  • D. Place the client flat in Trendelenburg.
C Low blood pressure and low urine output after a perfusion insult support hypovolemia/prerenal AKI, so a prescribed fluid challenge can restore kidney perfusion.
A, B, D Contrast can worsen AKI, nitroprusside is not appropriate for hypotension, and positioning should support venous return without an unsafe flat Trendelenburg default.
2

Which interventions fit a client who has postrenal AKI from metastatic cancer and a creatinine of 5 mg/dL? Select all that apply.

  • A. Provide protein support as prescribed for the catabolic state.
  • B. Assess urine for blood, stones, or particles.
  • C. Monitor for intermittent anuria.
  • D. Weigh the client once each week.
  • E. Use NSAIDs for pain control.
A, B, C AKI can require protein support, obstruction surveillance, and monitoring for intermittent anuria.
D, E Daily weight is needed for fluid retention, and NSAIDs are nephrotoxic.
3

Which actions should the nurse include for a client who has stage 4 CKD? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assess for jugular venous distention.
  • B. Provide frequent mouth rinses.
  • C. Auscultate for a pleural friction rub.
  • D. Encourage a high-sodium diet.
  • E. Monitor for dysrhythmias.
A, B, C, E Stage 4 CKD can cause fluid overload, uremic breath/mouth discomfort, respiratory findings from fluid and acid-base imbalance, and dysrhythmias from hyperkalemia.
D Sodium is commonly restricted rather than increased.
4

Which lab finding best matches stage 4 CKD?

  • A. BUN 15 mg/dL.
  • B. GFR 20 mL/min.
  • C. Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL.
  • D. Potassium 5.0 mEq/L.
B Stage 4 CKD is severe kidney damage with severe GFR reduction, roughly 15 to 29 mL/min.
A, C, D BUN and creatinine are expected to rise substantially, and potassium is typically above the expected range when hyperkalemia develops.
5

Which findings should the nurse expect with prerenal AKI? Select all that apply.

  • A. Reduced BUN.
  • B. Elevated cardiac enzymes.
  • C. Reduced urine output.
  • D. Elevated blood creatinine.
  • E. Elevated blood calcium.
C, D Prerenal AKI commonly reduces urine output and raises creatinine as perfusion falls and waste products accumulate.
A, B, E BUN is expected to rise, cardiac enzymes point to cardiac tissue injury, and calcium is more likely to be reduced in this context.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 60

Infections of the Renal and Urinary System

Renal infection questions are priority questions: protect kidney tissue, prevent ascending infection and sepsis, treat the organism with the full antibiotic course, and watch high-risk clients for atypical or systemic findings.

TL;DR · Treat Infection Before It Ascends

For UTI, antibiotics are the priority because untreated infection can progress to pyelonephritis, urosepsis, septic shock, CKD, and death. For pyelonephritis, track fever, flank/CVA pain, urine output, cultures, BUN/creatinine, and sepsis cues. For glomerulonephritis, watch fluid overload, hypertension, cola-colored urine, proteinuria, and falling GFR.

UTI logic

  • Lower UTI includes cystitis, urethritis, and prostatitis; upper UTI includes pyelonephritis.
  • Common findings include urgency, frequency, dysuria, bladder discomfort, incomplete emptying, hematuria, pyuria, cloudy/foul urine, fever, vomiting, nocturia, and small voids.
  • Older adults can present with confusion, incontinence, appetite loss, nocturia/dysuria, or urosepsis findings instead of classic symptoms.

Kidney involvement logic

  • Pyelonephritis often starts as lower-tract bacteria ascending into the kidney pelvis and can scar renal tissue after repeated infections.
  • Chronic pyelonephritis can lead to CKD, hypertension, and septic shock if infection enters the bloodstream.
  • Glomerulonephritis is immune-mediated glomerular injury that can follow infection or systemic disease and can progress to ESKD.

Core Concepts

Urinary Tract Infection

ATI source-authored

Risk factors and findings

General risk factors: Risk rises with alkaline urine, indwelling urinary catheters, stool incontinence, bladder distention, urinary stasis/anomalies/calculi/residual urine, diabetes mellitus, and possible genetic factors.

Female risk factors: Female risk factors include short urethra, urethra-to-rectum proximity, decreased estrogen with aging, intercourse, feminine hygiene products, spermicides, pregnancy, poorly fitted diaphragm, synthetic underwear, wet bathing suits, baths/hot tubs, and vaginal flora changes.

Older adult risk factors: Older adult risks include incomplete bladder emptying from prostate problems, bladder prolapse, neurogenic bladder, poor perineal hygiene, hypoestrogenism, fewer functioning nephrons, and decreased fluid intake.

Expected findings: Expected findings include lower back or suprapubic discomfort, bladder tenderness, nausea, urgency/frequency, dysuria, bladder cramping/spasms, incomplete emptying, retention, perineal itching, hematuria, pyuria, fever, vomiting, nocturia, urethral discharge, and cloudy or foul-smelling urine.

Diagnostics and treatment

Urine testing: Urinalysis/culture can show bacteria, sediment, WBCs, RBCs, leukocyte esterase, and nitrites; collect clean-catch or catheterized specimens correctly.

Urosepsis concern: If urosepsis is suspected, monitor WBC/differential for elevation and left shift.

STI rule-out: STI testing can be needed because chlamydia, gonorrhea, herpes simplex, trichomoniasis, and candida can mimic UTI manifestations.

Complicated cases: Complicated cases can require cystoscopy, cystourethroscopy, CT for pyelonephritis, ultrasonography, or transrectal ultrasound for male prostate/bladder conditions.

Medication treatment: Administer prescribed antibiotics promptly; phenazopyridine can relieve bladder discomfort but does not treat infection.

Priority nursing care

Antibiotics: Administer antibiotics as prescribed; this is the priority intervention when active infection threatens renal injury and sepsis.

Fluid guidance: Consult the provider about fluid restrictions before encouraging extra fluids.

Catheter prevention: Avoid indwelling urinary catheters when possible to reduce infection risk.

Pregnancy: Pregnant clients need rapid and effective treatment to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm labor.

Comfort care: Warm sitz baths can support comfort but do not replace antimicrobial treatment.

Client teaching

Antibiotic course: Take the full prescribed antibiotic course even when symptoms improve; take medication with food when directed and report watery diarrhea.

Sun sensitivity: Fluoroquinolones and sulfonamides can increase sun sensitivity; take them with a full glass of water and increase fluids when allowed.

Phenazopyridine: Phenazopyridine can turn urine orange and should be taken with food.

Hydration and voiding: Drink about 2 L/day when not restricted, empty the bladder every 3 to 4 hr and with urgency, urinate before/after intercourse, bathe daily, and wipe front to back.

Moisture avoidance: Avoid bubble baths, perfumed feminine products, wet bathing suits, pantyhose with slacks, tight clothing, and synthetic underwear that traps moisture.

Pyelonephritis

Ascending kidney infection

Acute vs chronic

Definition: Pyelonephritis is infection/inflammation of the kidney pelvis, calyces, and medulla; organisms usually ascend from the lower urinary tract.

Acute pyelonephritis: Acute pyelonephritis is an active bacterial infection that can cause interstitial inflammation, tubular cell necrosis, abscess formation, and temporary kidney-function change.

Chronic pyelonephritis: Chronic pyelonephritis results from repeated infections, progressive inflammation, scarring, calyx thickening, fibrosis, and permanent renal tissue damage.

Risk factors: Risk factors include older age with prostate problems, chronic stones, spinal cord injury with reflux, pregnancy, congenital malformations, bladder tumors, chronic illness, alkaline urine, incomplete emptying, and older-adult thermoregulation changes.

Findings and testing

Assessment: Assess for chills, colicky abdominal pain, nausea, malaise, fatigue, burning/urgency/frequency, costovertebral angle tenderness, flank/back pain, nocturia, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, vomiting, and bacteremia.

Chronic effects: Chronic pyelonephritis can impair urine concentration and sodium conservation.

Labs: Labs include urinalysis/culture, WBC/differential, blood cultures when systemic infection is suspected, serum creatinine, BUN, C-reactive protein, and ESR.

Imaging: Imaging can include KUB, ultrasound, gallium scan, and IV pyelogram to evaluate calculi, obstruction, infection, inflammation, or structural/vascular problems.

Nursing care and medications

Monitoring: Monitor nutrition, intake/output, fluid/electrolyte balance, temperature, and pain onset, quality, duration, and severity.

Supportive care: Increase fluid intake to about 2 L/day when not contraindicated, give antipyretics and analgesics as prescribed, support hygiene and rest/activity balance, and provide emotional support.

Anti-infective route: Mild to moderate pyelonephritis can be treated at home with prescribed oral anti-infectives; severe pyelonephritis can require hospitalization and IV antibiotics for initial stabilization.

Surgical care: For surgical care, assess dressings/incision, teach infection monitoring, and support nutrition and fluid intake.

Procedures and complications

Procedures: Procedures can include pyelolithotomy for a large infected obstructing stone, nephrectomy when infection cannot be cleared, or ureteroplasty to repair/revise the ureter and preserve kidney function.

Teaching: Teach clients to maintain nutrition, drink about 2 L/day unless restricted, report acute pain or fever, express fears, rest as needed, and follow up as directed.

Complications: Complications include septic shock from bloodstream spread, CKD from inflammation/fibrosis/scarring and filtration damage, and hypertension from fluid/sodium retention.

Glomerulonephritis

Immune-mediated glomerular injury

Assessment cues

Origin: Glomerulonephritis can begin in the kidneys or follow another health disorder such as lupus or diabetic nephropathy.

Time course: Acute glomerulonephritis often follows infection; chronic glomerulonephritis develops over decades and can progress to ESKD.

Risk cues: Risk cues include recent skin or upper-respiratory infection, bacterial/viral/fungal/parasitic exposure, systemic disease, recent surgery, or illness.

Expected findings: Expected findings include anorexia, nausea, dysuria, oliguria, fatigue, hypertension, difficulty breathing, crackles, S3 heart sound, weight gain, and reddish-brown or cola-colored urine.

Older adults: Older adults can show circulatory-overload findings that resemble heart failure.

Monitoring and care

Labs: Labs can show RBCs and protein in urine, decreased GFR, elevated BUN/creatinine, elevated antistreptolysin O after streptococcal infection, decreased C3 complement, cryoglobulins, ANA presence, and electrolyte changes including hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia.

Biopsy: Kidney biopsy can confirm the diagnosis, determine prognosis, and guide treatment.

Coordinated care: Coordinate care to conserve energy, determine fluid restrictions with the provider, administer antibiotics and antihypertensives as prescribed, monitor blood pressure, respiratory status, fluids, and electrolytes.

Restrictions and therapies: Collaborate on potassium/protein restriction when indicated and prepare for dialysis or plasmapheresis if needed.

Teaching: Teach full antibiotic-course completion, daily weights with reporting of increases, adherence to diet/fluid restrictions, and infection-control practices such as hand hygiene.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Chronic Pyelonephritis Teaching

Active Learning Scenario

Alteration and complications

  • Chronic pyelonephritis is repeated infection and inflammation of the kidney pelvis, calyces, and medulla, usually from bacteria ascending from a lower UTI.
  • Septic shock can occur when microorganisms from the infected kidney enter the bloodstream.
  • CKD can develop from inflammation, fibrosis, scarring, and damage to the kidney filtration structures.
  • Hypertension can signal CKD from fluid/sodium retention after filtration-system destruction.

Teaching points

  • Drink at least 2 L of fluid daily unless restricted.
  • Take all medications as prescribed.
  • Notify the provider of acute, rapid onset of pain.
  • Discuss fears and anxiety, and balance rest with activity.

Application Exercises

1

Which actions should the nurse include for a client who has chronic pyelonephritis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Refer the client for nutrition counseling.
  • B. Encourage fluid intake of only 1 L/day.
  • C. Gently palpate the costovertebral angle.
  • D. Monitor urinary output.
  • E. Administer prescribed antibiotics.
A, C, D, E Nutrition supports healing, CVA tenderness can indicate kidney inflammation/infection, output shows renal response, and antibiotics treat bacteriuria and reduce progressive kidney damage.
B When not contraindicated, teaching supports about 2 L/day to maintain dilute urine.
2

A client has a UTI. Which intervention has priority?

  • A. Offer a warm sitz bath.
  • B. Recommend cranberry juice for prevention.
  • C. Encourage increased fluids when allowed.
  • D. Administer the prescribed antibiotic.
D Antibiotics are the priority because the greatest risk is renal injury and sepsis from untreated infection.
A, B, C These can support comfort or prevention, but they do not treat the active infection first.
3

Which teaching should the nurse include for a female client who has frequent UTIs? Select all that apply.

  • A. Avoid sitting in a wet bathing suit.
  • B. Wipe from back to front after elimination.
  • C. Empty the bladder when there is an urge to void.
  • D. Wear synthetic-fabric underwear.
  • E. Take a shower daily.
A, C, E Avoiding wet bathing suits, voiding with urgency, and showering daily reduce bacterial growth and urinary stasis.
B, D Wipe front to back, and choose cotton underwear that absorbs moisture.
4

Which clients are at risk for developing pyelonephritis? Select all that apply.

  • A. A client who is 32 weeks pregnant.
  • B. A client who has kidney calculi.
  • C. A client who has urine pH 4.2.
  • D. A client who has neurogenic bladder.
  • E. A client who has diabetes mellitus.
A, B, D, E Pregnancy can promote reflux/retention, stones harbor bacteria, neurogenic bladder causes retention, and diabetes can promote bacterial growth when glucose is present in urine.
C Alkaline urine promotes bacterial growth; pH 4.2 is acidic.
5

Which urinalysis result supports a urinary tract infection?

  • A. Positive hyaline casts.
  • B. Positive leukocyte esterase.
  • C. Positive ketones.
  • D. Positive crystals.
B Positive leukocyte esterase supports UTI.
A, C, D Hyaline casts can occur with proteinuria or after exercise, ketones suggest starvation or poor diabetes control, and crystals suggest stone risk.

Unit 8 · Renal Disorders · Chapter 61

Renal Calculi

Renal calculi questions usually hinge on pain pattern, obstruction, infection, urine straining, procedure teaching, medication safety, and stone-specific recurrence prevention.

TL;DR · Pain, Passage, and Obstruction

Renal colic is severe and wave-like as a stone moves. Strain all urine, save the stone, promote fluids/ambulation if not contraindicated, treat pain and spasms safely, and report anuria or obstruction immediately because kidney damage can become permanent.

Assessment cues

  • Most stones are calcium phosphate or calcium oxalate; other types include uric acid, struvite, and cystine.
  • Flank pain suggests kidney or ureter location; flank pain radiating to the abdomen, scrotum, testes, or vulva suggests ureter or bladder involvement.
  • Frequency or dysuria can occur with bladder stones; fever, diaphoresis, pallor, nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, tachypnea, blood pressure changes, oliguria/anuria, and hematuria can occur.

Priority cues

  • Obstruction with diminished or absent urine output is a medical emergency; notify the provider and prepare for calculus removal.
  • ESWL breaks calculi into fragments; teach moderate sedation, expected bruising/hematuria, and urine straining after the procedure.
  • Prevention is stone-specific: calcium oxalate means avoid oxalate sources such as black tea and spinach; calcium phosphate means limit animal protein and sodium.

Core Concepts

Assessment and Diagnostics

ATI source-authored

Risk and location

Definition: Urolithiasis means stones are present in the urinary tract; many stones pass without invasive procedures depending on composition, size, and location.

Recurrence risk: Recurrence risk rises with family history or first stone before age 25.

Risk factors: Risk factors include male sex, damaged urinary tract lining, concentrated or particle-containing urine, metabolic defects, high urine alkalinity or acidity, urinary stasis/retention, immobilization, dehydration, decreased fluid intake, and older-adult dehydration risk.

Stone location: Nephrolithiasis forms in the kidney and commonly causes acute costovertebral pain; ureterolithiasis forms in the ureter and often causes wave-like excruciating pain.

Findings and tests

Assessment: Assess severe renal colic, flank pain, radiating pain, urinary frequency, dysuria, fever, diaphoresis, pallor, nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, tachypnea, pain-related hypertension, shock-related hypotension, oliguria/anuria, and rusty/smoky hematuria.

Urinalysis: Urinalysis evaluates pH, specific gravity, osmolarity, odor/turbidity, RBCs, WBCs, bacteria, crystals, calcium, phosphate, and uric acid.

Urine pH: Decreased urine pH supports uric acid or cystine stones; increased pH supports calcium or struvite stones.

KUB or IVP: KUB or IVP can locate calculi, but IVP is contraindicated if urinary obstruction is present.

Advanced imaging: Noncontrast helical CT or MRI can identify cystine or uric acid stones that standard x-rays can miss; renal ultrasound or cystoscopy can confirm the diagnosis.

Nursing Care and Medication Safety

Pain and passage

Core nursing care

Stone passage: Report lab and diagnostic findings, provide pre/postprocedure care, administer prescribed medications, and strain all urine to check for stone passage.

Stone analysis: Save passed stones for laboratory analysis.

Fluid and mobility: Encourage oral intake up to 3 L/day unless contraindicated, administer IV fluids as prescribed, and encourage ambulation to promote passage.

Comfort: Hot baths and moist heat can promote comfort.

Spontaneous passage: Closely monitor clients attempting spontaneous passage, especially when stones are small enough to pass without intervention.

Ongoing assessment: Assess pain, intake/output, and urinary pH.

Medication cautions

Morphine: Morphine can be used early for moderate to severe acute stone pain; monitor sedation, hypotension, and respiratory depression, especially in older adults or clients with asthma/emphysema.

Ketorolac: Ketorolac can treat mild to moderate pain, fever, and inflammation, but monitor bleeding and renal function/perfusion risk.

Oxybutynin: Oxybutynin decreases bladder spasms; check glaucoma history and monitor dizziness, tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation, nausea, and voiding problems.

Antibiotics: Gentamicin and cephalexin can treat UTIs; give with food if directed, and monitor gentamicin for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

Prevention medications: Thiazides and allopurinol can support prevention depending on stone type and provider plan.

Procedures and Complications

Obstruction watch

Procedures

ESWL: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy uses sound, laser, or shock-wave energy to break stones into fragments; moderate sedation and ECG monitoring are used.

After ESWL: After ESWL, strain all urine, monitor the site, and teach that bruising at the wave site and hematuria can be expected.

Chemolysis: Nonsurgical chemolysis uses chemical agents to dissolve the calculus.

Ureteroscopy: Stenting can dilate the ureter and help stone passage during ureteroscopy; retrograde ureteroscopy uses a basket, forceps, or loop to remove the stone.

Percutaneous or open procedures: Percutaneous ureterolithotomy/nephrolithotomy uses an ultrasonic or laser lithotripter with basket/forceps extraction; open surgery is reserved for large, impacted, or refractory stones.

Complications

Urosepsis: Urosepsis can occur with struvite stones when UTI spreads to the bloodstream; monitor infection cues, culture/sensitivity results, WBC elevation, shock, urine turbidity/odor, fever, tachycardia, and dysuria.

Obstruction: Obstruction can block urine flow into the kidney, ureter, or bladder; diminished or absent urine output requires immediate provider notification and preparation for removal.

Hydroureter: Hydroureter can occur when urine flow is blocked and the ureter enlarges.

Hydronephrosis: Hydronephrosis occurs when backed-up urine distends the kidney and can cause permanent kidney damage.

Antibiotics: Antibiotics can be used prophylactically before invasive treatment or to treat existing infection.

Stone-Specific Prevention

Diet and recurrence

Calcium and struvite patterns

Calcium phosphate: For calcium phosphate stones, limit animal protein and sodium; calcium restriction is individualized.

Calcium medications: Thiazide diuretics can increase calcium reabsorption, orthophosphates can decrease urine calcium oxalate saturation, and sodium cellulose phosphate can reduce intestinal calcium absorption.

Calcium oxalate: For calcium oxalate stones, avoid oxalate sources such as spinach, black tea, rhubarb, cocoa, beets, pecans, strawberries, peanuts, okra, chocolate, wheat germ, lime peel, and Swiss chard; also limit sodium.

Struvite: For struvite stones, avoid high-phosphate foods such as dairy products, red/organ meats, and whole grains.

Uric acid and cystine patterns

Uric acid diet: For uric acid stones, decrease purine sources such as organ meats, poultry, fish, gravies, red wine, and sardines.

Urine alkalinization: Lemon or orange juice can help alkalinize urine when recommended.

Uric acid medications: Allopurinol can help prevent uric acid stone formation; potassium citrate, sodium citrate, or sodium bicarbonate can alkalinize urine.

Cystine: For cystine stones, limit animal protein; alpha mercaptopropionylglycine and captopril can lower urine cystine.

Recurrence prevention: Teach adherence to prescribed diet and medications to prevent recurrence.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Morphine and Oxybutynin for Renal Calculi

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic uses and complications

  • Morphine treats moderate to severe pain during the early acute renal calculi period.
  • Oxybutynin reduces bladder spasms that can occur with renal calculi.
  • Morphine complications include respiratory depression, euphoria, sedation, and decreased GI motility.
  • Oxybutynin complications include dizziness, tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation, and nausea.

Nursing interventions

  • Use morphine cautiously with asthma or emphysema and monitor respirations, sedation, blood pressure, and constipation prevention.
  • If respirations are 12/min or less after morphine, stop the medication and notify the provider immediately.
  • Before oxybutynin, check for glaucoma history because intraocular pressure can increase.
  • With oxybutynin, monitor dizziness, tachycardia, and urinary retention; teach clients to report palpitations, voiding problems, or constipation.
  • Teach dry-mouth measures such as hard candy, oral hygiene, and increased dietary fiber/bulk as appropriate.

Application Exercises

1

Which finding should the nurse expect during admission assessment of a client who has renal calculi?

  • A. Bradycardia.
  • B. Diaphoresis.
  • C. Nocturia.
  • D. Bradypnea.
B Diaphoresis can occur with renal calculi and severe pain.
A, C, D Tachycardia, oliguria, and tachypnea are more consistent expected findings than bradycardia, nocturia, or bradypnea.
2

Which discharge instructions fit spontaneous passage of a calcium phosphate renal calculus? Select all that apply.

  • A. Limit foods high in animal protein.
  • B. Reduce sodium intake.
  • C. Continue straining urine for 48 hr after the calculus has passed.
  • D. Report burning with urination.
  • E. Increase fluid intake to 2 to 3 L/day unless restricted.
A, B, D, E Calcium phosphate recurrence prevention includes limiting animal protein and sodium, reporting UTI cues, and maintaining adequate fluid intake if not restricted.
C Once the calculus has passed, continued urine straining is not needed for that passed stone.
3

Which statement shows understanding of ESWL teaching?

  • A. "I will be fully awake during the procedure."
  • B. "Lithotripsy will prevent future stones."
  • C. "I should report any bruising at the wave site."
  • D. "I need to strain my urine after the procedure."
D Urine is strained after lithotripsy to verify passage of stone fragments.
A, B, C Moderate sedation is used, lithotripsy breaks stones but does not prevent recurrence, and bruising can be expected.
4

A client has a left renal calculus and an indwelling urinary catheter. Which finding is the priority to report?

  • A. Flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen.
  • B. Nausea.
  • C. Absent urine output for 1 hr.
  • D. WBC count 15,000/mm3.
C Anuria can indicate obstruction of urine flow and places kidney function at greatest risk.
A, B, D These are relevant findings, but obstruction with absent urine output is the priority escalation.
5

Which foods should a client who passed a calcium oxalate calculus avoid to reduce recurrence risk? Select all that apply.

  • A. Red meat.
  • B. Black tea.
  • C. Cheese.
  • D. Whole grains.
  • E. Spinach.
B, E Black tea and spinach are oxalate sources and should be avoided with calcium oxalate stones.
A, C, D Animal protein is limited for calcium phosphate, struvite, uric acid, or cystine patterns; dairy and whole grains are more relevant to other stone-type restrictions.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 62

Diagnostic and Therapeutic Procedures for Female Reproductive Disorders

Female reproductive procedure questions often test preparation details, specimen handling, expected discomfort or spotting, restrictions after biopsy, STI test interpretation, mammography teaching, and hysterectomy complication surveillance.

TL;DR · Prep, Pads, and Reportable Bleeding

Empty the bladder before pelvic procedures, support the client during specimen collection, expect mild discomfort or small spotting after many tests, and escalate heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain, foul drainage, low urine output, or hysterectomy shock/thrombosis cues.

Screening and biopsy logic

  • Pap testing identifies precancerous or cancerous cervical cells; HPV testing identifies HPV infections that can lead to cervical cancer.
  • Colposcopy and cervical biopsy follow atypical or abnormal Pap results and can cause temporary discomfort, cramping, and some bleeding.
  • After cervical biopsy, rest briefly, avoid intercourse, douching, vaginal creams, tampons, and heavy lifting until healing/discharge resolves as instructed.

Procedure safety logic

  • For mammography, avoid deodorant, lotion, or powder on the breasts/axilla because residue can alter imaging.
  • Hysterosalpingography uses contrast to view the cervix, uterus, and fallopian tubes; confirm last menstrual period and assess iodine allergy.
  • After hysterectomy, monitor bleeding, vital signs, breath/bowel sounds, urine output, incision, Hgb/Hct, thrombosis cues, infection, and psychological response.

Core Concepts

Pelvic Exam, Pap/HPV, Colposcopy, and Biopsy

ATI source-authored

Pelvic exam with Pap/HPV

Preparation: Prepare by having the client empty the bladder, placing the client in lithotomy position, draping appropriately, explaining the procedure, and having specimen equipment ready.

Scheduling: Schedule Pap testing when the client is not menstruating; vaginal medications, douching, or intercourse within 24 hr can alter results.

During procedure: During the procedure, remain with the client, provide support, transfer specimens to slides, and apply fixative when needed.

After procedure: Afterward, provide perineal pads/tissues, teach that minimal cervical bleeding can occur, and reinforce follow-up for abnormal results.

Colposcopy and cervical biopsy

Purpose: Colposcopy examines vaginal and cervical tissue with magnification; biopsy can follow abnormal Pap findings.

Procedure options: Endocervical curettage, cone biopsy, cryosurgery, laser, or LEEP can be used depending on the lesion and treatment goal.

Preparation: Provide psychological support, prepare similarly to Pap testing, and have a sterile biopsy container ready.

Expected discomfort: Teach that tissue collection can cause temporary discomfort and cramping.

After biopsy: After cervical biopsy, provide pads/tissues, teach rest for the first 24 hr, avoid intercourse/douching/vaginal creams/tampons until discharge stops, avoid heavy lifting for about 2 weeks, avoid aspirin if bleeding risk is a concern, and report excessive bleeding, fever, or foul-smelling drainage.

Endometrial Biopsy, STI Testing, and Imaging

Diagnostics and teaching

Endometrial biopsy

Purpose: Endometrial biopsy samples endometrial tissue to evaluate uterine cancer, menstrual irregularities, infertility causes, and abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding.

Before biopsy: Before endometrial biopsy, obtain menstrual history, give analgesic as prescribed, prepare as for pelvic exam, witness consent, teach that the client is awake, and encourage bladder emptying and relaxation.

After biopsy: After endometrial biopsy, allow rest until cramping decreases; spotting can occur for 1 to 2 days, results can be available in about 72 hr, and intercourse/douching/vaginal creams/tampons are avoided until discharge stops.

STI tests

Syphilis: Syphilis screening can use VDRL or RPR; reactive screening is confirmed with treponemal testing such as FTA-ABS or microhemagglutination assay.

HIV: HIV screening uses EIA, which can become positive weeks to months after infection; a positive EIA is confirmed with Western blot assay.

Genital herpes: Genital herpes confirmation can use viral culture, PCR testing, or antibody testing.

Mammography and ultrasound

Mammography purpose: Screening mammography detects breast lesions before symptoms; diagnostic mammography follows abnormal screening findings or breast cancer manifestations.

Mammography preparation: Before mammography, avoid deodorant, lotion, or powder on the breast/axillary area and avoid mammography if pregnant unless directed by the provider.

Mammography teaching: Teach that breast compression can cause brief discomfort, and reinforce regular breast inspection and provider-directed follow-up timing.

Ultrasound: Ultrasound can assess masses, cysts, fibroids, treatment effects, or mammography lesions; transvaginal ultrasound requires an empty bladder, while abdominal ultrasound can require a full bladder.

Hysterosalpingography

Purpose: Hysterosalpingography visualizes the cervix, uterus, and fallopian tubes with contrast and is performed shortly after menstruation to avoid harm to an existing pregnancy.

Before and after: Before hysterosalpingography, confirm last menstrual cycle date, assess iodine allergy, witness consent, and prepare as for pelvic exam; after, teach minimal bleeding, prescribed analgesics for cramping, possible shoulder referred pain, and reporting prolonged bleeding or infection signs.

Hysterectomy

Therapeutic procedure

Types and indications

Types: Total hysterectomy removes uterus and cervix; subtotal removes uterus only; bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy removes ovaries and fallopian tubes.

Extensive types: Panhysterectomy removes uterus, cervix, ovaries, and fallopian tubes; radical hysterectomy removes uterus, cervix, upper vagina, and adjacent tissue including lymph nodes.

Approaches: Approaches include abdominal, vaginal, and laparoscopy-assisted vaginal hysterectomy.

Indications: Indications include uterine cancer and noncancerous conditions such as fibroids, endometriosis, and genital prolapse that cause pain, bleeding, or emotional stress.

Presenting cues: Presenting cues can include painful intercourse, heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, urinary urgency/frequency, and constipation.

Preprocedure priorities

Medication holds: Ensure anticoagulants, aspirin, NSAIDs, or vitamin E have been discontinued as prescribed.

Preoperative steps: Rule out pregnancy, administer preoperative antibiotics, place anti-embolism stockings, maintain NPO status, and verify informed consent.

Teaching and support: Complete psychological assessment and teach turning, coughing, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and medication expectations.

Urinary catheter: After surgery, an indwelling urinary catheter is usually placed intraoperatively and remains initially postoperatively.

Postprocedure monitoring

Bleeding: Monitor vaginal bleeding; excessive bleeding is more than one saturated perineal pad in 4 hr.

Priority assessments: Priority assessments include vital signs, breath sounds, bowel sounds, urine output, incision integrity/infection/dehiscence, Hgb/Hct, and signs of thrombophlebitis.

Urine output: Report urine output below 30 mL/hr.

Thromboembolism precautions: Use thromboembolism precautions, including sequential compression devices and ambulation as prescribed.

Fluids: Provide IV fluid/electrolyte replacement until bowel sounds return.

Teaching and complications

Nutrition: Teach high-protein/high-vitamin C intake for wound healing and iron-rich intake if anemic.

Ovary removal: If ovaries are removed, menopausal manifestations can develop and hormone therapy considerations might be discussed with the provider.

Restrictions: Restrict heavy lifting, strenuous activity, driving, stairs, and sexual activity as prescribed; avoid tampons.

Reportable findings: Report fever, foul-smelling drainage, incision pain/redness, calf swelling, or burning with urination.

Complications and coping: Monitor for hypovolemic shock, infection, and psychological responses; support groups can help with coping after surgery.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure - Total Abdominal Hysterectomy

Active Learning Scenario

Preprocedure nursing actions

  • Maintain NPO status and ensure informed consent is complete.
  • Rule out pregnancy.
  • Confirm prescribed discontinuation of anticoagulants, aspirin, NSAIDs, or vitamin E.
  • Administer preoperative antibiotics and place anti-embolism stockings as prescribed.
  • Teach turning, coughing, deep breathing, incentive spirometer use, early ambulation, and medication expectations.
  • Complete psychological assessment.

Postprocedure nursing actions

  • Monitor vaginal bleeding; more than one saturated pad in 4 hr is excessive.
  • Maintain the indwelling urinary catheter and monitor urine output; expected output is at least 30 mL/hr.
  • Monitor vital signs, breath sounds, bowel sounds, Hgb/Hct, incision status, and thrombosis cues.
  • Assist with ambulation and use thromboembolism precautions.
  • Provide IV fluid and electrolyte replacement until bowel sounds return.
  • Teach wound-healing diet, activity restrictions, tampon avoidance, reportable infection/bleeding/thrombosis/urinary cues, and hormone-therapy considerations if ovaries were removed.

Application Exercises

1

Which information should the nurse include when teaching a new employee about HIV testing?

  • A. EIA is typically reactive within 72 hr after infection.
  • B. Western blot assay is used to confirm HIV diagnosis after a positive screening result.
  • C. PCR testing confirms HIV diagnosis.
  • D. CD4+ counts are elevated in HIV infection.
B HIV confirmation is a two-step process in this source pattern: positive EIA screening is confirmed with Western blot assay.
A, C, D EIA reactivity can take weeks to months, PCR is listed for herpes confirmation, and CD4+ counts decrease rather than elevate with HIV progression.
2

Which instruction should the nurse give before an initial mammogram?

  • A. Avoid aspirin products before the mammogram.
  • B. Do not apply deodorant the day of the exam.
  • C. Avoid sexual intercourse the day before the mammogram.
  • D. Avoid exercise before the exam.
B Deodorant, powders, or lotions can create shadows or interfere with mammography accuracy.
A, C, D These actions do not alter mammogram accuracy in the source teaching.
3

Which statement should the nurse include before an initial Pap test?

  • A. "You should urinate immediately after the procedure."
  • B. "You will not feel any discomfort."
  • C. "You may have some bleeding after the procedure."
  • D. "You will need to hold your breath during the procedure."
C A small amount of bleeding can occur after cervical scraping.
A, B, D The client empties the bladder before the procedure, can feel discomfort, and should use relaxation/deep breathing rather than breath-holding.
4

A client's RPR is positive. Which test confirms syphilis diagnosis?

  • A. Venereal Disease Research Laboratory.
  • B. D-dimer.
  • C. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed.
  • D. Sickledex.
C FTA-ABS is used to confirm syphilis after a reactive screening test.
A, B, D VDRL is another screening test, D-dimer evaluates fibrin/clotting activity, and sickledex screens for sickle cell disease.
5

Which teaching should the nurse include before cervical biopsy? Select all that apply.

  • A. "The procedure is painless."
  • B. "Avoid heavy lifting for about 2 weeks after the procedure."
  • C. "Heavy bleeding is common during the first 12 hr."
  • D. "Plan to rest for the first 72 hr after the procedure."
  • E. "Avoid tampons until the cervix has healed."
B, E Avoid heavy lifting and tampons until healing; the source timeframe for cervical healing/discharge restrictions is about 2 weeks.
A, C, D Temporary discomfort/cramping can occur, heavy bleeding is a complication, and rest is focused on the first 24 hr rather than 72 hr.
