Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 63

Female Physiologic Processes

Female physiologic-process questions often test normal menstrual timing, when bleeding becomes abnormal, PMS/PMDD treatment patterns, endometriosis infertility risk, menopause lab/assessment cues, and hormone therapy safety.

TL;DR · Cycles, Symptoms, and Estrogen Shift

Know the cycle anchors: menarche averages 12.4 years, typical cycles range 23 to 35 days, day 1 is the first day of bleeding, ovulation is around day 14, and menstruation can last up to 9 days. Escalate excessive bleeding, infertility risk from endometriosis, and hormone therapy thrombotic or cancer warning cues.

Menstrual-process logic

  • Assessment is indicated if menstruation has not begun by 16.5 years.
  • Menorrhagia means excessive amount/duration of menstrual bleeding; metrorrhagia means bleeding between periods.
  • Amenorrhea can indicate pregnancy, thyroid or structural disorders, strenuous activity with low body fat, or anorexia nervosa.

Menopause logic

  • Perimenopause can last about 4 years before menopause and can still involve pregnancy risk.
  • Menopause is complete after 12 months without menses and can be natural or surgically induced.
  • Expected findings include hot flashes, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, mood/sleep changes, decreased bone density, decreased HDL, increased LDL, and increased FSH.

Core Concepts

Menstrual Disorders and Endometriosis

ATI source-authored

Normal timing and abnormal bleeding

Average menarche is 12.4 years, with a possible range from 9 to 17 years.

Typical menstrual cycles are 28 days, with a normal range of 23 to 35 days; day 1 is the first day of menstruation.

Ovulation typically occurs around day 14, and menstruation begins about 14 days after ovulation.

Menstruation typically lasts 4 to 6 days but can continue up to 9 days.

Dysmenorrhea is painful menstruation and is common in adolescents and young clients.

DUB can include menorrhagia and metrorrhagia and is associated with hormonal imbalance.

PMS/PMDD and endometriosis

PMS is associated with estrogen/progesterone imbalance; manifestations can vary between clients and cycles.

Expected PMS findings include irritability, impaired memory, depression, poor concentration, mood swings, binge eating, breast tenderness, bloating, weight gain, headache, and back pain.

PMDD is a severe form of PMS that interferes with daily activities.

Endometriosis occurs when endometrial tissue grows outside the uterus into the fallopian tubes, ovaries, or pelvis.

Endometrial tissue can block fallopian tubes and cause infertility.

Assessment and diagnostics

Assess menstrual history, sexual history, nutritional history, flow characteristics, pain location/characteristics, pelvic tenderness, and metabolic disorders such as thyroid disease.

Hgb/Hct can be low from excessive blood loss.

CA-125 can be elevated in ovarian cancer, endometriosis, and other conditions.

Endometrial biopsy can evaluate the relationship between menstrual flow and hormone cycle and identify pathologic bleeding causes such as uterine cancer.

Transvaginal ultrasound can identify fibroids, endometrial abnormalities, or leiomyomas.

Treatments

Hormonal contraceptives can decrease PMS, PMDD, dysmenorrhea, DUB, and can be an initial endometriosis treatment.

Spironolactone can reduce bloating and weight gain with PMS/PMDD.

Leuprolide lowers FSH/LH, suppresses estrogen/testosterone, can treat DUB and endometriosis, and requires reliable contraception due to birth-defect risk.

NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can relieve pain/discomfort and inhibit prostaglandins.

Iron treats anemia associated with DUB; SSRIs such as fluoxetine and sertraline treat emotional and physical PMS/PMDD manifestations.

D&C, endometrial ablation, hysterectomy, or laparoscopic removal of ectopic tissue/adhesions can be used when indicated.

Perimenopause and Menopause

Estrogen decline and risk prevention

Perimenopause

Perimenopause is approximately the 4 years before menopause, when ovarian function declines and cycles can become anovulatory.

Irregular bleeding can include spotting for 2 to 3 days followed by 1 to 2 days of heavy bleeding.

Genitourinary findings can include vaginal/urethral atrophy, dryness, vaginitis, dyspareunia, and postcoital bleeding.

Vasomotor findings include hot flashes/flushes, irregular menses, night sweats, dizziness, numbness/tingling, and headaches.

Sleep loss, fatigue, depression, and reduced emotional control can occur.

Pregnancy can still occur during perimenopause, so contraception is needed if pregnancy is not desired.

Menopause findings

Menopause is cessation of menses and is complete when no menses occur for 12 months.

Expected findings include hot flashes, irregular menses, atrophic vaginitis, decreased vaginal secretions, dyspareunia, incontinence, mood swings, sleep changes, decreased REM sleep, decreased bone density, decreased skin elasticity, hair loss, and breast tissue changes.

Cardiovascular changes include decreased HDL and increased LDL.

FSH increases during menopause; hormone levels can also be evaluated in blood, urine, or saliva.

Diagnostics can include pelvic exam/Pap for abnormal bleeding, breast exam/mammogram for breast changes, uterine lining biopsy for unexplained bleeding after age 40 or postmenopausal bleeding, and DXA to assess osteoporosis risk.

Hormone Therapy and Complication Prevention

Risk-benefit teaching

HT teaching

HT can reduce hot flashes, prevent vaginal tissue atrophy, and reduce fracture risk from osteoporosis.

Clients with a uterus receive estrogen plus progestin; clients without a uterus can receive estrogen alone.

HT can be oral, transdermal, intravaginal, or intramuscular and can be continuous combined or cyclic.

Use the shortest appropriate duration when HT is needed, based on provider risk-benefit discussion.

Risks include coronary heart disease, MI, DVT, stroke, breast cancer, and possible ovarian/endometrial cancer patterns with some long-term regimens.

Stop smoking, learn self-administration, and report unilateral leg pain, edema, warmth, or redness.

Risk reduction

Avoid restrictive knee-high stockings, tight socks/clothing, and prolonged sitting; walk, do ankle pumps, and move/stretch legs to promote circulation.

Female MI manifestations can include dyspnea, jaw discomfort, indigestion, and pain between the shoulders; seek help immediately.

For oral HT nausea, taking medication with food can help.

For vaginal estrogen creams/suppositories, avoid insertion before intercourse to reduce partner exposure.

Ask about complementary therapies such as black cohosh, ginseng, red clover, phytoestrogens, vitamin E, or vitamin B6 because evidence varies and interactions are possible.

Reduce osteoporosis risk with weight-bearing exercise, high-protein/high-calcium intake, alcohol/caffeine/tobacco avoidance, and calcium with vitamin D supplements as recommended.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - PMS Manifestation Journal

Active Learning Scenario

Why journal symptoms

  • PMS/PMDD manifestations begin a few days before menstruation and end a few days after menstruation begins.
  • Journaling helps connect symptoms to the menstrual cycle and supports diagnosis.
  • Patterns can vary from one cycle to the next, so repeated tracking matters.

Expected findings to track

  • Irritability, impaired memory, depression, poor concentration, and mood swings.
  • Binge eating, breast tenderness, bloating, and weight gain.
  • Headache and back pain.

Application Exercises

1

Which menstruation teaching should the school nurse include? Select all that apply.

  • A. Average onset of menstruation is age 10.
  • B. A typical cycle range is 23 to 35 days.
  • C. The first day of the cycle is the last day of the period.
  • D. Ovulation typically occurs around day 14.
  • E. A menstrual period can last as long as 9 days.
B, D, E A normal cycle can range from 23 to 35 days, ovulation is often around day 14, and menses can continue up to 9 days.
A, C Average menarche is 12.4 years, and day 1 is the first day of bleeding.
2

Which medications can be used to treat PMS? Select all that apply.

  • A. Fluoxetine.
  • B. Spironolactone.
  • C. Ethinyl estradiol/drospirenone.
  • D. Ferrous sulfate.
  • E. Methylergonovine.
A, B, C SSRIs, spironolactone, and oral contraceptives can reduce emotional and physical PMS manifestations.
D, E Iron treats anemia related to DUB, and methylergonovine is used for postpartum hemorrhage.
3

Which statements show understanding of dysfunctional uterine bleeding? Select all that apply.

  • A. "My heavy bleeding can be due to a hormonal imbalance."
  • B. "If I have menstrual pain, I should take aspirin."
  • C. "Oral contraceptives are contraindicated for heavy uterine bleeding."
  • D. "A D&C can help identify what is causing abnormal bleeding."
  • E. "This condition is more common in clients in their 30s."
A, D DUB is linked with hormonal imbalance, and D&C can collect endometrial tissue for evaluation.
B, C, E Avoid aspirin because it can increase bleeding, contraceptives can be prescribed for DUB, and DUB is more common near menopause or in adolescence.
4

Which complication can occur with endometriosis?

  • A. Insulin resistance.
  • B. Infertility.
  • C. Vaginitis.
  • D. Pelvic inflammatory disease.
B Endometrial tissue can block the fallopian tubes, causing infertility.
A, C, D Insulin resistance is associated with PCOS, vaginitis is usually infectious, and PID is infection of pelvic organs.
5

Which findings should the nurse expect in a menopausal client? Select all that apply.

  • A. Increased vaginal secretions.
  • B. Decreased bone density.
  • C. Increased HDL.
  • D. Decreased skin elasticity.
  • E. Increased pubic hair growth.
  • F. Decreased FSH.
B, D Menopause is associated with decreased bone density and decreased skin elasticity.
A, C, E, F Vaginal secretions decrease, HDL decreases while LDL increases, pubic/head hair can decrease, and FSH increases.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 64

Disorders of Female Reproductive Tissue

Female reproductive tissue questions often test which structure is protruding, whether the client needs pessary/Kegel or surgical teaching, what to report after repair, and how fibrocystic breast condition differs from cancer warning cues.

TL;DR · Prolapse, Pessary, and Benign Breast Lumps

Separate cystocele from rectocele by the symptoms: cystocele points to urinary stasis, urgency, stress incontinence, and frequent UTIs; rectocele points to constipation, rectal pressure, fecal incontinence, and needing vaginal pressure to evacuate stool. Teach pessary care, Kegel technique, postoperative restrictions, infection reporting, and that fibrocystic breast condition is benign and does not increase breast cancer risk.

Prolapse logic

  • Cystocele is bladder protrusion through the anterior vaginal wall; rectocele is rectal wall protrusion through the posterior vaginal wall.
  • Risk patterns include aging, postmenopausal estrogen loss, obesity, family history, multiparity, pregnancy pressure, childbirth strain, pelvic-structure defects, and constipation.
  • Pelvic exam with bearing down helps confirm anterior or posterior wall bulging.

Care priorities

  • Pessary clients need fit checks, cleaning teaching, latex-allergy screening if rubber is used, and reporting of pain, discomfort, or discharge.
  • Kegels require pelvic contraction, 10-second hold and 10-second relaxation, multiple positions, and relaxed abdominal muscles.
  • Fibrocystic breast condition causes painful rubberlike upper-outer quadrant lumps and can be treated with analgesics, hormonal therapy, or diuretics.

Core Concepts

Pelvic Organ Prolapse: Cystocele and Rectocele

ATI source-authored

Definitions and prevention

Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when pelvic floor muscles and ligaments weaken or become damaged.

Cystocele involves bladder protrusion through the anterior vaginal wall.

Rectocele involves rectal protrusion through the posterior vaginal wall.

Uterine prolapse is another form of pelvic organ prolapse.

Health promotion includes weight loss when obesity is present, high-fiber intake, and adequate fluids to prevent constipation and chronic bearing down.

Risk factors

Cystocele and rectocele are more likely in older adult female clients, especially after menopause.

Cystocele risk factors include obesity, advanced age with estrogen loss, family history, multiparity, pregnancy-related abdominal pressure, and vaginal-birth strain or injury.

Rectocele risk factors include pelvic-structure defects, obesity, aging, constipation, family history, and difficult vaginal childbirth that required tear repair.

Chronic constipation can worsen displacement because repeated bearing down stresses weakened pelvic structures.

Cystocele cues

Urinary frequency, urgency, stress incontinence, and frequent urinary tract infections can occur from urinary stasis.

Clients can report vaginal fullness, dyspareunia, fatigue, back pain, or pelvic pain.

Pelvic examination can show anterior vaginal wall bulging when the client bears down.

Bladder ultrasound can measure residual urine; urine culture and sensitivity can evaluate UTI; cystography or x-ray can help define the degree of protrusion.

Rectocele cues

Constipation and the need to press inside the vagina to complete stool evacuation point toward rectocele.

Expected findings include a vaginal mass sensation, pelvic or rectal pressure/pain, dyspareunia, fecal incontinence, uncontrollable flatus, and hemorrhoids.

Pelvic examination can show posterior vaginal wall bulging with bearing down.

Rectal examination can confirm the presence of a rectocele.

Prolapse Treatment and Postoperative Safety

Pessary, Kegels, and repair

Nonoperative care

Intravaginal estrogen can be used after menopause to reduce pelvic muscle atrophy.

Bladder training supports continence when urinary symptoms are present.

A vaginal pessary is a removable rubber, plastic, or silicone device that supports pelvic structures and blocks organ protrusion.

Teach pessary insertion, removal, and cleaning; verify latex allergy status if a rubber pessary is prescribed.

Clients need routine provider checks for fit and complications and should report pain, discomfort, or vaginal discharge.

Kegel technique

Contract circumvaginal and perirectal muscles as though stopping urine flow or flatus.

Gradually increase contraction time to 10 seconds, followed by a 10-second relaxation period.

Perform exercises while lying down, sitting, and standing.

Complete 30 to 80 contractions daily.

Keep abdominal and thigh muscles relaxed during contractions.

Surgical options

Transvaginal repair can support pelvic organs using mesh or tape as a sling.

Anterior-posterior repair addresses both cystocele and rectocele.

Hysterectomy can be performed at the same time as prolapse repair when indicated.

Anterior colporrhaphy tightens pelvic muscles to improve bladder support for cystocele.

Posterior colporrhaphy tightens pelvic muscles to reduce rectal protrusion into the vaginal canal.

Postoperative teaching

Administer prescribed analgesics, antimicrobials, and stool softeners or laxatives.

Warm abdominal compresses, frequent sitz baths, and a low-residue diet until bowel function returns can reduce discomfort and strain.

Report fever, increased pulse or respirations, foul-smelling or purulent vaginal discharge, or persistent pain.

Avoid straining, sneezing/coughing without pelvic support, prolonged sitting/walking/standing, strenuous activity, lifting more than 5 lb, and intercourse for about 6 weeks or as prescribed.

Absorbable sutures do not require removal; dyspareunia and mesh/tape-related erosion or serious infection are possible complications.

Fibrocystic Breast Condition

Benign breast tissue changes

Assessment and diagnostics

Fibrocystic breast condition is a noncancerous breast condition associated with cyclic hormonal changes.

It is more common in younger or premenopausal clients and less common after menopause.

Postmenopausal hormone therapy is a risk factor.

Expected findings include breast pain and tender, rubberlike palpable lumps, often in the upper outer quadrant.

Breast ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration can help confirm the diagnosis; aspiration can also decrease pain from fluid buildup.

Care and medication teaching

Teach that fibrocystic breast condition does not increase breast cancer risk.

Supportive measures include reducing salt intake before menses, wearing a supportive bra, and applying local heat or cold for temporary pain relief.

Encourage the client to follow the provider's plan and journal the effectiveness of interventions.

Analgesics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can reduce pain.

Oral contraceptives or other hormonal therapy can suppress estrogen/progesterone secretion for severe manifestations, but clients need risk teaching such as liver disease and stroke.

Diuretics can reduce breast engorgement.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Fibrocystic Breast Condition

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic uses

  • Analgesics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen are used to relieve breast pain.
  • Oral contraceptives or hormonal medication therapy can suppress estrogen/progesterone secretion when manifestations are severe.
  • Diuretics can decrease breast engorgement.

Teaching focus

  • Ask the client to track pain, lump tenderness, and response to medications across cycles.
  • Discuss medication risks before hormonal therapy is started.
  • Keep follow-up appointments for breast evaluation and imaging as prescribed.

Application Exercises

1

Which instructions should the nurse include when teaching Kegel exercises? Select all that apply.

  • A. Perform the exercises about 50 times each day.
  • B. Contract the circumvaginal and perirectal muscles.
  • C. Gradually increase contraction time to 10 seconds.
  • D. Relax for at least 10 seconds after each contraction.
  • E. Practice while lying, sitting, and standing.
  • F. Tighten the abdominal muscles during each contraction.
A, B, C, D, E Kegels are performed 30 to 80 times daily by contracting pelvic muscles, building to a 10-second hold, relaxing 10 seconds, and practicing in multiple positions.
F Abdominal and thigh muscles should remain relaxed during pelvic-floor contractions.
2

Which client statement best supports the indication for an anterior colporrhaphy?

  • A. "I have to press inside my vagina to pass stool."
  • B. "I have pain and bleeding with bowel movements."
  • C. "I keep getting urinary tract infections."
  • D. "I have uncontrollable flatus."
C Anterior colporrhaphy treats cystocele; urinary stasis from cystocele can cause frequent UTIs.
A, B, D Stool pouching, bowel-movement pain/bleeding, and uncontrollable flatus are rectocele cues and align with posterior repair.
3

Which finding is a risk factor for cystocele?

  • A. BMI of 18.
  • B. Nulliparity.
  • C. Chronic constipation.
  • D. Postmenopausal status.
D Postmenopausal status is associated with aging and estrogen loss, which increase cystocele risk.
A, B, C Obesity and multiparity are cystocele risks; constipation is emphasized as a rectocele risk.
4

Which discharge instruction should the nurse give after anterior and posterior colporrhaphy?

  • A. "Avoid bending over for at least 6 weeks."
  • B. "You may lift objects that weigh up to 10 lb."
  • C. "Avoid sexual intercourse for about 6 weeks or as prescribed."
  • D. "Foul-smelling drainage is expected during the first week."
C Intercourse is restricted while the repair heals, commonly about 6 weeks or according to provider instructions.
A, B, D Bending is not the specific restriction, lifting should stay below 5 lb, and foul-smelling drainage can indicate infection.
5

Which assessment finding should the nurse expect with fibrocystic breast condition?

  • A. Palpable rubberlike lump in the upper outer breast quadrant.
  • B. BRCA1 gene mutation.
  • C. Elevated CA-125.
  • D. Peau d'orange dimpling of the breast.
A Fibrocystic breast condition commonly causes painful, rubberlike lumps in the upper outer quadrant.
B, C, D These findings point to other cancer-related concerns rather than benign fibrocystic breast condition.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 65

Diagnostic Procedures for Male Reproductive Disorders

Male reproductive diagnostic questions often test prostate screening order, what an abnormal PSA or DRE means, TRUS latex/enema teaching, and which tests evaluate infection, anemia, erectile dysfunction, or prostate-cancer risk.

TL;DR · PSA First, Then DRE

Draw PSA before the DRE because prostate palpation can raise PSA. A PSA above 4 ng/mL needs follow-up, EPCA-2 at 30 ng/mL or greater strongly suggests prostate cancer, and abnormal DRE findings include a large, hard, irregular, or nodular prostate. TRUS uses sound waves through a rectal probe, can guide biopsy, and is contraindicated with latex allergy.

Screening sequence

  • PSA is a blood test for a protein produced by the prostate gland.
  • Perform PSA before DRE because palpation can irritate the gland and raise PSA.
  • DRE palpates the posterior prostate through the rectal wall to assess size, shape, consistency, and lumps.

Follow-up cues

  • Weak urine stream, urinary retention, or hematuria can indicate BPH or prostate cancer.
  • TRUS is used after elevated PSA or abnormal DRE and can guide needle biopsy.
  • Penile Doppler ultrasonography evaluates penile anatomy and blood flow; avoid erectile-dysfunction medications for 2 days before the test.

Core Concepts

PSA, EPCA-2, and Digital Rectal Exam

ATI source-authored

Purpose and order

Diagnostic procedures for male reproductive disorders include PSA, EPCA-2, DRE, Doppler ultrasonography, urinalysis/urine culture, CBC, and TRUS.

PSA measures a prostate-produced protein in the bloodstream using a blood sample.

PSA is collected before DRE because prostate irritation during palpation can raise PSA.

EPCA-2 measures a protein produced only by abnormal prostate cells.

DRE is performed in an office or clinic with the client leaning over the table, side-lying, or in lithotomy position.

Risk and screening discussion

Prostate changes are common with aging; enlargement can be benign, and prostate cancer is common in male clients.

Clients should have an informed provider discussion about screening benefits, risks, and uncertainty.

Screening discussion timing is age 50 for average risk, age 45 for high risk, and age 40 for higher risk.

Risk discussion includes age greater than 50 years, African American descent, and family history of prostate cancer.

Some providers use EPCA-2 instead of biopsy because of its sensitivity, and it can also monitor treatment response.

Interpretation

PSA can increase with prostate cancer, prostatitis, BPH, or recent urinary tract infection.

For a client younger than 50 years, 2.5 ng/mL is within expected range.

A PSA value greater than 4 ng/mL requires additional evaluation.

A urinary tract infection can elevate PSA for up to 6 weeks.

EPCA-2 at 30 ng/mL or greater is highly suggestive of prostate cancer.

DRE and client presentation

DRE evaluates the posterior prostate through the rectal wall for abnormalities in size, shape, consistency, or lumps.

Abnormal DRE findings include an abnormally large, hard, irregularly shaped, or nodular prostate.

If DRE reveals an abnormality, ultrasonography can localize the lesion and biopsy can confirm findings.

As prostate enlargement encroaches on the urethra, clients can have diminished urine flow and urinary retention.

Hematuria can also be present and can indicate BPH or prostate cancer.

TRUS, Penile Doppler, and Infection Labs

Diagnostic teaching

Transrectal ultrasound

TRUS uses a rectal probe and sound waves to create an image of the prostate gland.

The client is placed in a left side-lying position for the procedure.

The provider can prescribe an enema before TRUS to improve visualization.

TRUS is contraindicated with latex allergy because the rectal probe is covered by a latex sac.

TRUS is done for elevated PSA or abnormal DRE; if an irregularity is found, imaging can guide needle biopsy.

Penile Doppler ultrasonography

Penile Doppler ultrasonography determines normal penile anatomy and blood flow.

It can identify conditions of the penis, including erectile dysfunction.

An injection increases penile blood flow and causes an erection so arterial flow can be measured.

Position the client supine with the penis in correct anatomical position against the abdomen.

Teach the client not to take erectile-dysfunction medications for 2 days before the test.

Infection and anemia evaluation

If prostatitis or infection is suspected, expressed prostatic fluid can be sent for culture and sensitivity.

Culture and sensitivity identifies the causative bacteria and guides antibiotic selection.

CBC can evaluate systemic infection.

CBC can also evaluate anemia related to hematuria.

High-yield distinctions

TRUS creates an image; biopsy or EPCA-2 is used to diagnose prostate cancer.

An enlarged and nodular prostate needs follow-up because it can indicate prostate cancer.

Weak urine stream needs follow-up because it can be a BPH manifestation.

Nocturia once can be expected in an older adult male; smegma can normally collect beneath the glans.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - PSA and DRE Teaching

Active Learning Scenario

Description of procedure

  • PSA is a blood test for a protein produced by the prostate gland and is collected first.
  • DRE follows PSA because the exam can irritate the prostate and increase PSA.
  • During DRE, the provider palpates the prostate through the rectal wall with a gloved, lubricated finger.

Indications and risk teaching

  • Discuss screening with older adult clients using shared decision-making language about benefits, risks, and uncertainty.
  • Risk factors to include are age greater than 50 years, African American descent, and family history of prostate cancer.
  • Teach that elevated PSA or abnormal DRE findings require follow-up rather than automatic cancer diagnosis.

Application Exercises

1

Which annual physical findings require additional prostate follow-up? Select all that apply.

  • A. PSA is 7.1 ng/mL.
  • B. DRE reveals an enlarged, nodular prostate.
  • C. The client reports a weak urine stream.
  • D. The client reports urinating once at night.
  • E. Smegma is present below the glans penis.
A, B, C PSA greater than 4 ng/mL, an enlarged/nodular prostate, and weak stream require follow-up.
D, E Urinating once at night can be expected in older adult male clients, and smegma can normally accumulate beneath the glans.
2

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client scheduled for TRUS?

  • A. "This procedure will determine whether you have prostate cancer."
  • B. "The procedure is contraindicated if you have an egg allergy."
  • C. "Sound waves will be used to create a picture of your prostate."
  • D. "Avoid having a bowel movement for 1 hour before the procedure."
C TRUS uses sound waves through a rectal probe to image the prostate.
A, B, D Biopsy or EPCA-2 is used for diagnosis, latex allergy is the contraindication, and an enema can be prescribed to reduce stool interference.

Unit 9 · Reproductive Disorders · Chapter 66

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia, Erectile Dysfunction, and Prostatitis

This chapter turns male reproductive diagnostics into treatment decisions: recognize BPH obstruction patterns, protect TURP clients from bleeding and catheter obstruction, screen ED medications for cardiovascular risk, and distinguish acute and chronic prostatitis teaching.

TL;DR · Flow, Bleeding, and Prostate Irritation

BPH causes obstruction and urinary stasis, so expect frequency, urgency, hesitancy, incontinence, incomplete emptying, dribbling, nocturia, weak stream, straining, hematuria, recurrent UTIs, and possible kidney damage. TURP care centers on three-way catheter/CBI patency, pink or lighter output, bleeding response, early ambulation, fluids, and discharge restrictions. ED and prostatitis questions hinge on medication safety, infection testing, and urinary-retention precautions.

BPH priorities

  • BPH is prostate enlargement that impairs urine outflow in older adult male clients.
  • DRE for BPH reveals an enlarged, smooth prostate.
  • Medication goals are to re-establish urine flow and reduce obstruction.

Safety flags

  • After TURP, bright-red bleeding with clots, obstruction, decreased output, or distention needs action.
  • Avoid NSAIDs after TURP because they increase bleeding risk.
  • For ED, avoid PDE-5 inhibitors with nitrates due to profound hypotension risk.

Core Concepts

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Assessment and Medications

ATI source-authored

Risk factors and findings

BPH is common in older adult male clients and occurs when prostate enlargement begins causing urinary dysfunction.

Risk factors include increased age, smoking, chronic alcohol use, sedentary lifestyle, obesity, Western high-fat/high-protein/high-carbohydrate/low-fiber diet, diabetes mellitus, and heart disease.

The International Prostate Symptom Score can rate lower urinary tract findings and quality-of-life impact.

Expected findings include urinary frequency, urgency, hesitancy, incontinence, incomplete emptying, post-void dribbling, nocturia, diminished stream, straining, and hematuria.

Urinary stasis and persistent retention promote recurrent UTIs; prolonged backflow can damage the kidneys.

Labs and diagnostics

Urinalysis/culture can show WBCs, hematuria, and bacteria if UTI is present.

CBC can show elevated WBCs with systemic infection and decreased RBCs from hematuria.

BUN and creatinine can rise with kidney damage.

PSA, TRUS with needle aspiration biopsy, or EPCA blood testing can help rule out prostate cancer.

DRE for BPH shows an enlarged, smooth prostate.

Medication patterns

BPH medications aim to re-establish uninhibited urine flow from the bladder.

Finasteride, a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, decreases DHT production and can shrink prostate tissue.

Finasteride is long-term therapy; effects can take many months to become evident.

Teach possible impotence, decreased libido, and the need to report breast enlargement.

Because finasteride is teratogenic to a male fetus and can be absorbed through skin, pregnant clients or clients who could become pregnant should avoid crushed/broken tablets and semen exposure from a client taking it.

Tamsulosin and conservative teaching

Tamsulosin relaxes the bladder outlet and prostate gland to decrease urethral pressure and improve urine flow.

Teach slow position changes because tachycardia, syncope, and postural hypotension can occur.

Cimetidine can potentiate hypotensive effects with tamsulosin.

Avoid large fluid volumes at one time; urinate when the urge first occurs.

Avoid bladder stimulants and medications that decrease bladder tone, including anticholinergics, decongestants, and antihistamines.

BPH Procedures and TURP Safety

Therapeutic procedure focus

Procedure options

Transurethral needle ablation uses low-level radiation to shrink the prostate.

Transurethral microwave therapy applies heat to decrease prostate size.

A prostatic stent can keep the urethra patent when a client is a poor surgical candidate.

Interstitial laser coagulation/contact laser prostatectomy, electrovaporization, transurethral incision, holmium laser enucleation, and surgical resection can relieve obstruction when conservative measures are inadequate.

TURP is the most common surgical procedure for BPH and removes excess tissue through the urethra to enlarge the passageway.

Immediate TURP care

Preoperatively, assess cardiovascular, respiratory, and renal systems and confirm that the client understands expected postoperative care.

Postoperative care usually includes a three-way indwelling catheter and continuous bladder irrigation with isotonic solution to prevent obstruction.

Adjust CBI to keep irrigation return pink or lighter; bright-red or ketchup-like bleeding with clots calls for increasing the CBI rate.

If obstruction occurs, such as bladder spasms or reduced irrigation outflow, stop CBI and irrigate with 50 mL or per protocol; notify the surgeon if unable to dislodge the clot.

Record irrigant instilled and total return; the difference equals urine output.

Catheter and bleeding logic

The catheter balloon is large, taped to the leg, and applies traction/pressure to help prevent bleeding.

Balloon pressure can create a continuous urge to void; teach the client not to void around the catheter because this can cause bladder spasms.

Monitor vital signs, urinary output, bleeding, Hgb trends, and catheter tubing for kinks.

Ambulate early to reduce immobility complications such as DVT.

Give prescribed analgesics, antispasmodics, antibiotics, and stool softeners.

Discharge teaching

After catheter removal, initial voiding can be uncomfortable, red, and contain clots; urine should trend toward amber in 2 to 3 days.

Expected output is 150 to 200 mL every 3 to 4 hr; contact the provider if unable to void.

Avoid heavy lifting, strenuous exercise, straining, and sexual intercourse for the prescribed period, often 2 to 6 weeks.

Drink 12 or more 8-oz glasses of water daily unless contraindicated.

Avoid NSAIDs, caffeine, and alcohol; if urine becomes bloody, stop activity, rest, and increase fluids.

Erectile Dysfunction and Prostatitis

Medication and infection teaching

Erectile dysfunction

ED is inability to achieve or maintain an erection for intercourse.

Organic ED has gradual reduction in function from causes such as diabetes, medications, or vascular disease; functional ED is linked with psychological causes such as high stress.

Risk factors include prostatectomy, pelvic fractures, lumbosacral injuries, hypertension/vascular disease, chronic neurologic conditions, endocrine disorders, smoking, alcohol use, antihypertensives, and poor overall health.

Penile Doppler ultrasonography evaluates penile anatomy and blood flow; avoid ED medications for 2 days before testing.

A cardiovascular workup is recommended before ED medication therapy.

ED interventions

PDE-5 inhibitors increase penile blood flow and are taken about 1 hr before intercourse.

Sildenafil and vardenafil require sexual stimulation within about 1/2 to 1 hr; tadalafil allows a longer period.

Avoid alcohol; adverse effects can include dyspepsia, headache, flushing, stuffy nose, cramps, nausea, and vomiting.

Avoid PDE-5 inhibitors with nitrates due to profound hypotension and reduced blood flow to vital organs.

Other options include injectable vasodilators, vacuum constriction device, penile implants, and alprostadil urethral suppository.

Prostatitis findings

Prostatitis is prostate inflammation, often associated with lower urinary tract findings and sexual dysfunction.

Organisms can reach the prostate through the urethra or bloodstream.

Acute prostatitis can cause fever, chills, dysuria, urethral discharge, boggy/tender prostate, and urethral discharge with WBCs after palpation.

Chronic prostatitis can cause urinary hesitancy/frequency, dysuria, difficulty starting/stopping flow, decreased urine strength/volume, back/perineal pain, and irregular prostate enlargement.

PSA greater than 4 ng/mL needs evaluation and can be elevated with prostate cancer, BPH, or acute prostatitis.

Prostatitis care

Use early morning urine for a concentrated specimen; if infection is suspected, obtain a midstream clean-catch sample.

Urine culture and sensitivity identifies the organism and antibiotic choice; WBC count rises with infection/inflammation.

Antimicrobials can be required for weeks or months and might require inpatient IV therapy.

Stool softeners prevent straining and rectal irritation of the prostate.

Use sitz baths, NSAIDs, and muscle relaxants if prescribed; avoid alcohol, tea, coffee, spicy foods, and OTC cold products with decongestants or antihistamines; complete the full medication course.

Sexual intercourse and masturbation can help manage chronic prostatitis; prostatitis is not infectious or contagious.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Finasteride for BPH

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic use

  • Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase, which converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.
  • Reduced DHT decreases testosterone activity in the prostate and can reduce prostate tissue size.
  • The goal is improved urine flow from decreased obstruction.

Client education

  • Take as long-term therapy; effects can take up to 1 year to become evident.
  • Impotence and decreased libido are possible.
  • Report breast enlargement to the provider.
  • Pregnant clients or clients who could become pregnant should avoid crushed/broken tablets and semen exposure from a client taking finasteride.

Application Exercises

1

Which history findings support BPH? Select all that apply.

  • A. Backache.
  • B. Frequent urinary tract infections.
  • C. Weight loss.
  • D. Hematuria.
  • E. Urinary incontinence.
B, D, E BPH causes urinary stasis, which can lead to UTIs, hematuria, and overflow incontinence from increased residual urine.
A, C Backache and weight loss raise concern for prostate cancer spread rather than typical BPH findings.
2

Which medication should the nurse expect for a client newly diagnosed with BPH?

  • A. Oxybutynin.
  • B. Diphenhydramine.
  • C. Ipratropium.
  • D. Tamsulosin.
D Tamsulosin relaxes the bladder outlet and prostate gland, improving urine flow.
A, B, C Anticholinergic or antihistamine effects can worsen urinary retention and are avoided in BPH.
3

Which TURP postoperative teaching should the nurse include?

  • A. "You might feel a continuous need to void even though you have a catheter."
  • B. "You will remain on bed rest for the first 2 days."
  • C. "You should limit fluids after the procedure."
  • D. "Your urine should be clear yellow the evening after surgery."
A The large catheter balloon applies pressure to reduce bleeding and can cause a continuous urge to void.
B, C, D Early ambulation is encouraged, fluids are increased unless contraindicated, and urine is expected to be pink during the first 24 hr.
4

Which discharge instructions should the nurse provide after TURP? Select all that apply.

  • A. Avoid sexual intercourse for 3 months.
  • B. If urine appears bloody, stop activity and rest.
  • C. Avoid caffeinated beverages.
  • D. Take a stool softener daily.
  • E. Treat pain with ibuprofen.
B, C, D Blood-tinged urine after activity means rest and fluids; caffeine can stimulate the bladder; stool softeners prevent straining and bleeding.
A, E Intercourse is typically restricted for 2 to 6 weeks or as prescribed, and NSAIDs can increase bleeding risk.

Unit 10 · Musculoskeletal Disorders · Chapter 67

Musculoskeletal Diagnostic Procedures

Musculoskeletal diagnostic questions usually ask what the test shows, what to screen for before the test, and what to teach afterward: arthroscopy needs neurovascular checks, nuclear scans need isotope teaching and fluids, DXA measures bone density, and EMG/nerve conduction require bleeding and infection precautions.

TL;DR · Image Bone, Test Nerves, Protect the Joint

Arthroscopy is a sterile joint procedure that can diagnose and repair tears; after it, check neurovascular status, ice/elevate, and report infection or thrombophlebitis. Bone/gallium/thallium scans use radionuclide timing and require bladder-emptying and postprocedure fluids. DXA estimates bone density without contrast. EMG/nerve conduction evaluates muscle weakness but requires anticoagulant, skin infection, and muscle-relaxant checks.

Procedure matching

  • Arthroscopy visualizes internal joint structures and can repair torn ligaments or meniscus.
  • Bone scans evaluate the entire skeleton; gallium/thallium scans are more sensitive for bone problems.
  • DXA scans estimate bone density, commonly in the hip or spine.

Safety checks

  • Nuclear scans require screening for radioisotope allergy, pregnancy, lactation, and kidney disease.
  • EMG requires review of anticoagulants, skin infection at the site, and muscle relaxants.
  • MRI requires metal screening; CT with contrast requires allergy assessment and adequate fluids afterward.

Core Concepts

Arthroscopy

ATI source-authored

Purpose and indications

Arthroscopy uses an endoscope to visualize internal structures of a joint.

It is commonly used for knee and shoulder joints and is performed in the operating room under sterile conditions.

Local or general anesthesia can be used.

Number and placement of incisions depend on the joint and extent of repair.

Potential uses include evaluating joint injury, repairing a torn ligament or meniscus, and performing synovial biopsy.

Contraindications and presentation

Infection in the joint is a contraindication.

Lack of joint mobility is a contraindication.

Client presentation can include joint swelling, pain, crepitus, and instability.

Preprocedure care includes confirming informed consent.

Teach that postoperative joint exercises, such as straight-leg raises or quadriceps-setting isometrics, can be prescribed.

Postprocedure priorities

Recovery actions depend on the type of sedation and extent of repair; arthroscopy is often outpatient.

Assess neurovascular status and dressings at least hourly or per facility protocol.

Assess color, temperature, pulse, pain, and sensation in the affected extremity.

Administer mild analgesics or opioids as prescribed depending on pain and whether repair was corrective.

Elevate the extremity for 12 to 24 hr and maintain activity restrictions.

Teaching and complications

Apply ice for the first 24 hr to control edema and discomfort.

Inspect the incision for infection cues such as redness, swelling, purulent drainage, and fever.

Report swelling, increased joint pain, thrombophlebitis cues, or infection cues.

A cast is not typically required after arthroscopy.

Infection is uncommon but possible with any procedure that disrupts skin integrity.

Nuclear Scans and DXA

Bone density and isotope teaching

Bone, gallium, and thallium scans

Bone scans evaluate the entire skeletal system.

A radionuclide is injected 2 to 3 hr before a bone scan; areas of abnormal bone formation appear brighter during scanning.

Bone scans can detect hairline fractures, tumors, fractures, osteomyelitis, osteoporosis, and vertebral compression fractures.

Gallium and thallium scans are more sensitive for bone problems and can detect disease in tissues such as brain, liver, and breast.

Gallium/thallium radionuclide injection occurs 4 to 6 hr before scanning; repeat scanning can occur at 24, 48, and 72 hr.

Nuclear scan care

Potential indications include degenerative bone disease, osteomyelitis, stress or vertebral compression fractures, nonhealing fractures, osteoporosis, primary or metastatic bone cancer, bone pain of unknown origin, and aseptic necrosis.

Assess for radioisotope allergy and conditions that prevent the procedure, including pregnancy, lactation, and kidney disease.

Teach the client to remain still and empty the bladder before the procedure to improve pelvic bone visualization.

After the procedure, radioactive precautions are not needed.

Increase fluids to promote excretion of the radioisotope in urine and feces.

DXA purpose

DXA estimates bone mass density, usually in the hip or spine.

DXA evaluates presence and extent of osteoporosis.

The scan uses two beams of radiation and a computer analyzes findings for radiologist interpretation.

Clients do not receive contrast material.

Clients lie on an x-ray table during hip or spine scanning.

DXA teaching

Indications include osteoporosis, postmenopausal state, and baseline testing for females in their 40s.

Client findings that can indicate need for DXA include loss of height, bone pain, and fractures.

DXA is not recommended for clients who are pregnant or lactating.

Clients can stay dressed but should remove metallic objects.

If bone loss is present, follow up with the provider to discuss supplements and medications.

EMG, Nerve Conduction, CT, MRI, Radiography, and US

Neuromuscular and soft-tissue evaluation

EMG and nerve conduction

EMG and nerve conduction studies determine the presence and cause of muscle weakness.

EMG places thin needles in the muscle being studied; electrodes connect to an oscilloscope and record activity during contraction.

Nerve conduction studies use surface or needle electrodes and low electrical current to record muscle response.

Potential diagnoses include neuromuscular disorders, motor neuron disease, and peripheral nerve disorders such as carpal tunnel.

Discomfort is possible during needle insertion and electrical current; the client can be asked to flex muscles during needle insertion.

EMG safety

Determine whether the client takes an anticoagulant because anticoagulation can be contraindicated due to bleeding risk within the muscle.

Check for skin infection in the assessment area because infection can spread to muscle with needle insertion.

Ask about muscle relaxants because they can be discontinued before testing for accurate results.

Teach the client to avoid cream or lotion on the area the day of the procedure.

Afterward, bruising can occur; report swelling or tenderness, and use ice to prevent hematoma or warm compresses for residual discomfort.

CT, MRI, radiography, US

These procedures provide detailed images of body structures, bone density, texture, and surgical hardware.

MRI, ultrasound, and CT provide visualization of soft tissues.

Potential diagnoses include tendon or ligament injuries, fractures of chest or pelvic bones, skull or vertebral fracture, and herniated disc.

Client presentation can include bone pain and joint instability.

Procedure-specific checks

For CT with contrast, assess for contrast allergy.

After contrast testing, ensure adequate fluid intake if not contraindicated.

For MRI, determine whether the client has metal in the body, such as a pacemaker.

Remove external metal such as jewelry and hair clips before MRI.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Gallium Scan Teaching

Active Learning Scenario

Description and indications

  • A gallium scan uses a radionuclide/radioisotope injection given 4 to 6 hr before scanning.
  • The radioisotope can migrate to bone and tissues such as brain, liver, and breast to help detect disease.
  • Indications include fractures, osteoporosis, bone lesions, osteomyelitis, and arthritis.

Nursing interventions

  • Before the procedure, assess for radioisotope allergy.
  • Assess for contraindicating conditions such as pregnancy, lactation, or kidney disease.
  • Have the client empty the bladder before the scan.
  • After the procedure, increase fluid intake to promote excretion of the radioisotope in urine and feces.

Application Exercises

1

Which teaching should the nurse include before shoulder arthroscopy? Select all that apply.

  • A. Avoid damage or moisture to the cast on the arm.
  • B. Inspect the incision daily for infection.
  • C. Apply ice packs to the area for the first 24 hr.
  • D. Keep the arm in a dependent position.
  • E. Perform prescribed isometric exercises.
B, C, E Arthroscopy teaching includes incision infection checks, ice for the first 24 hr, and prescribed isometric exercises.
A, D A cast is not typical after arthroscopy, and the extremity should be elevated for 12 to 24 hr rather than kept dependent.
2

Which actions should the nurse take after knee arthroscopy? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assess color and temperature of the extremity.
  • B. Apply warm compresses to incision sites during the first 24 hr.
  • C. Place pillows under the extremity.
  • D. Administer analgesic medication.
  • E. Assess pulse and sensation in the foot.
A, C, D, E Check circulation and sensation, elevate the extremity, and administer analgesics for postoperative arthroscopy care.
B Cold/ice is used for the first 24 hr to decrease swelling and pain.
3

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client scheduled for a bone scan?

  • A. "You will receive a radioactive isotope when scanning begins."
  • B. "You will be inside a tube-like structure during the procedure."
  • C. "Use radioactive precautions with your urine for 24 hr afterward."
  • D. "You will need to urinate just before the procedure."
D Emptying the bladder before the procedure promotes visualization of pelvic bones.
A, B, C The isotope is injected 2 to 3 hr before scanning, a tube-like structure is associated with MRI, and urine precautions are not needed afterward.
4

Which DXA scan teaching should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

  • A. The test requires contrast material.
  • B. The hip and spine are usual scan areas.
  • C. The scan detects osteoarthritis.
  • D. Bone pain can indicate a need for the scan.
  • E. Females should have a baseline scan during their 40s.
B, D, E DXA commonly scans hip/spine, can be indicated by bone pain, and baseline testing for females in their 40s supports later comparison.
A, C DXA does not require contrast and detects osteoporosis rather than osteoarthritis.
5

Which actions should the nurse include for a client having EMG? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assess for bruising after the test.
  • B. Administer aspirin before the procedure.
  • C. Determine whether the client takes a muscle relaxant.
  • D. Tell the client they might be asked to flex muscles during needle insertion.
  • E. Expect swelling, redness, and tenderness at insertion sites.
A, C, D Bruising can occur; muscle relaxants can affect results; and the client can be asked to flex muscles during needle insertion.
B, E Anticoagulant/bleeding risk is screened rather than aspirin given, and swelling/redness/tenderness should be reported as possible infection.

Suggested template type

Unit 10 · Musculoskeletal Disorders · Chapter 68

Arthroplasty

Arthroplasty replaces damaged joint structures with prosthetic components. The ATI priorities are infection screening before surgery, DVT/PE prevention after surgery, neurovascular checks, joint-specific positioning, and hip precautions that prevent dislocation.

TL;DR · Replace the Joint, Protect the Prosthesis

For knee and hip arthroplasty, think: rule out active infection and unstable comorbidities, prepare the client for postoperative therapy, prevent VTE, check neurovascular status every 2 to 4 hr, keep the knee extended after knee replacement, and prevent hip flexion beyond 90 degrees after hip replacement.

Before surgery

  • Assess for recent or active infection, arterial impairment, inability to follow the regimen, and unstable chronic conditions.
  • Review CBC, urinalysis, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, chest x-ray, and ECG findings as prescribed.
  • Teach surgical-site antiseptic scrub, clean clothes/linens, allowed morning medications, pain control, drains, exercises, transfer limits, and activity limits.

After surgery

  • Monitor bleeding, Hgb/Hct trends, incision infection cues, and neurovascular status of the surgical extremity.
  • Promote early mobility with ordered weight-bearing limits and assistive/adaptive devices.
  • Report calf pain/swelling/redness, shortness of breath, chest pain, acute hip pain, pop sensation, leg shortening, or abnormal rotation.

Arthroplasty Priorities

Joint Replacement Overview

ATI source-authored

What is replaced

Arthroplasty removes a diseased joint and replaces damaged structures with artificial components made from metal and/or plastic.

Total joint replacement replaces all parts of an articulating joint.

Total knee arthroplasty replaces distal femur, tibial plate, and patellar button components when conservative treatment fails.

Total hip arthroplasty replaces the acetabular cup, femoral head, and femoral stem.

Hemiarthroplasty replaces half of a joint and can be used for femoral neck fracture repair.

Why it is done

Goals include pain relief, restored joint motion, improved function, and better quality of life.

Common conditions include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, osteonecrosis, trauma, and congenital joint problems.

Expected findings can include weight-bearing pain, joint stiffness, crepitus, swelling, and limited motion.

Skin redness over a joint suggests infection rather than an expected degenerative finding.

Preprocedure Screening and Teaching

Rule out infection

Contraindication cues

Recent or active infection can seed the surgical site and cause prosthesis failure.

Arterial impairment in the affected extremity can compromise healing.

The client must be able to follow the postoperative regimen.

Uncontrolled diabetes, uncontrolled hypertension, advanced osteoporosis, progressive inflammatory disease, or unstable cardiac/respiratory status can delay or contraindicate surgery.

Pre-op teaching

Discuss postoperative incentive spirometry, transfusion possibility, drains, dressings, pain control, transfers, exercises, and activity limits.

Autologous blood donation can be considered before surgery.

Use prescribed antiseptic soap the night before and morning of surgery, then wear clean clothing and sleep on clean linens.

Take only the morning medications the surgeon allows, with a sip of water.

Knee Arthroplasty Nursing Care

Avoid flexion contractures

Immediate priorities

Prevent anemia, infection, neurovascular compromise, DVT, and PE.

Monitor movement, sensation, color, pulse, and capillary refill every 2 to 4 hr and compare with the other extremity.

Assess for overt bleeding and hypovolemia cues such as hypotension and tachycardia.

Monitor compression dressing, wound suction drainage, and any autotransfusion drainage system.

Support pain control so the client can participate in early ambulation.

Position and mobility

A continuous passive motion machine can be prescribed immediately after surgery to support knee motion, circulation, and prevention of scar tissue formation.

Check CPM settings against the prescription, follow duration orders, and turn the device off during meals.

Avoid knee gatch and pillows behind the knee because flexion positions promote contractures.

Place one pillow under the lower calf and foot or keep the knee flat to maintain slight extension.

Keep heels off the bed to prevent pressure injury; PT often begins mobility on the first postoperative day with weight-bearing as prescribed.

Hip Arthroplasty Nursing Care

Prevent dislocation

Post-op monitoring

Check the dressing and surgical drains frequently for bleeding and drainage amount.

Monitor Hgb and Hct because levels can continue to fall during the first 48 hr after surgery.

Assess neurovascular status every 2 to 4 hr and compare with the other extremity.

Give prescribed analgesics, prophylactic antibiotics, and anticoagulants.

Use early ambulation with walker, raised toilet seat, grab bars, shower chair, and provider-directed weight-bearing limits.

Hip precautions

Keep the client supine with the head slightly elevated and the affected leg in neutral alignment.

Use an abduction pillow or regular pillow between the legs when turning to the unaffected side if prescribed.

Avoid turning to the operative side unless allowed by policy or provider prescription.

Use elevated seating, a raised toilet seat, straight chairs with arms, and long-handled adaptive equipment.

Avoid hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, low chairs, crossing the legs, and internal toe rotation.

Complication Watch

VTE, infection, anemia, dislocation

VTE and bleeding

Older adults are at increased risk for complications because chronic disease can reduce physiologic reserve.

Monitor for DVT cues such as calf swelling, redness, and pain.

Monitor for PE cues such as shortness of breath and chest pain.

Assess for bleeding, especially when anticoagulant therapy is prescribed.

Joint and wound safety

Maintain aseptic technique during dressing care.

Teach daily incision cleaning with soap and water if prescribed and report fever, increased redness, swelling, or purulent drainage.

Follow mobility and positioning prescriptions to protect the prosthesis.

For hip dislocation, watch for acute pain, a reported popping sensation, internal/external rotation, or shortening of the affected extremity.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Enoxaparin After Knee Arthroplasty

Active Learning Scenario

Expected action

  • Enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulant.
  • After orthopedic surgery, it is used to reduce the risk of DVT that can progress to PE.

Nursing interventions

  • Do not expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe before injection.
  • Rotate injection sites.
  • Monitor for unexplained bleeding.

Client teaching

Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor, avoid over-the-counter medications unless the provider approves them, and avoid supplements that can increase bleeding risk, including garlic, ginger, ginkgo, and feverfew.

Application Exercises

1

Which finding should make the nurse question whether a client is ready for total joint arthroplasty?

  • A. Age of 78 years
  • B. History of cancer
  • C. Prior joint replacement
  • D. Bronchitis 2 weeks ago
D A recent infection can allow organisms to migrate to the surgical area and threaten prosthesis success.
A, B, C These findings are not automatic contraindications unless paired with unstable comorbidities or other surgical risks.
2

Which actions are appropriate for a client admitted after total knee arthroplasty? Select all that apply.

  • A. Verify continuous passive motion settings.
  • B. Palpate pedal pulses.
  • C. Place a pillow behind the knee.
  • D. Elevate the heels off the bed.
  • E. Apply heat to the incision.
A, B, D CPM settings must match the prescription, pulses support neurovascular assessment, and heel elevation helps prevent pressure injury.
C, E A pillow behind the knee promotes flexion contracture, and cold rather than heat is used for postoperative swelling.
3

Which discharge instructions should the nurse include after total hip arthroplasty? Select all that apply.

  • A. Clean the incision daily with soap and water if prescribed.
  • B. Turn the toes inward when sitting or lying.
  • C. Use a straight-backed chair with arms.
  • D. Bend at the waist to put on socks.
  • E. Use a raised toilet seat.
A, C, E Incision care reduces infection risk, and elevated/straight seating reduces hip flexion that can dislocate the prosthesis.
B, D Internal toe rotation and bending past 90 degrees increase dislocation risk.
4

Which expected findings can the nurse anticipate in a client scheduled for knee arthroplasty? Select all that apply.

  • A. Reddened skin over the joint
  • B. Pain with weight bearing
  • C. Joint crepitus
  • D. Swelling of the affected joint
  • E. Limited joint motion
B, C, D, E Degenerative joint disease can cause pain with weight bearing, crepitus, swelling, and limited motion.
A Redness over the joint can indicate infection and is not an expected finding for routine arthroplasty planning.
5

Which teaching should the nurse include before total hip arthroplasty? Select all that apply.

  • A. Consider autologous blood donation.
  • B. Use a low reclining chair after discharge.
  • C. Roll onto the operative hip for positioning.
  • D. Use an abduction pillow when turning if prescribed.
  • E. Practice prescribed isometric exercises.
A, D, E Autologous blood can be planned preoperatively, abduction positioning protects the hip, and isometric exercises help maintain muscle tone and reduce clot risk.
B, C Low seating and turning onto the operative side increase hip-dislocation risk unless specifically allowed by the provider.

Unit 10 · Musculoskeletal Disorders · Chapter 69

Amputations

Amputation care starts before the operation with prevention, perfusion assessment, and body-image support, then shifts to hemorrhage control, residual-limb healing, phantom pain, prosthesis preparation, and contracture prevention.

TL;DR · Preserve Perfusion, Shape the Limb, Prevent Contracture

For amputations, think: prevent lower-extremity loss with glucose control, smoking cessation, safe equipment use, and foot care; assess perfusion before surgery; handle traumatic amputations as a hemorrhage emergency; keep residual-limb care clean and perfused; treat phantom pain as real; and prevent hip/knee flexion contractures with positioning and prone time.

Highest-yield risks

  • Peripheral vascular disease and diabetes mellitus are major drivers of lower-extremity amputation.
  • Trauma, thermal injury, malignancy, chronic osteomyelitis, and congenital conditions can also lead to amputation.
  • The amputation level depends on whether blood flow is adequate for healing.

Care after surgery

  • Monitor bleeding, vital signs, drainage, infection, and tissue perfusion at the residual limb.
  • Use shrinkage interventions so the residual limb can fit a prosthesis when healing allows.
  • Discourage prolonged sitting and use prone positioning several times daily to prevent flexion contractures.

Amputation Priorities

Prevention and Perfusion Assessment

ATI source-authored

Risk reduction

Encourage smoking cessation, healthy weight, and regular exercise to reduce vascular disease risk.

Clients who have diabetes should keep blood glucose within the expected range.

Teach good foot care and early reporting of nonhealing wounds.

Use safety measures with heavy machinery and around electrical or burn hazards.

Peripheral vascular disease causes most lower-extremity amputations.

Expected perfusion findings

Assess pain, altered pulses, temperature changes, pallor/cyanosis/gangrene, open wounds, infection, and reduced sensation.

Compare extremities when checking capillary refill, pulses, temperature, edema, and skin changes.

Use Doppler when pulses are difficult to assess.

Angiography, Doppler/ultrasound, transcutaneous oxygen pressure, and ankle-brachial index can help determine blood flow at amputation levels.

Traumatic Amputation and Immediate Care

Hemorrhage first

Emergency response

Activate emergency medical services.

Apply direct pressure with gauze or a clean cloth to control life-threatening bleeding.

Elevate the injured extremity above heart level to decrease blood loss when appropriate.

Wrap the severed part in dry sterile gauze or a clean cloth, seal it in a plastic bag, and place the bag in ice water for transport with the client.

Post-op priorities

Prevent hypovolemia, pain, and infection.

Assess the surgical site for bleeding and monitor vital signs frequently.

Assess residual-limb warmth, proximal pulse comparison, drainage, and wound healing.

For open amputation, administer antibiotics and change dressings as prescribed.

Pain, Phantom Pain, and Body Image

Pain is real

Differentiate pain type

Incisional pain is treated with analgesics.

Phantom limb pain is felt where the removed limb was and is related to severed nerve pathways.

Phantom pain can occur immediately after surgery, weeks later, or continue longer term.

Burning, cramping, shooting, aching, sharp, or stabbing descriptions can guide medication choices.

The nurse should recognize phantom pain as real and treat it accordingly.

Pain and psychosocial support

Antiepileptic medications can help sharp, stabbing, or burning phantom pain.

Other options can include calcitonin early after amputation, beta blockers, antispasmodics, antidepressants, massage, heat, TENS, ultrasound, biofeedback, acupuncture, and relaxation.

Teach supported downward pressure of the residual limb toward the bed when prescribed to reduce phantom pain and prepare for prosthesis use.

Assess grief, depression, anger, withdrawal, altered self-concept, self-esteem, and motivation for rehabilitation.

Residual-Limb Preparation and Prosthesis Planning

Shape and shrink safely

Shrinkage interventions

The residual limb must heal, shrink, and be shaped before prosthetic training.

Wrap with elastic bandages in a figure-eight pattern to reduce edema without restricting blood flow.

A residual-limb shrinker sock can be easier for the client to apply.

An air splint can protect and shape the limb while allowing wound inspection.

Client teaching

Teach residual-limb care, wrapping, and strengthening exercises.

Teach correct prosthesis application and care when the client is ready.

Support safe transfers, mobility devices, and adaptive aids.

Closed amputation closes a skin flap over the residual limb; open amputation allows infection drainage and is closed later.

Contracture Prevention and Rehab Team

Position early

Prevent contractures

Hip or knee flexion contractures are more likely when positioning is poor after amputation.

Start range-of-motion exercises and proper positioning early as prescribed.

Have the client lie prone for 20 to 30 min several times daily to help prevent hip flexion contracture.

Discourage prolonged sitting and teach standing with the residual limb in extension when able.

Interprofessional roles

A certified prosthetic orthotist fits the prosthesis after the wound heals and the residual limb shrinks.

A physical therapist trains the client in prosthesis application, prosthesis care, and mobility aids.

A psychologist can support adjustment to limb loss.

A social worker can connect the client with financial resources, support groups, and community organizations.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Amputation Discharge Team

Active Learning Scenario

Team members

  • Certified prosthetic orthotist: fits the prosthesis once healing and residual-limb shrinkage are adequate.
  • Physical therapist: teaches prosthesis use, prosthesis care, transfers, ambulation, and mobility aids.
  • Psychologist: assists the client and family with adjustment to limb loss and altered body image.
  • Social worker: helps with financial concerns and links the client to resources and support groups.

Nursing focus

  • Include rehabilitation planning early, not only at discharge.
  • Assess readiness, support grief work, and reinforce safe home mobility.
  • Coordinate follow-up teaching for residual-limb care, phantom pain management, and prosthesis preparation.

Application Exercises

1

Which teaching should the nurse include to reduce the risk of amputation? Select all that apply.

  • A. Consider smoking cessation programs.
  • B. Keep blood glucose within the expected range.
  • C. Unplug electrical equipment before repairs.
  • D. Maintain good foot care with vascular disease.
  • E. Drive 2 hr after taking pain medication.
A, B, C, D Smoking cessation, glucose control, electrical safety, and foot care reduce vascular, injury, and infection risks that can lead to amputation.
E Driving after pain medication can increase injury risk and is not prevention teaching.
2

Which findings should the nurse expect in an extremity with poor perfusion from arteriosclerosis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Cool skin from mid-calf to toes
  • B. Increased sensitivity to fine touch
  • C. Palpable pounding pedal pulse
  • D. Lack of hair on the lower leg
  • E. Blackened areas on several toes
A, D, E Coolness, decreased hair growth, and gangrenous color changes are expected with decreased vascularization.
B, C Poor perfusion is associated with decreased sensation and diminished or absent pulses, not increased fine touch or pounding pulses.
3

Which actions should the nurse take after a below-the-elbow amputation? Select all that apply.

  • A. Encourage dependent positioning of the residual limb.
  • B. Inspect for presence and amount of drainage.
  • C. Implement residual-limb shrinkage interventions.
  • D. Wrap the residual limb in a circular manner with gauze.
  • E. Assess for feelings related to body image changes.
A, B, C, E Dependent positioning can promote perfusion, drainage assessment detects infection, shrinkage prepares for prosthesis fitting, and body-image assessment supports rehabilitation.
D The residual limb is wrapped in a figure-eight pattern to reduce edema without restricting blood flow.
4

A client after an above-the-knee amputation reports sharp, stabbing phantom pain. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Remove the initial pressure dressing.
  • B. Encourage cold therapy.
  • C. Question whether the pain is real.
  • D. Administer an antiepileptic medication.
D Antiepileptic medications can relieve sharp, stabbing phantom limb pain.
A, B, C The initial pressure dressing is not removed for phantom pain, heat rather than cold can be used as an alternative therapy, and phantom pain should be treated as real.
5

Which action should the nurse include to prevent flexion contractures 24 hr after below-the-knee amputation?

  • A. Limit all residual-limb exercise for the first 48 hr.
  • B. Position the client prone several times each day.
  • C. Wrap the residual limb in a figure-eight pattern.
  • D. Encourage sitting in a chair during the day.
B Prone positioning for 20 to 30 min several times daily helps prevent hip flexion contractures.
A, C, D ROM is used to prevent contractures, figure-eight wrapping prepares for prosthesis fitting, and prolonged sitting increases flexion contracture risk.

Suggested template type

Unit 10 · Musculoskeletal Disorders · Chapter 70

Osteoporosis

Osteoporosis is low bone density from bone resorption outpacing formation, making fractures more likely. ATI priorities cluster around prevention, recognizing height loss/kyphosis/fracture cues, DXA screening, fall safety, medication precautions, and vertebral-fracture care.

TL;DR · Build Bone, Prevent Falls, Protect the Spine

For osteoporosis, think: calcium/vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, DXA screening, fall-proof the home, avoid excess alcohol/caffeine/carbonated beverages, monitor high-risk medications, give oral bisphosphonates with strict upright teaching, avoid raloxifene with DVT history, and keep vertebroplasty clients supine for 1 to 2 hr.

Risk and recognition

  • Risk increases with low body weight, family history, menopause/low estrogen, low calcium or vitamin D, smoking, high alcohol intake, malabsorption, immobility, and prolonged corticosteroid or anticonvulsant use.
  • Expected findings include loss of 2 to 3 inches in height, kyphosis, back pain after lifting/bending, spinal deformity, limited movement, and fracture history.
  • Fractures are the leading complication; wrists, hips, and spine are common sites.

Prevention and safety

  • Teach calcium/vitamin D sources, moderate sun exposure with sunscreen, and weight-bearing activity.
  • Assess home safety: remove throw rugs and clutter, improve lighting, clear walkways, mark thresholds, and use prescribed assistive devices.
  • Use rubber-bottomed shoes and avoid slippery surfaces, jarring activity, strenuous lifting, and trunk twisting with vertebral pain.

Osteoporosis Priorities

Risk Factors and Prevention

ATI source-authored

What drives bone loss

Osteopenia is low bone mineral density that can precede osteoporosis.

Bone density peaks in young adulthood, then decreases; postmenopausal estrogen loss accelerates bone resorption.

Thin body build, family history, low calcium/vitamin D intake, malabsorption, smoking, high alcohol intake, excess caffeine, high phosphorus intake, immobility, and older-adult fall risk all raise concern.

Secondary osteoporosis can occur with endocrine, inflammatory, respiratory, and metabolic conditions or with long-term loop diuretics, corticosteroids, thyroid medications, and anticonvulsants.

Prevention teaching

Encourage adequate calcium and vitamin D from food and/or supplements.

Vitamin D sources include fish, egg yolks, and fortified milk/cereals; calcium sources include dairy, leafy greens, fortified juice/cereal, beans, figs, and fortified soy/rice products.

Use weight-bearing exercise such as walking or lifting weights to promote bone rebuilding and maintenance.

Limit excess caffeine, alcohol, and carbonated beverages because they can contribute to bone loss.

Assessment and Diagnostic Testing

DXA and fracture cues

Expected findings

Reduced height of 2 to 3 inches can suggest vertebral compression fractures.

Back pain after lifting or bending can worsen with activity and improve with rest.

Assess restricted movement, spinal deformity, kyphosis, localized tenderness, and history of wrist, femur, or thoracic spine fractures.

Labs can help rule out other metabolic bone disease and can include calcium, vitamin D, phosphorus, hematocrit, ESR, alkaline phosphatase, 24-hr urine calcium excretion, and bone turnover markers.

Imaging logic

Radiographs can show low bone density and fractures.

DXA screens for early bone-density changes, usually at the hip or spine; peripheral DXA can assess heel, forearm, or finger.

DXA uses two radiation beams, provides T-score and Z-score comparisons, and does not require clothing removal, but metallic objects should be removed.

Peripheral quantitative ultrasound is portable and low risk; quantitative CT predicts spinal/hip fractures but uses more radiation than DXA; MRI/MRS can assess bone density without radiation.

Nursing Care and Home Safety

Prevent falls and fractures

Daily care teaching

Teach dietary calcium sources and calcium/vitamin D supplementation, often taken with food.

Encourage moderate sun exposure with sunscreen and provider-guided weight-bearing activity.

Encourage adequate protein, magnesium, vitamin K, and trace minerals needed for bone formation.

Exercise can reduce vertebral fracture risk; isometric exercises can strengthen the core.

Home safety

Remove throw rugs and clutter from walkways.

Provide adequate lighting, especially around doorways, thresholds, and steps.

Use prescribed assistive devices and safety equipment.

Wear rubber-bottomed shoes and avoid slippery surfaces.

Medication Priorities

Bone resorption and DVT checks

Supplements and bone agents

Calcium and vitamin D can slow or prevent osteoporosis; vitamin D toxicity can cause weakness, fatigue, nausea, constipation, and kidney stones.

Calcitonin decreases bone resorption; calcitonin salmon can be subcutaneous, intramuscular, or intranasal.

Teriparatide stimulates osteoblasts and calcium absorption, is given subcutaneously, is limited to 2 years of use, and can cause orthostatic hypotension up to 4 hr after dosing.

Teriparatide is contraindicated with hypercalcemia, bone cancer history, radiation, or Paget's disease.

High-yield safety checks

Oral bisphosphonates can cause esophagitis or esophageal ulcers; teach early-morning dosing with 8 oz water before eating and remaining upright for 30 min.

Clients receiving IV bisphosphonates or denosumab should have dental evaluation/prevention to reduce osteonecrosis of the jaw risk.

Denosumab is contraindicated with hypocalcemia, is given subcutaneously, and requires calcium monitoring.

Raloxifene decreases bone resorption, is avoided with DVT history, requires liver-function monitoring, and should be stopped 72 hr before prolonged bed rest.

Procedures and Fracture Care

Spine protection

Orthotics and arthroplasty

Orthotic devices can immobilize the spine after compression fracture, support posture, and decrease pain.

Teach skin checks under orthotic devices, good posture/body mechanics, log rolling when getting out of bed, and heat/back rubs for muscle relaxation.

Joint repair or arthroplasty can be needed when osteoporosis weakens a joint, especially the hip.

Physical therapy can help establish aerobic exercise and weightlifting plans, and rehabilitation can be needed after fractures or disability.

Vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty

These minimally invasive procedures inject bone cement into a fractured vertebral space, with or without balloon inflation.

Mild sedation is used, and the client lies supine for 1 to 2 hr afterward while the cement hardens.

Monitor vital signs, shortness of breath, puncture-site bleeding, and neurologic status; apply cold therapy to the injection site.

Teach no driving for 24 hr, keep the dressing dry, remove the dressing the next day if prescribed, monitor for infection, resume walking the next day, and gradually increase activity.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Raloxifene for Osteoporosis

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic uses

  • Raloxifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator.
  • It decreases bone resorption and increases bone density.
  • It is used for postmenopausal osteoporosis and can reduce breast cancer risk.

Nursing interventions

  • Avoid administration to clients who have a history of DVT.
  • Teach the client to report unusual calf pain or tenderness.
  • Assess liver function tests periodically.
  • Review calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

Effectiveness cues

Expected outcomes include improved bone mineral density, no further loss in height, and no cancer metastasis when used for breast cancer risk reduction.

Application Exercises

1

Which findings are risk factors or cues for osteoporosis? Select all that apply.

  • A. History of one glass of wine daily
  • B. Loss of 2 in of height
  • C. Body mass index of 18
  • D. Kyphotic curve of the upper thoracic spine
  • E. History of lactose intolerance
B, C, D, E Height loss and kyphosis can reflect vertebral fractures; low BMI and lactose intolerance can signal low bone mass/calcium intake risk.
A Osteoporosis risk is associated with high alcohol intake, not one glass of wine daily.
2

Which action should the nurse take after a thoracic vertebroplasty?

  • A. Apply heat to the puncture site.
  • B. Place the client supine.
  • C. Turn the client every 1 hr.
  • D. Ambulate the client within the first hour.
B The client remains supine for 1 to 2 hr after vertebroplasty while the cement hardens.
A, C, D Cold therapy is used at the puncture site, and turning/ambulation are delayed during the immediate supine period.
3

Which food should the nurse include when teaching about calcium-rich foods?

  • A. White bread
  • B. Kale
  • C. Apples
  • D. Brown rice
B Green leafy vegetables such as kale are calcium-rich foods.
A, C, D These foods can provide other nutrients but are not the best calcium-rich choice in this item.
4

Which clients have osteoporosis risk factors? Select all that apply.

  • A. A 40-year-old client taking prednisone for 4 months
  • B. A 30-year-old client who jogs 3 miles daily
  • C. A 45-year-old client taking phenytoin for seizures
  • D. A 65-year-old client with a sedentary lifestyle
  • E. A 70-year-old client who has smoked for 50 years
A, C, D, E Prolonged corticosteroid use, anticonvulsants, sedentary lifestyle, and smoking increase osteoporosis risk.
B Weight-bearing activity decreases risk by stressing bone and supporting maintenance/rebuilding.
5

Which home-safety teaching should the nurse include for a client who has osteoporosis? Select all that apply.

  • A. Remove throw rugs in walkways.
  • B. Use prescribed assistive devices.
  • C. Remove clutter from the environment.
  • D. Wear soft-bottomed shoes.
  • E. Maintain lighting in doorway areas.
A, B, C, E Removing trip hazards, using assistive devices, clearing clutter, and maintaining lighting reduce fall and fracture risk.
D Rubber-bottomed shoes are preferred to reduce slipping.
