Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 82

Diabetes Mellitus Management

Diabetes mellitus management is built around matching food, activity, insulin or non-insulin medication, and monitoring so glucose stays in range and complications are prevented. Nursing priorities are to recognize hypo/hyperglycemia fast, teach insulin and medication safety, support nutrition/exercise/illness plans, protect feet and skin, and screen for vascular, eye, nerve, kidney, and sexual-health complications.

TL;DR · Match Insulin, Food, Activity, and Monitoring

Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune beta-cell destruction with insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes is progressive insulin resistance plus reduced beta-cell insulin production. Management depends on screening, A1C/glucose interpretation, SMBG, consistent meals, physical activity, insulin or non-insulin therapy, sick-day rules, and complication prevention. Hypoglycemia below 70 mg/dL is treated first with 15 to 20 g rapid carbohydrate if awake; severe symptoms need glucagon or IV dextrose. Hyperglycemia needs fluids, insulin as prescribed, ketone checks, and provider contact if it progresses.

Control tools

  • A1C reflects average glucose over about 120 days and guides treatment effectiveness.
  • SMBG records should include time, date, glucose, insulin dose, food intake, activity, illness, and other glucose-changing events.
  • Type 1 clients need insulin even when NPO, usually with basal insulin continued while rapid mealtime insulin is adjusted.

Safety anchors

  • Rapid-acting insulin is given with meals; glargine/detemir are not mixed with other insulin and are never IV.
  • Foot care is daily: inspect, wash, dry between toes, avoid soaking/heating pads/callus removers, and wear closed shoes.
  • Sick days require glucose checks every 2 to 4 hr, continued diabetes medication, hydration, carbohydrate intake, ketone testing, and provider calls for danger signs.

Diabetes Management Priorities

Types, Prevention, and Screening

ATI source-authored

Type 1 vs type 2

Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune beta-cell destruction, causing inadequate insulin production.

Type 2 diabetes is progressive insulin resistance plus reduced insulin production by beta cells.

Type 2 diabetes is linked to obesity, sedentary lifestyle, heredity, and often metabolic syndrome.

Diabetes contributes to cardiovascular disease, hypertension, kidney disease, neuropathy, retinopathy, peripheral vascular disease, and stroke.

Prevention and screening

Type 1 diabetes cannot be prevented; lifestyle changes can reduce type 2 risk and reduce complications after diagnosis.

Teach weight management, exercise, and nutrition patterns that support glucose and cardiovascular risk control.

Screen clients with BMI over 25 plus risk factors such as first-degree family history, age 45 or older, sedentary lifestyle, vascular disease, polycystic ovary syndrome, gestational diabetes, large-for-gestational infant history, high-risk ancestry, hypertension, A1C above 5.7%, impaired fasting glucose/tolerance, low HDL, or high triglycerides.

Screening uses fasting blood glucose or A1C.

Risk and Assessment Pattern

Metabolic syndrome and classic findings

Metabolic syndrome

Metabolic syndrome is at least three factors that increase cardiovascular-event risk and type 2 diabetes risk.

Factors include central obesity, triglycerides above 150 mg/dL or triglyceride medication, low HDL, blood pressure above 130/85 or hypertension medication, and fasting glucose at or above 100 mg/dL or hyperglycemia medication.

Prediabetes is glucose above expected range but below diabetes criteria, such as impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance.

Older adults can need support with transportation, finances, vision/hearing changes, medication metabolism, ADLs, foot care, wound care, and glucose monitoring.

Expected findings

Polyuria occurs from osmotic diuresis; polydipsia occurs from dehydration.

Dehydration cues include poor skin turgor, warm dry skin, dry mucous membranes, weakness, malaise, rapid weak pulse, and hypotension.

Polyphagia occurs when cells cannot use glucose and the body uses fat/protein for energy; weight loss can occur.

Other cues include Kussmaul respirations, recurrent infections, fruity breath, headache, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, difficulty concentrating, fatigue, vision changes, slow wound healing, decreased LOC, seizures, and coma.

Labs and Self-Monitoring

Glucose, A1C, ketones, SMBG

Diagnostic and trend labs

Diagnostic criteria include repeated findings such as diabetes manifestations plus casual glucose above 200 mg/dL, fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL, 2-hr oral glucose tolerance test glucose above 200 mg/dL, or A1C above 6.5%.

For fasting glucose testing, hold antidiabetic medication until after the level is drawn and fast for 8 hr except water.

Oral glucose tolerance testing begins with fasting glucose, then glucose intake, with glucose checks every 30 min for 2 hr and assessment for hypoglycemia.

A1C is the best indicator of average glucose over the past 120 days and is recommended quarterly or twice yearly depending on control.

Urine ketones with hyperglycemia above 300 mg/dL are a medical emergency.

SMBG safety

Use control solution to check strip accuracy, match the meter code to the strip bottle when applicable, and store strips closed in a dry location.

Use hand hygiene, fresh lancets, adequate blood sample, and never share monitoring equipment.

Record time, date, glucose level, insulin dose, food intake, activity, illness, and other events that change glucose metabolism.

Supplemental short-acting insulin can be prescribed for elevated premeal glucose levels.

Insulin Map

Timing, mixing, peaks

Insulin types

Insulin therapy mimics basal insulin and prandial insulin needs.

Rapid-acting insulin lispro/aspart/glulisine and inhaled insulin control postprandial rise and are given before meals.

Regular insulin is short-acting; U-100 can be given IV, but U-500 is reserved for insulin resistance and is never IV.

NPH is intermediate-acting, used between meals and at night, given subcutaneously only, and is the only insulin mixed with short-acting insulin.

Glargine and detemir are long-acting, given subcutaneously only, never IV, and not mixed; ultra-long options last longer than 24 hr.

Administration teaching

Observe self-administration and reinforce teaching as needed.

Monitor hypoglycemia at insulin peak times: sweating, weakness, dizziness, confusion, headache, tachycardia, and slurred speech.

Rotate injection sites within one anatomic area to prevent lipohypertrophy or lipoatrophy while keeping absorption consistent.

Inject at 90 degrees, or 45 degrees for a thin client; aspiration is not needed.

When mixing rapid- or short-acting insulin with a longer-acting insulin, draw up the shorter-acting insulin first.

Eat at regular intervals, avoid alcohol, match insulin to exercise and food, and wear medical identification.

Non-Insulin Medication Map

Oral and injectable safety

Oral antidiabetics

Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production, improves insulin sensitivity, and slows carbohydrate absorption; monitor GI effects and lactic acidosis risk, especially with kidney/liver disease.

Hold metformin 24 to 48 hr before elective iodinated-contrast testing and restart 48 hr after as prescribed.

Sulfonylureas and meglitinides stimulate insulin release; monitor hypoglycemia, give sulfonylureas before meals, and omit meglitinides if the meal is skipped.

Pioglitazone improves insulin sensitivity but needs monitoring for fluid retention, heart failure, liver injury, and lipid changes.

Acarbose/miglitol slow carbohydrate absorption; take with first bite and treat hypoglycemia with glucose rather than table sugar.

DPP-4 inhibitors increase incretin effect and can cause upper respiratory symptoms or pancreatitis signs.

SGLT2 inhibitors increase urinary glucose excretion; monitor for UTI, genital yeast infection, and postural hypotension.

Non-insulin injectables

Exenatide/liraglutide mimic incretin hormone, decrease glucagon, promote insulin release, slow gastric emptying, and reduce fasting/postprandial hyperglycemia.

Exenatide is given before morning and evening meals; do not give after a meal.

Separate oral medications from exenatide timing because effectiveness can be reduced; use caution with oral contraceptives and antibiotics.

Report severe abdominal pain with or without vomiting as a possible pancreatitis cue.

Pramlintide suppresses glucagon and controls postprandial glucose; premeal rapid/short insulin doses are reduced when it starts to reduce hypoglycemia risk.

Give pramlintide immediately before major meals and at least 2 inches from an insulin injection site.

Hypoglycemia and Hyperglycemia Response

Treat the current glucose first

Hypoglycemia

Hypoglycemia manifestations include shakiness, confusion, sweating, palpitations, headache, poor coordination, blurred vision, seizures, and coma.

Slow glucose decline often causes CNS symptoms such as headache, confusion, fatigue, and drowsiness; rapid decline often causes sympathetic symptoms such as tachycardia, diaphoresis, and nervousness.

If glucose is below 70 mg/dL and the client can swallow, give 15 to 20 g readily absorbable carbohydrate, recheck in 15 min, and repeat if symptoms continue or glucose is not above 70.

If the next meal is more than 1 hr away after glucose normalizes, add a carbohydrate/protein snack.

If unconscious, place lateral to prevent aspiration, give glucagon subcutaneously or IM or IV dextrose as prescribed, notify the provider, and repeat glucagon in 10 min if still unconscious.

Hyperglycemia

Teach hot dry skin and fruity breath as hyperglycemia cues.

Encourage sugar-free fluids to prevent dehydration.

Administer insulin as prescribed.

Test urine for ketones and report results outside the expected range.

Consult the provider if manifestations progress.

Daily Nursing Care and Nutrition

Food, feeds, activity, skills

Care monitoring

Monitor glucose and factors affecting glucose, intake/output, weight, skin/wound healing, recurrent infections, sensory changes, vision changes, diet, exercise, SMBG skill, and self-medication skill.

Adjust therapy when NPO, on clear liquids, or receiving enteral/parenteral nutrition.

Type 1 clients need continued insulin while NPO to prevent DKA, often with basal insulin continued and rapid-acting insulin adjusted.

Continuous enteral/parenteral feeding requires scheduled blood glucose monitoring and possible insulin injections at even intervals.

Nutrition and exercise

Dietitian teaching should cover meal planning, food intake, weight, lipid, and glucose management.

Keep meal timing and food composition consistent; do not skip meals.

Count carbohydrates; 15 g carbohydrate equals 1 carbohydrate exchange.

Use fiber to improve carbohydrate metabolism and cholesterol control; reduce saturated and trans fats and include omega-3 sources.

Exercise only when glucose is 80 to 250 mg/dL and ketones are absent; carry diabetes identification and check glucose more often for 24 hr after intensive exercise.

Foot Care and Sick-Day Rules

Prevent injury, dehydration, DKA risk

Foot care

Inspect feet daily; wash with mild soap and warm water, test water with the arm or thermometer, and do not soak feet.

Dry gently, especially between toes; avoid lotion between toes and use mild powder for sweaty feet.

Do not use commercial callus/corn remedies; consult a podiatrist.

Wear closed-toe, closed-heel shoes that fit, slippers with soles, and clean absorbent socks; do not go barefoot.

Avoid heating pads/hot water bottles, prolonged sitting/standing, and crossing legs.

Clean cuts with warm water and mild soap, apply a dry dressing, monitor healing, and seek care promptly.

Sick days

Notify the provider when ill and monitor blood glucose every 2 to 4 hr.

Continue insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents unless directed otherwise.

Drink 8 to 12 oz sugar-free noncaffeinated fluid every hour; use sugar-containing fluids if glucose is below provider parameters.

Meet carbohydrate needs with soft food or liquids equal to usual carbohydrate content.

Test urine ketones every 3 to 4 hr or when glucose exceeds 240 mg/dL, and report abnormal results.

Call the provider for moderate/large ketones, ketonuria more than 24 hr, glucose above 250 not resolving, fever above 101.5 F or lasting more than 24 hr, confusion, rapid breathing, persistent GI losses, inability to tolerate liquids, or illness longer than 2 days.

Chronic Complication Surveillance

Vessels, eyes, nerves, kidneys

Vascular, eye, nerve

Consistent glucose control is the best protection against complications.

Cardiovascular/cerebrovascular prevention includes blood pressure at each visit, tobacco cessation, lipid-lowering medication and aspirin adherence as prescribed, yearly lipids, and A1C every 3 months.

Diabetic retinopathy can cause impaired vision and blindness; teach yearly eye exams and reporting vision changes that do not fluctuate with glucose.

Neuropathy can cause numbness, pain, foot deformities, ulcers, exercise intolerance, painless MI, gastroparesis, reflux, early satiety, urinary retention, and reduced hypoglycemia awareness.

Kidney and other concerns

Diabetic nephropathy can follow prolonged hyperglycemia and dehydration; monitor hydration, intake/output, creatinine, and blood pressure.

Report urine output below 30 mL/hr and decreased output.

Teach yearly urinalysis, BUN, microalbumin, and creatinine testing.

Sexual dysfunction can occur from nerve and vascular damage; discuss concerns and offer referral when desired.

Other complications include periodontal disease and integumentary disorders such as infections, color changes, and sclerosing.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Type 1 Diabetes Sick-Day Care

Active Learning Scenario

Labs and provider calls

  • Test urine ketones if blood glucose is above 240 mg/dL.
  • Report moderate to large ketones or ketonuria that lasts more than 24 hr.
  • Call the provider if glucose remains above 250 mg/dL despite treatment.
  • Call for fever above 101.5 F or increasing, illness longer than 2 days, inability to take fluids, confusion, rapid breathing, or persistent nausea/vomiting/diarrhea.

Self-care plan

  • Monitor blood glucose every 3 to 4 hr, or more often as directed.
  • Continue insulin as prescribed.
  • Drink 8 to 12 oz sugar-free liquid every hour; use sugar-containing fluids if blood glucose is below provider parameters.
  • If unable to eat soft foods, drink liquids equal to usual carbohydrate content.
  • Rest and seek help early when danger signs appear.

Application Exercises

1

A client has blood glucose 52 mg/dL and is lethargic but arousable. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Recheck blood glucose in 15 min.
  • B. Provide a carbohydrate and protein food.
  • C. Provide 15 g of simple carbohydrates.
  • D. Report findings to the provider.
C The immediate priority is injury prevention from hypoglycemia, so give 15 to 20 g rapidly absorbed carbohydrate when the client can swallow.
A, B, D Recheck after carbohydrate treatment, add protein/carbohydrate snack after glucose normalizes if the meal is delayed, and report after treating the urgent low glucose.
2

Which action should the nurse take before giving morning insulin aspart to a client who has type 1 diabetes?

  • A. Check blood glucose immediately after breakfast.
  • B. Administer insulin when breakfast arrives.
  • C. Hold breakfast for 1 hr after insulin administration.
  • D. Clarify the prescription because insulin should not be given now.
B Insulin aspart is rapid-acting and should be given when the meal is available to reduce hypoglycemia risk.
A, C, D Glucose is checked before insulin, the client should eat within minutes of rapid-acting insulin, and aspart is appropriate at mealtime.
3

A client needs morning insulin glargine and regular insulin for glucose 278 mg/dL. Which action should the nurse take?

  • A. Draw up regular insulin and then glargine insulin in the same syringe.
  • B. Draw up glargine insulin then regular insulin in the same syringe.
  • C. Draw up and administer regular and glargine insulin in separate syringes.
  • D. Administer regular insulin, wait 1 hr, then administer glargine insulin.
C Glargine is not compatible for mixing with regular insulin, so each is administered as a separate injection.
A, B, D Do not mix glargine with another insulin; separating by 1 hr is not needed.
4

Which nutrition habits help prevent type 2 diabetes mellitus? Select all that apply.

  • A. Eat at regular intervals.
  • B. Decrease intake of saturated fats.
  • C. Increase daily fiber intake.
  • D. Limit saturated fat intake to 15% of daily calories.
  • E. Include omega-3 fatty acids in the diet.
A, B, C, E Regular eating, lower saturated fat, more fiber, and omega-3 fatty acids support glucose, lipids, weight, and heart-risk control.
D The recommended saturated fat intake is lower than 15% of daily calories.
5

Which foot-care instructions should the nurse include for a client who has diabetes mellitus? Select all that apply.

  • A. Remove calluses using over-the-counter remedies.
  • B. Apply lotion between toes.
  • C. Test water temperature with the fingers before bathing.
  • D. Trim toenails straight across.
  • E. Wear closed-toe shoes.
D, E Trimming straight across and wearing closed-toe shoes help prevent soft-tissue injury.
A, B, C A podiatrist should manage calluses/corns, moisture between toes increases infection risk, and water temperature should be checked with the wrist/arm or thermometer.

Unit 12 · Endocrine Disorders · Chapter 83

Complications of Diabetes Mellitus

Diabetes emergencies move fast because water, electrolytes, insulin, and serum osmolarity all shift at once. Separate DKA from HHS, then treat perfusion, insulin needs, potassium safety, neurologic status, and recurrence prevention in that order.

TL;DR · DKA Has Ketones; HHS Has Extreme Osmolar Dehydration

DKA is rapid hyperglycemia with metabolic acidosis and ketones, most often tied to insulin deficiency, illness, infection, or missed insulin. HHS is gradual, profound hyperglycemia with severe dehydration and hyperosmolarity but little to no ketosis, most often in older adults who have type 2 diabetes.

Emergency pattern

  • DKA: glucose usually above 300 mg/dL, ketones present, acidosis, Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, abdominal pain.
  • HHS: glucose usually above 600 mg/dL, osmolarity above 320 mOsm/L, profound dehydration, neurologic decline, no ketones.
  • Both can show polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, weakness, blurred vision, and mental-status changes.

Priority response

  • Restore intravascular volume with isotonic fluid first unless sodium status changes the prescription.
  • Give IV regular insulin and monitor glucose hourly; add dextrose when glucose reaches about 250 mg/dL.
  • Monitor potassium closely because insulin and correction of acidosis can quickly shift potassium into cells.

DKA and HHS Priorities

DKA vs HHS

ATI source-authored

Both emergencies begin with hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis, but the acid-base and ketone patterns tell the nurse which complication is unfolding.

DKA: insulin is too low to use glucose, so fat breakdown produces ketones and metabolic acidosis.

HHS: enough endogenous insulin remains to limit ketosis, but not enough to prevent extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration.

Timing: DKA develops rapidly; HHS usually develops over days and can progress to coma or death if untreated.

Risk group: DKA is strongly linked with type 1 diabetes; HHS is most common in older adults who have type 2 diabetes.

Risk Triggers

ATI source-authored

DKA Triggers

New, untreated, or poorly controlled type 1 diabetes.

Missed, reduced, or incorrectly dosed insulin.

Infection, the most common precipitating cause.

Physical or emotional stress that increases counterregulatory hormones.

HHS Triggers

Undiagnosed or poorly managed type 2 diabetes with inadequate fluid intake or impaired kidney function.

Older adulthood, especially with reduced thirst perception and delayed care seeking.

Stressors such as myocardial infarction, stroke, sepsis, or other severe illness.

Medications including glucocorticoids, thiazide diuretics, phenytoin, beta blockers, and calcium channel blockers.

Expected Findings

ATI source-authored

Both DKA and HHS: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, dehydration, blurred vision, headache, weakness, orthostatic hypotension, and mental-status changes.

DKA-specific clues: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath, Kussmaul respirations, metabolic acidosis, and blood or urine ketones.

HHS-specific clues: severe neurologic changes, seizures, myoclonic jerking, reversible paralysis, and coma risk as osmolarity rises above 350 mOsm/L.

Older adult warning: dehydration can be severe before the client recognizes thirst or seeks care, so mental status and intake history matter.

Serial Laboratory Pattern

ATI source-authored

DKA Labs

Glucose greater than 300 mg/dL, often rising much higher.

Ketones present in blood and urine.

pH below 7.35 and low bicarbonate, reflecting metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

BUN and creatinine rise with dehydration.

HHS Labs

Glucose greater than 600 mg/dL.

Ketones absent in blood and urine.

Serum osmolarity greater than 320 mOsm/L.

pH usually greater than 7.4 and bicarbonate greater than 20 mEq/L.

Fluid and Insulin Management

ATI source-authored

Assess vital signs frequently until stable, then continue scheduled monitoring.

Look for dehydration indicators: weight loss, poor skin turgor, oliguria, rapid weak pulse, and orthostatic hypotension.

Begin with rapid IV isotonic fluid replacement to support perfusion to vital organs; clients with elevated sodium can require a different prescribed solution.

As glucose approaches 250 mg/dL, add dextrose-containing fluid to reduce hypoglycemia and cerebral edema risk from rapid osmolar shifts.

Use IV regular insulin for immediate effect, with hourly glucose checks and continued insulin/dextrose in DKA until acidosis resolves and subcutaneous insulin can resume.

Potassium and Acidosis Safety

ATI source-authored

Potassium can appear normal or high at first because dehydration and acidosis shift potassium out of cells.

Insulin, fluid expansion, and acidosis correction move potassium back into cells, so hypokalemia can emerge during treatment.

Begin potassium replacement as prescribed when the level falls below 5 mEq/L, and verify adequate urine output before giving potassium.

Monitor cardiac rhythm and report weak pulse, shallow respirations, malaise, muscle weakness, confusion, abdominal distention, or paralytic ileus.

Severe acidosis can require slow IV sodium bicarbonate; potassium replacement is often paired unless hyperkalemia is present.

Older Adult and Prevention Teaching

ATI source-authored

Teach older adults to check glucose every 1 to 4 hr when ill and to continue prescribed insulin.

Stress hydration because thirst sensation can be diminished and mental-status changes can delay treatment.

Teach medical alert identification and daily dehydration prevention.

During illness, check glucose at least every 4 hr, check ketones if glucose is above 240 mg/dL, and use carbohydrate/electrolyte liquids when solid food is not tolerated.

Notify the provider for illness longer than 24 hr, glucose above 250 mg/dL, inability to tolerate food or fluids, ketones for more than 24 hr, or fever that persists.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - DKA Plan of Care

Active Learning Scenario

Fluid Replacement

  • Rapidly infuse prescribed IV 0.9% sodium chloride, then transition to maintenance fluids as ordered.
  • Monitor BUN, creatinine, serum osmolarity, electrolytes, and glucose response.
  • Replace potassium as prescribed and continue hydration assessment.

Insulin Administration

  • Administer IV regular insulin bolus if prescribed.
  • Continue IV regular insulin infusion as prescribed.
  • Evaluate blood glucose hourly and continue therapy until DKA resolution criteria are met.

Application Exercises

1

A nurse is reviewing the health history of a client who has type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which findings increase the risk for HHS? Select all that apply.

  • A. Recent myocardial infarction
  • B. BUN 35 mg/dL
  • C. Calcium channel blocker therapy
  • D. Age 77 years
  • E. Daily insulin injections
A, B, C, D Stress illness, impaired kidney function, calcium channel blockers, and older age increase HHS risk.
E Insulin use does not increase HHS risk; insulin helps reduce progression to diabetic ketoacidosis during hyperglycemia.
2

A client has DKA and ketones in the urine. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

  • A. Weight gain
  • B. Fruity odor of breath
  • C. Abdominal pain
  • D. Kussmaul respirations
  • E. Metabolic acidosis
B, C, D, E Ketones and acidosis cause fruity breath, abdominal pain, deep rapid respirations, and metabolic acidosis.
A Weight loss is more expected because of dehydration and catabolism.
3

A nurse is reviewing laboratory reports for a client who has HHS. Which finding should the nurse expect?

  • A. Blood pH 7.2
  • B. Blood osmolarity 350 mOsm/L
  • C. Blood potassium 3.8 mEq/L
  • D. Blood creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
B HHS causes marked hyperosmolarity; values greater than 320 mOsm/L are expected.
A, C, D Acidosis points toward DKA; normal potassium and creatinine are not the expected dehydration pattern.
4

A client is beginning therapy for DKA. Which prescription should the nurse expect?

  • A. Administer IV regular insulin at 0.3 unit/kg/hr.
  • B. Administer a slow IV infusion of 3% sodium chloride.
  • C. Rapidly administer IV 0.9% sodium chloride.
  • D. Add glucose to the IV infusion when blood glucose is 350 mg/dL.
C Initial DKA management prioritizes isotonic fluid replacement to restore perfusion to vital organs.
A, B, D IV regular insulin is usually lower-dose continuous therapy, 3% saline is not routine DKA fluid, and dextrose is added closer to 250 mg/dL.
5

Which discharge instructions should the nurse include to help prevent recurrent DKA? Select all that apply.

  • A. Drink about 2 L of fluids daily unless contraindicated.
  • B. Monitor blood glucose every 4 hr when ill.
  • C. Continue insulin as prescribed when ill.
  • D. Notify the provider when blood glucose is 200 mg/dL.
  • E. Report ketones in urine after 24 hr of illness.
A, B, C, E Hydration, frequent illness monitoring, continued insulin, and reporting prolonged ketonuria help prevent recurrence.
D Provider notification is emphasized when glucose remains above 250 mg/dL despite treatment.

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 84

Immune and Infectious Disorders Diagnostic Procedures

Immune and infectious diagnostic work starts with identifying the organism, inflammatory pattern, or allergen. Read the WBC differential first, protect the neutropenic client, then match allergy testing to the risk of provoking a reaction.

TL;DR · WBC Pattern, Neutropenia Risk, Allergy Test Safety

Microscopy and lab testing identify pathogens and cell patterns so treatment can target the cause. Leukocytosis suggests inflammation or infection, leukopenia can signal severe infection or drug toxicity, and neutropenia requires protective precautions when infection risk is high.

WBC anchors

  • Total WBC reference range is about 5,000 to 10,000/mm3.
  • Leukopenia is less than 4,000/mm3; leukocytosis is greater than 10,000/mm3.
  • Neutropenia is neutrophils less than 2,000/mm3; ANC less than 1,000 means protective precautions are essential.

Allergy testing

  • Blood allergy testing measures allergen-specific IgE and avoids provoking a dangerous allergic reaction.
  • Skin testing can be scratch, prick, or intradermal; have anaphylaxis equipment available.
  • Withhold antihistamines and corticosteroids before skin testing as instructed because they can alter results.

Diagnostic Priorities

Specimen and Microscopy Logic

ATI source-authored

The source priority is identification: blood, body fluid, and tissue specimens can reveal pathogenic microorganisms and cell characteristics that guide infectious disease treatment.

WBCs stimulate inflammatory response and defend against infection and foreign antigens.

The differential reports the proportion of neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils for a total of 100%.

When one WBC type rises, the relative percentages of the other types fall.

Older adults can have severe bacterial infection without leukocytosis or fever, so absence of classic signs does not rule out infection.

Total WBC and Neutrophil Safety

ATI source-authored

Leukopenia: WBC less than 4,000/mm3; can occur with drug toxicity, autoimmune disease, bone marrow failure, or overwhelming infection.

Leukocytosis: WBC greater than 10,000/mm3; can occur with infection, inflammation, malignancy, trauma, dehydration, stress, steroid use, and thyroid storm.

Neutropenia: neutrophils less than 2,000/mm3; increases infection risk and can follow viral infection, overwhelming bacterial infection, radiation, or chemotherapy.

ANC: calculate from total WBC and neutrophil plus band percentages to estimate infection risk severity.

Left shift: increased immature neutrophils during acute infection; the released bands are not fully capable of phagocytosis.

Neutropenic Precautions

ATI source-authored

Use protective precautions when ANC is below 1,000.

Restrict visitors and prohibit visits from people who have infection symptoms.

Avoid exposure to live, cut, or potted plants.

Restrict fresh fruits and vegetables when ordered for neutropenic protection.

Avoid rectal temperatures and IM injections to reduce exposure to the client's own bacterial flora and tissue trauma.

WBC Differential Patterns

ATI source-authored

Common Increases

Neutrophils: acute bacterial infection, trauma, rheumatoid arthritis, myelocytic leukemia.

Lymphocytes: chronic bacterial or viral infection, measles, mumps, mononucleosis, hepatitis, lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma.

Monocytes: chronic inflammation, protozoal infection, tuberculosis, viral mononucleosis.

Allergy and Stress Cues

Eosinophils rise with allergic reactions, parasitic infection, eczema, leukemia, and autoimmune disease.

Basophils participate in inflammation, allergy, and hypersensitivity responses and can rise with leukemia.

Stress and corticosteroids can decrease eosinophils; corticosteroid therapy can also decrease monocytes.

Blood Allergy Testing

ATI source-authored

Blood allergy testing, including RAST, evaluates sensitivity to selected allergens by measuring allergen-specific IgE response.

It can complement skin testing or serve as an alternative when skin exposure could trigger a dangerous hypersensitivity reaction.

Advantages: does not precipitate an allergic reaction and can be quicker than skin testing.

Limitations: often tests smaller allergen panels at one time and can be less sensitive than skin testing.

Potential false results can occur with conditions that alter immunoglobulins or with corticosteroid exposure before testing.

Skin Testing for Allergens

ATI source-authored

Skin testing uses scratch, prick, or intradermal exposure to small amounts of potential allergens.

Intradermal testing has higher hypersensitivity risk and can follow inconclusive scratch testing.

A wheal-and-flare response is a positive reaction; larger reactions indicate greater sensitivity.

Prepare the back or forearm with soap and water, remove oil with alcohol, and keep equipment available for anaphylaxis.

Apply controls, assess after 15 to 20 min, document responsible allergens, remove solutions, and treat itching as prescribed.

Client Teaching

ATI source-authored

Before skin testing, withhold antihistamines and corticosteroids for the ordered window, often 48 hr to 2 weeks depending on the medication and provider direction.

Tell the client that histamine control sites can itch during testing.

After testing, follow avoidance and desensitization instructions for confirmed allergens.

Dietary avoidance can be needed for food allergens, such as gluten avoidance when indicated.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Radioallergosorbent Test

Active Learning Scenario

Indications

  • Possible environmental or food allergy.
  • History of hypersensitivity reactions such as hives, asthma, GI symptoms, rhinitis, dermatitis, or angioedema.

Interpretation and Action

  • Results reflect allergen-specific IgE levels and degree of sensitivity on a graded scale.
  • Intraprocedure nursing action is to obtain the blood sample.

Application Exercises

1

A client has a WBC count of 20,000/mm3. Which conclusion should the nurse make?

  • A. Neutropenia
  • B. Leukocytosis
  • C. Left shift
  • D. Leukopenia
B Leukocytosis is a WBC count greater than 10,000/mm3 and can indicate infection or inflammation.
A, C, D Neutropenia refers to low neutrophils, left shift refers to increased immature neutrophils, and leukopenia is a WBC count below 4,000/mm3.
2

A nurse reviews laboratory findings for a client who has measles. Which WBC type should the nurse expect to be increased?

  • A. Neutrophils
  • B. Basophils
  • C. Lymphocytes
  • D. Eosinophils
C Lymphocytes increase with viral infections such as measles, mumps, and mononucleosis.
A, B, D Neutrophils rise with acute bacterial infection, basophils with leukemia/allergy patterns, and eosinophils with allergy or parasitic infection.
3

Which actions should the nurse take before a scratch test for suspected food and environmental allergies? Select all that apply.

  • A. Cleanse the skin with povidone-iodine.
  • B. Ask about previous reactions to allergens.
  • C. Ask about medications taken over the past several days.
  • D. Tell the client itching can occur at one control site.
  • E. Have emergency resuscitation equipment available.
B, C, D, E Prior reactions, recent antihistamine/corticosteroid use, expected histamine-control itching, and emergency equipment all matter before testing.
A Use soap and water for cleansing; povidone-iodine can interfere with allergen testing.

Suggested template type

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 85

Immunizations

Immunization questions are usually safety questions: identify active versus passive protection, match the vaccine product to the client, screen for contraindications, teach expected local reactions, and document the administration record completely.

TL;DR · Immunity Type, Live-Vaccine Cautions, Documentation

Vaccines stimulate active immunity, while immune globulins give temporary passive protection after exposure. Screen for anaphylaxis history, pregnancy, severe illness, immune compromise, and product-specific allergies before administration.

Protection logic

  • Active immunity takes weeks to months to develop and is long-lasting.
  • Passive immunity transfers antibodies from another person or animal and is temporary.
  • Immune globulin is used when immediate postexposure protection is needed.

Safety anchors

  • Do not repeat a vaccine after anaphylaxis to that vaccine or a shared component.
  • Live-virus vaccines such as MMR and varicella are avoided in pregnancy and severe immune compromise.
  • Document VIS date, route, site, type, manufacturer, lot number, expiration date, and administration date.

Immunization Priorities

Active vs Passive Immunity

ATI source-authored

ATI frames immunizations around how protection is produced and how fast the client needs it.

Active-natural immunity: the client produces antibodies after natural exposure to a pathogen.

Active-artificial immunity: vaccination exposes the client to killed or attenuated antigen so the client produces antibodies.

Passive-natural immunity: antibodies pass from mother to fetus/newborn through the placenta or breast milk.

Passive-artificial immunity: immune globulin supplies antibodies for rapid, temporary protection after exposure.

Use the word temporary as the clue for passive immunity and long-lasting antibody production as the clue for active immunity.

Adult Schedule Cues

ATI source-authored

Td booster is given every 10 years; adults who have not previously received Tdap should substitute one dose with Tdap.

Pregnant clients receive Tdap during each pregnancy to help protect the fetus/newborn from pertussis.

MMR is used for adults who lack documentation of immunization, prior infection, or laboratory evidence of immunity; pregnancy is a contraindication.

Varicella is used for adults without evidence of prior infection; pregnancy, certain cancers, immune deficiency, immunosuppressive therapy, and hypersensitivity to neomycin or gelatin are key cautions.

Hepatitis A is a two-dose series for high-risk clients; hepatitis B is a three-dose series for high-risk clients who have not completed the series.

Influenza Product Selection

ATI source-authored

Influenza vaccination is recommended annually for adults.

Inactivated influenza vaccine is approved for clients who are pregnant.

Recombinant influenza vaccine is approved for adults 18 years and older.

Live attenuated influenza vaccine is a nasal spray option only for adults under age 50 who are not pregnant and not immunocompromised.

Prior Guillain-Barre syndrome after influenza vaccine and prior severe reaction require careful provider review; severe egg allergy requires administration where a provider and emergency equipment are available.

High-Yield Product Cautions

ATI source-authored

Live or immune-sensitive vaccines

MMR: contraindicated in pregnancy; use caution after recent antibody-containing blood products and with tuberculin skin testing.

Varicella: contraindicated in pregnancy and avoided with immune compromise; recent antivirals, extended corticosteroids, and cancer are precautions.

Zoster: contraindicated in pregnancy, immune compromise, and treatment with medications that alter immune response.

Allergy component cues

MMR and varicella: screen for hypersensitivity to gelatin or neomycin.

Hepatitis A: severe latex allergy is a contraindication; pregnancy is a precaution.

Hepatitis B and HPV: severe yeast allergy is a contraindication; HPV is also contraindicated in pregnancy.

Expected Reactions and Red Flags

ATI source-authored

Common reactions include injection-site redness, swelling, tenderness, low-grade fever, malaise, headache, and myalgia depending on vaccine type.

Td, DTaP, and Tdap can cause mild local findings; serious neurologic reactions are rare but are key prior-dose cautions.

MMR can cause rash, fever, swollen glands, joint discomfort, and rare thrombocytopenia or neurologic complications.

Live attenuated influenza vaccine can cause nasal congestion, cough, fever, headache, myalgia, vomiting, or diarrhea.

HPV vaccine can cause mild local reaction, fever, headache, and fainting shortly after administration.

Nursing Administration and Comfort

ATI source-authored

Keep emergency medications and equipment available because anaphylaxis is rare but possible.

Follow vaccine storage and reconstitution instructions exactly.

Provide the written vaccine information sheet, review it with the client, and document the VIS publication date.

For expected local discomfort or fever, administer an antipyretic as prescribed, apply a cool compress, and encourage use of the affected extremity.

Teach the client to observe for complications and notify the provider if adverse effects occur.

Documentation and Adult Injection Sites

ATI source-authored

Document vaccine date, route, site, type, manufacturer, lot number, and expiration date.

Also document the client's identifying information and signature when required, the administrator's name and title, and the address where the permanent record is kept.

For adults, give subcutaneous immunizations in the outer upper arm or anterolateral thigh.

For adults, give intramuscular immunizations in the deltoid muscle.

Evaluate effectiveness by the intended development of immunity.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication - Influenza Vaccine Selection

Active Learning Scenario

Product match

  • IIV: inactivated influenza vaccine; approved for clients who are pregnant.
  • RIV: recombinant influenza vaccine; approved for adults 18 years and older.
  • LAIV: live attenuated nasal spray; limited to adults under age 50 who are not pregnant and not immunocompromised.

Nursing considerations

  • Screen for prior severe influenza-vaccine reaction and prior Guillain-Barre syndrome after influenza vaccination.
  • If the client has severe egg allergy symptoms beyond hives, administer where a provider and emergency equipment are present.

Application Exercises

1

A client exposed to hepatitis A is prescribed immune globulin. Which teaching statement is most appropriate?

  • A. "This gives permanent immunity to hepatitis A."
  • B. "This is a series of three injections over several months."
  • C. "This gives protection faster than your body can make antibodies."
  • D. "This contains weakened virus so your body can create antibodies."
C Immune globulin provides passive-artificial immunity by supplying antibodies for rapid, temporary protection after exposure.
A, B, D Passive protection is temporary, hepatitis A immune globulin is not a vaccine series, and immune globulin contains antibodies rather than attenuated virus.
2

Before giving a varicella immunization, which question is the priority?

  • A. "Are you allergic to eggs?"
  • B. "Are you allergic to baker's yeast?"
  • C. "Are you pregnant?"
  • D. "Do you have a history of Guillain-Barre syndrome?"
C Varicella vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy.
A, B, D Egg allergy is most relevant to influenza products, yeast allergy to hepatitis B/HPV, and Guillain-Barre history to influenza or tetanus-toxoid precautions.
3

Which comfort strategies should the nurse teach after an immunization? Select all that apply.

  • A. Massage the injection site for several minutes.
  • B. Apply a cool compress to the injection site.
  • C. Take acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed.
  • D. Use the affected extremity.
  • E. Apply antimicrobial ointment to the injection site.
B, C, D Cool compresses, antipyretic/analgesic medication as prescribed, and moving the extremity can reduce expected local discomfort.
A, E Prolonged massage can worsen discomfort, and antimicrobial ointment is not indicated for routine immunization care.
4

Which information should be documented after a meningococcal vaccine is administered? Select all that apply.

  • A. Client age as the vaccine identifier
  • B. Vaccine manufacturer
  • C. Vaccine expiration date
  • D. Date of administration
  • E. Vaccine serial number instead of lot number
B, C, D Document manufacturer, expiration date, and date of administration, along with route, site, type, lot number, VIS date, and administrator details.
A, E The client's age is not the vaccine identifier, and the lot number is documented rather than a serial number.
5

A client asks about contraindications to immunizations. Which response is best?

  • A. "Using insulin means you should not receive immunizations."
  • B. "An anaphylactic reaction to one vaccine rules out every vaccine."
  • C. "A common cold means immunization must be delayed."
  • D. "Your provider will weigh the risks if you have had adverse effects."
D Prior adverse effects require provider review of the risks and benefits of immunization.
A, B, C Insulin use is not a contraindication, anaphylaxis applies to that vaccine or shared components, and minor illness such as a common cold is not a contraindication.

Suggested template type

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 86

HIV/AIDS

HIV care centers on transmission prevention, early testing, staging by CD4 pattern, viral-load monitoring, strict antiretroviral adherence, and fast reporting of infection. The nurse protects nutrition, fluids, skin, respiratory status, neurologic status, and psychosocial support while watching for opportunistic disease.

TL;DR · CD4 Stage, Viral Load, No Missed Doses

HIV targets CD4+ T lymphocytes and is transmitted through blood and selected body fluids. Confirm infection with supplemental antibody testing, track disease with CD4 and viral load, and teach that missed antiretroviral doses can cause medication resistance.

Assessment anchors

  • Acute infection can feel flu-like within 2 to 4 weeks and can include rash, sore throat, fever, night sweats, chills, headache, and muscle aches.
  • Chronic asymptomatic infection can last years while viral replication slowly destroys CD4+ cells.
  • AIDS is the late stage with life-threatening opportunistic infections or CD4+ count below 200 cells/mm3.

Nursing anchors

  • Use standard precautions and teach condoms, abstinence, and avoiding shared needles.
  • Monitor CBC, CD4+ count, CD4 percentage/ratio, viral load, liver profile, weight, intake/output, skin, respiratory status, and neurologic status.
  • Teach infection prevention, safe food choices, hydration, medication adherence, follow-up CD4/viral-load monitoring, and immediate reporting of infection.

HIV/AIDS Priorities

Transmission and Immune Target

ATI source-authored

HIV is a retrovirus that reshapes the host immune system by targeting CD4+ T lymphocytes.

Transmission occurs through blood and body fluids such as semen and vaginal secretions.

HIV is not commonly transmitted through casual contact; epidemiologic data make urine, feces, tears, saliva, and similar fluids unlikely sources.

All clients who are pregnant should be screened for HIV.

Prevention teaching includes condoms, abstinence, avoiding shared needles, and maintaining recommended immunizations.

Use standard precautions when caring for a client who has HIV.

Disease Stages and CD4 Pattern

ATI source-authored

Progression/acute infection: manifestations can begin 2 to 4 weeks after infection and resemble influenza; viral load rises rapidly while CD4+ cells drop.

Chronic asymptomatic infection: the client can remain clinically silent for years while antibodies are present and viral replication continues.

AIDS: late stage marked by life-threatening opportunistic infections; without treatment, death occurs within a few years.

Stage 1: CD4+ count 500 cells/mm3 or more, or CD4 percentage 29% or more.

Stage 2: CD4+ count 200 to 499 cells/mm3, or CD4 percentage 14% to 28%.

Stage 3/AIDS: AIDS-defining condition, CD4+ count below 200 cells/mm3, or CD4 percentage below 14%.

Risk Factors and Expected Findings

ATI source-authored

Risk factors include unprotected vaginal, anal, or oral sex; multiple sex partners; occupational exposure; perinatal exposure; IV drug use with contaminated needles; and older adulthood.

Older adults can go undiagnosed because manifestations can resemble other common illnesses.

Older adult women have increased risk related to vaginal dryness and thinning of the vaginal wall.

Expected findings can include chills, rash, anorexia, nausea, weight loss, weakness, fatigue, headache, sore throat, and night sweats.

CBC and differential can show anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia; platelet count can be below 150,000/mm3.

Diagnostic and Monitoring Tests

ATI source-authored

Positive HIV antibody screening is confirmed by supplemental testing such as Western blot or indirect immunofluorescence assay.

CD4+ count helps classify the stage of HIV disease.

HIV RNA quantification determines viral load before treatment and monitors disease progression, adherence, treatment response, and medication resistance.

HIV drug resistance testing guides medication changes when resistance occurs or CD4+ counts fall despite therapy.

After a positive confirmatory test, explain that HIV exposure/infection does not automatically mean the client has clinical AIDS.

Core Nursing Care

ATI source-authored

Assess risk factors, including sexual practices and IV drug use.

Monitor fluid intake, urinary output, daily weight, nutrition, electrolytes, pain, vital signs, and temperature.

Assess skin integrity for rashes, open areas, and bruising.

Assess respiratory status and lung sounds, especially diminished breath sounds.

Assess neurologic status for confusion, dementia, or visual changes.

Encourage activity balanced with rest, and provide oxygen, analgesia, and skin care as indicated.

Antiretroviral Therapy and Adherence

ATI source-authored

Highly active antiretroviral therapy combines several HIV medications to reduce resistance, adverse effects, and dosing burden.

Medication classes include fusion inhibitors, entry inhibitors, nucleoside and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, and integrase inhibitors.

Monitor CBC, WBC, and liver function tests because antiretrovirals can affect liver enzymes, bilirubin, MCV, HDL, cholesterol, and triglycerides.

Monitor CD4+ T lymphocyte count, CD4 percentage, and CD4-to-CD8 ratio; a ratio below 1 indicates more severe manifestations.

Teach clients to take antiretroviral medications on schedule and not miss doses because missed doses can cause drug resistance.

Ask about herbal products because alternative therapies can alter prescribed medication effects.

Infection Prevention Teaching

ATI source-authored

Practice good hygiene and frequent hand hygiene.

Avoid crowds, travel to areas with poor sanitation, and exposure to family or friends who have cold or influenza symptoms.

Avoid raw fruits and vegetables and undercooked meat, fish, or eggs when immune risk is high.

Avoid cleaning pet litter boxes to reduce toxoplasmosis risk.

Use hot water for dishes, bathe daily with antimicrobial soap, and keep the home environment clean.

Report manifestations of infection immediately.

Complications, Nutrition, and Fluids

ATI source-authored

Opportunistic infections and malignancies can include bacterial disease, tuberculosis, pneumonia, septicemia, Kaposi's sarcoma, lymphoma, viral infections, fungal disease, and protozoal disease.

Maintain antiretroviral therapy and administer prescribed antineoplastics, antibiotics, analgesics, antifungals, antidiarrheals, and appetite stimulants.

For wasting syndrome, monitor weight, calorie counts, intake/output, and nutrition; provide between-meal supplements and small frequent high-protein feedings.

Reduce fat content when fat intolerance worsens GI symptoms.

For mouth pain, rinses with saline or sodium bicarbonate and sterile water can support intake.

Encourage 2,000 to 3,000 mL/day of fluids when appropriate, and implement seizure precautions for HIV encephalopathy.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - AIDS Nursing Care

Active Learning Scenario

Priority assessments

  • Assess risk factors, fluid intake and urinary output, daily weight, nutritional intake, and electrolytes.
  • Assess skin integrity, pain, vital signs with temperature, lung sounds, respiratory status, and neurologic status.

Priority teaching

  • Adhere to antiretroviral dosing schedules and keep CD4+/viral-load follow-up.
  • Report signs of infection immediately and use daily infection-prevention routines.

Application Exercises

1

A client reports night sweats, fatigue, cough, nausea, diarrhea, and an oral temperature of 38.1 C (100.6 F) and is worried about HIV. Which actions should the nurse take first? Select all that apply.

  • A. Perform a physical assessment.
  • B. Determine when the manifestations began.
  • C. Begin teaching about HIV transmission immediately.
  • D. Draw blood for HIV testing immediately.
  • E. Obtain a sexual history.
A, B, E The priority is assessment: collect physical data, clarify timing, and obtain a sexual history to understand risk and possible exposure.
C, D Teaching and testing can be appropriate later, but the ATI priority in this scenario is to gather assessment data first.
2

Which tests confirm HIV infection? Select all that apply.

  • A. Western blot
  • B. Indirect immunofluorescence assay
  • C. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count
  • D. HIV RNA quantification
  • E. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis
A, B Positive supplemental antibody tests, such as Western blot or indirect immunofluorescence assay, confirm HIV infection.
C, D, E CD4+ count stages disease, HIV RNA quantification monitors viral load and treatment, and CSF analysis is not used to confirm HIV infection.
3

Which statement by a client who has stage 3 HIV disease shows correct infection-prevention teaching?

  • A. "I will wear gloves while changing the pet litter box."
  • B. "I will rinse raw fruits with water before eating them."
  • C. "I will wear a mask when around family members who are ill."
  • D. "I will cook vegetables before eating them."
D Cooking vegetables reduces bacterial exposure that can cause opportunistic infection.
A, B, C The client should avoid cleaning litter boxes, avoid raw produce when immune risk is high, and avoid contact with ill people rather than relying on a mask.
4

Which findings are HIV risk factors? Select all that apply.

  • A. Perinatal exposure
  • B. Pregnancy alone
  • C. One mutually monogamous sex partner
  • D. Older adult woman
  • E. Occupational exposure
A, D, E Perinatal exposure, older adult female genital changes, and occupational exposure are ATI-supported HIV risk factors.
B, C Pregnancy prompts screening but is not itself a risk factor; a mutually monogamous partner is not listed as a risk factor.
5

A client who has stage 2 HIV is having difficulty maintaining weight. Which statement shows correct nutrition teaching?

  • A. "I will choose a diet high in fat to help gain weight."
  • B. "I will eat three large meals each day."
  • C. "I will limit liquids to about 1 liter daily."
  • D. "I will add high-protein foods to my diet."
D High-protein, high-calorie intake supports weight maintenance and nutrition.
A, B, C High-fat foods can worsen fat intolerance, small frequent meals are better tolerated, and fluids are often encouraged up to 2 to 3 L/day when appropriate.

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 87

Lupus Erythematosus, Gout, and Fibromyalgia

This chapter compares three chronic inflammatory or pain patterns. SLE is autoimmune and multisystem, gout is uric-acid crystal inflammation, and fibromyalgia is chronic pain with fatigue, sleep disturbance, and functional impairment.

TL;DR · SLE Kidneys, Gout Uric Acid, Fibromyalgia Sleep-Pain Cycle

For SLE, watch autoimmune flare patterns, kidney injury, skin/sun teaching, and immunosuppression safety. For gout, connect uric acid, great-toe pain, kidney function, diet, and medication adherence. For fibromyalgia, treat pain, fatigue, sleep, mobility, and coping as one care cluster.

SLE clues

  • Autoimmune disorder with flares/remissions and possible kidney, heart, lung, GI, neurologic, and vascular involvement.
  • Expected labs can include positive ANA, decreased C3/C4, elevated ESR, pancytopenia, proteinuria, RBCs in urine, and increased BUN/creatinine.
  • Report edema, hypertension, chest pain, infection, and Raynaud-type color changes promptly.

Gout and fibromyalgia clues

  • Gout: severe painful swollen joint, often great toe; monitor uric acid, BUN/creatinine, and joint fluid results.
  • Fibromyalgia: burning or gnawing trigger-point pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, sensory sensitivity, and functional impairment.
  • Teach low-purine gout care and regular low-impact activity/sleep routines for fibromyalgia.

Disorder Priorities

Autoimmune and Chronic Pain Frame

ATI source-authored

ATI presents these disorders as chronic patterns where symptom control, flare reduction, and functional support are the major nursing through-lines.

Autoimmune disorders occur when antibodies attack healthy tissue; triggers can include toxins, medications, bacteria, and viruses.

SLE can involve multiple organ systems and has no cure; treatment aims to reduce manifestations and flare frequency.

Gout is a systemic uric-acid disorder with crystal deposits in joints and body tissues.

Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome with stiffness, sleep disturbance, weakness, fatigue, and tender trigger points.

Autoimmune disorders become more common with age, and older-adult presentations can be delayed or confused with other conditions.

SLE Assessment Pattern

ATI source-authored

Lupus can be discoid, systemic, or medication-induced; systemic lupus can lead to major organ failure.

Risk is higher in females ages 20 to 40 and in clients of Asian, Hispanic, or Native American descent.

Expected findings include fatigue, malaise, alopecia, blurred vision, pleuritic pain, anorexia, weight loss, depression, weakness, and joint pain, swelling, or tenderness.

Physical findings can include fever, anemia, lymphadenopathy, butterfly rash, pericarditis/friction rub, and Raynaud phenomenon.

During exacerbations, assess kidney, heart, lung, GI, vascular, neurologic, joint, and connective-tissue involvement.

SLE Labs and Kidney Warning Signs

ATI source-authored

ANA can be positive because antibodies are produced against the client's own DNA.

SLE-related immune activity can decrease serum complement C3 and C4 and elevate ESR.

BUN and creatinine can increase with kidney involvement; urinalysis can show protein and RBCs.

CBC can show pancytopenia.

Monitor blood pressure, edema, urine output, BUN, creatinine, nutritional status, and signs of lupus nephritis.

SLE Medication and Self-Care Teaching

ATI source-authored

NSAIDs reduce inflammation and arthritic pain but are contraindicated with impaired kidney function; monitor for hepatitis.

Prednisone reduces inflammation and suppresses immune response; monitor for fluid retention, hypertension, and kidney effects, and taper as prescribed.

Methotrexate, azathioprine, and belimumab suppress immune response; monitor for infection, bone marrow suppression, and increased liver enzymes.

Avoid live vaccines before immunosuppressant therapy as instructed.

Hydroxychloroquine can reduce synovitis, fever, fatigue, and photosensitive lesions; teach frequent eye examinations.

Use sun protection, mild shampoo, gentle skin care, steroid creams as prescribed, and daily skin inspection.

SLE Complication Watch

ATI source-authored

Lupus nephritis can progress to chronic kidney disease and possible transplant need; monitor periorbital/lower-extremity edema, hypertension, creatinine, and BUN.

Pericarditis and myocarditis can occur with SLE; monitor for chest pain, fatigue, arrhythmias, and fever.

Teach the client to report chest pain, peripheral or periorbital edema, and evidence of infection.

Illness and stress can precipitate exacerbations, so avoidance strategies and medication adherence matter.

Pregnancy risk and treatment medication effects should be reviewed with the provider.

Gout Assessment and Diagnostics

ATI source-authored

Primary gout involves uric acid production exceeding kidney excretion and can progress through asymptomatic hyperuricemia, acute gouty arthritis, and chronic gout.

Secondary gout can be caused by chronic kidney failure, some cancers, or excessive diuretic use.

Risk factors include obesity, heredity, postmenopause, cardiovascular disease, trauma, alcohol use, starvation dieting, diuretics, chemotherapy agents, and chronic kidney failure.

Expected findings include severe joint pain, redness, swelling, warmth, and exquisite pain with touch or motion, often at the great toe.

Diagnostics include elevated ESR, repeated serum uric acid measurements, urinary uric acid, BUN/creatinine, and synovial fluid aspiration for uric acid crystals.

Gout Medications and Teaching

ATI source-authored

Acute gout: colchicine, NSAIDs, or corticosteroids can decrease pain and inflammation; kidney impairment changes medication safety.

Chronic gout: allopurinol or febuxostat lowers production and supports uric acid control; take after meals with a full glass of water and increase fluids as instructed.

Probenecid promotes uric acid excretion; monitor uric acid and avoid aspirin because it reduces medication effectiveness.

Pegloticase can be used for refractory gout and requires close monitoring for allergic reaction or anaphylaxis.

Teach a low-purine diet without organ meats or shellfish, limited alcohol, avoidance of starvation diets and diuretics when possible, increased fluids, stress management, and medication adherence.

Fibromyalgia Assessment Pattern

ATI source-authored

Fibromyalgia pain is often described as burning or gnawing and can be elicited by palpating trigger points.

Risk factors include female sex ages 30 to 50, rheumatologic conditions, chronic fatigue syndrome, Lyme disease, influenza-like illness, trauma, and deep sleep deprivation.

Expected findings include fatigue, sleep disturbance, numbness/tingling, sensory sensitivity, headache, jaw pain, depression, and concentration or memory difficulty.

Cardiovascular, GI, genitourinary, and visual complaints can also occur.

Pain and tenderness can vary with stress, activity, and weather conditions.

Fibromyalgia Care and Teaching

ATI source-authored

Assess pain, mobility, and fatigue; provide emotional support to the client and family.

Pregabalin and duloxetine can decrease nerve pain; teach no alcohol and monitor for drowsiness or sleepiness.

NSAIDs can reduce pain and inflammation but are contraindicated with impaired kidney function; take with food.

Amitriptyline, nortriptyline, and trazodone can support sleep and pain control; older adults need monitoring for confusion and orthostatic hypotension.

Teach sleep routines, low-impact exercise, physical therapy, support groups, and complementary strategies such as stress management, tai chi, acupuncture, or hypnosis when appropriate.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Fibromyalgia Teaching

Active Learning Scenario

Alteration and findings

  • Chronic pain syndrome with burning or gnawing trigger-point pain, stiffness, chronic fatigue, sleep disturbance, and functional impairment.
  • Findings can include numbness/tingling, sensory sensitivity, headaches, jaw pain, depression, memory or concentration difficulty, GI symptoms, GU symptoms, and visual changes.

Medication teaching

  • Pregabalin or duloxetine can decrease nerve pain; avoid alcohol and monitor for drowsiness.
  • NSAIDs require kidney-function caution and should not be taken on an empty stomach.
  • Tricyclic antidepressants can improve sleep and pain; older adults need monitoring for confusion and orthostatic hypotension.

Application Exercises

1

A client who has SLE reports fatigue, joint tenderness, swelling, and difficulty urinating. Which laboratory findings should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Positive ANA titer
  • B. Increased hemoglobin
  • C. 2+ urine protein
  • D. Increased serum C3 and C4
  • E. Elevated BUN
A, C, E SLE can produce positive ANA, proteinuria from kidney involvement, and elevated BUN with renal injury.
B, D Pancytopenia can occur rather than increased hemoglobin, and C3/C4 are expected to decrease with SLE immune activity.
2

Which statement by a client who has SLE shows correct self-care teaching?

  • A. "I should limit my time in the tanning bed."
  • B. "I will apply powder to any skin rash."
  • C. "I should use a mild hair shampoo."
  • D. "I will inspect my skin once a month for rashes."
C Mild shampoo helps avoid scalp irritation and supports gentle hair care.
A, B, D Avoid tanning/UV exposure, use prescribed steroid creams rather than powder, and inspect skin daily.
3

Which findings are risk factors for gout? Select all that apply.

  • A. Diuretic use
  • B. Obesity
  • C. Deep sleep deprivation
  • D. Depression
  • E. Cardiovascular disease
A, B, E Diuretic use, obesity, and cardiovascular disease are ATI-supported gout risk factors.
C, D Deep sleep deprivation is associated with fibromyalgia risk, and depression is not listed as a gout risk factor.
4

Which finding should the nurse expect in a client who has a new diagnosis of SLE?

  • A. Weight gain
  • B. Petechiae on thighs
  • C. Systolic murmur
  • D. Alopecia
D Alopecia is an expected finding with SLE.
A, B, C Weight loss is more expected; the source emphasizes butterfly rash and cardiac friction rub rather than petechiae or systolic murmur.
5

A client who has SLE is experiencing Raynaud phenomenon. Which finding should the nurse anticipate?

  • A. Swelling of finger joints
  • B. Pallor of toes with cold exposure
  • C. Feet reddened with ambulation
  • D. Intense heat in the fingers
B Raynaud phenomenon involves vasospasm and pallor with cold or stress exposure.
A, C, D Joint swelling can occur with SLE but is not specific to Raynaud phenomenon; cold/stress color changes and pain are the priority cue.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

System Disorder, Medication, Diagnostic Procedure, Basic Concept, and Nursing Skill: systemic lupus erythematosus, discoid lupus, medication-induced lupus, lupus nephritis, pericarditis/myocarditis, Raynaud phenomenon, ANA testing, complement C3/C4, hydroxychloroquine, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, gout, synovial fluid aspiration, colchicine, allopurinol/febuxostat, probenecid, pegloticase, low-purine diet, fibromyalgia, trigger-point pain, sleep routine, low-impact exercise, pregabalin, duloxetine, and tricyclic antidepressants. Worked AMS Templates will be linked after source-supported examples are built.

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 88

Rheumatoid Arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic autoimmune synovitis that attacks joints bilaterally and symmetrically, often starting in the hands and upper joints. Early recognition, joint protection, medication safety, and activity-rest balance can preserve mobility and reduce permanent deformity.

TL;DR · Symmetric Synovitis, DMARD Lag, Systemic Complications

RA causes inflammatory synovitis, thickened synovium, cartilage/bone/tendon/ligament damage, and late joint deformities. Monitor inflammation labs, protect joints during ADLs, teach medication warning signs, and report fever, infection, pleuritic pain, or substernal chest pain.

Pattern clues

  • Bilateral, symmetric joint involvement; upper joints commonly affected first.
  • Morning stiffness, pain at rest and with movement, swelling, warmth, erythema, and decreased range of motion.
  • Late hand deformities include ulnar deviation, swan-neck, and boutonniere patterns.

Safety clues

  • DMARD relief can take weeks; monitor for infection, low WBCs/platelets, liver enzyme elevation, and pregnancy contraindications when relevant.
  • NSAIDs can cause GI distress, fluid retention, hypertension, renal dysfunction, and GI bleeding.
  • RA can affect eyes, lungs, blood vessels, pleura, pericardium, and other connective tissues.

RA Priorities

Disease Process and Prevention

ATI source-authored

RA is a chronic, progressive inflammatory autoimmune disease. WBCs attack synovial tissue, causing thickening and inflammation that can spread into surrounding joint structures.

Inflammation can damage cartilage, bone, tendons, and ligaments, reducing range of motion and function.

The disease course includes exacerbations and remissions.

Early diagnosis and treatment can prevent permanent joint damage.

Use adaptive devices to prevent deformity during ADLs.

Continue using affected joints and ambulating within tolerance to maintain function and range of motion.

Risk Factors and Expected Findings

ATI source-authored

Risk factors include female sex, age 30 to 60, genetic predisposition, bacterial or viral infection such as Epstein-Barr virus, stress, smoking, environmental factors, and older age.

Expected findings can include pain at rest and with movement, morning stiffness, pleuritic pain, xerostomia, anorexia, weight loss, fatigue, paresthesias, recent illness or stressor, joint pain, and loss of function.

Joint swelling, warmth, and erythema are common; joint deformity is a late manifestation.

Fingers, hands, wrists, knees, and feet are often affected; proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints are common hand sites.

Other findings can include subcutaneous nodules, low-grade fever, muscle weakness or atrophy, red sclera/eye changes, and lymph node enlargement.

Labs and Diagnostic Procedures

ATI source-authored

Anti-CCP antibodies are sensitive for RA and can be positive before manifestations develop.

Rheumatoid factor can support diagnosis; higher titers correlate with more severe disease, but other autoimmune disorders can also increase RF.

ESR and CRP indicate inflammation and can help diagnose or monitor disease activity and response to anti-inflammatory therapy.

ANA can be positive; WBCs can increase during exacerbation and RBCs can decrease with anemia.

Arthrocentesis evaluates synovial fluid; monitor the needle site for bleeding or fluid leak, and teach ice/rest for 24 hr.

X-ray can show bony erosions and narrowed joint spaces and track joint destruction over time.

Nursing Care and Function

ATI source-authored

Encourage physical activity within the client's capability to maintain joint mobility.

Monitor for fatigue and teach strategies to maximize function and minimize pain.

Monitor skin closely and maintain a safe environment.

Refer for physical therapy, occupational therapy, assistive devices, support organizations, and home assistance as needed.

Monitor medication effectiveness through reduced pain and improved mobility.

Encourage foods high in vitamins, protein, and iron, plus small frequent meals when needed.

NSAIDs, COX-2 Blockers, and Corticosteroids

ATI source-authored

NSAIDs often begin treatment and provide analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects.

Teach NSAID use with food, water, or milk; watch for coffee-ground emesis or dark tarry stools and avoid alcohol to reduce GI risk.

Monitor for fluid retention, hypertension, and renal dysfunction.

COX-2 blockers can cause less GI distress but can increase cardiac risk and are not recommended after myocardial infarction.

Corticosteroids can be used for acute exacerbations or advanced disease but are not preferred long-term due to osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, immunosuppression, and cataract risk.

Teach steroid warning signs: vision changes, blood glucose changes, impaired healing, black tarry stools, weight gain, infection avoidance, and tapering/alternate-day dosing as prescribed.

DMARDs and Immune Suppression Safety

ATI source-authored

Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs slow RA progression and suppress the immune response that drives pain and inflammation.

Relief can take several weeks, so the client should not expect immediate symptom improvement.

Examples include hydroxychloroquine, minocycline, sulfasalazine, etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, penicillamine, methotrexate, leflunomide, cyclophosphamide, and azathioprine.

Monitor for allergic reaction, low WBCs, low platelets, and increased liver enzymes, especially with leflunomide.

Teach infection avoidance, allergy reporting, alcohol avoidance for liver protection, and reporting hair loss or diarrhea with leflunomide.

Leflunomide is contraindicated during pregnancy due to fetal birth-defect risk.

Procedures, Supports, and Self-Management

ATI source-authored

Plasmapheresis can remove circulating antibodies during severe, life-threatening exacerbations.

Total joint arthroplasty can replace severely deformed joints that do not respond to medication therapy.

Synovectomy removes the synovial membrane around affected joints.

Use heat or cold based on response: hot shower for morning stiffness, heated paraffin for hand/finger pain, and cold therapy for edema.

Conserve energy by spacing activities, taking rest periods, and asking for help when needed.

Report fever, infection, pain with inspiration, or substernal chest pain promptly.

Systemic Complication Watch

ATI source-authored

Sjogren's syndrome causes dry eyes, mouth, and vagina; provide eye drops, artificial saliva, vaginal lubricants, and fluids with meals.

Secondary osteoporosis can result from immobilization; encourage weight-bearing exercise as tolerated.

Vasculitis can reduce blood flow to organs, often affecting skin, eyes, and brain; monitor skin lesions, vision changes, and cognitive changes.

Respiratory complications can include pleurisy, pneumonitis, interstitial fibrosis, and pulmonary hypertension; monitor dyspnea and support oxygen therapy as prescribed.

Cardiac inflammation can cause pericarditis or myocarditis; administer anti-inflammatory agents as prescribed and report concerning chest symptoms.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Rheumatoid Arthritis Self-Management

Active Learning Scenario

Potential complications

  • Sjogren's syndrome with dryness of the eyes, mouth, and vagina.
  • Vasculitis causing organ ischemia, often affecting the brain, eyes, and skin.

Client education

  • Use fluids with meals, eye drops, artificial saliva, or vaginal lubricants as needed for dryness.
  • Report vision or cognitive changes, fever, infection, pleuritic pain, or substernal chest pain.
  • Use heat/cold, remain active within tolerance, and use approved nonpharmacologic pain strategies.

Application Exercises

1

A client who has RA reports increased joint tenderness and swelling. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

  • A. Recent influenza
  • B. Decreased range of motion
  • C. Hypersalivation
  • D. Increased blood pressure
  • E. Pain at rest
A, B, E Recent illness can precipitate RA exacerbation, and decreased range of motion plus pain at rest are expected RA findings.
C, D RA can cause dry mouth rather than hypersalivation; increased blood pressure is not a characteristic RA manifestation.
2

Which teaching should the nurse include for a client with a new diagnosis of RA?

  • A. "You can have morning stiffness when you get out of bed."
  • B. "You can have abdominal pain as the key joint symptom."
  • C. "You can expect weight gain."
  • D. "You can experience low blood sugar."
A Morning stiffness on rising is a classic RA teaching point.
B, C, D RA is associated with pleuritic pain, weight loss, fatigue, and joint symptoms rather than abdominal pain, weight gain, or hypoglycemia.
3

Which laboratory tests are used to diagnose or support diagnosis of RA? Select all that apply.

  • A. Urinalysis
  • B. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  • C. BUN
  • D. Antinuclear antibody titer
  • E. WBC count
B, D, E ESR, ANA titer, and WBC count are ATI-supported lab tests used in RA diagnostic evaluation.
A, C Urinalysis and BUN are useful for kidney assessment but are not RA diagnostic tests in this source question.

Related ATI Templates

Suggested template type

System Disorder, Medication, Diagnostic Procedure, Basic Concept, and Nursing Skill: rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory synovitis, anti-CCP antibodies, rheumatoid factor, ESR, CRP, ANA, arthrocentesis, X-ray for joint destruction, NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, corticosteroids, DMARDs, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, leflunomide, biologic response modifiers, plasmapheresis, total joint arthroplasty, synovectomy, adaptive devices, Sjogren's syndrome, vasculitis, osteoporosis, respiratory complications, and pericarditis/myocarditis.
