Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 89

General Principles of Cancer

Cancer care starts with recognizing abnormal cell growth, reducing modifiable risks, identifying warning patterns early, and watching for complications that can become emergencies before a specific cancer diagnosis is fully staged.

TL;DR · Mutated Cells, Early Screening, Emergency Red Flags

Cancer is uncontrolled abnormal cell growth that can invade locally, spread through lymph or blood, and still keeps the name of the original tissue. Nursing priorities are prevention, early screening, staging awareness, nutrition support, survivorship planning, and urgent recognition of oncologic emergencies.

High-yield anchors

  • Differentiate benign local growth from malignant invasion and metastasis.
  • Link tissue origin to cancer naming: carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, sarcoma, leukemia, lymphoma, or myeloma.
  • Use TNM staging and grading language to interpret spread and tumor aggressiveness.

Do-not-miss care

  • Teach modifiable prevention: tobacco avoidance, healthy diet, vaccines, skin protection, exercise, and risk-reducing screening.
  • Support intake early because cancer and treatment can drive anorexia, nausea, taste changes, dry mouth, diarrhea, and early satiety.
  • Escalate SIADH, hypercalcemia, superior vena cava syndrome, sepsis, spinal cord compression, and tumor lysis syndrome findings.

Cancer Foundations

Abnormal Growth and Metastasis

ATI source-authored

Cancer begins when genetic changes disrupt normal cell growth, division, and death. Abnormal cells can keep proliferating, build new blood supply for continued growth, invade nearby tissues, and move through blood or lymph to distant sites.

Triggers: inherited mutations or external factors such as viruses, chemicals, physical agents, hormones, family history, and lifestyle patterns.

Metastasis rule: name the cancer by the original tissue, even after it spreads.

New symptom clue: new bone pain can suggest bone metastasis; bowel or bladder tone changes can suggest nervous-system involvement.

Benign Versus Malignant and Tissue Origin

ATI source-authored

A tumor is an abnormal cell collection, but not every tumor is cancer. Benign tumors can compress nearby structures as they enlarge, while malignant tumors invade, access blood or lymph, and can spread beyond the first site.

Carcinomas: epithelial tissue.

Adenocarcinomas: glandular organs.

Sarcomas: mesenchymal tissue.

Leukemias: blood-forming cells.

Lymphomas: lymph tissue; myelomas: plasma cells.

Prevention, Screening, and Risks

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

ATI source-authored

Primary prevention is a teaching-heavy nursing role: reduce exposures, support protective habits, and connect clients with vaccines or preventive medications when indicated by the provider.

Encourage a low-fat eating pattern with fruits, vegetables, lean protein, healthy weight, and routine activity.

Limit processed/red meats, sugar, salt, nitrates, nitrites, alcohol, and tobacco exposure.

Reduce risk from recreational drug use, needle sharing, unprotected sex, radiation, chemicals, and UVA/UVB exposure.

Teach HPV vaccination for cancers linked to HPV and hepatitis B vaccination to reduce liver-disease progression risk.

Know chemoprevention examples: aspirin or celecoxib for colon-cancer risk reduction and tamoxifen or vitamin D for breast-cancer risk reduction when prescribed.

Screening Foundation

ATI source-authored

Clients should discuss benefits, risks, timing, and personal risk with the provider. Higher-risk clients can need earlier or more frequent screening than average-risk clients.

Breast screening includes mammography and clinical breast exams based on age and health status.

Colorectal options include colonoscopy, fecal occult or immunochemical testing, and stool DNA testing at source-supported intervals.

Prostate screening is shared decision-making after discussion of benefits, risks, and uncertainty, with earlier discussion for higher-risk clients.

Gene-mutation screening can be indicated with strong family history of breast or colon cancer.

Pap/HPV testing and low-dose helical CT for qualifying current or former smokers are included in the source screening foundation.

Cancer Risk Pattern

ATI source-authored

Risk assessment should combine age, immune status, tissue injury, racial/ethnic patterns, genetics, infection history, exposures, lifestyle, chronic disease, obesity, GERD, poverty-related access barriers, and air pollution.

Older female clients commonly develop colorectal, breast, lung, pancreatic, and ovarian cancers.

Older male clients commonly develop lung, colorectal, prostate, pancreatic, and gastric cancers.

Viral and bacterial links include hepatitis B/C with liver cancer, human T-cell leukemia virus with leukemia/lymphoma, Epstein-Barr virus with lymphoma, HPV with cervical cancer, HIV with lymphoma and Kaposi's sarcoma, and Helicobacter pylori with stomach cancer or stomach-lining lymphoma.

Dietary risk rises with high fat, red or processed meat, preservatives/additives, and low fiber.

Assessment, Staging, and Prognosis

Expected Findings and Diagnostics

ATI source-authored

Findings depend on the tissue involved. Pain and physiologic changes usually reflect disruption of local organ or tissue function, compression, invasion, or metastatic spread.

Laboratory testing can include tumor markers and screening labs such as PSA.

Diagnostic procedures identify tumor location and size and can include biopsy, MRI, CT, fluoroscopy, PET, and nuclear imaging.

Biopsy and imaging are covered in the next chapter; this chapter frames why staging information matters.

TNM Staging and Tumor Grading

ATI source-authored

TNM staging describes primary tumor size/extent, regional lymph-node involvement, and distant metastasis. Grading describes how much the cells resemble normal tissue and how aggressively they are likely to behave.

T: TX cannot evaluate primary tumor; T0 no evidence; Tis in situ; T1 through T4 increasing size or extent.

N: NX cannot evaluate nodes; N0 no regional node evidence; N1 through N3 increasing node involvement or spread.

M: MX cannot evaluate distant metastasis; M0 no distant metastasis; M1 distant metastasis present.

Grade: well-differentiated cells look closer to normal and grow more slowly; poorly differentiated cells look less normal and spread more quickly.

Prognosis and Survivorship Planning

ATI source-authored

Early diagnosis generally improves prognosis, but some cancers metastasize before symptoms appear. Minority populations can have worse cancer outcomes because of access, socioeconomic, and care-seeking barriers.

After successful treatment, help create a survivorship plan.

Continue prevention and screening for recurrence or new cancer.

Watch for metastasis manifestations and coordinate ongoing needs such as pain management, fertility support, or treatment-effect care.

Complications and Emergencies

Malnutrition, Constipation, and Gastric Stasis

ATI source-authored

Cancer raises metabolic demand and can impair intake, digestion, absorption, and desire or ability to eat. Treatment can add nausea, vomiting, taste changes, anorexia, pain, diarrhea, dry mouth, thick saliva, early satiety, and GI irritation.

Monitor nutrition-related labs such as albumin, ferritin, and transferrin.

Give antiemetics and antacids as prescribed, encourage oral hygiene, include food preferences, and limit liquids with meals to reduce early satiety.

For constipation or slowed gastric emptying, anticipate cancer effects, treatment effects, and opioid-related slowed motility; use stool softeners/laxatives as prescribed and encourage fluids, fiber, and activity as tolerated.

Paraneoplastic Syndromes

ATI source-authored

Paraneoplastic syndromes occur when immune cells attack normal cells instead of cancer cells, producing neurologic changes in movement, sensation, or mental function.

Recognize altered neurologic function early and provide a safe environment until baseline mental status returns.

Administer prescribed therapies that reduce the immune response, which can include steroids, immune factors, plasmapheresis, or irradiation.

Use vision or hearing aids when deficits affect safety or communication.

Oncologic Emergencies

ATI source-authored

Oncology clients can deteriorate from endocrine, electrolyte, vascular, hematologic, infectious, neurologic, or cell-lysis complications. These findings should trigger prompt escalation and ordered emergency interventions.

SIADH: most associated with lung and brain cancers; watch nausea/vomiting, behavior change, lethargy, hostility, seizures, coma, hyponatremia, and low osmolality.

Hypercalcemia: watch anorexia, nausea/vomiting, shortened QT interval, kidney stones, bone pain, and mental-status changes.

Superior vena cava syndrome: head/upper-body venous obstruction can cause facial/periorbital edema, upper-body erythema, dyspnea, and epistaxis; place in high-Fowler's initially.

Hematologic emergencies: bone-marrow invasion can reduce RBCs, platelets, and neutrophils; leukemia or adenocarcinoma can trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Sepsis: neutropenia increases risk; anticipate cultures, lactate, antibiotics, crystalloid fluids, and vasopressors if fluids are insufficient.

Spinal cord compression: worsening back pain, sensation or strength changes, reduced deep tendon reflexes, and bowel/bladder retention need immediate action.

Tumor lysis syndrome: rapid tumor destruction can cause hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, kidney injury, and cardiac-function changes.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Cancer Risk Factors Teaching

Scenario: A nurse is preparing community health-fair teaching about cancer risk factors. Complete the System Disorder template by organizing risk groups, lifestyle risks, and infection-related cancer links.

  • Risk factors: older adult women have increased incidence of colorectal, breast, lung, pancreatic, and ovarian cancers; older adult men have increased incidence of lung, colorectal, prostate, pancreatic, and gastric cancers.
  • Race-linked examples: risk patterns include testicular, breast, colorectal, pancreatic, liver, and renal pelvis cancers in specific racial/ethnic groups.
  • Diet-related risks: high fat, high red meat, and low fiber.
  • Lifestyle-related risks: multiple sexual partners or STIs, ultraviolet/radiation exposure, tobacco use, and alcohol use.
  • Infectious links: hepatitis B/C with liver cancer, human T-cell leukemia virus with lymphoma/leukemia, Epstein-Barr virus with lymphoma, HPV with cervical cancer, HIV with lymphoma/Kaposi's sarcoma, and H. pylori with stomach cancer or stomach-lining lymphoma.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · SIADH Escalation

A client who has lung cancer is showing manifestations consistent with SIADH. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

  1. Behavioral changes
  2. Headache
  3. Urine output 40 mL/hr
  4. Nausea
  5. Increased urine specific gravity
A, B, D Behavior changes, headache, and nausea can indicate cerebral edema associated with SIADH and should be reported.
C, E A urine output of 40 mL/hr and increased urine specific gravity can occur with SIADH but were not the priority reportable findings in the source item.

Exercise 2 · Screening Teaching

Which client statement shows understanding of cancer-screening prevention teaching?

  1. "I will have a mammogram every 2 years starting at age 45."
  2. "I should have a colonoscopy every 15 years starting at age 60."
  3. "I need a clinical breast exam every year after age 40."
  4. "I should complete fecal occult blood testing every 3 years."
C The source teaching supports annual clinical breast examination after age 40.
A, B, D These choices misstate the source screening timing for mammogram transition, colonoscopy interval/starting age, or fecal occult blood testing.

Exercise 3 · Cancer-Related Malnutrition

A nurse is planning care for a client who has malnutrition related to cancer. Which interventions belong in the plan? Select all that apply.

  1. Encourage a food diary.
  2. Encourage toothbrushing before and after meals.
  3. Review the ferritin value.
  4. Eat nutrient-dense foods last.
  5. Limit fluids during meals.
A, B, C, E Food diaries track intake, oral hygiene can improve salivation and taste, ferritin supports nutrition assessment, and limiting fluids during meals can reduce early satiety.
D Nutrient-dense foods should be eaten first when intake is limited.

Exercise 4 · TNM Interpretation

The pathology report after ovarian-cancer staging reads T2-N3-MX. Which finding supports this notation?

  1. The primary tumor has moderate size or extent.
  2. No lymph nodes contain cancer cells.
  3. The tumor is responding to current medication therapy.
  4. The cancer has confirmed distant metastasis.
A T2 describes primary tumor size and extent within the TNM staging system.
B, C, D N3 indicates node involvement, TNM does not describe medication response, and MX means distant metastasis cannot be evaluated.

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 90

Cancer Screening and Diagnostic Procedures

Cancer screening and diagnosis combine client-reported changes, focused assessment, biopsy confirmation, laboratory testing, imaging, and procedure-specific nursing actions so the team can identify tumor origin, spread, and treatment targets.

TL;DR · Biopsy Confirms, Imaging Maps, Consent Protects

Screening notices concerning changes; diagnostic procedures define cancer location, tissue origin, spread, and complications. The nurse gathers a careful history, recognizes red flags, prepares the client for biopsy/labs/imaging/endoscopy, protects safety during sedation or contrast use, and teaches self-assessment plus follow-up.

Diagnostic flow

  • Start with new body-function changes, masses, pain, weight or appetite changes, and metastatic clues.
  • Use biopsy to identify the site of origin and cell characteristics.
  • Use labs and imaging to evaluate severity, response, spread, and recurrence.

Safety priorities

  • Obtain informed consent when required and explain why further testing is needed.
  • Monitor bleeding, oxygenation, sedation recovery, and contrast-dye reaction.
  • Teach self-examination and reportable changes rather than waiting for routine visits.

Screening Assessment

Client Presentation and Metastasis Clues

ATI source-authored

Cancer screening can begin with broad, sometimes subtle findings. The nurse should connect altered body function, structural change, asymmetry, pain, and systemic findings with the need for provider evaluation.

Possible cancer cues: fatigue, weakness, anorexia, weight change, masses, pain, nausea, vomiting, body-structure change, or new body-symmetry change.

Possible metastasis cues: secondary discomfort sites, swollen or tender lymph nodes, masses, altered function in another body system, and bone pain.

Teaching phrase: unexpected or persistent changes deserve screening rather than watchful delay.

Focused Assessment Techniques

ATI source-authored

Assessment should include health history, family history of cancer or genetic disorders, client-reported findings, and head-to-toe techniques aimed at detecting altered tissue or organ function.

Inspect: changes in color, symmetry, movement, or body function.

Auscultate: heart, lung, bowel, main-artery, mass, or discomfort-area sounds for altered function.

Palpate: masses or tissue abnormalities using appropriate pressure; some exams are provider-only.

Percuss: sound changes over organs; dullness can suggest consolidation, tumor, inflammation, or enlarged liver borders.

Report unexpected findings and explain why further testing or evaluation is needed.

Self-Assessment and Reportable Findings

ATI source-authored

Client education should make screening concrete. Teach self-examination practices and general warning signs that should be reported for further screening.

Report bowel or bladder habit changes and changes in body or skin shape or texture.

Report difficulty eating, chewing, swallowing, or persistent decreased appetite.

Report nonhealing sores or wounds, persistent cough, hoarseness, unexplained pain, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss or gain, and unusual bleeding or discharge.

Use breast and testicular self-examination as source-supported self-assessment examples.

Biopsy and Laboratory Testing

Biopsy Confirms Cell Origin

ATI source-authored

Biopsy provides the definitive diagnosis by identifying the site of origin, cell type, and cell characteristics such as receptors. Samples can be collected during procedures such as endoscopy, laparoscopy, or thoracotomy.

Shave biopsy: samples outer skin layers from raised lesions with a scalpel or razor blade.

Needle biopsy: aspirates tissue or fluid from a tumor near the skin surface; bone marrow aspiration is used for leukemia and lymphoma diagnosis.

Incisional/excisional biopsy: removes part or all of a tumor; punch biopsy removes a small skin plug.

Sentinel lymph node biopsy: uses dye or colloid mapping to sample the node closest to the cancer; negative nodes suggest surrounding nodes are cancer-free, while positive nodes can lead to dissection.

Biopsy Nursing Actions

ATI source-authored

Biopsy safety centers on consent, asepsis, bleeding prevention, sedation recovery, oxygenation, and positioning based on the procedure.

Obtain signed informed consent and assemble supplies for aseptic technique.

Prevent bleeding by withholding anticoagulants as prescribed and monitoring coagulation studies.

Monitor for bleeding, including dressing drainage, hypotension, and tachycardia.

Maintain a safe recovery environment until sedation effects are minimal; keep bed rest, withhold oral intake, and support oxygenation as indicated.

Use procedure-specific positioning, such as right-side positioning after liver biopsy.

Laboratory and Genetic Tests

ATI source-authored

Laboratory tests can screen for cancer, evaluate cancer effects on the body, monitor treatment response, and watch for recurrence.

Liver function test elevation can indicate primary liver cancer or metastasis from another cancer.

Tumor marker assays detect elevated proteins or DNA patterns in urine, stool, tissue, blood, or body fluids; examples include carcinoembryonic antigen, PSA, and alpha-fetoprotein.

Tumor markers can help detect cancer, measure severity, or monitor response; expected treatment response is marker decrease or return to expected range.

Genetic tests use blood or saliva to detect genes or mutations linked to cancer risk or rapid tumor growth, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2.

Some genetic testing requires informed consent and can warrant genetic-counselor support for risk interpretation.

Imaging and Endoscopy

Imaging Maps Tumor Borders and Spread

ATI source-authored

Imaging is usually a secondary tool near diagnosis to show tumor borders, detect metastasis, measure severity, monitor remission, and guide treatment planning.

Common tools include CT, MRI, PET, ultrasound, x-ray, nuclear imaging, bone scan, gallium scan, and thyroid scan.

Dye or contrast can enhance visualization; monitor for allergic reaction signs such as dyspnea, tachycardia, and restlessness.

Digital imaging improves accuracy and helps share results across the interprofessional team.

ECG, echocardiogram, or multigated acquisition scan can evaluate cardiac function before treatment or identify treatment-related damage.

Modality-Specific Teaching

ATI source-authored

Each test answers a different question. Client teaching should match the procedure rather than treating all imaging as the same experience.

CT: combines x-ray images into cross-sectional views; contrast can be oral or IV.

MRI: uses magnetic fields and radio waves; clients with clips, pacemakers, or metal implants should not have MRI.

Ultrasound: uses sound waves and can guide biopsy.

Nuclear imaging: uses an oral or IV radioactive tracer; cancerous tissue can absorb more or less tracer than expected.

PET: measures uptake of radioactive sugar, which is more rapid in cancer; PET can be combined with CT.

Endoscopy Nursing Actions

ATI source-authored

Endoscopy uses flexible scopes and cameras to visualize internal structures, including respiratory, GI, joint, body-cavity, and organ sites. Preparation and recovery depend on the specific procedure.

Obtain signed informed consent.

Prepare the client according to the procedure type.

Provide a safe environment until sedation effects are minimal, including bed rest and withholding oral intake.

Ensure adequate oxygenation during recovery.

Interpretation and Nursing Care

Interpreting Findings

ATI source-authored

Any finding that indicates or increases suspicion of cancer must be evaluated further. Multiple tests can work together to clarify tumor involvement, tumor type, metastatic areas, and cancer complications.

Educate clients about routine cancer screening as health promotion and disease prevention.

Provide care before, during, and after procedures according to procedure type.

Give self-care resources for the home environment so clients know when and how to follow up.

Active Learning Scenario

Diagnostic Procedure - Collecting Cancer Screening Findings

Scenario: A nurse manager is reviewing how to collect findings during cancer screening. Complete the Diagnostic Procedure template by organizing metastasis cues, assessment techniques, and self-assessment teaching.

  • Metastasis findings: secondary-site discomfort, swelling or tenderness of lymph nodes or body areas, masses, altered function of another body system, and bone pain.
  • Assessment techniques: inspect for color/symmetry/movement/function changes, auscultate for adventitious sounds, palpate for masses or tissue abnormalities, and percuss for altered organ sounds.
  • Client education: teach breast and testicular self-examinations as self-assessment practices that can identify data for follow-up.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy

A client is scheduled for sentinel lymph node biopsy. Which teaching should the nurse include?

  1. Dye is used during the procedure.
  2. The lymph nodes closest to the tumor are removed during the biopsy.
  3. A small amount of chemotherapy is used to test the lymph node response.
  4. A 2 mm plug of tissue is removed during the biopsy.
A Dye or colloid is used as a tracer to identify lymph nodes during sentinel lymph node biopsy.
B, C, D Node removal can occur later if positive, chemotherapy is not used for this biopsy, and a tissue plug describes punch biopsy.

Exercise 2 · Nuclear Imaging Teaching

Which statement should the nurse give to a client scheduled for nuclear imaging for suspected cancer?

  1. "This test identifies a liver enzyme."
  2. "You will receive a radioactive substance."
  3. "An endoscope will be inserted through your mouth."
  4. "The tumor will be aspirated."
B Nuclear imaging uses an oral or IV radioactive tracer to identify cancerous tissue.
A, C, D These describe liver testing, endoscopy, and needle biopsy rather than nuclear imaging.

Exercise 3 · Possible Cancer Findings

Which findings should the nurse identify as possible indications of cancer? Select all that apply.

  1. Temperature 102 F (38.9 C) for more than 48 hr
  2. Sore that does not heal
  3. Difficulty swallowing
  4. Unusual discharge
  5. Weight gain of 4 lb (1.8 kg) in 2 weeks
B, C, D, E Nonhealing sore, difficulty swallowing, unusual discharge, and unexpected weight change are possible cancer warning findings.
A Extended fever was not the source-supported cancer warning finding; unexplained night sweats were emphasized instead.

Exercise 4 · Shave Biopsy Understanding

Which statement indicates understanding of a shave biopsy for suspected cancer?

  1. "A test of my bone marrow will be performed."
  2. "A lymph node will be removed."
  3. "A needle will be inserted into the mass."
  4. "A small skin sample will be obtained."
D A shave biopsy samples the outer skin layer using a scalpel or razor blade.
A, B, C These describe bone marrow aspiration, sentinel node biopsy, and needle biopsy.

Exercise 5 · Genetic Testing Plan

Which intervention should the nurse include when planning care for genetic testing for suspected cancer?

  1. Determine whether informed consent is needed.
  2. Send results to the client's insurance agency.
  3. Verify a prescription for a tumor marker assay.
  4. Place the client in a recovery position after testing.
A Some genetic testing requires signed informed consent.
B, C, D Genetic results are confidential, tumor marker assays are separate lab tests, and blood/saliva genetic testing does not require recovery positioning.

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 91

Cancer Treatment Options

Cancer treatment is guided by the primary cell of origin, even after metastasis, and can combine surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, hormone therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, photodynamic therapy, and supportive services.

TL;DR · Primary Origin, Cytotoxic Safety, Radiation Distance

Cancer treatment removes or destroys malignant cells and can be curative, palliative, or adjuvant. Nursing priorities are procedure recovery, chemotherapy handling and adverse-effect management, neutropenic and bleeding precautions, radiation safety, skin/oral/nutrition care, and supportive referrals.

Treatment map

  • Treat metastasis according to the primary tumor origin.
  • Use surgery for removal, staging, palliation, prophylaxis, reconstruction, or lymph-node evaluation.
  • Use chemotherapy, radiation, hormone therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, or photodynamic therapy based on cancer type and client factors.

Safety map

  • Use PPE and proper disposal for chemotherapy, including oral agents.
  • Report fever quickly in neutropenia and protect against bleeding in thrombocytopenia.
  • For internal radiation, limit time, maximize distance, use shielding, and follow source/linen/excretion precautions.

Treatment Foundation

Treatment Goals and Planning

ATI source-authored

Cancer treatment is chosen according to cell of origin, client factors, and whether the goal is cure, control, palliation, or support after the primary standard treatment.

Consider age, pregnancy or childbearing desire, current health, and expected lifespan.

Adjuvant treatment is added to the primary treatment and can include hormone therapy, radiation, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or chemotherapy.

Collaborate with supportive therapies, counseling, and transfer-of-care planning at discharge.

Surgery and Tumor Procedures

ATI source-authored

Procedures can reduce, destroy, remove, stage, prevent, palliate, or reconstruct after cancer treatment.

Tumor reduction can use cryosurgery, laser therapy, ablation, or artery embolization.

Tumor excision removes the tumor and surrounding margin; a negative margin means the outer removed tissue has no cancer cells.

Lymph node dissection or sentinel lymph node biopsy evaluates spread or risk of spread.

Prophylactic surgery removes precancerous or high-risk tissue; reconstructive surgery improves appearance or function.

Nursing care includes perioperative care, complication prevention, pain control, drain/wound/device teaching, psychological support, and compensatory strategies for lost function.

Chemotherapy and Cytotoxic Safety

Chemotherapy Routes and Handling

ATI source-authored

Chemotherapy uses systemic or local cytotoxic medications that damage DNA or destroy rapidly dividing cells. Normal rapidly dividing cells in GI mucosa, hair follicles, and bone marrow are also vulnerable.

Routes can include topical, oral, parenteral, IV, intra-arterial, intraventricular, intracavitary, intravesicular, intrapleural, or intrathecal administration.

Oral anticancer medications are still toxic and should not be crushed, split, broken, or chewed.

Anyone preparing, giving, or disposing of chemotherapy should use proper PPE and agency disposal procedures.

Central venous access or an implanted port is often used for long-term therapy or vesicants.

Monitor IV therapy closely for extravasation and know the medication-specific antidote or neutralizing solution.

Immunosuppression and Neutropenic Precautions

ATI source-authored

Neutropenia from bone marrow suppression is a major chemotherapy adverse effect. Clients might not develop high fever or purulent drainage even when infection is present.

Monitor temperature, WBC count, and ANC; report fever greater than 37.8 C (100 F) immediately.

Initiate neutropenic precautions when ANC is below 1,000/mm3 or per protocol.

Use a private room, dedicated equipment, frequent hand hygiene, visitor screening, and a mask during transport.

Avoid infection sources such as live plants, stagnant water, contaminated equipment, undercooked foods, fresh fruits/vegetables when restricted, and ill visitors.

Teach daily temperature checks and immediate reporting of bacterial or viral infection manifestations.

Nausea, Anorexia, Mucositis, and Stomatitis

ATI source-authored

Chemotherapy can cause nausea, vomiting, anorexia, altered taste, mucositis, and stomatitis. Prevention and early symptom control help preserve intake and reduce infection risk.

Give antiemetics before chemotherapy and for several days after treatment as prescribed.

Remove nausea cues, use nonpharmacologic methods, track calories, offer supplements, and use mouth care before meals.

Teach small frequent meals, cold foods, low-fat dry foods, limited liquids during meals, and nutrient-dense high-protein/high-calorie foods.

For mucositis, inspect the mouth, culture new lesions, avoid glycerin swabs and alcohol mouthwash, use topical anesthetic before meals, and avoid salty, acidic, spicy, rough, or hard foods.

Encourage gentle brushing/flossing, bland soft foods, infection-control medications as prescribed, and adequate water intake if not restricted.

Anemia, Thrombocytopenia, Neuropathy, and Cognition

ATI source-authored

Myelosuppression and neurologic effects drive many chemotherapy safety interventions. Connect the lab problem to the bedside precaution.

Anemia: monitor fatigue, pallor, dizziness, dyspnea, Hgb response, and schedule rest with activity.

Thrombocytopenia: monitor petechiae, ecchymosis, gum/nose bleeding, and occult or frank blood; use bleeding precautions, small-gauge needles if needed, prolonged pressure, and avoid NSAIDs.

Peripheral neuropathy: monitor numbness, tingling, redness, loss of hand/foot sensation, orthostatic hypotension, taste changes, constipation, and injury/fall risk.

Cognitive impairment: support reports of decreased concentration, learning difficulty, or memory loss and provide cognitive-training resources.

Radiation and Other Therapies

Internal and External Radiation Safety

ATI source-authored

Radiation targets tissue with high-energy radiation. Effects depend on dose, exposure duration, intensity, distance, and whether the source is internal or external.

External beam radiation does not make the client radioactive.

Internal radiation can make body fluids and waste radioactive until the isotope is eliminated.

For brachytherapy, use a private room, warning sign, dosimeter badge, limited visits, visitor distance, lead apron, and source-retrieval equipment if indicated.

Pregnant individuals, people trying to conceive, and children should not enter the room for internal radiation.

Keep linens/dressings in the room or follow facility policy so the source is not lost in trash or laundry.

Radiation Skin, Oral, and Fatigue Care

ATI source-authored

Radiation can cause skin changes, hair loss, debilitating fatigue, oral effects, difficulty swallowing, gastroenteritis, and decreased platelets or WBCs.

Do not remove radiation tattoos or markings.

Wash irradiated skin gently with mild soap and water, pat dry, and avoid powders, ointments, lotions, deodorants, perfumes, sun, heat, tight clothing, and washcloth friction unless prescribed.

For mucositis, avoid spicy, salty, and acidic foods and try cold foods.

Schedule activity with rest periods and use energy-saving measures.

Monitor skin, mucous membranes, CBC, and treatment-field-specific effects.

Hormone, Immunotherapy, and Targeted Therapy

ATI source-authored

Hormone therapy works for hormone-supported or hormone-suppressed tumors. Immunotherapy alters the biologic response to cancer cells. Targeted therapy acts on cancer-cell components and must be taken as a significant part of treatment.

Hormone therapy examples include LH-RH agonists, androgen antagonists, estrogen receptor down-regulators, and estrogen antagonists.

Monitor hormone therapy for cardiac, blood pressure, pulmonary edema, CBC, calcium, liver enzyme, clotting, lipid, neurologic, and cardiovascular changes as source-supported by medication type.

Immunotherapy includes interleukins, interferons, monoclonal antibodies, biologic response modifiers, and cancer vaccines.

Monitor BRM therapy for inflammation, edema, orthostatic hypotension, peripheral neuropathy, neurologic effects, and skin peeling/pruritus/dryness.

Targeted therapies include small molecule inhibitors and monoclonal antibodies; monitor adverse effects specific to the agent and reinforce adherence.

Photodynamic and Supportive Treatment

ATI source-authored

Photodynamic therapy uses a photosensitizing agent followed by targeted light after the agent remains mainly in cancer cells. Supportive treatment addresses function, coping, nutrition, communication, pain, sexuality, body image, and transitions of care.

Photodynamic therapy is used for selected esophageal, ocular, upper-airway, and nonmelanoma skin cancers.

It is contraindicated when a tumor has major blood-vessel involvement; rapid tumor death can cause bleeding.

Teach sun avoidance after photodynamic therapy per source guidance.

Coordinate home health, hospice, rehabilitation, therapy services, dietitian/nutrition support, counseling, communication aids, assistive devices, and pain-management consultation as needed.

Ask about complementary or alternative therapies and incorporate safe preferred strategies when possible.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Chemotherapy-Induced Alopecia

Scenario: A nurse is teaching a client who is receiving chemotherapy and has alopecia. Complete the System Disorder template by linking pathophysiology, teaching, and nursing care.

  • Pathophysiology: chemotherapy can affect rapidly proliferating hair-follicle cells, disrupting the hair life cycle and causing temporary hair loss.
  • Client education: use head coverings, avoid damaging hair-care measures, use a soft brush or wide-tooth comb, avoid sun exposure, and expect hair to return after chemotherapy stops.
  • Nursing care: discuss the impact on self-image, encourage expression of feelings, provide reliable alopecia resources, and refer to a cancer support group.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · Thrombocytopenia Precaution

A client has a platelet count of 10,000/mm3. Which intervention should the nurse include?

  1. Apply prolonged pressure after blood sampling.
  2. Administer epoetin alfa as prescribed.
  3. Place the client in a private room.
  4. Have the client use an oral topical anesthetic before meals.
A Severe thrombocytopenia requires bleeding precautions, including prolonged pressure after punctures.
B, C, D These fit anemia, neutropenia, and mucositis care rather than thrombocytopenia.

Exercise 2 · Mucositis Care

A client receiving chemotherapy has mucositis. Which action should the nurse take?

  1. Use a glycerin-soaked swab for oral hygiene.
  2. Encourage citrus fruit juices.
  3. Obtain a culture of the lesions.
  4. Provide alcohol-based mouthwash.
C New oral lesions should be cultured to identify pathogens and guide treatment.
A, B, D Avoid glycerin swabs, acidic foods or drinks, and alcohol-based mouthwash with mucositis.

Exercise 3 · Neutropenic Precautions

Which interventions belong in the plan for a client receiving chemotherapy who is on neutropenic precautions? Select all that apply.

  1. Encourage a high-fiber diet.
  2. Eliminate standing water in the room.
  3. Have the client wear a mask when leaving the room.
  4. Keep client-specific equipment in the room.
  5. Eliminate raw foods from the diet.
B, C, D, E Remove standing water, mask for transport, keep dedicated equipment, and avoid raw foods to reduce infection exposure.
A A high-fiber diet is not a neutropenic precaution in the source item.

Exercise 4 · Chemotherapy Nausea Teaching

A client receiving chemotherapy reports severe nausea. Which statement should the nurse make?

  1. "Your nausea will lessen with each course of chemotherapy."
  2. "Hot food is better tolerated because of the aroma."
  3. "Try eating several small meals throughout the day."
  4. "Increase your red meat intake as tolerated."
C Several small meals are usually better tolerated with chemotherapy-related nausea.
A, B, D Nausea can recur with each treatment; cold foods are often better tolerated, and red meat can become unpalatable.

Exercise 5 · Brachytherapy Precautions

A client with cervical cancer is scheduled for brachytherapy. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

  1. Permit visitors to stay for 30 min at a time.
  2. Allow pregnant visitors into the room once daily.
  3. Wear a dosimeter in the client's room.
  4. Place soiled dressings in regular trash after bagging.
  5. Place soiled linens in the hallway hamper.
A, C Visitors should be time-limited and maintain distance, and staff should wear a dosimeter when caring for a client receiving brachytherapy.
B, D, E Pregnant individuals should not enter, and contaminated dressings or linens must follow radiation-safety policy rather than routine disposal.

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 92

Cancer Disorders

Specific cancers share the same abnormal-growth foundation, but each disorder has a distinct risk profile, warning pattern, screening approach, diagnostic pathway, treatment emphasis, and complication watch.

TL;DR · ABCDE Skin, Blood Cell Failure, Silent Pelvic Patterns

Cancer-disorder questions often hinge on the signature clue: melanoma ABCDE changes, leukemia bleeding/infection from marrow crowding, pancreatic late jaundice and severe pain, liver bleeding/ascites, renal hematuria or paraneoplastic effects, bladder hematuria and intravesical precautions, breast skin/nipple changes, ovarian vague abdominal findings, cervical HPV/Pap follow-up, prostate PSA/DRE/urinary symptoms, and testicular self-exam.

Recognition map

  • Skin: suspicious mole or lesion changes, especially asymmetry, irregular border, uneven color, larger diameter, or evolving features.
  • Blood/lymph: infection, anemia, bleeding, bone pain, enlarged nodes, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and fatigue.
  • GI/hepatobiliary/renal: weight loss, pain, jaundice, altered stool or urine, hematuria, ascites, and organ-function changes.

Care map

  • Protect clients with blood cancers from infection, bleeding, injury, and exhaustion.
  • Use ostomy, urinary diversion, stoma, and drain teaching after bowel, bladder, or pelvic cancer surgery.
  • Discuss body image, sexuality, fertility, menopause, erectile function, and support resources after breast, pelvic, prostate, or testicular cancer care.

Skin and Blood/Lymph Cancers

Skin Cancer and Melanoma

ATI source-authored

Ultraviolet exposure is the leading skin-cancer risk. Squamous and basal cell cancers are usually sun-exposed lesions, while malignant melanoma has rapid invasion/metastasis risk and needs fast recognition of suspicious mole changes.

Teach sun avoidance/reduction, sunscreen with UVA/UVB protection, protective clothing, sunglasses, lip protection, and avoidance of tanning beds.

Use ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter larger than about a pencil eraser/pea, and evolving shape, size, color, height, texture, bleeding, or itching.

Risk rises with chronic sun damage, severe skin injury, immunosuppression, chronic scars/burns, many moles, family/personal melanoma history, light skin that burns easily, older age, high elevation, and proximity to the equator.

Diagnostics include self/clinician assessment, body mapping, punch/shave/excisional biopsy, lymph node biopsy/dissection, and blood tests for organ involvement when melanoma is diagnosed.

Therapies can include topical chemotherapy, imiquimod, interferon, targeted therapy, biotherapy, radiation for selected older/poor surgical candidates, cryosurgery, curettage/electrodessication, excision, or Mohs surgery.

Leukemias and Lymphomas

ATI source-authored

Leukemia crowds the bone marrow with nonfunctional white blood cells, lowering mature leukocytes, platelets, and erythrocytes. Lymphomas involve lymphocytes and lymph nodes and can spread to many organs.

Acute leukemia findings can include bone pain, joint swelling, hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss, fever, poor wound healing, anemia findings, bleeding, headache, behavior change, and decreased attention.

Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present with enlarged lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, unplanned weight loss, fatigue, and infections.

Diagnostics include CBC, coagulation time, cytogenetic studies, bone marrow biopsy, CT for Hodgkin staging, lymph node biopsy, chest x-ray, CT, PET, and bone scan.

Care priorities are infection prevention/neutropenic precautions, bleeding/injury prevention, energy conservation, nutrition, fluids, sleep, visitor screening, hand hygiene, and monitoring WBC/platelets.

GI, Hepatic, Renal, and Bladder Patterns

Colorectal and Pancreatic Cancer

ATI source-authored

Colorectal care emphasizes screening, biopsy confirmation, bowel preparation, resection/ostomy teaching, and obstruction watch. Pancreatic cancer often has vague findings, late diagnosis, high mortality, and palliative pain/nutrition priorities.

For average-risk colorectal screening in the source, colonoscopy begins at age 50 every 10 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and fecal occult blood testing annually.

Colorectal diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy during endoscopic procedures; surgery can include colon resection, colectomy with temporary/permanent ostomy, or abdominal-perineal resection.

After colorectal surgery, assess a reddish-pink moist stoma, monitor output, manage pain/NG suction/diet progression, discuss incontinence, sexual function, body image, and provide ostomy support.

Pancreatic clues include boring back/abdominal pain radiating to the back, fatigue, anorexia, pruritus, weight loss, mass, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, late jaundice, clay stools, dark frothy urine, ascites, glucose intolerance, and GI bleeding.

Pancreatic care often focuses on palliation, opioids, glucose monitoring/insulin, enteral or parenteral nutrition, stenting/bypass, and monitoring after Whipple procedure for anastomotic drainage, peritonitis, thromboembolism, and metabolic complications.

Liver Cancer

ATI source-authored

Liver cancer is often metastatic, though hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer. Prevention overlaps with cirrhosis and hepatitis risk reduction.

Teach avoiding excessive alcohol, low-fat diet/healthy BMI, hepatitis B vaccination, and hepatitis B/C precautions.

Findings can include right upper quadrant, epigastric, or back pain; anorexia; weakness/fatigue; edema; weight loss; hepatomegaly; jaundice; ascites; pruritus; encephalopathy; bleeding/bruising; and anemia.

Diagnostics include biopsy, AFP, CEA with AFP interpretation, liver-function-related labs, and contrast-enhanced ultrasound or CT.

Nursing care includes right-side positioning after biopsy, hemorrhage monitoring, blood products as prescribed, small frequent high-calorie/moderate-fat meals, vitamin replacement, fluid restriction with ascites, alcohol avoidance, abdominal girth, nutrition, pain, and medication caution with impaired liver metabolism.

Treatments can include sorafenib, hepatic arterial infusion, embolization/chemoembolization/radioembolization, ablation, tunneled abdominal drain, radiation, resection, or liver transplantation.

Kidney/Renal Pelvis and Bladder Cancer

ATI source-authored

Renal cell cancer can produce paraneoplastic effects; bladder cancer commonly presents with hematuria and can require intravesical therapy, urinary diversion, or cystectomy care.

RCC findings can include smoky or cola urine, late hematuria, flank/abdominal pain, mass, renal bruit, weight loss, fever, hypertension, urinary obstruction, and hormone-related changes.

RCC paraneoplastic effects can include anemia, erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, liver dysfunction, increased sedimentation rate, and hypertension.

After nephrectomy, monitor bleeding, adrenal insufficiency, Hgb/Hct/WBC, urine output, and remaining-kidney function; teach avoiding heavy lifting and protecting kidney function.

Bladder cancer risks include tobacco, chemical/fume exposure, rubber/paint/electric cable contact, chronic urinary inflammation, long-term cyclophosphamide, male sex, older age, and schistosomiasis.

Intravesical BCG requires dwell-time precautions: sit to void, perineal cleansing, fluid restriction before therapy, toilet disinfection, private toilet if possible, washing urine-contaminated linen/clothing, and avoiding intercourse for 24 hr.

After urinary diversion or neobladder, monitor output, drains, pouch/stoma skin, decreased or absent urine, nutrition, and self-catheterization timing if applicable.

Breast and Gynecologic Patterns

Breast Cancer

ATI source-authored

Breast cancer can be noninvasive or invasive. Common metastasis sites are bone, lung, brain, and liver; triple-negative disease is aggressive because cells lack estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors.

Prevention and risk reduction include screening mammography, healthy weight, exercise, fruits/vegetables, minimized alcohol, breastfeeding when applicable, and avoiding hormone replacement therapy or environmental estrogens when appropriate.

Risk factors include BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations, previous breast cancer, dense breast tissue, atypical hyperplasia, female sex, older age, first-degree relative, early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity or first pregnancy after 30, obesity, alcohol, smoking, radiation, hormone therapy, and triple-negative risk in African American and Puerto Rican females.

Findings can include appearance/texture changes, lump, soreness, peau d'orange, dimpling, small irregular firm nontender nonmobile tumor, erythema, increased vascularity, nipple discharge/retraction/ulceration, and enlarged nodes.

Male clients can report a hard painless areolar mass, nipple inversion, ulceration, chest swelling, lymphedema, or gynecomastia.

Ovarian and Uterine Cancer

ATI source-authored

Ovarian cancer has no single screening test and is often staged during surgery. Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer and is associated with prolonged estrogen exposure.

Ovarian risk factors include age over 40, nulliparity or first pregnancy after 30, family history of ovarian/breast/colon cancer, BRCA1/BRCA2, HNPCC mutation, diabetes, endometriosis, infertility, early menarche/late menopause, and high-fat diet.

Ovarian findings can include abdominal pain/swelling, dyspepsia, gas, distention, abdominal mass, urinary frequency/incontinence, unexpected weight loss, and vaginal bleeding.

Ovarian treatment can include chemotherapy, intraperitoneal therapy, exploratory laparotomy, debulking, and total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy/oophorectomy; monitor voiding, bowel sounds, sexuality, menopause, and infection/discharge teaching.

Endometrial cancer risk rises with obesity, unopposed estrogen, tamoxifen, nulliparity, late menopause, diabetes, HNPCC, uterine polyps, and personal/family cancer history.

Endometrial findings include irregular or postmenopausal bleeding and low-back, abdominal, or pelvic pain; standard diagnosis uses transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy.

Cervical Cancer

ATI source-authored

Cervical cancer is slow-growing and often asymptomatic early, which makes HPV vaccination and Pap/HPV screening central prevention tools.

Prevention includes HPV vaccination before first sexual contact, Pap and pelvic exams, HPV co-testing in the source age group, condom use, limiting sexual partners, and smoking avoidance.

Risk factors include high-risk HPV, chronic cervical inflammation/infections, HIV/immunosuppression, STI history, early sexual activity, multiple partners, low economic status, family history, African American descent, and smoking.

Findings can include painless bleeding between menses, dysuria, hematuria, watery blood-tinged early discharge, dark foul late discharge, weight loss, pelvic pain, pain with/after intercourse, rectal bleeding, cough/chest pain, and late leg pain or edema.

Pap is screening, not diagnosis; abnormal Pap needs follow-up such as colposcopy with biopsy and HPV DNA testing.

Treatment can include conization, cryotherapy, laser ablation, hysterectomy, LEEP, radiation, chemotherapy, or exenteration; teach reportable bleeding, foul drainage, fever, drain/diversion care, and perineal wound care.

Male Reproductive Patterns

Prostate Cancer

ATI source-authored

Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and can resemble BPH. Active surveillance can be appropriate for selected clients, while treatment depends on spread, age, life expectancy, and symptom progression.

Teach diet low in animal fat with omega-3 foods, fruits/vegetables, exercise, and provider discussion of PSA screening at age 50 or earlier for higher-risk clients.

Risk factors include age, family history, African American heritage, high-fat/low-fiber diet, hereditary prostate cancer genes, BRCA1/BRCA2, rapid prostate growth, and environmental toxins.

Findings can include hesitancy, weak stream, urgency, frequency, nocturia, recurrent bladder infection, retention, late blood in urine/semen, painful ejaculation, bone pain, weight loss, sexual dysfunction, discharge or scrotal swelling, residual urine, and groin nodes.

Diagnostics include DRE, biopsy with Gleason score, genetic testing, PSA before DRE, EPCA-2, TRUS, urinalysis, and imaging for metastasis.

Treatment can include sipuleucel-T, LH-RH agonists, androgen blockers, chemotherapy, radiation, radical prostatectomy, orchiectomy, catheter care, bladder antispasmodics, and sexuality/body-image support.

Testicular Cancer Self-Examination

ATI source-authored

Testicular cancer is rare but most common in clients ages 15 to 34, and early detection has a high cure rate. Teaching should normalize the exam and clarify what must be reported.

Best timing is during or after a bath or shower when the scrotum is relaxed.

Move the penis aside and examine one testicle at a time.

Use both hands, rolling the testicle gently between thumbs and fingers.

Report hard lumps, smooth rounded bumps, or changes in size, shape, or consistency.

One testicle can normally be larger or hang lower, and the epididymis can feel like a lump; noncancer causes of swelling include hydrocele and varicocele.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder - Prostate Cancer Teaching

Scenario: A nurse is teaching a client with a new diagnosis of prostate cancer. Complete the System Disorder template by organizing medications, prostatectomy teaching, and nursing care.

  • Medications: LH-RH agonists such as leuprolide, androgen receptor blockers such as flutamide, chemotherapy such as docetaxel, ketoconazole to block androgen production when needed, and estrogen therapy such as diethylstilbestrol.
  • Therapeutic procedure: prostatectomy removes the prostate gland, seminal vesicles, bladder cuff, and regional lymph nodes by open or laparoscopic approach through suprapubic, perineal, or retropubic access.
  • Nursing care: ask about body image and sexuality, offer intimacy counseling referral, provide catheter care, and administer bladder antispasmodics as prescribed.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · Leukemia With Thrombocytopenia

A client who has leukemia develops thrombocytopenia. Which action should the nurse take first?

  1. Instruct the client to take rest periods throughout the day.
  2. Encourage repositioning in bed every 2 hr.
  3. Check temperature every 4 hr.
  4. Monitor platelet counts.
D The priority risk with thrombocytopenia is bleeding, so platelet monitoring and bleeding precautions come first.
A, B, C Rest, repositioning, and temperature checks matter, but they do not address the immediate bleeding priority.

Exercise 2 · Ovarian Cancer Risk

Which findings are risk factors for ovarian cancer? Select all that apply.

  1. Previous treatment for endometriosis
  2. Family history of colon cancer
  3. First pregnancy at age 24
  4. First period at age 14
  5. Use of oral contraceptives for 10 years
A, B Endometriosis and family history of breast, ovarian, or colon cancer are source-supported ovarian cancer risks.
C, D, E First pregnancy before 30 is not the risk pattern, early menarche is the risk pattern, and oral contraceptives offer protection in the source item.

Exercise 3 · Liver Lobectomy Monitoring

A client is 24 hr after liver lobectomy for hepatocellular carcinoma. Which laboratory report should the nurse monitor?

  1. Urine specific gravity
  2. Blood glucose
  3. Serum amylase
  4. D-dimer
B Blood glucose should be monitored during the first 24 to 48 hr after liver lobectomy due to decreased gluconeogenesis and surgical stress on the liver.
A, C, D These are not the expected source priority after liver lobectomy.

Exercise 4 · Colon Cancer Screening

Which teaching should the nurse include for adults ages 45 to 65 learning about colon cancer?

  1. Colonoscopy starts at age 40 for clients without family history.
  2. Sigmoidoscopy is recommended every 5 years beginning at age 60.
  3. Fecal occult blood testing should be done annually beginning at age 50.
  4. MRI provides definitive diagnosis of colon cancer.
C The source item supports annual fecal occult blood testing beginning at age 50.
A, B, D Colonoscopy begins at 50 every 10 years for average risk, sigmoidoscopy begins at 50, and biopsy confirms diagnosis.

Exercise 5 · Melanoma Clues

Which skin findings are indicative of malignant melanoma? Select all that apply.

  1. Diffuse vesicles
  2. Uniformly colored papule
  3. Area with asymmetric borders
  4. Rough, scaly patch
  5. Irregular colored mole
C, E Asymmetric borders and uneven pigmentation are suspicious melanoma findings.
A, B, D These are more consistent with allergy, benign pigment/skin injury, or irritation in the source rationale.

Exercise 6 · Testicular Self-Examination

Which client statement shows understanding of testicular self-examination?

  1. "It is best to examine the testicles before bathing."
  2. "Small lumps do not need reporting unless they are painful."
  3. "I will examine one testicle at a time."
  4. "I will use my palms to feel for abnormalities."
C The client should examine one testicle at a time.
A, B, D Exam after bathing/showering, report any lump or swelling, and use thumbs/fingers rather than palms.

Unit 13 · Immune System and Connective Tissue Disorders · Chapter 93

Pain Management for Clients Who Have Cancer

Cancer pain can come from tumor invasion, pressure, surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immobility, or nerve changes. Effective care starts with believing the client's report, matching the pain type to the intervention, and layering pharmacologic, procedural, and nonpharmacologic strategies.

TL;DR · Verbal Report, Multimodal Relief, Procedure Safety

Cancer-pain questions often test the pain source, the most reliable assessment cue, medication class safety, and protection after invasive pain procedures. Use the client's report as the core assessment, expect multimodal analgesia for persistent cancer pain, monitor opioids and neuraxial analgesia for respiratory depression/sedation/hypotension, and protect numb or catheterized areas from injury and infection.

Assessment map

  • Neuropathic: nerve injury with numb, tingling, burning, shooting, or radiating pain.
  • Visceral/deep: internal-organ pain that can be hard to localize and can feel deep or sharp.
  • Somatic: bone or connective-tissue pain that is often localized, sharp, dull, or throbbing.

Care map

  • Use around-the-clock opioids for acute severe pain rather than relying only on PRN dosing.
  • Pair opioids with constipation prevention, sedation/respiratory checks, and naloxone readiness.
  • Teach TENS, relaxation, imagery, distraction, heat/cold limits, acupuncture, hypnosis, and peer support as adjuncts.

Pain Assessment and Care Goals

Cancer Pain Framework

ATI source-authored

Pain is subjective and can include physical and emotional components. Cancer pain can be acute after surgery or chronic from nerve changes, tumor growth, tissue destruction, or pressure on nearby structures.

The client's verbal report is the most reliable pain indicator.

Assess location, quality, intensity, timing, setting, associated findings, triggers, and relieving factors.

Observe acute nonverbal cues such as agitation, grimacing, elevated vital signs, diaphoresis, pupil dilation, and splinting.

Observe chronic pain cues such as depression, lethargy, anger, and weakness.

Barriers include inadequate assessment, inadequate education, provider knowledge gaps, reluctance to report pain, fear of addiction, and underdosing.

Palliative pain management aims to improve quality of life, dignity, comfort, and mental clarity rather than cure the cancer.

Medication Strategy

Nonopioids, NSAIDs, and Opioids

ATI source-authored

Many clients need a multimodal plan that combines two or more analgesic classes. Nonopioids and NSAIDs fit mild to moderate pain; opioids fit moderate to severe pain and breakthrough pain.

Nonopioid/NSAID examples include acetaminophen, ketorolac, aspirin, ibuprofen, and celecoxib.

Monitor NSAIDs for GI bleeding, bruising/bleeding, tinnitus or hearing loss, renal risk, and cardiovascular adverse effects.

Avoid acetaminophen in clients who have liver disease; keep total daily dosing within source limits and lower long-term adult limits.

Opioid examples include morphine, meperidine, hydromorphone, oxycodone, fentanyl, and combination products for breakthrough pain.

Use caution with older adults, monitor constipation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, nausea/vomiting, sedation, and respiratory depression.

Prevent opioid constipation with stimulant laxatives and teach no alcohol, no hazardous activity until effects are known, slow position changes, and bowel-support measures.

Adjuvant Analgesics

ATI source-authored

Adjuvant medications help when cancer pain has neuropathic, inflammatory, swelling-related, muscle-spasm, or localized procedural components.

TCAs and SNRIs can improve mood, sleep, serotonin/norepinephrine effects, and neuropathic pain; monitor suicide risk and anticholinergic, CNS, weight, sedation, memory, sweating, and tremor effects.

Anticonvulsants such as gabapentin, pregabalin, phenytoin, and carbamazepine fit neuralgia and neuropathic pain; monitor electrolytes, liver function, blood counts, levels, tremors, and life-threatening rash.

Corticosteroids such as prednisolone or dexamethasone reduce pain by decreasing swelling; taper gradually and monitor glucose, infection, behavior, confusion, weakness, joint pain, and fever.

Clonidine can support neuropathic pain or epidural/local infusions with bupivacaine; monitor hypotension and teach slow position changes.

Baclofen can be paired with other pain medications for cancer-related muscle spasms; monitor seizure activity and teach food use, driving caution, drowsiness, and dizziness.

Local anesthetics such as lidocaine, bupivacaine, and ropivacaine can be infused into targeted spaces; monitor pain relief, hypotension, infection, motor impairment, sedation, and catheter protection.

Routes and Procedures

Administration Routes

ATI source-authored

Route selection depends on onset need, pain pattern, blood counts, available nursing support, and whether systemic or local relief is needed.

Oral is the first-choice route when appropriate and includes short- and long-acting formulations.

Transdermal fentanyl has slow onset, consistent dosing, and long duration.

Rectal administration is not appropriate with low WBC or platelet counts.

Subcutaneous and IV morphine or hydromorphone have rapid onset and require nursing support; monitor infiltration risk.

Epidural or intrathecal therapy can be more effective than IV analgesia immediately after surgery but requires monitoring for infection, pruritus, urinary retention, sedation, and respiratory depression.

Sublingual/buccal medications absorb under the tongue or between the cheek and gum; teach clients to avoid eating, drinking, or smoking during use.

Nerve Blocks, Catheters, and Ablation

ATI source-authored

Invasive pain procedures can target isolated or refractory pain, but safety hinges on vital-sign monitoring, block assessment, neurologic checks, and infection surveillance.

Regional nerve blocks use anesthetic and sometimes corticosteroid near a nerve root; establish IV access, obtain baseline vital signs, monitor during and after, and protect the numb area.

Watch for local anesthetic systemic effects such as metallic taste, ringing in ears, perioral numbness, and seizures.

Epidural or intrathecal catheters can provide chronic upper abdominal, thoracic, or below-umbilicus pain control by continuous infusion or PRN injection.

Monitor neuraxial therapy for hypotension, anaphylaxis, muscle weakness, seizures, dura puncture, respiratory depression, sedation, hematoma, infection, CSF leakage, sensory block level, and leg strength before ambulation.

Neurolytic ablation interrupts or destroys pain-transmitting nerve pathways; it is irreversible, reserved for ineffective noninvasive methods, and can affect sensory, motor, or autonomic function.

Radiofrequency ablation uses heat from an electrical probe to destroy selected cancer cells or nerve endings, including selected lung or bone tumor pain targets.

Nonpharmacologic and Alternative Approaches

TENS, Relaxation, Distraction, and Support

ATI source-authored

Alternative approaches are used in addition to pain medications and procedures. They can reduce anxiety, stress, and pain while giving clients more control over symptoms.

TENS uses low-voltage impulses near or over the painful area; remove hair, place electrodes on clean hairless intact skin, monitor for burns/rash, and continue other pain medication as needed.

Do not use TENS for clients who have pacemakers or dysrhythmias, during pregnancy, near the head, or over the heart.

Relaxation and imagery can include deep breathing, progressive relaxation, meditation, and peaceful visualization with or without audio recordings.

Distraction can include music, television, exercise, family/friends, repetitive actions, focused breathing, a visual focal point, or a change of scenery.

Heat, cold, pressure, massage, and vibration can support comfort, but avoid heat or cold directly on skin with radiation damage and avoid irritating fragile skin.

Acupuncture, hypnosis, and peer group support can alter pain perception, strengthen coping, provide social connection, and connect clients/families with community resources.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Alternative Pain Approaches

Scenario: A nurse manager is leading an oncology-unit discussion about alternative approaches to cancer-pain management. Complete the Basic Concept template by naming approaches, nursing actions, and teaching points.

  • TENS: monitor electrode sites, offer pain medications, avoid use with pacemakers/dysrhythmias or pregnancy, and teach clean hairless intact skin placement away from the head and heart.
  • Relaxation, imagery, and distraction: coach deep breathing, progressive relaxation, meditation, peaceful imagery, music, television, exercise, family involvement, focused breathing, or a change of scenery.
  • Heat/cold, massage, acupuncture, hypnosis, and peer support: avoid heat/cold on radiation-damaged skin, avoid excessive skin irritation, refer to trained/community resources, and include family support when helpful.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · Permanent Epidural Catheter

A client has chronic cancer pain and a permanent epidural catheter for fentanyl/bupivacaine. Which findings should the nurse monitor for? Select all that apply.

  1. Respiratory depression
  2. Hypotension
  3. Sedation
  4. Muscle spasticity
  5. Sensory blockage
A, B, C, E Epidural analgesics can cause respiratory depression, hypotension, sedation, and sensory block.
D Muscle weakness, not spasticity, is the expected concern in the source rationale.

Exercise 2 · Neurolytic Ablation Purpose

A client scheduled for neurolytic ablation asks why the procedure is being done. Which response should the nurse give?

  1. "It can provide long-lasting relief by destroying pain-transmitting nerves."
  2. "It prevents adverse effects from pain medication."
  3. "It increases infection-fighting cells."
  4. "It increases cells that stop bleeding."
A Neurolytic ablation destroys nerves that transmit pain from a specific area and is used after other methods are ineffective.
B, C, D It can reduce analgesic need, but it does not prevent medication adverse effects or treat myelosuppression or thrombocytopenia.

Exercise 3 · TENS Application

A client has a prescription for TENS for cancer pain. Which action should the nurse take?

  1. Remove hair before applying the electrodes.
  2. Apply alcohol to the skin before electrode placement.
  3. Place electrodes over painful incisions or damaged skin.
  4. Avoid pain medications while the TENS unit is in use.
A Hair should be removed before TENS electrodes are applied.
B, C, D Skin should be clean and intact, electrodes should not go over damaged areas, and pain medication can still be administered.

Exercise 4 · Gabapentin Monitoring

A client receives gabapentin for neuropathic cancer pain. Which adverse effect should the nurse monitor for?

  1. Constipation
  2. Urinary retention
  3. Insomnia
  4. Dizziness
D Gabapentin can cause dizziness; teach the client to avoid driving until medication effects are known.
A, B, C Constipation and urinary retention are opioid concerns, and sedation rather than insomnia is expected.

Unit 14 · Nursing Care of Perioperative Clients · Chapter 94

Anesthesia and Moderate Sedation

Anesthesia and moderate sedation suppress pain, memory, awareness, or movement to different degrees. The nursing priority is to protect airway and oxygenation while monitoring medication effects, reversal needs, and rapid complications such as malignant hyperthermia or local anesthetic toxicity.

TL;DR · Airway First, Titrate Carefully, Reverse Fast

Anesthesia questions usually hinge on airway, oxygenation, and drug-specific rescue. General anesthesia removes awareness and reflexes, regional blocks a body region, local numbs tissue, and moderate sedation keeps the client arousable with protective reflexes and a patent airway. Watch older adults closely, keep emergency equipment ready, use flumazenil for benzodiazepine reversal and naloxone for opioid reversal, and treat malignant hyperthermia with stopping surgery, 100% oxygen, IV dantrolene, cooling, labs, urine monitoring, and ICU transfer.

Anesthesia map

  • General: loss of sensation, consciousness, reflexes, and memory for major surgery or complete relaxation.
  • Regional: reduced sensation in a selected area through peripheral nerve or spinal-cord blockade.
  • Local: topical or infiltrated anesthetic at skin, mucosa, or incision tissue.

Moderate sedation map

  • Client relaxes enough for a minor procedure but responds to verbal stimuli.
  • Protective reflexes remain, the client is easily arousable, and airway stays independently patent.
  • An RN with no other duties continuously monitors before, during, and immediately after the procedure.

Anesthesia Foundations

Types and Risk Patterns

ATI source-authored

Anesthesia depresses central nervous system activity to produce analgesia, amnesia, loss of awareness, or muscle relaxation. Risk recognition starts before the procedure because anesthesia safety depends on airway, cardiopulmonary reserve, and medication clearance.

  • General anesthesia risk factors include family history of malignant hyperthermia, respiratory disease, cardiac disease, gastric contents/aspiration risk, and alcohol or substance use disorder.
  • Local anesthesia risk factors include allergy to ester-type anesthetics and altered peripheral circulation.
  • Older adults are especially susceptible to anesthetic agents; titration should be careful and airway patency remains the top priority.
  • Inhalation agents include halothane, isoflurane, and nitrous oxide with oxygen.
  • IV agents include benzodiazepines, etomidate, propofol, ketamine, and short-acting barbiturates.
  • Propofol is common and can be used for mechanical ventilation, monitored anesthesia, procedural sedation, and surgery-related anesthesia.

Adjunct Medications and Safety

ATI source-authored

Clients often receive adjunct medications during anesthesia to deepen sedation, reduce anxiety, prevent nausea, reduce secretions or bradycardia, or relax skeletal muscles.

  • Opioids such as fentanyl, sufentanil, and alfentanil provide sedation and analgesia but can depress respirations, delay awakening, constipate, cause urinary retention, and trigger nausea/vomiting.
  • Benzodiazepines such as diazepam and midazolam reduce anxiety, promote amnesia, and create sedation; rapid administration or stacking doses can cause cardiac and respiratory arrest.
  • Antiemetics such as ondansetron, metoclopramide, and promethazine reduce nausea/vomiting and aspiration risk; monitor for dry mouth, dizziness, extrapyramidal effects, tardive dyskinesia, respiratory depression, or apnea depending on agent.
  • Anticholinergics such as atropine and glycopyrrolate reduce bradycardia risk and secretions but can cause urinary retention, tachycardia, and dry mouth; glaucoma is a contraindication.
  • Sedatives such as pentobarbital and secobarbital can cause respiratory depression and should be avoided within 14 days of starting or stopping an MAOI.
  • Neuromuscular blockers such as succinylcholine and vecuronium relax skeletal muscle and support airway placement; they produce flaccid paralysis and require mechanical ventilation.

Complication Watch

Malignant Hyperthermia

ATI source-authored

Malignant hyperthermia is an inherited muscle disorder and life-threatening anesthesia emergency triggered by inhalation anesthetics or succinylcholine.

  • Early cues include increased carbon dioxide, decreased oxygen saturation, and tachycardia.
  • Progression can include dysrhythmias, muscle rigidity, hypotension, tachypnea, mottling, cyanosis, myoglobinuria, and very high late temperature.
  • Assist with terminating surgery as soon as malignant hyperthermia is suspected.
  • Administer IV dantrolene and 100% oxygen.
  • Monitor ABGs and hyperkalemia labs; treat metabolic acidosis and dysrhythmias as prescribed.
  • Cool with iced IV fluids, cooling blanket, ice to axillae/groin/neck/head, and iced lavage; insert urinary catheter to monitor output and hematuria; transfer to ICU.

Anesthetic Toxicity, Hypoventilation, and Awareness

ATI source-authored

Complications can come from anesthetic toxicity, medication interactions, poor ventilation, intubation injury, or unintended awareness during anesthesia.

  • Toxicity risk rises in older adults and in clients with poor liver or kidney function.
  • Unrecognized hypoventilation can cause cardiac arrest, hypoxia, brain damage, and death; monitor end-tidal carbon dioxide and manually ventilate if equipment fails.
  • Intubation can injure teeth, lips, vocal cords, or neck; risk rises with small mouth, limited mouth opening, or oral tumors.
  • Anesthesia awareness means the client remembers events unexpectedly; the client might not be able to alert the surgical team during the event.
  • When regional or local systemic toxicity occurs, prioritize airway support, oxygen, and treatment for CNS/cardiovascular deterioration.

Regional, Local, and Moderate Sedation

Regional and Local Anesthesia

ATI source-authored

Regional anesthesia can be a peripheral nerve block, epidural, spinal, or field block. Local anesthesia is applied topically or infiltrated into tissue and is often paired with regional anesthesia.

  • Clients receiving regional anesthesia remain awake; maintain a calm environment and avoid unnecessary alarming comments.
  • Epinephrine can be added to local anesthetic to prolong effect and decrease systemic toxicity risk.
  • Local anesthesia is not appropriate when the incision is large enough that the needed amount would be toxic.
  • Early injection-site complications can include edema/inflammation, with risk for gangrene, necrosis, or tissue abscess.
  • Systemic toxicity findings include restlessness, altered speech, blurred vision, metallic taste, tremors, and tachycardia; it can progress to hypotension, cardiac arrest, apnea, and death.

Moderate Sedation Workflow

ATI source-authored

Moderate sedation uses sedatives, hypnotics, and/or opioids for procedures such as endoscopy, bone marrow aspiration, lumbar puncture, cardioversion, wound care, fracture reduction, and device/tube procedures.

  • Only qualified providers administer moderate sedation; an ACLS-certified RN can assist under supervision according to facility policy.
  • Preprocedure: obtain history, allergies, medications, preexisting conditions, prior sedation/anesthesia reactions, baseline vital signs, cardiac rhythm, level of consciousness, NPO status, IV access, consent verification, monitoring equipment, and denture removal.
  • Intraprocedure: remain with the client, allow other staff to assist the provider, continuously monitor LOC, cardiac rhythm, respirations, vital signs, and older-adult sensory/cardiopulmonary needs.
  • Keep emergency cart/medications, airway and ventilatory equipment, defibrillator, IV supplies, 100% oxygen, airways, manual resuscitation bag, suction, ECG, noninvasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, capnography, thermometer, and stethoscope within reach.
  • Postprocedure: monitor vital signs and consciousness until fully awake and back to presedation criteria.
  • Discharge criteria include baseline LOC, stable vital signs, cough/deep-breath ability, oral fluid tolerance, urination, no nausea/vomiting/shortness of breath/dizziness, no obvious bleeding, and capnography showing adequate respiratory status.

Moderate Sedation Rescue

ATI source-authored

Moderate sedation dosing is highly individualized and requires careful titration. Complications require stopping or reversing sedation and supporting the problem system immediately.

  • Medication examples include opioids such as morphine, fentanyl, and alfentanil; anesthetics such as etomidate and propofol; and benzodiazepines such as midazolam and diazepam.
  • Use naloxone to reverse opioid adverse effects and flumazenil to reverse benzodiazepine adverse effects.
  • Airway obstruction, dysrhythmias, hypotension, and anaphylaxis require rapid response.
  • For airway obstruction or respiratory depression, administer oxygen/reversal agents as indicated and insert an oral airway with suction.
  • For cardiac arrhythmias, obtain a 12-lead ECG and provide antidysrhythmics and fluids as prescribed.
  • For hypotension, provide fluids and vasopressors; for anaphylaxis, administer epinephrine.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Moderate Sedation for Colonoscopy

Scenario: A nurse is preparing to administer moderate sedation to a client who will undergo a colonoscopy. Complete the Basic Concept template by linking medication classes, underlying principles, and nursing actions.

  • Related content: fentanyl is an opioid, propofol is an anesthetic, and midazolam is a benzodiazepine.
  • Underlying principle: moderate sedation relaxes the client enough to prevent procedural discomfort while the client can respond to verbal stimuli, retain gag reflex, remain easily arousable, and maintain the airway.
  • Preprocedure: attach monitoring equipment, initiate IV access, verify informed consent, and have emergency cart, oxygen, and suction equipment ready.
  • Intraprocedure/postprocedure: monitor LOC, cardiac status, respiratory status, vital signs, ability to cough/deep breathe/swallow, and nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, or dizziness before discharge.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · Midazolam Reversal

A client receives IV midazolam before a procedure and then has hypotension and tachycardia. Which IV medication should the nurse administer?

  1. Naloxone
  2. Morphine
  3. Flumazenil
  4. Atropine
C Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, so flumazenil reverses its effects.
A, B, D Naloxone reverses opioids, morphine can worsen hypotension/respiratory depression, and atropine treats bradycardia.

Exercise 2 · Nitrous Oxide Induction Priority

A client receives nitrous oxide by face mask during induction of anesthesia. Which nursing action has priority?

  1. Assess oxygen saturation.
  2. Measure blood pressure.
  3. Palpate pulse rate.
  4. Check temperature.
A Hypoxia is the greatest immediate risk during induction, so oxygen saturation is the priority.
B, C, D Cardiovascular and temperature assessment matter, but oxygenation is the priority in this source item.

Exercise 3 · Malignant Hyperthermia Actions

Which actions should the nurse take for malignant hyperthermia? Select all that apply.

  1. Infuse iced IV fluids.
  2. Provide 100% oxygen.
  3. Place a cooling blanket on the client.
  4. Treat while the surgeon continues surgery.
  5. Administer IV dantrolene.
A, B, C, E Cooling, 100% oxygen, and IV dantrolene are source-supported emergency actions.
D Surgery should be terminated as soon as malignant hyperthermia is suspected.

Exercise 4 · Regional Block Toxicity

A client develops a systemic toxic reaction after a regional block. Which action should the nurse take?

  1. Monitor blood creatinine levels.
  2. Provide airway support.
  3. Turn the client to the right side.
  4. Administer a diuretic.
B Systemic toxicity can cause CNS depression, so airway patency and oxygen support are the priority.
A, C, D Labs can be monitored, but positioning does not treat toxicity and diuresis can worsen progression to hypotension.

Exercise 5 · Post-Epidural Headache

A client reports headache after an epidural regional nerve block. Which action should the nurse take?

  1. Decrease the client's fluid intake.
  2. Apply pressure to the puncture site.
  3. Place the head of the bed flat.
  4. Instruct the client to lie prone.
C A flat head-of-bed position can decrease headache intensity from cerebrospinal fluid leakage.
A, B, D Hydration is encouraged, pressure does not relieve the leak-related headache, and prone positioning can worsen or fail to improve pain.
