Unit 14 · Nursing Care of Perioperative Clients · Chapter 95

Preoperative Nursing Care

Preoperative nursing care runs from the surgery decision until transfer to the operating suite. The nurse reduces preventable harm by identifying risk factors, confirming consent and readiness, reinforcing teaching, preparing the body safely, and catching abnormalities before the client leaves for surgery.

TL;DR · Risk Screen, Consent Witness, Readiness Check

Preoperative questions usually test whether the nurse catches risk before the procedure. Report abnormal renal function, hyperglycemia, infection signs, fever, missing consent understanding, unsafe NPO timing, and medication issues. The provider explains the procedure and risks; the nurse verifies understanding, witnesses the signature, documents questions, and escalates confusion back to the provider.

Report fast

  • Elevated temperature can indicate infection and can delay/cancel surgery.
  • Elevated creatinine, blood glucose, or WBC requires provider follow-up before surgery.
  • Late solids, unclear consent, or impaired decision-making blocks safe transfer.

Teach clearly

  • Take approved cardiac/other medications with a sip of water when prescribed.
  • Splint, cough/deep breathe, use incentive spirometry, and ambulate early after surgery.
  • Use stockings or pneumatic compression plus ROM to reduce DVT risk.

Preoperative Assessment

Surgical Risk Patterns

ATI source-authored

Surgery can be curative, palliative, cosmetic, functional, diagnostic, or transplant-related. Procedures can be emergent, urgent, elective, inpatient, or outpatient; risk assessment is a major preoperative responsibility.

  • Airway/oxygenation risks include obstructive sleep apnea, pregnancy-related fetal anesthesia risk, COPD, pneumonia, asthma, obesity, and older-adult physiologic reserve changes.
  • Cardiovascular and perfusion risks include heart failure, myocardial infarction, hypertension, dysrhythmias, coagulation defect, anemia, hypovolemia, and VTE risk.
  • Metabolic/organ risks include diabetes mellitus, liver disease, kidney disease, thyroid/adrenal disorders, immune disorders, malnutrition, and multibody-system disease.
  • Medication/substance risks include antihypertensives, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, tricyclic antidepressants, herbal or OTC products, tobacco, and alcohol.
  • Allergy and family-history risks include latex, anesthetic agents, malignant hyperthermia history, and food clues that suggest latex or medication-related cross-risk.
  • Psychosocial risks include anxiety, inability to cope, limited support, and cultural or communication needs.

Assessment and Diagnostics

ATI source-authored

The preoperative assessment establishes baseline status and identifies conditions that need treatment before surgery proceeds.

  • History includes medical/surgical history, anesthesia tolerance, medications, complementary/herbal practices, psychosocial history, cultural considerations, substance use, support systems, occupation, and understanding of surgery.
  • Allergy assessment includes medications, latex, contrast, and foods; banana/kiwi can suggest latex risk, egg or soybean oil is a propofol contraindication, and shellfish can indicate povidone-iodine reaction risk in the source.
  • Baseline assessment includes anxiety level, coping/support, head-to-toe assessment, vital signs, oxygen saturation, and VTE risk.
  • Diagnostics can include urinalysis, blood type/crossmatch, CBC, pregnancy test, clotting studies, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, ABGs, chest x-ray, and ECG based on age/history/procedure.
  • Report abnormal findings such as impaired renal function, elevated glucose, elevated WBC, fever, or other signs suggesting infection or physiologic instability.

Readiness, Consent, and Teaching

Preoperative Readiness Care

ATI source-authored

Readiness care protects the client from aspiration, infection, bleeding, hypothermia, medication complications, wrong-site surgery, VTE, and falls.

  • Verify completed, signed, witnessed consent and confirm the correct surgical site with the client and team before site marking.
  • Keep the client NPO according to source guidance: at least 6 hr for solids and 2 hr for clear liquids before general anesthesia; document last intake.
  • Prepare bowel or skin as prescribed; remove hair only if necessary using electric clippers or chemical depilatory.
  • Remove jewelry, dentures, prosthetics, makeup, nail polish, and glasses; protect valuables through family or secure storage.
  • Use a warmed lightweight blanket to prevent hypothermia, which increases wound infection risk and can alter medication metabolism, coagulation, and cardiac rhythm.
  • Establish large-bore IV access when indicated, administer prescribed preoperative medications, have the client void before sedating medication, monitor response, raise side rails, and complete the checklist.
  • Give prophylactic antibiotics within 1 hr of incision and continue beta-blockers preoperatively when prescribed for clients already taking them.

Informed Consent Roles

ATI source-authored

Consent is a provider responsibility; the nurse witnesses and protects the process. The nurse can clarify already-provided information but cannot add new procedural information that the provider did not explain.

  • The provider explains the procedure, participants, anesthesia risks, expected benefits, possible harm/pain/discomfort, alternatives, and the right to refuse.
  • The client must consent voluntarily, receive enough information to decide, and be competent/legal age or have an authorized person consent.
  • The nurse verifies that the provider gave needed information, the client understands, and the client is capable of consent.
  • Notify the provider if the client has questions, appears confused, or lacks understanding.
  • Witness the signature, document questions and reinforcement, and use a trained medical interpreter rather than family/friends when needed.
  • Consent is needed for surgery, invasive procedures, sedation/anesthesia, radiation exposure, and procedures with increased complication risk.

Client Education

ATI source-authored

Teaching prepares the client to participate in postoperative recovery and reduces preventable respiratory, clotting, pain, and medication complications.

  • Explain the purpose/effects of preoperative medications and approved medication instructions.
  • Teach pain-control methods such as medication, immobilization, PCA pumps, splinting, and use of a pain scale.
  • Teach splinting, coughing, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, ROM exercises, and early ambulation to reduce respiratory and thrombotic complications.
  • Teach antiembolism stockings and pneumatic compression device use.
  • Teach bowel/skin prep, invasive lines, postoperative diet, and procedure-specific restrictions.
  • For elective surgery, source guidance supports stopping aspirin 1 week before surgery and asking the provider before herbal or OTC products because of bleeding/anesthesia risks.
  • Teach avoidance of smoking, alcohol, and illicit drugs because they can interfere with surgical medications and increase complication risk.

Complication Prevention

Medication-Related Complications

ATI source-authored

Many immediate postoperative complications begin with preoperative medications or fluids, so prevention starts before transfer.

  • Sedatives such as benzodiazepines or barbiturates can cause respiratory depression, drowsiness, and dizziness; monitor respirations/oxygen saturation, give oxygen, and administer flumazenil when prescribed.
  • Opioids can cause respiratory depression, drowsiness, dizziness, constipation, and urinary retention; monitor respirations/oxygen saturation, give oxygen, use naloxone when prescribed, and catheterize if prescribed for retention.
  • IV fluids such as 0.9% sodium chloride or lactated Ringer's can contribute to fluid overload or hypernatremia; monitor I&O, slow fluids, and administer diuretics when prescribed.
  • GI medications such as antiemetics, antacids, and H2 blockers can relate to alkalosis, cardiac effects, and drowsiness; obtain cardiac history and monitor electrolytes.
  • Other postoperative risks to anticipate include poor wound healing, infection/sepsis, anemia, hypovolemia/circulatory shock, and electrolyte imbalance.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Preventing Surgical Complications

Scenario: A nurse is planning care for a client scheduled for surgery. Complete the Basic Concept template by linking likely complications, causes, and prevention.

  • Respiratory depression: can follow overmedication with benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or opioids; monitor closely and administer prescribed reversal agents.
  • Fluid overload: can occur with excess IV fluids and limited excretion; obtain cardiac/pulmonary history, monitor I&O, slow IV fluids, and administer prescribed diuretic.
  • Deep-vein thrombosis: can result from lower-extremity blood stasis; apply antiembolism stockings or pneumatic compression devices, administer prescribed anticoagulants, and teach ROM.
  • Infection: can occur from wound contamination; administer prophylactic antibiotic within 1 hr before incision.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · Preoperative Lab Reports

Which preoperative laboratory results should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

  1. Potassium 3.9 mEq/L
  2. Sodium 145 mEq/L
  3. Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL
  4. Blood glucose 235 mg/dL
  5. WBC 17,850/mm3
C, D, E Elevated creatinine, glucose, and WBC can indicate renal impairment, hyperglycemia needing treatment, or infection requiring preoperative follow-up.
A, B The listed potassium and sodium values are within expected ranges in the source item.

Exercise 2 · Abdominal Surgery Teaching

Which teaching should the nurse include before abdominal surgery? Select all that apply.

  1. Take prescribed heart medication with a sip of water before surgery.
  2. Splint the abdominal incision with a pillow when coughing and deep breathing.
  3. Bed rest is recommended for the first 48 hr.
  4. Antiembolism stockings are applied before surgery.
  5. Solid foods are allowed up to 4 hr before surgery.
A, B, D Some cardiac/other medications can be taken with a sip of water, splinting supports coughing/deep breathing, and antiembolism stockings help prevent DVT.
C, E Early ambulation is important after abdominal surgery, and solid foods should stop at least 6 hr before surgery in the source item.

Exercise 3 · Informed Consent Verification

When verifying informed consent for paracentesis, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

  1. Explain the purpose of the procedure.
  2. Inform the client of procedure risks.
  3. Ensure the client understands the procedure information.
  4. Witness the client signing the consent form.
  5. Determine whether the client can understand the reason for the procedure.
C, D, E The nurse verifies understanding/capacity and witnesses the signature.
A, B The provider explains the purpose and risks.

Exercise 4 · Fever Before Surgery

A client scheduled for exploratory laparotomy has an oral temperature of 39 C (102.2 F). Which action should the nurse take?

  1. Inform the surgeon of the elevated temperature.
  2. Transfer the client to the preoperative unit.
  3. Apply ice packs to the groin.
  4. Encourage increased clear liquids.
A The surgeon should be notified immediately because fever can indicate infection and might require delaying surgery.
B, C, D Transfer, cooling packs, or fluids do not address the need to evaluate possible infection before surgery; NPO status also limits intake.

Exercise 5 · Colon Resection Readiness

Which action should the preoperative nurse take for a client having colon resection?

  1. Encourage voiding after preoperative medication administration.
  2. Administer antibiotics 2 hr before incision.
  3. Remove hair with a manual razor.
  4. Remove nail polish from fingers and toes.
D Nail polish should be removed so nail beds can be assessed for color and circulation.
A, B, C The client should void before sedating medication, antibiotics are given within 1 hr of incision, and hair removal should use clippers or depilatory if needed.

Unit 14 · Nursing Care of Perioperative Clients · Chapter 96

Postoperative Nursing Care

Postoperative nursing care begins with transfer to PACU and continues through discharge teaching. The first priority is airway, breathing, and circulation, followed by pain control, fluid balance, wound/drain surveillance, mobility, and early recognition of complications.

TL;DR · ABC First, Urine 30, Wound Covered

PACU questions start with airway, breathing, and circulation. Position an unresponsive client laterally, monitor oxygenation and breath sounds, watch bleeding and perfusion, report urine output below 30 mL/hr, and use Aldrete scoring for recovery readiness. For evisceration, call for help, stay with the client, cover the wound with sterile saline-moistened dressing, bend hips/knees, and do not reinsert organs.

PACU anchors

  • Airway patency and ventilation are the immediate postoperative priorities.
  • General anesthesia needs frequent respiratory assessment; epidural/spinal anesthesia needs motor and sensory checks.
  • Discharge from PACU requires anesthesia approval, stable criteria, and an Aldrete score in the source range.

Unit anchors

  • Cough/deep breathe at least hourly while awake and use incentive spirometry every 1 to 2 hr while awake.
  • Reposition every 2 hr and ambulate early with rest periods.
  • Advance diet only after gag reflex and peristalsis return, as prescribed and tolerated.

PACU Priorities

PACU Transfer and Risk Pattern

ATI source-authored

The anesthesia provider transfers the client to PACU, and the circulating nurse gives hand-off report. PACU nurses monitor anesthesia recovery, prevent complications, manage pain, and determine discharge readiness.

  • Risk factors include immobility, anemia, hypovolemia, hypothermia, cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, immune disorder, diabetes mellitus, coagulation defect, malnutrition, obesity, and older adult physiology.
  • Older adults can need warming, delayed orientation monitoring, medication-response monitoring, skin protection, and nutrition attention for wound healing.
  • Postoperative diagnostics can include CBC, metabolic profile, ABGs, glucose, PT, and INR based on procedure and health problems.
  • Outpatient discharge requires spontaneous breathing, safe swallowing, safe ambulation with assistance, and a responsible person to receive instructions and transport the client home.

Airway, Breathing, and Circulation

ATI source-authored

On PACU arrival, perform a full-body assessment with priority to airway, breathing, and circulation. Artificial airways stay until the client can keep the airway open independently.

  • Assess breath-sound symmetry, chest movement, respiratory pattern/rate/depth, lung sounds, and continuous oxygen saturation.
  • Absent left breath sounds can suggest right-mainstem intubation or pneumothorax; snoring or stridor can signal poor oxygen exchange.
  • Suction secretions if the client cannot cough; extubation depends on command response, head-lift ability, and thoracic breathing.
  • Assess internal/external bleeding, abdominal distention, hematoma, tachycardia, hypotension, restlessness, increased pain, skin color/temperature/sensation, capillary refill, cyanosis, pulses, and DVT signs.
  • Trend vital signs; report significant blood pressure change from baseline or downward pressure trends according to the source guidance.
  • Position responsive clients in semi-Fowler's if allowed; keep unresponsive clients lateral due to aspiration risk; elevate legs and lower head of bed if hypotension or shock develops.

Monitoring and Management

Fluid, Wound, Pain, and Mentation

ATI source-authored

After immediate ABC stabilization, postoperative monitoring focuses on fluid balance, wound/drain output, pain control, and neurologic recovery from anesthesia or sedation.

  • Review potassium, sodium, creatinine, BUN, hemoglobin, hematocrit, I&O, drains, NG output, urine, estimated blood loss, IV fluids, and blood products.
  • Urine output below 30 mL/hr can indicate hypovolemia; palpate the bladder and monitor drainage devices.
  • Check dressings and drainage tubes for patency/function; outline drainage with date/time and report excessive or increasing drainage.
  • Give pain medication according to recovery status, monitor for respiratory depression and oxygen desaturation, and add nonpharmacologic pain strategies.
  • Monitor LOC, mental status, stimulation needed for arousal, and orientation compared with baseline; older adults can have postoperative delirium from anesthesia, dehydration, hypoxia, blood loss, or electrolyte imbalance.
  • Use Aldrete scoring to evaluate activity, consciousness, respiration, oxygen saturation, and circulation before PACU discharge.

Postsurgical Unit Care

ATI source-authored

On transfer from PACU, repeat a full-body ABC-focused assessment to create a postsurgical baseline and detect changes quickly.

  • Monitor pulse oximetry, assist coughing/deep breathing at least every hour while awake, provide splinting, and assist incentive spirometry every 1 to 2 hr while awake.
  • Avoid coughing after cosmetic, eye, or intracranial surgery as directed.
  • Reposition every 2 hr and encourage early regular ambulation with rest; avoid pillows under knees because they reduce venous return.
  • Use prescribed IV fluids, ice chips/fluids as tolerated, frequent oral hygiene, PCA/epidural/intrathecal pain control when prescribed, and around-the-clock pain prevention during early postoperative hours.
  • Monitor opioid effects, give analgesia before ambulation or painful procedures, and use naloxone for opioid overmedication as prescribed.
  • Keep the client NPO until gag reflex and peristalsis return; monitor bowel sounds/flatus, maintain NG patency, and advance diet as prescribed and tolerated.
  • Prevent thromboembolism with pneumatic compression, stockings, repositioning, early ambulation, and prescribed anticoagulants or antiplatelets.

Incisions, Drains, Healing, and Discharge

ATI source-authored

Wound monitoring catches hemorrhage, infection, dehiscence, and delayed healing while discharge teaching prepares the client to recover safely at home.

  • Expected drainage should progress from sanguineous to serosanguineous to serous.
  • Expected incision findings include pink edges, slight swelling under sutures/staples, and slight drainage crusting; report redness, excessive tenderness, or purulent drainage.
  • Monitor wound drains with each vital-sign check; empty closed suction as needed to maintain compression and report drainage increases.
  • Use surgical asepsis for dressing changes after the surgeon's first dressing change when applicable.
  • Use an abdominal binder as prescribed for clients who are obese or debilitated, encourage splinting, administer prophylactic antibiotics, and remove sutures/staples as prescribed.
  • Support healing with high-calorie, high-protein, vitamin C-rich nutrition and glycemic control for diabetes.
  • Teach medications, activity restrictions, diet, wound/catheter/assistive-device care, emergency contacts, unrelieved pain reporting, and infection reporting.

Complication Watch

Airway, Shock, Ileus, Wound Failure, and DVT

ATI source-authored

Postoperative complication questions usually test first action: open the airway, oxygenate, restore perfusion, assess bowel function, protect an open wound, or prevent clot formation.

  • Airway obstruction can present with stridor, snoring, choking, irregular respirations, low oxygen saturation, or cyanosis; use head-tilt/chin-lift, humidified oxygen, suction/airways, and notify anesthesia for possible reintubation.
  • Hypoxia requires oxygen, coughing/deep breathing, head-of-bed elevation, and turning every 2 hr.
  • Hypovolemic shock can cause low BP/urine output, tachycardia, tachypnea, narrow pulse pressure, and slow capillary refill; give oxygen, supine legs-elevated positioning, IV fluids, and vasopressors as prescribed.
  • Paralytic ileus after abdominal surgery/trauma requires bowel-sound monitoring, ambulation, diet advancement after bowel activity/flatus, prokinetics as prescribed, and NG decompression when needed.
  • For dehiscence or evisceration, call for help, stay with the client, cover with sterile saline-moistened dressing/towel, do not reinsert organs, position low-Fowler's with hips/knees bent, monitor shock, and notify the provider.
  • DVT prevention includes heparin/warfarin as prescribed, stockings, pneumatic compression, ROM, early ambulation, no pressure behind knees, avoiding prolonged leg dangling, and hydration.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept - Postoperative Complications

Scenario: A nurse is reviewing several health records to identify postoperative complications. Complete the Basic Concept template by linking the complication, likely cause, and intervention.

  • Paralytic ileus: absent peristalsis after abdominal surgery or trauma; monitor bowel sounds, encourage ambulation, and use NG decompression as prescribed.
  • Wound evisceration: abdominal contents protrude through an incision after wound failure; call for help, cover with sterile saline-soaked dressings, and position with hips/knees bent.
  • Airway obstruction: laryngeal/tracheal swelling or spasm, mucus, or relaxed tongue causes stridor/snoring; notify anesthesia, open airway, give humidified oxygen, elevate HOB if allowed, and prepare for reintubation.
  • Hypovolemic shock: blood loss causes decreased BP/urine output and increased heart/respiratory rates; give oxygen, elevate legs while supine, and administer IV fluids/vasopressors as ordered.

Application Exercises

Exercise 1 · Postoperative Risk Factors

Which PACU clients are at risk for postoperative complications? Select all that apply.

  1. A client who has WBC 22,500/uL
  2. A client who uses an insulin pump
  3. A client who takes warfarin daily
  4. A client who has heart failure
  5. A client who has BMI 26
A, B, C, D Infection, diabetes, anticoagulation, and heart failure increase postoperative complication risk.
E BMI 26 is within the expected source reference pattern and is not the risk cue in this item.

Exercise 2 · Hypovolemia Findings

Which findings require action for a PACU client with hypovolemia? Select all that apply.

  1. Urine output less than 25 mL/hr
  2. Hematocrit 53%
  3. BUN 24 mg/dL
  4. Tenting of skin over the sternum
  5. Apical pulse 62/min
A, B, C, D Low urine output, hemoconcentration, elevated BUN, and tenting indicate hypovolemia/dehydration and require fluid intervention.
E Apical pulse 62/min is not the hypovolemia manifestation in the source item.

Exercise 3 · Unresponsive PACU Client

A client arrives in PACU after total hip arthroplasty and does not respond to verbal stimuli. Which action should the nurse perform first?

  1. Compare peripheral pulses.
  2. Apply a warm blanket.
  3. Assess dressings.
  4. Place the client in a lateral position.
D An unresponsive client is at greatest risk for aspiration, so lateral positioning helps keep the airway clear.
A, B, C Circulation, warming, and dressing checks matter, but airway protection comes first.

Exercise 4 · Atelectasis Prevention

Which interventions help prevent postoperative atelectasis? Select all that apply.

  1. Encourage incentive spirometer use every 2 hr.
  2. Teach splinting while coughing and deep breathing.
  3. Reposition every 2 hr.
  4. Administer antibiotic therapy.
  5. Assist with early ambulation.
A, B, C, E Spirometry, splinting with coughing/deep breathing, repositioning, and early ambulation expand lungs and mobilize secretions.
D Antibiotics prevent/treat infection, not atelectasis in this source item.

Exercise 5 · Nausea and Vomiting After Surgery

A client reports nausea and vomiting 2 days after hysterectomy. Which action should the nurse perform first?

  1. Assess bowel sounds.
  2. Administer antiemetic medication.
  3. Restart prescribed IV fluids.
  4. Insert a prescribed nasogastric tube.
A Assess first to check for peristalsis and guide further interventions.
B, C, D Antiemetic, fluids, or NG tube can be appropriate later, but assessment is first.
